He frequently appears as a commentator and analyst on Argentine sports television and radio programs, offering insights based on his extensive experience playing in multiple leagues and countries. He resides in Buenos Aires with his family. While he didn’t achieve international caps for the senior Argentina national team, his career represents a solid and adaptable professional journey spanning Argentina, Italy and England.

title: Winston Churchill
text:
Winston Leonard Spencer-Churchill was born on November 30, 1874, at Blenheim Palace in Oxfordshire, England, the son of Lord Randolph Churchill, a Conservative politician, and Jennie Jerome, an American socialite. His early childhood was largely marked by emotional distance from his parents; he was primarily raised by his nanny, Elizabeth Everest. He attended Harrow School in 1888, achieving moderate academic success but demonstrating a particular aptitude for history and English. He initially pursued a military career, entering the Royal Military College, Sandhurst in 1893. 

Commissioned as a Second Lieutenant in the 4th Queen’s Own Hussars in 1895, Churchill sought active service and quickly found it, reporting as a war correspondent for the *Pioneer* and *Morning Post* newspapers during the Second Anglo-Boer War in South Africa beginning in 1899. He gained public attention for his daring escape from a Boer prisoner-of-war camp in December 1899, a feat that fueled his burgeoning reputation for courage and initiative. Upon his return to Britain, he resigned his commission and entered politics, being elected as the Conservative Member of Parliament for Oldham in 1900. 

Churchill's early parliamentary career saw him frequently crossing the political floor. He defected to the Liberal Party in 1904, disagreeing with Conservative policies on trade tariffs. He served as President of the Board of Trade from 1908 to 1910 under Prime Minister H.H. Asquith, introducing social reforms like labour exchanges and minimum wages. He then became Home Secretary in 1910, a position he held until 1911, during which he dealt with industrial unrest and suffragette protests. From 1911 to 1915, he served as First Lord of the Admiralty, modernizing the Royal Navy and preparing it for war. 

The disastrous Gallipoli Campaign in 1915, which he heavily advocated for, led to his demotion and temporary removal from the Admiralty. He served with the Royal Scots Fusiliers on the Western Front in France from 1916, before returning to government as Minister of Munitions in 1917 under David Lloyd George.  He played a significant role in coordinating war production. After the war, he served as Secretary of State for War and Air from 1919 to 1921, advocating for intervention against the Bolsheviks in Russia.

The 1920s and 1930s were a politically challenging period for Churchill.  He rejoined the Conservative Party in 1924 and served as Chancellor of the Exchequer under Stanley Baldwin from 1924 to 1929, controversially returning Britain to the gold standard in 1925. He lost his seat in the 1929 general election but was re-elected in 1931.  Throughout the 1930s, he became a vocal and largely isolated critic of the policy of appeasement towards Nazi Germany, warning of the growing threat posed by Adolf Hitler. He accurately predicted the increasing aggression of Germany in numerous speeches and writings.

Upon the outbreak of World War II in September 1939, Churchill was reappointed to the Admiralty.  Following Neville Chamberlain’s resignation in May 1940, Churchill became Prime Minister and Minister of Defence, forming a national government. His powerful oratory, particularly his speeches like “We shall fight on the beaches” (June 4, 1940) and “Their Finest Hour” (June 18, 1940), rallied the British public during the darkest days of the war. He forged a crucial alliance with the United States, working closely with President Franklin D. Roosevelt and later Harry S. Truman. He participated in key wartime conferences, including the Atlantic Conference (1941), the Casablanca Conference (1943), and the Yalta Conference (1945).

Despite leading Britain to victory in 1945, Churchill’s Conservative Party lost the general election in July of that year to Clement Attlee’s Labour Party. He served as Leader of the Opposition from 1945 to 1951. He was re-elected as Prime Minister in 1951, serving until 1955, focusing on foreign policy and maintaining Britain's international standing.  In 1953, he suffered a stroke, which impacted his health for the remainder of his life. He received the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1953 "for his mastery of historical and biographical description as well as for his brilliant oratory."  

Winston Churchill died on January 24, 1965, at his home in Chartwell, Kent, at the age of 90, following complications from his stroke. He was given a state funeral, attended by dignitaries from around the world, marking his lasting legacy as one of the 20th century’s most significant leaders.

title: Tony Bellew
text:
Anthony Joshua Bellew, born August 30, 1983, in Toxteth, Liverpool, England, is a former professional boxer who competed from 2007 to 2018. His upbringing was marked by a challenging environment; he grew up in a tough area and was involved in street fights from a young age, leading to numerous arrests as a teenager. He began boxing at the age of 10 at the Rotunda Amateur Boxing Club in Liverpool, initially to channel his aggression and avoid further trouble. He had around 80 amateur fights, winning the ABA Championships in 2006 at light heavyweight, defeating Courtney Fry. 

Bellew turned professional in March 2007, signing with Matchroom Sport under promoter Eddie Hearn. His professional debut took place on March 3rd, 2007, at the Liverpool Echo Arena, where he defeated Sid Razak via TKO in the first round. He quickly built a record, initially fighting primarily in the light heavyweight division. Early career highlights included a points victory over former world champion Michael Magnesi in December 2009, taking his record to 14-0. However, a significant setback came in February 2010, when he suffered his first professional loss against Nathan Cleverly, losing a 12-round decision for the vacant Commonwealth light-heavyweight title.

Bellew moved up to cruiserweight in 2016, a decision driven by difficulty consistently making the 175lb light heavyweight limit. This proved to be a transformative move. On May 29, 2016, at the Goodison Park football stadium in Liverpool, he defeated Ilunga Makabu to win the WBC cruiserweight title via third-round TKO. This victory was particularly poignant as he fought at the home of his beloved Everton Football Club, fulfilling a lifelong dream. He defended the title once, against David Haye on March 4, 2017, at the O2 Arena in London. Despite being a significant underdog, Bellew overcame a troublesome Achilles injury sustained in the sixth round to win by eleventh-round TKO. 

The Haye victory propelled Bellew to mainstream recognition. He then took on the challenge of heavyweight champion Deontay Wilder for the WBC heavyweight title on January 19, 2018, at the Barclays Center in Brooklyn, New York. Though Bellew showed considerable courage and resilience, he was ultimately defeated by Wilder via first-round knockout. This was his third and final professional loss.

Bellew’s final fight was a rematch against David Haye on May 5, 2018, also at the O2 Arena. He secured a conclusive fifth-round TKO victory, ending their rivalry decisively. He retired from boxing shortly after, citing concerns about his health and a desire to spend more time with his family. His professional record stands at 30 wins, 3 losses, with 20 victories by knockout.

Following retirement, Bellew transitioned into a career in acting and broadcasting. He played the role of ‘Pretty Boy’ in the fourth *Creed* film, *Creed III*, released in 2023, alongside Michael B. Jordan. He has also become a prominent boxing analyst and commentator for DAZN and other platforms, offering insightful commentary and analysis. 

Bellew is married to Rachael Roberts, and they have four children. He remains a vocal supporter of Everton Football Club and frequently participates in charitable work within his local community. He has been open about his struggles with mental health and uses his platform to advocate for awareness and support. He frequently discusses the challenges of his youth and the positive impact boxing had on his life, becoming a role model for young people facing similar difficulties.

title: Alexandre Hohagen
text:
Alexandre Hohagen was born on October 14, 1908, in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, to a German father, Hermann Hohagen, a successful businessman involved in coffee exports, and a Brazilian mother, Maria Joaquina de Albuquerque. His early life was marked by privilege and exposure to both Brazilian and European cultures. Hermann, recognizing Alexandre’s artistic inclinations, encouraged his son’s education in drawing and painting from a young age, initially with private tutors. He attended the Escola Nacional de Belas Artes (National School of Fine Arts) in Rio de Janeiro, beginning his studies in 1926, a period of significant artistic ferment in Brazil as modernism gained traction. 

Hohagen’s initial artistic direction leaned towards conventional portraiture and landscapes, exhibiting work in the annual Salões de Belas Artes (Fine Arts Salons) starting in 1928. However, he quickly became dissatisfied with the academic constraints and began experimenting with more avant-garde styles. A pivotal moment came in 1930 with a trip to Paris, funded by his father, where he encountered the works of Pablo Picasso, Georges Braque, and Fernand Léger firsthand. This exposure profoundly impacted his artistic vision, steering him towards Cubism and a more abstract form of expression.

Returning to Brazil in 1931, Hohagen became a key figure in the development of modern art within the country. He co-founded the Grupo Frente Única de Arte (United Art Front) in 1932, alongside artists such as Ivan Serpa and Milton Tonetti. This group aimed to promote socially conscious art and engage with the political and economic realities of Brazil during the turbulent years of Getúlio Vargas’s rise to power. Hohagen’s contributions to the Grupo Frente Única de Arte included participating in exhibitions and actively debating artistic theory.

Throughout the 1930s and 40s, Hohagen’s style continued to evolve, incorporating elements of Constructivism and Surrealism alongside his Cubist foundations. He increasingly focused on depicting urban landscapes and scenes of industrial life, reflecting the rapid modernization occurring in Brazil at the time.  He held his first solo exhibition in 1937 at the Galeria de Arte Moderna (Modern Art Gallery) in Rio de Janeiro, a landmark event that solidified his reputation as a leading modernist painter. 

In 1945, Hohagen joined the faculty of the Escola Nacional de Belas Artes, teaching painting and drawing, and influencing a new generation of Brazilian artists. He remained a professor there until 1968. During the 1950s, he began to explore informalism, a movement characterized by its emphasis on spontaneity and abstract expression. This shift saw a move away from the geometric rigor of his earlier work towards a more gestural and emotionally charged style. 

Hohagen's work was exhibited internationally, including participation in the 1951 São Paulo Biennial, a prestigious event that brought Brazilian art to a global audience. He received the Prêmio Nacional de Artes Plásticas (National Arts Award) in 1965, recognizing his significant contribution to Brazilian art.  He continued to paint prolifically throughout the 1960s and 70s, experimenting with new materials and techniques.

Alexandre Hohagen married Maria Helena de Albuquerque in 1935, and they had two children, a son and a daughter.  His later life was marked by a quiet dedication to his art, living and working in Rio de Janeiro.  He passed away on February 23, 1991, at the age of 82, leaving behind a substantial body of work – over 300 paintings and numerous drawings – that continues to be celebrated for its innovative spirit and its insightful depiction of Brazilian society and modernity. His works are held in major collections, including the Museu de Arte de São Paulo (MASP) and the Museu Nacional de Belas Artes in Rio de Janeiro.

title: Aleksandar Kolarov
text:
Aleksandar Kolarov was born on November 10, 1985, in Belgrade, Serbia, then part of Yugoslavia. His early footballing education began at Red Star Belgrade’s youth academy in 1995, where he spent the next eight years developing his skills. Initially a central midfielder, coaches recognised his powerful left foot and versatility, gradually shifting him to the left-back position. He made his senior debut for Red Star on March 26, 2004, in a Yugoslav League match against FK Sutjeska Nikšić. He quickly established himself as a regular, playing 38 matches and scoring four goals across all competitions for the club. 

His performances attracted attention from abroad, and in the summer of 2006, Kolarov moved to OFK Belgrade for a reported fee of €600,000. He spent one season with OFK, featuring in 28 league games and scoring twice. This period further honed his attacking prowess from full-back, contributing with assists and powerful shots. His consistent displays caught the eye of Lazio sporting director Igli Tare, leading to a transfer to the Italian club in July 2007 for approximately €3.5 million.

Kolarov’s time at Lazio, under coach Delio Rossi, proved pivotal. He immediately became a key player, showcasing his dynamism, crossing ability and set-piece expertise. He played 171 games for the *Biancocelesti* across all competitions, scoring 25 goals. A standout moment came on November 22, 2009, when he scored a stunning free-kick against Livorno, demonstrating the power and accuracy that would become a trademark of his game. He also helped Lazio win the Coppa Italia in 2009, defeating Sampdoria 6-5 on penalties after a 1-1 draw, playing the full 120 minutes of the final.

His consistently impressive form led to a move to Manchester City in July 2010, under manager Roberto Mancini, for a reported fee of around £16 million. He became a crucial component of City's evolving squad, providing width and attacking threat. During his seven seasons at the Etihad Stadium, Kolarov amassed 247 appearances, scoring 22 goals. He was a key figure in City’s Premier League title wins in 2012 and 2014, as well as their FA Cup triumph in 2011 and League Cup victories in 2014, 2016 and 2018. He captained Manchester City on several occasions, demonstrating his leadership qualities.

In July 2017, at the age of 31, Kolarov made a surprising move to Roma, joining the Italian side for a fee of around €5 million. He reunited with former Manchester City manager Eusebio Di Francesco. He quickly adapted to his new surroundings, becoming a mainstay in the Roma defence and contributing significantly in attack.  He played 95 games for Roma, scoring nine goals. He experienced a Champions League semi-final run with Roma in the 2017-18 season, where they were narrowly defeated by Liverpool. 

Kolarov also enjoyed a long and successful international career with Serbia. He earned his first cap on November 15, 2008, in a friendly against Poland. He represented Serbia at the 2010 FIFA World Cup, the 2014 FIFA World Cup, and the 2018 FIFA World Cup. He captained the national team for a significant period, accumulating 94 caps and scoring 11 goals, making him one of the most capped players in Serbian history. He retired from international football in March 2021.

Following his departure from Roma in August 2020, Kolarov returned to Serbia to play for his boyhood club, Red Star Belgrade, on a one-year contract. He retired from professional football in June 2022, bringing an end to a distinguished 17-year career.  After retirement, Kolarov transitioned into a coaching role, taking on a position as an assistant coach with the Serbia national team in August 2023, working under Dragan Stojković.

title: Marcus Aurelius
text:
Marcus Aurelius was born Marcus Annius Verus on April 26, 121 AD, in Rome. His family was of high social standing, belonging to the equestrian order, not the traditional patrician nobility, though they had risen in prominence through service to the empire. His father, Marcus Annius Verus, was a wealthy and respected man who held several important positions, including serving as a suffect consul in 138 AD. His mother, Domitia Lucilla, came from a powerful family; her brother, Lucius Verus, would later become co-emperor with Marcus. Marcus’s early life was privileged, receiving a comprehensive education that included rhetoric, Greek literature, and philosophy, particularly Stoicism. He was deeply influenced by the teachings of Rusticus, a Stoic philosopher who became his mentor around 132 AD.

Marcus’s trajectory shifted significantly in 138 AD when Emperor Hadrian, recognizing the boy’s potential, adopted him as his son and designated him as his successor. This adoption came with a new name, Marcus Aurelius Verus. Hadrian insisted on a thorough education continuing, stressing both practical skills and philosophical grounding. Following Hadrian’s death in 138 AD, his chosen successor, Antoninus Pius, ascended the throne. Antoninus, in turn, adopted both Marcus and Lucius Verus as his sons and designated them as joint heirs. This arrangement, though unusual, was intended to ensure a stable succession. 

Antoninus Pius proved to be a benevolent and effective ruler, and Marcus benefitted immensely from his guidance. He served in various administrative and military roles throughout Antoninus’s reign, gaining practical experience in governance. From 161 AD onwards, he served as Antoninus’s colleague, effectively a co-emperor, though Antoninus remained the senior emperor. Antoninus Pius died on March 7, 161 AD, leaving Marcus, aged 40, and Lucius Verus as joint emperors.

The early years of their joint reign were dominated by the Marcomannic Wars, a series of conflicts with Germanic tribes along the Danube frontier. Lucius Verus took command of the military operations in the east against the Parthian Empire in 162-166 AD, while Marcus remained in Rome to manage the empire’s administration. While Lucius’s campaign saw initial successes, it was hampered by disease and logistical problems. Marcus, despite his preference for philosophical pursuits, proved a capable administrator, dealing with financial difficulties brought on by the wars and a devastating plague that swept through the empire in 165-180 AD, known as the Antonine Plague, likely smallpox. It is estimated to have killed around 5 million people, significantly impacting the empire’s population and economy.

Following Lucius Verus’s death in 169 AD, Marcus Aurelius became sole emperor. He spent the majority of the remaining 12 years of his reign personally leading military campaigns along the Danube frontier, facing constant threats from various Germanic tribes like the Quadi, Marcomanni, and Sarmatians. He wasn't a natural military leader, preferring diplomacy, but he displayed resilience and strategic thinking, personally overseeing sieges and battles. He established defensive fortifications and implemented policies to resettle displaced populations. 

Throughout his reign, Marcus Aurelius remained dedicated to Stoic philosophy. He is best known for his personal writings, *Meditations*, written in Greek, likely during military campaigns between 166 and 180 AD. *Meditations* is not a systematic philosophical treatise, but rather a collection of personal reflections on duty, virtue, mortality, and the nature of the universe, offering insights into his inner life and philosophical principles.

Marcus Aurelius died on March 17, 180 AD, in Vindobona (modern-day Vienna), while campaigning against the Germanic tribes. He was succeeded by his biological son, Commodus, whose reign marked a turning point in the empire’s history, signaling a decline from the relative peace and prosperity of the previous decades. Marcus Aurelius is remembered as the "philosopher-emperor," a ruler who combined military and administrative competence with a deep commitment to Stoic principles, leaving behind a legacy of wisdom and duty.

title: Emcee N.I.C.E.
text:
Nicholas “N.I.C.E.” Pimentel was born on February 17, 1969, in the Bronx, New York City, a borough steeped in the nascent sounds of hip-hop. His upbringing in the South Bronx, specifically the Castle Hill Houses, profoundly shaped his artistic perspective. He was the son of Dominican immigrants, and the cultural blend within his household and neighborhood – the vibrancy of Latin music alongside the emerging energy of breakbeats and rhyming – formed the foundation of his unique style. He wasn’t initially focused on rapping; as a young child, N.I.C.E. demonstrated a talent for visual arts, particularly drawing and painting, a pursuit encouraged by his mother. However, the magnetic pull of the burgeoning hip-hop scene proved too strong.

The early 1980s saw N.I.C.E. begin to seriously engage with rap music. He started as a DJ, learning the fundamentals of beatmatching and record selection, skills honed at block parties and local gatherings. By age 14, around 1983, he transitioned from DJing to MCing, adopting the moniker N.I.C.E. – an acronym standing for “Naturally Intelligent Creative Energy.” He quickly gained recognition within the local scene, participating in battles and cyphers, developing a reputation for complex rhyme schemes and a lyrical dexterity that distinguished him from many of his peers. He wasn’t interested in the more boastful or aggressive styles popular at the time; instead, N.I.C.E. focused on conscious lyrics, intricate storytelling, and a sophisticated vocabulary.

In 1989, N.I.C.E. joined the legendary Juice Crew, a collective led by DJ Mr. Magic and featuring artists like Big Daddy Kane and Kool G Rap. This was a pivotal moment, placing him alongside some of the most respected lyricists in hip-hop.  His debut single, “Doin’ It Nice,” released on Profile Records in 1990, immediately showcased his skills. The song, produced by Marley Marl, received significant radio play on stations like WBLS and Hot 97, and garnered positive reviews in publications like *The Source* and *Rap Pages*.  

His debut album, *Adventures of a Spaceman*, followed in 1991, also on Profile Records. The album was critically acclaimed for its lyrical depth, sophisticated production, and N.I.C.E.’s distinctive flow. Tracks like “Space Odyssey” and “Workin’ On A Ph.D.” demonstrated his intellectual approach to hip-hop. While not a commercial blockbuster, *Adventures of a Spaceman* became a cult classic, influencing a generation of rappers with its emphasis on lyrical substance. 

Despite the critical success, N.I.C.E. faced challenges navigating the music industry. Profile Records encountered financial difficulties in the mid-1990s, hindering promotional efforts for his work.  He released a second album, *Understanding the Roots*, in 1994, but it received less support and failed to achieve the same recognition as his debut. He continued to record and perform, releasing independent projects and collaborating with other artists, including work with Pete Rock and Diamond D. 

Throughout the late 1990s and 2000s, N.I.C.E. remained a respected figure within the underground hip-hop community, known for his consistent lyrical quality. He became increasingly involved in community activism, working with youth organizations in the Bronx and using his platform to promote education and positive change. He released several independent albums and mixtapes, including *The Rhyme Pays* (2003) and *Inner City Blues* (2007). 

In 2017, N.I.C.E. released *The New Era*, a collaborative album with producer Ayatollah, receiving widespread acclaim and reintroducing him to a new generation of hip-hop fans. He continued to perform and create music, remaining committed to the principles of lyrical artistry and conscious rap that defined his career. Nicholas Pimentel passed away on November 27, 2023, at the age of 54, leaving behind a legacy as a true lyricist and a significant, if often underappreciated, figure in hip-hop history. He is remembered for his complex rhymes, insightful lyrics, and dedication to his community.

title: Jeff Beukeboom
text:
Jeff Beukeboom was born on March 20, 1966, in Petrolia, Ontario, Canada, a small town known for its oil industry. He was the youngest of three children born to John and Shirley Beukeboom. His father, a mechanic, instilled in him a strong work ethic, and his mother encouraged his academic pursuits. Beukeboom’s early athletic interests weren't solely focused on hockey; he also excelled in baseball and track and field. However, hockey quickly became his primary passion, playing minor hockey in the Lambton Jr. Sting organization, progressing through the ranks and demonstrating a natural talent for defensive play. 

Beukeboom's junior hockey career began in 1982 with the Belleville Bulls of the Ontario Hockey League (OHL). Over four seasons with the Bulls, from 1982 to 1986, he established himself as a reliable and physically imposing defenseman. He wasn't a prolific scorer, but his strength lay in his shutdown abilities, consistently preventing opponents from getting scoring chances. In his final OHL season, 1985-86, he was named the OHL’s Most Outstanding Player and was a First Team All-Star. He totalled 35 points (7 goals and 28 assists) in 62 games that season, while also amassing 156 penalty minutes, indicative of his physical style.

His performance attracted the attention of NHL scouts, and Beukeboom was drafted 89th overall in the 1984 NHL Entry Draft by the Hartford Whalers. He opted to finish his OHL career before turning professional. He joined the Binghamton Whalers, Hartford’s American Hockey League affiliate, in 1986, playing 58 games and registering 21 points. His strong play earned him a call-up to the NHL, where he debuted with the Hartford Whalers on February 26, 1987. 

Beukeboom played seven seasons with the Whalers, becoming a key member of their defense corps. He played in 443 games for Hartford, accumulating 144 points (28 goals and 116 assists). While never a star player in terms of offensive output, he was consistently relied upon to play tough minutes against opposing teams’ top lines.  He quickly gained a reputation as one of the league’s most physical players and a master of intimidation, leading the team in penalty minutes several times.

In the summer of 1993, Beukeboom was traded to the New York Islanders along with forward Pat Verbeek for Stéphane Richer. This trade proved pivotal for Beukeboom’s career.  He quickly integrated into the Islanders’ system and found a role that maximized his strengths.  He played five seasons on Long Island, from 1993 to 1998, playing in 336 games and contributing 84 points (15 goals and 69 assists). 

His most significant NHL success came when he was traded to the Colorado Avalanche in March 1998, alongside Claude Lemieux. He joined a team already stacked with talent, including Joe Sakic, Peter Forsberg, and Patrick Roy. Beukeboom played a crucial role in the Avalanche’s Stanley Cup victories in 1999 and 2001.  His physical presence and defensive reliability were instrumental in shutting down opposing offenses during the playoffs. He played in 168 regular season games for Colorado, adding 46 points (8 goals and 38 assists).

Beukeboom retired from professional hockey after the 2001 Stanley Cup victory. He finished his NHL career with 1,147 regular season games played, 248 points (41 goals and 207 assists), and 1,533 penalty minutes. He also played in 125 playoff games, winning two Stanley Cups.

Following his playing career, Beukeboom remained involved in hockey. He worked as a scout for the Colorado Avalanche for several years. He also became involved in youth hockey coaching, sharing his knowledge and experience with young players in the Denver area. He currently resides in Centennial, Colorado, with his wife, Lisa, and their two children.  He has largely remained out of the public spotlight, focusing on family and contributing to the hockey community at a grassroots level.

title: Phil Vickery (rugby union)
text:
Philip David Vickery MBE, born on March 14, 1976, in Barnstaple, Devon, England, is a retired English rugby union prop, renowned for his powerful scrummaging and significant contribution to the sport over a 14-year international career. His early life was steeped in sporting tradition; his father, John Vickery, was a Royal Marine and a keen rugby player who instilled a strong work ethic and discipline in his son. Phil began playing rugby at the age of eight for Barnstaple RFC, quickly demonstrating a natural aptitude for the front row. He attended Braunton Academy, where he continued to excel at rugby, captaining the school’s first XV. 

Vickery’s club career began with the North Devon club, before he moved to Gloucester Rugby in 1995. He rapidly progressed through the ranks at Kingsholm, making his first team debut in 1996. His consistent performances for Gloucester soon attracted the attention of national selectors. He made his England debut on November 22, 1997, against Australia at Twickenham, earning cap number 686. This marked the beginning of a remarkable international career that saw him become a mainstay of the England pack. 

Vickery’s international career was characterized by his reliability and dominance in the scrum. He quickly established himself as the first-choice tighthead prop, amassing a total of 73 caps for England. He was a key member of the England team that won the Six Nations Championship in 2000, 2001 and 2003, playing a crucial role in the Grand Slam victory in 2003. However, his most significant achievement came in the 2003 Rugby World Cup in Australia. Vickery was an integral part of the England team that defeated Australia 20-17 in extra time in the final at Stadium Australia in Sydney on November 22, 2003, securing England’s only Rugby World Cup title to date. He played in every match of the tournament, becoming a national hero.

He also represented the British & Irish Lions on two tours, in 2001 to Australia and in 2005 to New Zealand. In 2005, he started in all three Test matches against the All Blacks, a testament to his world-class ability. Although the Lions series was lost, Vickery’s performances were widely praised.  He captained England for the first time on November 12, 2005, against Canada at Twickenham, a proud moment in his career. 

Throughout his career, Vickery battled with several injuries, notably neck and back problems, which required multiple surgeries. These setbacks threatened to derail his career on several occasions, but he demonstrated remarkable resilience and determination to return to the highest level of the game each time. He moved from Gloucester to Wasps in 2006, spending three seasons with the club before returning to Gloucester in 2009. He announced his retirement from professional rugby in March 2010 at the age of 34, citing ongoing injuries as the primary reason. He finished his club career with 231 appearances for Gloucester.

Following his retirement from playing, Vickery transitioned into a successful career in broadcasting and business. He became a regular commentator and pundit for Sky Sports, providing expert analysis on rugby union matches. He also embarked on entrepreneurial ventures, establishing a successful catering company, 'The Scrumptious Suppers', specializing in locally sourced produce.  In 2011, he was appointed a Deputy Lieutenant of Cornwall. 

In 2014, Vickery was inducted into the World Rugby Hall of Fame, recognizing his outstanding contribution to the sport. He was awarded an MBE in the 2004 Queen’s Birthday Honours List for his services to rugby. He continues to be a prominent figure in the rugby community, involved in charitable work and mentoring young players. He is married to Kath and they have two children, both of whom are involved in sport.

title: Ingo Titze
text:
Ingo Titze was born on January 23, 1933, in Altenbruch, Germany, a small village near Cuxhaven. His father, Friedrich Titze, was a Lutheran pastor, and his mother, Elisabeth (née Evers), a homemaker. Growing up during World War II and its aftermath deeply impacted Titze, fostering a lifelong interest in understanding complex systems and the human voice. He received his early education in local schools, demonstrating an aptitude for mathematics and physics. In 1951, he began studies in Electrical Engineering at the Technical University of Hanover, Germany, completing his Diplom-Ingenieur degree in 1956. This foundation in engineering would prove crucial to his future work.

Following his studies, Titze emigrated to the United States in 1957, initially working as a research engineer at the Boeing Company in Seattle, Washington. While at Boeing, he focused on antenna design and signal processing, gaining valuable experience in acoustic and vibration analysis. However, his interests gradually shifted towards the biological aspects of sound production, particularly the human voice. This transition began in 1962 when he started taking voice lessons to improve his singing, sparking a curiosity about the mechanics of laryngeal function.

In 1968, Titze enrolled at the University of Utah in Salt Lake City, pursuing a PhD in acoustics under the guidance of David G. Taylor. He completed his doctoral studies in 1970 with a dissertation titled "The Dynamics of Voice Production," a work that laid the groundwork for much of his subsequent research. During this time, he also began a long-term collaboration with the National Center for Voice and Speech (NCVS), initially as a consultant, and later as a core member of the research team. 

Titze’s career at NCVS, which became the National Center for Voice and Speech Research (NCVSR) in 1983, became the defining chapter of his professional life. He devoted over four decades to studying the physiology and acoustics of voice production, developing groundbreaking computational models and biomechanical analyses. He moved from a primarily engineering approach to one integrating biology, medicine and acoustics. He pioneered the development of the “laryngeal video kymograph,” a device allowing for high-speed visualization of vocal fold vibration, and the “Titze-Starling vocal fold model,” a three-dimensional computer simulation that revolutionized understanding of vocal fold behavior. 

A significant achievement was his development of glottal area waveforms, a method for analyzing the shape of the vocal folds during vibration, providing insights into vocal pathology and efficiency. His research contributed significantly to understanding vocal fatigue, phonotrauma, and the effects of aging on the voice. He authored or co-authored over 200 peer-reviewed publications, including the influential textbook “Principles of Voice Production” (1994), which remains a standard reference in the field.  He also served as editor of the *Journal of Voice* from 1987 to 2006, shaping the direction of voice research.

Throughout his career, Titze received numerous awards and accolades, including the Silver Medal in Physical Acoustics from the Acoustical Society of America in 1998 and the Voice Foundation's Lifetime Achievement Award in 2007. He held adjunct professorships at several universities, including the University of Iowa and the University of Colorado at Boulder, mentoring numerous students who went on to become leaders in the field of voice science. 

After formally retiring from the NCVSR in 2008, Titze remained actively involved in research, continuing to refine his models and explore new avenues of investigation. He established Voice Science Works, a company dedicated to developing and distributing voice analysis software and educational materials.  Ingo Titze passed away on July 22, 2023, in Salt Lake City, Utah, at the age of 90. His legacy endures through his extensive body of work, which continues to inform clinical practice and inspire research in the fields of speech-language pathology, otolaryngology, and voice pedagogy.

title: Jamie Cripps
text:
Jamie Cripps was born on February 28, 1992, in Northampton, Western Australia, to parents Brian and Dianne Cripps. He grew up in the small coastal town of Horrocks, approximately 450 kilometers north of Perth, where his early sporting pursuits were heavily influenced by the local environment. While proficient in a variety of sports, including basketball and cricket, Australian Rules Football quickly became his primary focus. He attended Champion Bay Senior High School in Geraldton, demonstrating athletic talent from a young age. Cripps’ formative football years were spent playing for Northampton Football Club in the Great Northern Football League, where he quickly established himself as a dynamic and versatile player, capable of playing as both a midfielder and a forward.

His talent caught the attention of West Coast Eagles scouts during the 2009 WAFL season while playing for East Perth, a club with a strong relationship with the AFL team. He had initially been overlooked in the 2009 AFL Draft, but the Eagles offered him a rookie listing in December 2009, believing in his potential. He spent the majority of the 2010 season developing with the Eagles’ reserves, playing consistently well and demonstrating rapid improvement. 

Cripps made his AFL debut in Round 18, 2011, against the Brisbane Lions at the Gabba on August 13th. He managed 12 disposals and a goal in a solid first outing, immediately showcasing his speed and goal sense. He played a further three games that season, demonstrating he could handle the step up to the elite level. In 2012, he secured a senior list position and played 21 games, cementing himself as a regular member of the West Coast Eagles’ forward line. He kicked 32 goals that year, finishing as the club’s second-highest goalkicker behind Josh Kennedy. 

Cripps continued to be a consistent performer for the Eagles throughout the 2013-2017 seasons, known for his high-energy play, penetrating kick and ability to take spectacular marks. He played in the 2015 Grand Final against Hawthorn, where the Eagles unfortunately lost by 46 points. Despite the defeat, Cripps had a respectable game with 16 disposals and a goal. He consistently polled well in the Brownlow Medal count during these years, although he never reached the top echelon of vote-getters. 

The pinnacle of his career arrived in 2018. He played a crucial role in the Eagles’ premiership campaign, kicking 23 goals for the season and performing strongly in the finals series. He was particularly effective in the Grand Final against Collingwood on September 29th, kicking three goals, including a crucial goal in the final quarter, to help the Eagles secure their fourth AFL premiership. He finished with 12 disposals, 6 marks and ultimately, a premiership medal.

Cripps continued to be a valuable contributor to the West Coast Eagles for several more seasons, playing his 200th AFL game in Round 19, 2021, against the Gold Coast Suns. His role evolved somewhat, becoming more of a pressure forward and utilizing his defensive running. In 2022, he signed a one-year contract extension, remaining committed to the club. He played 14 games in 2023, showcasing his continued dedication despite battling various injuries. 

In October 2023, at the age of 31, Cripps announced his retirement from AFL football, bringing an end to a 14-year career with the West Coast Eagles. He finished his career having played 222 games and kicked 254 goals for the club. Beyond his on-field contributions, Cripps was known for his professionalism, positive attitude and dedication to the West Coast Eagles community. Following his retirement, he has expressed interest in remaining involved in football, potentially in a coaching or development role, and continues to reside in Perth with his wife, Chelsea, and their family.

title: Karyn Pugliese
text:
Karyn Pugliese was born on November 29, 1966, in Toronto, Ontario, Canada, to Italian immigrant parents, Maria and Joseph Pugliese. Her father was a tool and die maker, and her mother worked in a variety of roles, including factory work and as a seamstress. Growing up in the west end of Toronto, specifically the Corso Italia neighbourhood, instilled in her a strong sense of community and a keen awareness of diverse perspectives, elements that would later influence her journalistic approach. She attended Runnymede Collegiate Institute, graduating in 1984, and then pursued a Bachelor of Arts degree in Political Science at the University of Toronto, completing it in 1988. 

Pugliese’s career in journalism began almost immediately after university. In 1988, she joined the *Toronto Star* as a library intern, quickly transitioning to a general assignment reporter covering a wide range of beats, including city hall and social services. This period proved formative, honing her skills in investigative reporting and building a network of sources. By 1993, she had moved to the *Star’s* Queen’s Park bureau, becoming a key member of the team covering provincial politics. She spent six years there, reporting on the governments of Bob Rae and Mike Harris, establishing a reputation for thoroughness and insightful analysis. 

A significant turning point came in 1999 when Pugliese joined the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation (CBC). Initially, she was a reporter and producer with CBC News, contributing to both television and radio broadcasts.  She quickly rose through the ranks, becoming a senior reporter specializing in investigative journalism. Her work at CBC focused heavily on issues of social justice, government accountability, and systemic discrimination. 

Pugliese’s investigative skills were prominently displayed in a series of high-profile investigations. In 2008, she led a team that produced “The Fifth Estate’s” investigation into the plight of Indigenous children in the child welfare system in Manitoba, titled “Stolen Sisters.” This investigation, which uncovered the disproportionate number of Indigenous children apprehended by the system and the challenges they faced, received widespread acclaim and won a Gemini Award for Best Investigative Report in 2009.  

Further recognition followed with her 2015 investigation, “Unnatural Causes,” which examined the deaths of several Indigenous women in Winnipeg, raising questions about police investigations and systemic racism within the justice system.  This work earned her a Canadian Association of Journalists (CAJ) Award for Investigative Journalism.  She continued to focus on Indigenous issues, leading a team that investigated the systemic failures that contributed to the tragic death of Tina Fontaine, a 15-year-old Indigenous girl, in 2014. This investigation, broadcast in 2017, resulted in further scrutiny of the child welfare and justice systems.

In 2018, Karyn Pugliese was appointed Executive Director, News and Current Affairs for CBC News, becoming the first woman to hold the position. This role placed her at the helm of Canada’s national public broadcaster’s news division, overseeing programs like *The National*, *World Report*, *The Fifth Estate* and CBC’s local news operations across the country.  During her tenure, she championed diversity and inclusion within the newsroom, advocating for greater representation of marginalized voices both on and off screen. 

Pugliese left CBC in July 2022, citing a desire to return to investigative reporting. She subsequently joined the University of Toronto’s Munk School of Global Affairs & Public Policy as a Distinguished Fellow. In this role, she researches and writes about issues of media ethics, investigative journalism, and systemic discrimination.  She also mentors young journalists and continues to contribute occasional investigative pieces to various publications. 

Throughout her career, Karyn Pugliese has received numerous awards and accolades, including the 2023 Atkinson Fellowship for public policy research. She has been a frequent speaker at journalism conferences and universities, advocating for responsible and impactful journalism.  She currently resides in Toronto with her family.

title: Sun Wenguang
text:
Sun Wenguang (孙文广, born December 27, 1911, in Yongjia County, Wenzhou, Zhejiang Province, China – died February 23, 1994, in Beijing) was a prominent Chinese nuclear physicist who played a pivotal role in the development of China’s atomic bomb. His contributions were largely focused on the crucial area of uranium enrichment, enabling the production of the fissile material necessary for nuclear weapons.

Sun’s early education took place in his hometown, followed by attendance at the Wenzhou Provincial Middle School. In 1929, he was admitted to the Department of Physics at Tsinghua University in Beijing, a prestigious institution known for sending students abroad for further study. In 1933, he received a Boxer Indemnity Scholarship and travelled to the United States, enrolling at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT). He earned his Bachelor of Science degree in Electrical Engineering from MIT in 1936. He continued his studies there, completing his Ph.D. in Physics in 1940 with a dissertation focused on the positive ray analysis of isotopes, specifically concerning the separation of isotopes. 

During his time in the United States, Sun’s research leaned towards isotope separation, a skill that would become invaluable to China’s nuclear program. He spent the following years as a research associate and lecturer at MIT and later at the University of California, Berkeley, where he worked with Ernest Lawrence, the inventor of the cyclotron. He also held a position at the Radiation Laboratory at Berkeley between 1940 and 1946, contributing to research related to the Manhattan Project, though his involvement was limited to fundamental research and not directly to bomb design. 

In 1948, responding to a call from the Chinese government following the establishment of the People's Republic of China, Sun returned to his homeland. He initially served as a professor at Tsinghua University, and in 1958, he was appointed as the director of the Institute of Physics, part of the Chinese Academy of Sciences. Crucially, he was tasked with leading the effort to establish a uranium enrichment program. 

Recognizing the limitations of relying solely on gaseous diffusion, the method initially pursued, Sun advocated for the development of the centrifugal separation method, a more efficient and cost-effective technology. He foresaw the significant advantages of this approach, despite the greater technical challenges. He actively promoted collaboration with Pakistani nuclear scientist Abdus Salam, who provided crucial theoretical insights into the dynamics of gas centrifuges.  Sun’s insistence on the centrifuge method, despite initial resistance, proved to be a turning point in China’s nuclear program. 

Between 1960 and 1970, Sun oversaw the construction and operation of China’s first uranium enrichment plant, located in Hanzhong, Shaanxi Province. This facility, built with limited resources and relying heavily on domestic engineering and scientific expertise, successfully produced enriched uranium, a critical component for the first Chinese atomic bomb, tested in 1964. He was a key figure in overcoming numerous technical hurdles, including material science challenges and the need to develop specialized precision engineering capabilities. 

Sun remained a leading figure in China’s nuclear energy development. In 1982, he was elected as an academician of the Chinese Academy of Sciences.  He continued to advise the government on nuclear policy and technology, shifting his focus towards peaceful applications of nuclear energy. In the late 1980s, he played a role in the development of China’s first commercial nuclear power plant at Daya Bay, Guangdong Province. 

Throughout his career, Sun Wenguang remained relatively low-profile, preferring to focus on the scientific and technical aspects of his work. He received numerous awards and honors from the Chinese government, including the State Science and Technology Progress Award in 1985. He passed away in Beijing on February 23, 1994, leaving behind a legacy as one of the founding fathers of China’s nuclear program and a dedicated scientist who significantly contributed to his nation’s scientific advancement.

title: Jennifer Sevilla
text:
Jennifer Sevilla was born on August 17, 1971, in Manila, Philippines, to parents Ricardo and Erlinda Sevilla. Her father was a businessman involved in import/export, and her mother was a schoolteacher specializing in English. Growing up in the affluent Makati district, Jennifer attended the Assumption College, a prestigious all-girls Catholic school, graduating in 1989. From a young age, she demonstrated a strong aptitude for mathematics and science, coupled with a keen interest in performing arts, participating in school theatre productions and debate clubs. 

Sevilla’s higher education began at Ateneo de Manila University in 1989, where she pursued a Bachelor of Science degree in Management Engineering, graduating magna cum laude in 1993. During her time at Ateneo, she was actively involved in student government, serving as Treasurer of the University Student Council in her junior year.  She also participated in several engineering design competitions, consistently placing in the top rankings.  Immediately following graduation, Sevilla accepted a position as a Management Consultant at McKinsey & Company in Manila. She worked on projects spanning various industries, including telecommunications, retail, and financial services, quickly earning a reputation for analytical rigor and client management skills. 

In 1996, Sevilla made a significant career shift, deciding to pursue an MBA at Harvard Business School in Boston, Massachusetts. She completed the program in 1998, concentrating in Finance and Strategy.  It was during her time at Harvard that she met her future husband, David Thompson, an American lawyer. They married in 2000 in a ceremony held in both Manila and Boston. After graduating, Sevilla joined Goldman Sachs in New York City, initially in the Investment Banking Division, focusing on mergers and acquisitions.  

Over the next decade, Sevilla steadily rose through the ranks at Goldman Sachs, becoming a Managing Director in 2008, at the age of 37.  Her expertise centered on the technology, media, and telecommunications sectors, advising companies like Yahoo! on its Alibaba stake sale in 2012, a transaction valued at over $7.1 billion.  She led several other high-profile deals, including the $4.4 billion acquisition of Skype by Microsoft in 2011, playing a crucial role in the financial structuring and negotiation process.  

In 2015, Sevilla transitioned from investment banking to a more operational role, joining Spotify as its Chief Financial Officer.  She was instrumental in guiding Spotify through its initial public offering (IPO) on the New York Stock Exchange in April 2018, raising approximately $2.65 billion.  During her tenure as CFO, Spotify's subscriber base grew from 60 million to over 144 million, and its revenue increased significantly.  She oversaw the company’s expansion into new markets and the development of its podcasting strategy. 

Sevilla stepped down as CFO of Spotify in February 2020, citing a desire to dedicate more time to philanthropic endeavors and family.  She joined the board of directors of Teach for America in March 2020, and in 2021, she established the Sevilla-Thompson Foundation, a non-profit organization focused on providing educational opportunities for underprivileged students in the Philippines. The foundation has since awarded over $5 million in scholarships and grants to various educational programs. 

Jennifer Sevilla Thompson, as she is now known, currently resides in Greenwich, Connecticut with her husband and their two children, born in 2003 and 2006.  She continues to serve on several corporate boards, including that of Duolingo, and remains an active mentor for young professionals, particularly women in finance and technology.  She was recognized by Forbes as one of the “Most Powerful Women in Finance” in both 2017 and 2019, and received the Ateneo de Manila University’s Distinguished Alumni Award for Professional Achievement in 2022.

title: León Dujovne
text:
León Dujovne was born on September 26, 1926, in Buenos Aires, Argentina, into a Jewish family of Eastern European descent. His father, Jacobo Dujovne, was a physician, and his mother, Celia Berliner, was a teacher. This background instilled in him a strong emphasis on intellectual pursuits and a commitment to social responsibility that would characterize his life and work. Dujovne received his primary and secondary education at the prestigious Colegio Nacional Buenos Aires, graduating with honors in 1944. He began studying law at the University of Buenos Aires, but quickly shifted his focus to economics, ultimately earning a degree in Economics from the same institution in 1949. 

Following graduation, Dujovne embarked on his academic career, initially working as an assistant professor at the University of Buenos Aires. He recognized the limitations of the prevailing economic thought in Argentina at the time, heavily influenced by Keynesianism and import substitution industrialization, and sought further training abroad. In 1951, he received a scholarship to study at the University of Chicago, a burgeoning center for neoclassical economics under the influence of figures like Milton Friedman and George Stigler. He completed his doctorate in Economics there in 1954, with a dissertation focused on monetary theory. 

Returning to Argentina in 1955, Dujovne faced a challenging political and economic climate. The country was experiencing significant instability, and his free-market oriented views were often at odds with the prevailing Peronist economic policies. Despite these obstacles, he continued to teach and research, becoming a full professor at the University of Buenos Aires in 1962. He also held positions at the Universidad Católica Argentina and the Torcuato Di Tella Institute, a newly founded institution dedicated to liberal economic thinking.  During the 1960s and 70s, he became a vocal critic of the interventionist policies that he believed were hindering Argentina's economic development. 

Dujovne’s contributions extended beyond academia. He served as a consultant to the Central Bank of Argentina on several occasions, beginning in 1964, though his influence was often limited by the political context. He actively participated in public debates, writing extensively for newspapers and journals, and advocating for fiscal responsibility, deregulation, and trade liberalization.  He was a founding member of the Centro de Estudios Económicos Argentina (CEEA) in 1977, a think tank that became a crucial voice for market-oriented reforms during the military dictatorship (1976-1983). While he maintained a degree of distance from the regime, CEEA provided a platform for promoting ideas that would later underpin the economic reforms of the 1990s.

The 1990s witnessed a significant shift in Argentina’s economic policy, largely driven by the reforms implemented under Economy Minister Domingo Cavallo. Dujovne played a key advisory role in these reforms, particularly the implementation of the Convertibility Plan in 1991, which pegged the Argentine peso to the US dollar. He served as a director of the Central Bank of Argentina from 1991 to 1993, and as Secretary of Economic Policy in 1993 and 1994.  During this period, he was instrumental in promoting privatization, deregulation, and fiscal austerity. 

However, Dujovne became increasingly critical of the rigidities of the Convertibility Plan as it became clear that it was hindering Argentina’s ability to respond to economic shocks. He warned of the dangers of maintaining an overvalued exchange rate and advocated for greater flexibility. The collapse of the Convertibility Plan in 2001 and the subsequent economic crisis deeply affected him. 

In his later life, Dujovne continued to write and lecture, reflecting on the lessons of Argentina’s economic history and advocating for sound economic policies. He remained a prominent voice in the debate over Argentina’s economic future.  He published several books, including "El Quiebre de la Convertibilidad" (The Breakdown of Convertibility) in 2002, analyzing the causes and consequences of the 2001 crisis. León Dujovne passed away in Buenos Aires on February 27, 2017, at the age of 90, leaving behind a legacy as one of Argentina’s most influential economists and a staunch defender of free market principles.

title: Settimo Mineo
text:
Settimo Mineo was born on November 22, 1901, in Palermo, Sicily, Italy, into a family deeply involved in the burgeoning world of Italian aviation. His father, Rosario Mineo, was a pioneering aeronautical engineer and builder who established the Società Anonima Costruzioni Aeronautiche (SACA) in 1917, one of the first Italian aircraft factories. This early exposure proved formative for Settimo, who quickly developed a passion for flight. He received his pilot’s license, number 423, on July 14, 1921, at the age of 19, from the Italian Royal Aviation School in Cameri, Novara.

Mineo’s early career was intrinsically linked to his father’s SACA company. He initially worked as a test pilot, gaining invaluable experience with a variety of aircraft designs.  He quickly distinguished himself with his skill and daring, participating in numerous air shows and competitions. In 1923, he began to make a name for himself in the realm of air racing, competing in the prestigious Challenge International de Navigation Aérienne, a long-distance air race. He flew a SACA-built aircraft, though he didn’t win, the experience honed his navigational and endurance skills.

The year 1926 marked a pivotal moment in Mineo’s career. He was selected, alongside Guido Manerba, as the pilot for an attempt to break the world endurance flight record.  Their aircraft, a modified Farman F.60 Goliath biplane christened “Italia,” was equipped with in-flight refueling capabilities – a relatively new and complex technology at the time. The flight took off from Montecelio airfield near Rome on May 26, 1926, and aimed to stay aloft for an extended period by refueling with gasoline transferred from a modified Fiat AS.2 reconnaissance aircraft piloted by Vincenzo Lo Re. 

After a grueling 52 hours, 31 minutes, and 30 seconds, the “Italia” landed on May 28, 1926, having shattered the previous endurance record of 33 hours and 12 minutes, held by Americans James Doolittle and Paul Davis. This achievement brought instant international fame to Mineo and Manerba, and cemented Italy’s position as a leader in aviation innovation.  The feat was celebrated with a medal from King Victor Emmanuel III and widespread public recognition.

The success of the endurance flight led to an even more ambitious project: a transatlantic flight from Italy to Brazil.  Again, Mineo and Manerba were selected as the pilots, and the “Italia” was modified for the longer journey.  They departed from Sesto Calende, Italy, on February 15, 1928, aiming for Rio de Janeiro.  The flight was fraught with difficulties, including severe weather conditions and mechanical issues. They successfully reached Fernando de Noronha, a Brazilian archipelago, on February 17th, but disaster struck during the final leg to Rio de Janeiro. 

On February 18, 1928, approximately 300 kilometers off the Brazilian coast, the “Italia” crashed into the Atlantic Ocean. Manerba was killed instantly. Mineo, despite suffering serious injuries, miraculously survived clinging to a floating portion of the fuselage for nearly 30 hours before being rescued by the Portuguese steamer “Sâo Tomé.” He was found unconscious and severely dehydrated, but alive. 

Following his rescue and recovery, Mineo received a hero’s welcome in Brazil and Italy.  He continued to work in the aviation industry, though he never again attempted such daring long-distance flights. He served as a director at SACA until its eventual absorption into the larger Fiat Aviazione company in 1930. He then held various administrative positions within the Italian aviation authority, focusing on air safety and regulation.  

Settimo Mineo spent his later years largely out of the public eye. He remarried in 1934 to Lidia Gallinaro, and they had two daughters. He remained a respected figure within the Italian aviation community, often consulted for his expertise. Settimo Mineo died on December 8, 1973, in Rome at the age of 72, leaving behind a legacy as a pioneering aviator and a symbol of Italian courage and innovation in the early days of flight.

title: Will Keane
text:
William “Will” Keane was born on January 21, 1993, in Cheshire, England, the younger brother of fellow professional footballer Michael Keane. His early footballing development took place within the youth system of Manchester United, joining the club at the age of 11 in July 2004. He progressed steadily through the ranks, demonstrating a natural goalscoring ability and playing in a variety of attacking positions. He was a key member of the United youth team that won the FA Youth Cup in 2011, scoring in both legs of the final against Sheffield United, a testament to his burgeoning talent. This success brought him to the attention of the first-team management.

Keane made his senior debut for Manchester United on September 27, 2011, in a League Cup third-round match against Leeds United at Elland Road, coming on as a 78th minute substitute for Dimitar Berbatov in a 3-0 victory. He made his Premier League debut on January 28, 2012, against Southampton, again appearing as a late substitute. However, opportunities in the Premier League remained limited, and he spent a loan period with Queens Park Rangers in February 2013, making 6 appearances and scoring 0 goals as the club battled relegation. 

A more impactful loan spell followed in November 2013, joining Wigan Athletic initially for a month, which was later extended until the end of the 2013-2014 season. At Wigan, playing in the Championship, Keane flourished, scoring 3 goals in 21 appearances and demonstrating a growing maturity to his game.  His performances earned him praise and solidified his reputation as a promising young striker.

Despite this, Keane didn’t establish himself as a regular starter at Manchester United upon his return.  On August 11, 2014, he joined Sheffield Wednesday on a season-long loan, where he played 26 times across all competitions, scoring 3 goals.  His time at Hillsborough was hampered by injuries, preventing him from consistently showcasing his potential. 

In August 2015, Keane officially left Manchester United, signing a two-year contract with Hull City, then also in the Championship. This marked a significant step in his career, seeking regular first-team football. He quickly became a pivotal player for Hull, forming a productive partnership with Abel Hernandez.  He enjoyed a successful 2016-2017 season, playing a crucial role in Hull’s promotion to the Premier League via the Championship play-off final, scoring 12 league goals and 15 in total. 

However, his Premier League return with Hull in the 2017-2018 season was less fruitful, as the team struggled and were ultimately relegated. He scored 2 Premier League goals during this period.  Following Hull’s relegation, Keane joined Ipswich Town on a two-year contract in July 2018. His time at Portman Road saw him score 8 goals in 37 appearances across all competitions.

In January 2020, Keane made a move to Wigan Athletic for a second spell, signing an 18-month contract. He quickly re-established himself as a key player, becoming the club’s leading scorer in the 2020-2021 season with 12 goals in League One, despite Wigan facing significant off-field financial difficulties.  He was instrumental in their survival, and his commitment to the club during a turbulent period was widely recognised.

In June 2022, Keane signed for Preston North End on a two-year contract. He has become a consistent performer for Preston, showcasing his goalscoring prowess and leadership qualities. As of November 2023, he has made over 70 appearances for the club, scoring over 20 goals, and has become a fan favourite at Deepdale. He has also captained the side on several occasions. 

Throughout his career, Keane has also represented England at various youth levels, including the Under-17, Under-19, and Under-20 teams. He was part of the England Under-20 squad that won the 2013 FIFA U-20 World Cup in Turkey, although he didn’t feature in the final. Will Keane continues to play professionally for Preston North End, maintaining a solid career built on perseverance and a consistent goalscoring record.

title: Yuu Watase
text:
Yuu Watase was born on August 5, 1970, in Shimane Prefecture, Japan. Her real name is Yumiko Watase (渡瀬 悠美子), with “Yuu” being the pen name she adopted for her manga work. Growing up in a rural environment, Watase demonstrated an early passion for storytelling and art, heavily influenced by folklore and traditional Japanese tales. She was a particularly avid reader of shōjo manga, the genre aimed at young girls and women, and this strongly shaped her artistic aspirations. While her family wasn’t directly involved in the creative industries, they supported her artistic endeavors. 

Watase’s formal education culminated in enrollment at the Kanazawa College of Art, where she studied design. However, she left before graduating, deciding to pursue her dream of becoming a manga artist professionally. This decision was fuelled by a desire to tell her own stories visually. In 1990, at the age of 20, she made her professional debut with a short story titled "Ryuu no Kodoku" (The Dragon's Solitude) published in the shōjo manga magazine *LaLa*. This early work, though not a major success, provided her with valuable experience and a foothold in the industry.

Her breakthrough arrived in 1992 with *Fushigi Yuugi* (Mysterious Play), which began serialization in *Shōjo LaLa*. This series, running until 1996 with a total of 18 volumes, catapulted Watase to national fame. *Fushigi Yuugi* is a fantasy romance centered around Miaka Yuuki, a high school student transported with her friend Yui Hongo into a mysterious book set in ancient China. The series’ popularity was driven by its complex characters, intricate plot, and romantic elements, and it was quickly adapted into a successful anime television series in 1995, running for 26 episodes, as well as several OVAs and stage plays. *Fushigi Yuugi* sold over 80 million copies in Japan alone, solidifying Watase’s position as a leading figure in shōjo manga.

Following the success of *Fushigi Yuugi*, Watase continued to create a diverse body of work. *W's* (Wish), which ran from 1996 to 2003 and spanned 17 volumes, explored themes of reincarnation and destiny with a more mature tone. This series, while popular, didn’t achieve the same widespread recognition as her previous hit.  She then began *Kanata* in 2004, a science fiction romance that ran for 7 volumes until 2008. In 2009, she launched *Arata Kangatari* (Arata the Magnificent), a lengthy epic fantasy series inspired by Japanese mythology, running until 2015 with 23 volumes.  Throughout these series, Watase consistently demonstrated her skill in character design, intricate world-building, and emotionally resonant storytelling.  Her style is characterized by detailed artwork and a focus on strong female protagonists.

Watase's work often features recurring themes of fate, destiny, reincarnation, and the power of love.  She frequently draws inspiration from Japanese history, mythology, and folklore, integrating these elements into her fantastical narratives.  Beyond her major serializations, she has also published numerous short stories and art collections.  

In recent years, Watase has continued to work steadily, though with a less frenetic pace. In 2017, she started *Sakura Hime: The Legend of Princess Sakura*, a historical fantasy series.  As of late 2023, this series is ongoing. While she doesn’t maintain a large public profile, she occasionally participates in art exhibitions and provides updates on her work through social media.  She remains a respected and influential figure within the manga industry, inspiring a new generation of artists with her unique style and captivating stories.  She is currently residing in Tokyo, Japan and continues to focus on her manga creations.

title: Pablo Ganet
text:
Pablo Ganet was born on August 12, 1903, in Buenos Aires, Argentina, to a family with a strong connection to journalism. His father, Emilio Ganet, was a prominent political journalist and director of the newspaper *La Nación*, a position that significantly influenced Pablo’s early intellectual and professional development. From a young age, Ganet was immersed in the world of newspapers, politics, and literature, accompanying his father on assignments and absorbing the nuances of Argentine public life. He received his primary and secondary education in Buenos Aires, attending the prestigious Colegio Nacional Buenos Aires. 

Ganet began his journalistic career exceptionally early, contributing articles to *La Nación* while still a teenager. He formally joined the newspaper’s staff in 1921, initially working as a theater and literary critic. This period allowed him to hone his writing skills and develop a keen eye for cultural trends. However, Ganet’s ambitions extended beyond cultural reporting. He quickly gravitated towards political and international affairs, demonstrating a talent for insightful analysis and nuanced reporting. He travelled extensively throughout Europe in the 1920s and 30s, reporting from key cities like Paris, Berlin, Rome, and London. These experiences broadened his perspective and allowed him to build a network of contacts that would prove invaluable throughout his career.

A pivotal moment in Ganet’s career came in 1936, when he was appointed *La Nación’s* correspondent in Washington D.C. This posting coincided with the rise of Franklin D. Roosevelt’s New Deal and the escalating tensions in Europe leading up to World War II. Ganet's reporting from the American capital was distinguished by its accuracy, objectivity, and depth. He provided Argentine readers with a sophisticated understanding of American politics, economics, and foreign policy, often offering critical perspectives that challenged prevailing narratives. He became a trusted source of information for the Argentine government, frequently consulted on matters relating to the United States.

During World War II, Ganet’s role became even more crucial. Despite Argentina’s initial neutrality, he maintained a vital link between Buenos Aires and Washington, reporting on the war’s progress and the shifting alliances. He was known for his ability to navigate the complex political landscape of wartime Washington, securing interviews with key figures like Cordell Hull, the US Secretary of State, and providing insightful analysis of the war’s impact on Latin America. In 1945, he covered the founding conference of the United Nations in San Francisco, offering detailed accounts of the negotiations and the establishment of the new international organization.

After returning to Argentina in 1946, Ganet continued his work at *La Nación*, becoming a leading voice in Argentine journalism. He was a staunch defender of democratic principles and a vocal critic of the growing authoritarianism under Juan Perón. His critical stance led to increasing pressure from the Perón government, culminating in his forced resignation from *La Nación* in 1949.  This dismissal was part of a broader crackdown on independent media during Perón’s first presidency. 

Despite the political challenges, Ganet remained active in journalism, founding and directing the news agency *Argentina News Features* in 1950. Through this agency, he continued to provide independent reporting and analysis, reaching a wider audience both domestically and internationally. He also authored several books, including “The Third American Republic” (1953), a critical examination of Peronism and its impact on Argentine society. 

In 1955, following the military coup that overthrew Perón, Ganet was briefly appointed as Argentina’s ambassador to the United States, a position he held for only a few months.  He found the diplomatic role restrictive and returned to journalism, continuing to write and comment on political affairs. 

Pablo Ganet died in Buenos Aires on November 26, 1975, at the age of 72.  He left behind a legacy as one of Argentina’s most respected and influential journalists, known for his integrity, intellectual rigor, and commitment to democratic values. His extensive reporting and insightful analysis provided a crucial window into the political and international events of the 20th century, shaping public understanding both in Argentina and abroad.

title: Sayaka Ando
text:
Sayaka Ando was born on December 28, 1983, in Fukuoka Prefecture, Japan. Her upbringing was unconventional; her mother, a single parent, ran a hostess club, a type of Japanese entertainment establishment, and Ando frequently accompanied her to work. This early exposure to a complex social environment, witnessing a range of human interactions and emotional displays, would later inform her acting style. Despite this unusual background, Ando excelled academically, demonstrating a particular aptitude for literature and languages. She initially harbored ambitions of becoming a teacher, even enrolling in courses related to education.

However, Ando’s path shifted dramatically when, at the age of 16, she was scouted by a talent agency while shopping in a local department store in Hakata, Fukuoka. She initially resisted, hesitant to enter the entertainment industry, but was eventually persuaded by the agency to audition. Her debut came in 2002, with a minor role in the television drama *Romanesque*, marking the beginning of her professional acting career. 

The early years of her career saw Ando taking on a variety of small roles in television dramas, gradually gaining experience and recognition. A significant breakthrough arrived in 2005 with her performance in the film *Ashura-jo* (Asura Castle), directed by Kazuhiro Kiyohara. This role garnered her attention for her raw and intense portrayal of a troubled young woman.  She continued to appear in a steady stream of television and film projects, often playing characters on the fringes of society – vulnerable, damaged, and emotionally complex. 

2009 proved to be a pivotal year. Ando starred in *Crossfire*, directed by Yoshihiro Nakamura, a crime drama that showcased her ability to convincingly portray both strength and fragility.  More importantly, she was cast in the lead role of Akari in *Walking on Water*, directed by Ryūichi Hiroki. The film, which premiered at the 2009 Venice Film Festival, garnered critical acclaim and earned Ando significant international recognition. She won the Best Actress award at the Venice Film Festival, becoming the first Japanese actress to receive the award in 15 years – a landmark achievement. *Walking on Water* explored themes of grief, motherhood, and the complexities of modern relationships, and Ando’s nuanced performance was widely praised.

Following her Venice win, Ando's career trajectory accelerated. She continued to choose roles that challenged her and allowed her to explore a wide emotional range.  She appeared in *Helped* (2012), a film dealing with assisted suicide, and *Rurouni Kenshin* (2014) and its sequel (2021), taking on the role of Tomoe Yukishiro, a complex antagonist. She also starred in *Flight into Darjeeling* (2013), a drama exploring familial bonds. Throughout this period, she consistently demonstrated a commitment to independent and art-house cinema alongside more mainstream productions.

Ando’s acting style is characterized by its naturalism and emotional honesty. She is known for her ability to embody characters fully, often drawing upon her own experiences and observations to create deeply compelling performances. She deliberately avoids over-acting, favouring subtle nuances and internal struggles. 

In 2019, Ando married a man outside the entertainment industry, a software engineer.  She largely maintains a private personal life, rarely discussing it in public. In recent years, she has continued to work consistently, appearing in films such as *Ride or Die* (2018), a yakuza action film directed by Ryuichi Kitamura, and *Violent Cop* (2018), a remake of the 1989 Takeshi Kitano film. In 2023, she starred in *Monster*, a critically acclaimed Hirokazu Kore-eda film that premiered at Cannes.  



As of late 2023, Sayaka Ando remains a highly respected and sought-after actress in Japanese cinema, known for her dedication to her craft and her willingness to tackle challenging and unconventional roles. She has earned over 20 awards and nominations for her work, solidifying her position as one of Japan’s leading contemporary actresses.

title: Chris Woakes
text:
Christopher David Woakes was born on July 1st, 1989, in Birmingham, West Midlands, England. He was raised in Leamington Spa, Warwickshire, and his early sporting interests weren't solely focused on cricket. He excelled at football and rugby, representing Warwickshire at both sports before committing fully to cricket around the age of 15. He attended Warwick School, a well-known cricketing school, where he honed his skills and captained the first XI. His father, Chris Woakes Senior, was a fast bowler for Warwickshire 2nd XI, providing early guidance and encouragement. 

Woakes’s journey through the county system began with Warwickshire. He debuted in first-class cricket for them in June 2006 against Worcestershire at New Road, taking 2-73 in the first innings. He continued to feature sporadically for Warwickshire, developing his all-round abilities. A significant move came in 2008 when he joined the Marylebone Cricket Club (MCC) Young Cricketers, a development programme designed to nurture emerging talent. This provided him with intensive coaching and more consistent match practice.

He returned to Warwickshire in 2009 and began to establish himself as a key player. His performances with both bat and ball steadily improved, showcasing his potential as a genuine all-rounder. A breakthrough season came in 2012, where he played a crucial role in Warwickshire winning the County Championship, taking 49 wickets at an average of 22.57 and scoring 434 runs. This success earned him his first call-up to the England Test squad in May 2013 for the series against New Zealand at Lord’s. He marked his debut with a first-innings wicket of Peter Fulton.

Although initially in and out of the England side, Woakes demonstrated his ability to perform at the highest level. He made his One Day International (ODI) debut against Ireland in September 2011, but it wasn’t until 2015 that he really began to cement his place in the limited-overs formats. The 2017 Champions Trophy, held in England and Wales, proved to be a watershed moment.
