He appeared in 39 games for the Jazz during the 2015-2016 NBA season, averaging 5.3 points in 13.8 minutes per game. 

In July 2016, Mitrou-Long was waived by the Jazz and subsequently signed with the Philadelphia 76ers on a non-guaranteed contract. After a brief stint, he was cut before the start of the regular season. He then spent the 2016-2017 season bouncing between the Delaware 87ers (the 76ers’ G League affiliate) and short-term 10-day contracts with the Milwaukee Bucks and the New Orleans Pelicans, appearing in a total of 16 NBA games.

Seeking more stable playing time, Mitrou-Long moved to Europe in the summer of 2017, signing with Gran Canaria of the Spanish Liga ACB.  He enjoyed a successful two-year stint with the club, averaging 12.3 points in 44 games during the 2017-2018 season and 14.5 points in 31 games in the 2018-2019 season. Following Gran Canaria, he played for Turk Telekom Ankara in Turkey (2019-2020), averaging 16.4 points per game. 

In 2020, Mitrou-Long returned to Canada and joined the Scarborough Shooting Stars of the National Basketball League of Canada (NBLC). He led the league in scoring during the 2021 season, averaging 25.8 points per game and was named the NBLC Finals MVP after leading the Shooting Stars to the championship. He continued with Scarborough through the 2023 season, remaining a key player. 

In 2024, Mitrou-Long signed with the Newfoundland Growlers of the Canadian Elite Basketball League (CEBL), further continuing his professional career in Canada. Beyond his playing career, Mitrou-Long has been involved in basketball camps and clinics, giving back to the Canadian basketball community that nurtured his development. He remains a popular figure amongst Canadian basketball fans and a role model for aspiring players.

title: Dominique Blake
text:
Dominique Blake, born on November 12, 1968, in New Orleans, Louisiana, emerged as a significant figure in the world of competitive ballroom dance, specifically excelling in International Standard style. Her early life was steeped in the vibrant culture of New Orleans, though her introduction to dance wasn’t immediate. She began formal ballet training at the age of seven with the New Orleans Ballet Association, studying under the direction of Beth Pirkey. However, it was a chance viewing of a televised ballroom competition that sparked a passion that would define her career. 

By age ten, Blake had transitioned to ballroom, initially training with local instructors in New Orleans. Recognizing her potential, her parents, Arthur and Evelyn Blake, made a substantial commitment to her development, eventually relocating to the New York metropolitan area in 1981. This move allowed Dominique access to higher-level coaching and a more competitive dance scene. She began studying with Eddie Espinoza, a renowned figure in American ballroom, and quickly progressed. 

Blake's competitive career began in earnest in the mid-1980s. She initially partnered with several dancers, achieving regional success, but her breakthrough came in 1988 when she began partnering with Alex Sharapov. Sharapov, a Russian-born dancer who had immigrated to the United States, proved to be a particularly strong match for Blake, both technically and artistically. Together, they quickly rose through the ranks of American and then international competition. 

The pair’s defining style centered around the elegance and precision of International Standard, focusing on Waltz, Tango, Viennese Waltz, Foxtrot, and Quickstep. They were known for their strong musicality, refined technique, and undeniable stage presence. In 1991, Blake and Sharapov claimed the United States National Professional American Smooth Championship, a significant achievement solidifying their status within the American dance community. However, their ambition extended beyond national prominence.

Throughout the 1990s, Dominique Blake and Alex Sharapov represented the United States in numerous international competitions. A peak moment arrived in 1994 at the World Ballroom Dance Championships in Hong Kong, where they finished 6th in the International Standard category. This was a landmark result for an American couple, as European dancers historically dominated the discipline. They consistently ranked among the top ten couples globally for the next several years, competing in prestigious events like the Blackpool Dance Festival in England, consistently placing within the semi-finals and quarter-finals. They also earned a notable 5th place finish at the 1996 International Championships held in Rotterdam, Netherlands. 

Blake and Sharapov's partnership extended for over a decade, concluding in 1999. Following their split, Dominique continued to be involved in the dance world, transitioning her focus toward coaching and choreography. She established the Dominique Blake Dance Studio in New York City, where she mentored aspiring dancers, focusing on technical skill, performance quality, and the artistic elements of ballroom. 

Beyond direct instruction, Blake became a sought-after judge at numerous national and international ballroom competitions, utilizing her extensive experience and keen eye for detail. She served as a judge for USA Dance, a governing body for the sport in the United States, for over fifteen years. She also contributed to dance education through workshops and masterclasses held across the country.  

Dominique Blake remained a prominent figure in the American ballroom scene until her passing on October 27, 2023, in Manhattan, New York, at the age of 54, after a battle with cancer. Her legacy extends beyond her competitive achievements, encompassing a dedication to nurturing the next generation of ballroom dancers and a lasting influence on the American style of International Standard dance. She is remembered as a graceful performer, a demanding but supportive coach, and a dedicated advocate for the art of ballroom dancing.

title: Julie Bishop
text:
Julie Bishop was born Julie Maxine Bishop on July 17, 1966, in Lobethal, South Australia, a small Adelaide Hills town with strong German heritage. Her parents, Doug and Margaret Bishop, were both involved in local politics; her father was a local councillor and her mother a schoolteacher. Bishop attended Lobethal Lutheran School and then Urrbrae Agricultural High School, excelling in debating and public speaking. She demonstrated early ambition and leadership qualities, becoming school captain in 1983. 

Bishop commenced a Bachelor of Arts degree at the University of Adelaide in 1984, majoring in Government and Public Policy. She deferred her studies in 1985 to work as a research assistant to Liberal Member for Mayo, Dudley Hausler. This experience sparked her interest in a political career and allowed her to gain practical insights into parliamentary processes. She completed her degree in 1988, graduating with Honours. Following university, Bishop worked as an associate to Justice Jane Matthews of the South Australian Equal Opportunity Tribunal, furthering her legal understanding.

She then pursued a legal career, qualifying as a solicitor in 1990 after completing the Law Society of South Australia’s Articles of Clerkship. Bishop worked at legal firms Minter Ellison and later Clayton Utz, specializing in commercial litigation. She became a partner at Clayton Utz in 1998, a significant accomplishment at the age of 32. During her time in legal practice, she handled a diverse range of cases, including complex commercial disputes and advising on corporate governance.

Bishop’s entry into federal politics came in 1998 when she successfully contested the Division of Curtin in Western Australia for the Liberal Party. She defeated longstanding Labor incumbent, Allan Griffiths, winning with a 5.8% swing. She was immediately appointed to the parliamentary secretary role assisting the Minister for Defence, John Moore. In 2003, she was promoted to Minister for Children and Youth, then, in 2005, Minister for Education and Youth. 

A key period in her career began in 2007 when she was appointed Shadow Minister for Treasury, a role she held until 2013. During this time, she was a vocal critic of the Labor government’s economic policies. Following the Liberal/National Coalition’s victory in the 2013 federal election, Bishop was appointed Minister for Foreign Affairs in Tony Abbott’s cabinet. 

As Foreign Minister, Bishop significantly raised Australia’s international profile. She focused on strengthening ties with countries in the Indo-Pacific region and played a key role in negotiating the Trans-Pacific Partnership trade agreement. She oversaw the response to the downing of Malaysia Airlines Flight MH17 in 2014, leading Australia’s efforts to secure justice for the victims. She also championed women’s leadership in foreign policy and advocated for human rights on the international stage. Bishop was the first woman to hold the position of Foreign Minister in Australia.

She retained the Foreign Affairs portfolio under Malcolm Turnbull, becoming the Deputy Leader of the Liberal Party in 2017 following the leadership change. This made her a key figure in the government. However, the Liberal Party lost the 2019 federal election, and Bishop subsequently resigned from her positions, including the deputy leadership. 

Since leaving parliament, Bishop has pursued a successful career in the private sector. In 2020, she joined the board of Palladium, an international development consultancy. She also serves on the boards of several other companies. Bishop has been a frequent commentator on political and international affairs, and in 2021, she published her memoir, "Halftime", which became a bestseller. In January 2024, she was appointed as the Chancellor of Murdoch University. She continues to be a prominent public figure, offering perspectives on current events and advocating for issues she is passionate about. Bishop remains unmarried and resides in Perth, Western Australia.

title: Diafra Sakho
text:
Diafra Sakho was born on November 24, 1989, in Thiès, Senegal. His early life was marked by a nomadic footballing journey across Europe before he eventually found a consistent foothold in professional football. Sakho didn’t begin his youth career in a formally structured academy system, instead initially playing for local Senegalese clubs before moving to France at the age of 15. He joined SC Bastia's youth setup in 2004, but spent only a short time there, before spells with several lower-league French clubs including AS Yzeure (2006-2007) and FC Villefranche Beaujolais (2007-2008). It was at Villefranche, playing in the Championnat de France amateur 2, that he began to attract attention with his goal-scoring prowess, netting 18 goals in 32 appearances during the 2008-2009 season.

This performance earned him a move to Valenciennes FC in Ligue 2 in the summer of 2009. Sakho spent two seasons with Valenciennes, gradually establishing himself as a key player. He made his professional debut on August 8, 2009, against Clermont Foot, and scored his first professional goal on November 20, 2009, against Tours. Over his time at the club, he contributed 16 goals in 64 league appearances. This form attracted the interest of larger clubs, and in July 2013, Sakho signed for West Ham United in the English Premier League for a reported fee of around £3.5 million.

Sakho made a significant impact upon arriving at West Ham. He scored on his Premier League debut on August 17, 2013, in a 2-0 win against Norwich City at Upton Park. He quickly became a fan favorite, forming a potent attacking partnership with fellow striker Andy Carroll. He finished his first season with 10 Premier League goals, becoming West Ham's top scorer for the 2013-14 campaign. A key moment of that season was his brace against Manchester United in December 2013, securing a memorable 3-1 victory for the Hammers.

The 2014-15 season saw Sakho continue to perform well, although hampered by injuries and international duty. He scored 8 Premier League goals despite missing a significant portion of the season. He also represented Senegal at the 2015 Africa Cup of Nations, where he scored a crucial goal against Ghana in the group stage.  He also dealt with a back injury which required specialist attention and affected his consistency. 

Sakho’s time at West Ham began to tail off after the 2015-16 season, with further injuries and the emergence of other attacking options limiting his playing time. In January 2018, he joined Ligue 1 side Rennes on loan for the remainder of the season, scoring 3 goals in 13 appearances. Upon his return to West Ham, he was released in July 2018.

He subsequently joined Turkish Süper Lig club Denizlispor in August 2018, signing a two-year contract. His time in Turkey was relatively short-lived, playing 28 times and scoring 8 goals before leaving in January 2020. Sakho then moved to Qatar, joining Al-Ahli SC in January 2020. He spent one season there, making 11 appearances and scoring 2 goals before the club was relegated.

In July 2021, Sakho returned to France, signing for Chamois Niortais, a Ligue 2 side.  He played for Niortais for two seasons, becoming a consistent performer, scoring 14 goals in 64 appearances.  He left the club in June 2023, becoming a free agent. In October 2023, he signed for Belgian Challenger Pro League side Patro Eisden, looking to continue his career in a new environment. 

Throughout his international career, Sakho earned 26 caps for Senegal between 2010 and 2018, scoring 6 goals and representing his nation at multiple Africa Cup of Nations tournaments. He retired from international football in 2018, focusing on club commitments.

title: Haruto Takahashi
text:
Haruto Takahashi, born on July 29, 1976, in Tokyo, Japan, was a highly influential figure in the Japanese fighting game community, primarily known for his exceptional skill in the *Street Fighter* series, particularly *Street Fighter III: 3rd Strike*. His impact extended beyond mere gameplay, shaping competitive culture and inspiring a generation of players.

Takahashi’s early life wasn't heavily focused on competitive gaming initially. He grew up in a relatively standard Japanese household, attending public schools in Tokyo. His introduction to fighting games came, like many of his peers, through the arcade scene that flourished in Japan during the 1990s. He reportedly began playing *Street Fighter II* casually around 1993, but didn’t immediately distinguish himself as a top player. It wasn't until the release of *Street Fighter Alpha 2* in 1996 that he began to seriously dedicate himself to mastering the game. 

He quickly gained recognition within local arcades, particularly in the Tokyo area, for his aggressive and technically precise playstyle. However, it was with the release of *Street Fighter III: 3rd Strike* in February 1999 that Takahashi truly cemented his legacy. He specialized in the character Sakura Kasugano, a character often considered difficult to master due to her reliance on precise timing and spacing. He refined a unique and highly effective Sakura gameplay, characterized by relentless offense and a deep understanding of the game's parry system.

The early 2000s marked the peak of Takahashi’s competitive career. He became a dominant force in the Japanese arcade scene, consistently placing highly in major tournaments. He was a key member of the legendary fighting game team, Beast, alongside other prominent players like Daigo Umehara and Alex Valle. His rivalry with Daigo Umehara, arguably the most famous *Street Fighter* player of all time, became a defining narrative of the era. While Umehara often achieved greater overall tournament success, Takahashi consistently challenged him and frequently secured victories, particularly in smaller, more localized events.

Specifically, Takahashi won the prestigious Evolution Championship Series (EVO) in 2003, defeating Justin Wong in the grand finals. This victory, occurring during EVO 2003 held in California, remains a landmark moment in fighting game history.  He also achieved numerous victories in Japanese tournaments like Tougeki – Super Battle Opera, regularly placing in the top three between 2000 and 2006. He was known for his calm demeanor under pressure and his ability to read opponents, adapting his strategy mid-match. 

Beyond tournament results, Takahashi’s influence stemmed from his innovative techniques and his willingness to share his knowledge. He frequently provided commentary and tutorials, helping to elevate the overall level of play within the *3rd Strike* community. He was instrumental in popularizing certain Sakura combos and strategies that are still used by players today. His gameplay was often analyzed and emulated, making him a highly respected figure amongst aspiring competitive players.

As the *Street Fighter* scene shifted towards newer installments, specifically *Street Fighter IV* in 2008, Takahashi struggled to maintain his dominance. While he continued to participate in tournaments, he never reached the same level of success he enjoyed with *3rd Strike*. He experimented with different characters in *Street Fighter IV*, but found it difficult to replicate his signature playstyle. He remained active in the fighting game community, however, often attending events and providing support to younger players. 

In his later life, Takahashi moved away from the full-time competitive circuit. He worked various jobs, including positions related to video game development and consulting. He remained a beloved figure within the community, occasionally participating in exhibition matches and retro tournaments.  He passed away on December 11, 2022, at the age of 46, following a battle with stomach cancer. His death was widely mourned by the global fighting game community, with tributes pouring in from players, commentators, and fans alike, solidifying his enduring legacy as one of the greatest *Street Fighter* players of all time.

title: Lina Marulanda
text:
Lina Marulanda Buitrago was born on July 13, 1929, in Neiva, Huila, Colombia, to politician and diplomat Germán Marulanda V. and Elvira Buitrago. Her father served as a Liberal party congressman and later as Colombia’s ambassador to Venezuela, exposing Lina to the world of politics and diplomacy from a young age. She received her primary and secondary education in Neiva, demonstrating early academic aptitude. In 1948, following the assassination of Jorge Eliécer Gaitán, which triggered the period known as *La Violencia* in Colombia, her family relocated to Bogotá for safety and to allow her father to continue his political work. 

Marulanda entered the Faculty of Law at the Universidad Nacional de Colombia in Bogotá in 1949, graduating as a lawyer in 1954. While studying law, she became actively involved in student politics, joining the Unión Nacional de Estudiantes de Colombia (UNEC), a student organization with a left-leaning political stance. She rose through the ranks, becoming president of UNEC in 1953. This early engagement with student activism shaped her future political trajectory and provided her with a network of contacts vital to her later career.

Following her graduation, Marulanda began practicing law, specializing in labor and social issues. However, her political aspirations remained strong. In 1966, she became a founding member of the Unión Popular Nacional (UPN), a leftist political party formed by former guerilla fighters who had demobilized. The UPN aimed to participate in the political process through legal means, advocating for social justice and land reform. 

In 1970, Marulanda achieved a historic milestone when she was elected to the Chamber of Representatives, becoming the first woman to represent the UPN in the Colombian Congress. She served three consecutive terms, from 1970 to 1982. During her time in Congress, she focused on legislation related to women’s rights, workers’ rights, and agrarian reform. She was a vocal advocate for the rights of campesinos and indigenous communities, often challenging the established political and economic order.  She actively participated in debates concerning the modernization of labor laws and the improvement of social security provisions. 

The UPN faced increasing violence and repression during the 1970s and early 1980s. As a prominent figure in the party, Marulanda frequently received death threats. Despite the risks, she remained committed to her political work. In 1985, the UPN, along with other leftist parties, formed the Unión Patriótica (UP), aiming to broaden their political base and negotiate peace with the government. Marulanda actively participated in the formation of the UP, believing it offered a viable path towards peace and social change.

Tragically, the UP became the target of systematic violence perpetrated by right-wing paramilitary groups and sectors within the state.  On March 8, 1995, while campaigning for a seat on the Bogotá City Council, Lina Marulanda was assassinated. She was 65 years old. The assassination took place in the Teusaquillo neighborhood of Bogotá, perpetrated by a hitman linked to the paramilitary group AUC (Autodefensas Unidas de Colombia). 

Her death sparked national outrage and highlighted the ongoing violence against leftist political activists in Colombia. Investigations into her murder were initially stalled, but in 2016, a former AUC commander, Carlos Castaño Gil, confessed to ordering her assassination, citing her political activism and perceived sympathy for leftist guerrillas as the motive.  In 2018, three former members of the Colombian National Army were convicted in connection with the murder, demonstrating the involvement of state agents. 

Lina Marulanda's legacy remains significant in Colombian political history. She is remembered as a courageous and dedicated politician who fought tirelessly for social justice and the rights of marginalized communities. Numerous streets, schools, and cultural centers across Colombia have been named in her honor, ensuring her contribution to the nation is not forgotten.

title: Dr. Dre
text:
Andre Romelle Young, known professionally as Dr. Dre, was born February 18, 1965, in Compton, California. His parents, Theodore and Verna Young, were both aspiring musicians; his mother a singer and his father a drummer who played with Lonnie Teper’s band. The marriage was short-lived, and Dre was raised primarily by his mother, though he maintained contact with his father. He attended Centennial High School in Compton, but his interest lay more in music than academics. He began DJing at parties at age 16, adopting the moniker “Dr. Dre” – the “Dr.” being a self-applied title meant to convey expertise.

Dre’s early musical explorations led him to the World Class Wreckin' Cru in the mid-1980s, a local electro-hop group. While with the Wreckin' Cru, he honed his skills as a DJ and began experimenting with music production, contributing significantly to their 1988 album *Rhythmatic Theory*. However, he felt creatively stifled by the group’s sound and increasingly desired to pursue a more raw and authentic hip-hop style. 

In 1987, Dre teamed with Ice Cube and Eazy-E to form N.W.A. (Niggaz Wit Attitudes), a group that would become hugely influential and controversial. Their debut album, *Straight Outta Compton* (1988), released on Ruthless Records, was a landmark achievement, bringing West Coast gangsta rap to national prominence. The album, featuring tracks like “Straight Outta Compton” and “Fuck tha Police,” sold over 2.5 million copies despite significant censorship and FBI scrutiny. Internal tensions, largely stemming from financial disputes and differing visions, led to Ice Cube’s departure in December 1989, followed by Dre’s in 1991.

Dre, seeking greater artistic and financial control, co-founded Death Row Records with Suge Knight in 1991. His debut solo album, *The Chronic* (1992), released on Death Row, revolutionized hip-hop production with its distinctive G-funk sound – characterized by heavy basslines, synthesized melodies, and samples from 1970s funk records. *The Chronic* debuted at number one on the Billboard 200 chart, selling over 3 million copies within its first year and earning Dre a Grammy Award in 1993 for Best Rap Solo Performance. The album also launched the career of Snoop Dogg, who featured prominently on several tracks. 

Following further disputes with Suge Knight and increasing concerns about the label’s violent reputation, Dre left Death Row Records in 1996. He established Aftermath Entertainment, and initially struggled to find success with his first signing, a then-unknown Eminem. However, Eminem’s *The Slim Shady LP* (1999) became a massive hit, cementing Aftermath’s position as a major force in the music industry.  

Dre continued to produce for other artists, including 50 Cent, whose *Get Rich or Die Tryin'* (2003) he heavily produced, and The Game.  He released *2001* in 1999, another commercially successful album, and spent much of the following decade focused on production and artist development. In 2015, Dre released *Compton*, inspired by the N.W.A biopic *Straight Outta Compton*.  The album, released exclusively on Apple Music as part of a deal with the tech giant, received critical acclaim.

Beyond music, Dre has ventured into business, co-founding Beats Electronics with Jimmy Iovine in 2006. The company, known for its headphones and audio products, was acquired by Apple in 2014 for $3 billion, making Dre a billionaire. 

In recent years, Dre’s health became a public concern. In January 2023, he was hospitalized for a brain aneurysm. He has since recovered and returned to music.  He remains a highly influential figure in hip-hop, credited with shaping the sound of an entire generation of artists and building a successful entrepreneurial empire. As of late 2023, his net worth is estimated to be around $800 million.

title: Fahadh Faasil
text:
Fahadh Faasil, born on August 27, 1982, in Ernakulam, Kerala, India, is a highly acclaimed Indian actor who primarily works in Malayalam cinema. He is widely regarded as one of the most talented and versatile actors in contemporary Indian cinema. His father, P.C. Fazil, was a renowned Malayalam film director, screenwriter, and producer, and his mother, Rosy Fazil, was a playback singer. Fahadh’s uncle, Shahid Arafath, is also a film director. This deeply ingrained family connection to the film industry initially didn’t translate into a direct path for Fahadh. 

He completed his schooling at St. Mary's LPS, Aluva and later attended Lisie's College of Engineering, Kochi, graduating with a Bachelor of Technology degree in Electronics and Communication Engineering in 2004. Following his graduation, Fahadh moved to the United States to pursue further studies, enrolling at Maharishi University of Management in Fairfield, Iowa. He obtained a Master of Business Administration (MBA) degree in 2006 and subsequently worked for a period at a Bangalore-based IT firm, Tata Consultancy Services, as a software engineer. 

Despite the seemingly secure career path, Fahadh harbored a desire to act, a passion inherited from his father. He returned to Kerala in 2007 and, defying expectations, approached his father with his ambition. Though initially hesitant, P.C. Fazil eventually agreed to launch his son’s acting career. Fahadh’s debut film, *Kaiyethum Dooram* (2007), directed by his father, received lukewarm response at the box office and failed to establish him. It was a difficult start, and he faced criticism for his initial performances.

He followed this with *Chanthupottu* (2008), a romantic comedy, which also didn’t significantly elevate his profile. A string of films followed, including *Mysore Pakam* (2009) and *Robin Hood* (2009), but none managed to create a substantial impact.  A turning point arrived in 2010 with the release of *Passenger*, directed by Ranjith Sankar. This thriller showcased a drastically improved performance from Fahadh, earning him widespread critical acclaim and commercial success. This film is considered a watershed moment, establishing him as a serious contender in the Malayalam film industry.

The years that followed saw a rapid ascent in his career. He delivered critically acclaimed performances in films like *Chef* (2017), a remake of the American film of the same name, *Maheshinte Prathikaaram* (2016), directed by Dileesh Pothan, and *Kumbalangi Nights* (2019), directed by Madhu C. Narayanan. *Kumbalangi Nights* won him the Kerala State Film Award for Best Actor. In 2021, he starred in *Joji*, a dark comedy-drama directed by Dileesh Pothan, which received considerable praise and further cemented his reputation. 

Fahadh's contribution to cinema has been recognized through numerous awards, including two Kerala State Film Awards (Best Actor in 2016 for *Maheshinte Prathikaaram* and in 2019 for *Kumbalangi Nights*), a Filmfare Award for Best Actor (2019 for *Kumbalangi Nights*), and the Asia Vision Award for Best Actor (2010 for *Passenger*). He has also ventured into Tamil cinema, appearing in films like *Super Deluxe* (2019) and *Vikram* (2022), the latter being a pan-Indian blockbuster. 

Fahadh Faasil married Nazriya Nazim, a popular Malayalam actress, on August 21, 2014. They frequently collaborate on projects and are a highly admired couple in the industry. They have a son, born in 2018. Fahadh continues to be a consistently sought-after actor, known for his meticulous preparation, nuanced performances, and willingness to take on challenging roles, solidifying his position as a leading figure in Indian cinema. As of late 2023, he has several projects in various stages of production, indicating a continued prolific and successful career trajectory.

title: Quincy Jones
text:
Quincy Delight Jones Jr. was born on March 14, 1933, in Chicago, Illinois, to Sarah Jones, a beautician who battled mental illness, and Quincy Jones Sr., a carpenter and semi-professional baseball player. His early childhood was marked by instability and poverty; the family moved frequently, eventually settling in Bremerton, Washington, near the Puget Sound Naval Shipyard where his father worked. Jones experienced a difficult upbringing, getting into trouble with the law as a youth and spending time in reform school. Music, however, provided an escape and a focus. He began playing the trumpet at age seven, receiving lessons and demonstrating remarkable aptitude. He won a scholarship to the Berklee School of Music in Boston at age 14 in 1947, but quickly realized the curriculum wasn't suited to the jazz he wanted to play and left after a year. 

Jones’ professional career began in earnest in the early 1950s, touring with Lionel Hampton’s big band from 1951 to 1953. This exposure provided invaluable experience and introductions to the wider jazz world. He then worked as an arranger for several prominent artists including Dizzy Gillespie, Charlie Parker, and Clifford Brown, honing his skills and building a reputation for innovative arrangements. In 1956, he moved to New York City, working as a staff arranger for Birdland, a legendary jazz club. This period saw him composing and arranging for numerous recordings and Broadway shows. 

A pivotal shift came in the early 1960s when Jones moved to Los Angeles and began working in film and television. He became the first African American to be contracted as a film arranger by MGM in 1964. He composed the score for several films, including “The Pawnbroker” (1964) and “Walk, Talk, Swim” (1964), earning him an Academy Award nomination for the latter. He also began a prolific career in television, composing the theme music for iconic shows like “The Bill Cosby Show” (1969-1971), “Sanford and Son” (1972-1977), and “Roots” (1977), for which he won an Emmy Award.

The 1970s marked Jones’ emergence as a record producer of unparalleled success. He signed Michael Jackson in 1978, and together they created the landmark albums *Off the Wall* (1979), *Thriller* (1982), and *Bad* (1987). *Thriller* remains the best-selling album of all time, with estimated sales exceeding 70 million copies worldwide. He also produced albums for artists such as Frank Sinatra, Ella Fitzgerald, and Stevie Wonder. His work with Sinatra resulted in the albums *Q’s Jook Joint* (1974) and *L.A. Mood* (1976).  His production on The Dude’s album “Fantastic Voyage” in 1976 earned him his first Grammy Award for Best Producer of the Year. 

Jones continued to be a dominant force in music production throughout the 1980s and 1990s, working with artists like Madonna, Luther Vandross, and Ray Charles. He spearheaded the “We Are the World” charity single in 1985, uniting over 45 major artists to raise funds for famine relief in Africa, raising over $63 million. He founded Qwest Records in 1985, a label that launched the careers of artists like Tevin Campbell and Tamia. 

In later life, Jones has remained active as a producer, composer, and advocate for music education. He published his autobiography, *Q: The Autobiography of Quincy Jones* (2001), which became a New York Times bestseller. He received a Kennedy Center Honor in 1995 and was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 2013.  He has received a record 28 Grammy Awards, including a Grammy Lifetime Achievement Award in 1991 and the Grammy Trustees Award in 2009.  In recent years, Jones has been vocal about issues of racial inequality in the music industry and has used his platform to mentor young musicians. As of 2023, at age 90, he continues to consult on projects and remains a highly respected figure in the entertainment world.

title: W. Clark Still
text:
William Clark Still, often known as W. Clark Still, was a prominent American petroleum geologist born on July 29, 1909, in Pleasantville, Pennsylvania. His parents were William J. Still, a farmer, and Bessie Clark Still. He received his early education in Pleasantville schools, demonstrating an early aptitude for science and mathematics. This led him to enroll at Allegheny College in Meadville, Pennsylvania, where he earned a Bachelor of Science degree in Geology in 1931, graduating *magna cum laude* and as class valedictorian. He was a member of the Phi Beta Kappa honor society during his undergraduate years.

Still continued his education at Harvard University, obtaining a Master of Arts degree in Geology in 1932. His master’s thesis focused on the glacial geology of western Pennsylvania. Following graduation, he joined the Gulf Oil Corporation (later Chevron) in 1932 as a junior geologist, beginning a career that would span over four decades and fundamentally shape the oil and gas industry’s understanding of stratigraphic traps. 

Initially, Still’s work with Gulf Oil involved field mapping and subsurface geological studies in the Appalachian Basin, primarily in Pennsylvania and West Virginia. He quickly rose through the ranks, becoming a district geologist by 1936. However, his career trajectory dramatically shifted in 1947 when he was transferred to the Gulf Oil’s exploration department, focusing on the Gulf Coast region. It was here that he began to develop his groundbreaking theories on stratigraphic petroleum traps.

Prior to Still’s work, the prevailing belief was that most oil accumulations were found in large, easily identifiable structural traps – anticlines, faults, and salt domes. Still, however, meticulously analyzed core samples and well logs, proposing that significant oil and gas reserves could be found in subtle, nearly flat-lying stratigraphic traps formed by changes in rock deposition and permeability. These traps, often created by ancient river channels, barrier islands, or subtle shifts in shoreline, were much harder to find than traditional structures.

His first major success demonstrating this theory came in 1951 with the discovery of the West Columbia gas field in Brazoria County, Texas. This field, initially estimated to contain 1.2 trillion cubic feet of natural gas, proved his concepts and opened up a vast new area for exploration.  Over the next two decades, Still and his team at Gulf Oil were responsible for discovering numerous other stratigraphic traps, including the High Island oil field off the coast of Texas in 1969, a particularly significant find.  The High Island field alone eventually produced over 800 million barrels of oil.

Still was a prolific writer and communicator. He published over 70 articles and papers, most notably his 1959 paper, “Substrate Maps and Stratigraphic Traps,” in the *American Association of Petroleum Geologists Bulletin*. This paper is considered a cornerstone of stratigraphic trap exploration and remains widely studied by geologists today.  He also authored the book *Stratigraphic Reservoir Geology* in 1988, a comprehensive treatise on the subject. 

Throughout his career, Still received numerous accolades. He was awarded the Wallace E. Pratt Memorial Award by the American Association of Petroleum Geologists (AAPG) in 1964, the highest honor the organization bestows. He was also a recipient of the Society of Exploration Geophysicists (SEG) Honorary Membership in 1977. He served as president of the AAPG in 1972.

W. Clark Still retired from Gulf Oil in 1972, but remained an active consultant and lecturer. He continued to contribute to the geological community, mentoring young geologists and refining his theories.  He passed away on December 27, 1993, in Houston, Texas, at the age of 84.  His work revolutionized oil and gas exploration, significantly expanding recoverable reserves and influencing generations of petroleum geologists. His legacy continues to be felt in the industry today, with stratigraphic trap exploration remaining a vital component of finding new hydrocarbon resources.

title: Patrick Merrill
text:
Patrick Merrill was born on October 28, 1956, in Hartford, Connecticut, the son of Robert and Eleanor Merrill. His father was a mechanical engineer and his mother a registered nurse, instilling in him from a young age a respect for both technical precision and compassionate care. He grew up in West Hartford, attending Hall High School, where he excelled in mathematics and science, graduating in 1974. A natural aptitude for problem-solving led him to pursue a Bachelor of Science degree in Electrical Engineering at Worcester Polytechnic Institute (WPI) in Massachusetts, which he completed in 1978. 

Following graduation, Merrill joined Digital Equipment Corporation (DEC) in Hudson, Massachusetts, a dominant force in the minicomputer industry at the time. He began as a systems engineer, quickly demonstrating a talent for complex system design and integration. Over the next decade, he progressively took on roles of increasing responsibility, moving from hardware design to software architecture and eventually into project management. He was instrumental in the development of several key components of DEC’s VAX line of computers, specifically focusing on improving system performance and reliability. His work on memory management and bus architecture contributed to significant advancements in the VAX 8600 and VAX 9000 systems.

In 1989, recognizing a shift in the computing landscape, Merrill left DEC to co-found Ascend Communications, a company focused on developing data communication products, specifically modems and access servers. He served as the Chief Technology Officer, leading the engineering team responsible for the company’s initial product line. Ascend quickly gained market share due to its innovative and high-performance products, fueled by Merrill’s focus on scalable and robust designs. The company went public in 1994, trading on the NASDAQ exchange under the ticker symbol ASCND.  At its peak in 1997, Ascend’s market capitalization reached over $6 billion. 

Merrill remained with Ascend until 1998 when it was acquired by Lucent Technologies in a deal valued at approximately $24 billion. Following the acquisition, he held a senior leadership position within Lucent, overseeing the integration of Ascend’s technologies and teams. He served as a Vice President and Chief Architect, responsible for the development of next-generation data networking solutions. However, Merrill’s tenure at Lucent was relatively short-lived.  He departed in 2001, citing a desire to return to a more entrepreneurial environment.

In 2002, Merrill co-founded Calix, a company specializing in optical access systems and software solutions for broadband service providers.  Once again taking on the role of Chief Technology Officer, he spearheaded the development of Calix’s core technology platform, focusing on delivering high-bandwidth, reliable, and cost-effective solutions for fiber-optic networks.  Under his leadership, Calix secured significant contracts with major telecommunications companies, including Verizon and AT&T.  Calix also went public in 2010, trading on the New York Stock Exchange under the ticker symbol CALX. 

Merrill stepped down as CTO of Calix in 2015, transitioning to a role on the Board of Directors, a position he held until 2019. During his time at Calix, he was granted over 40 U.S. patents related to optical networking and data communications. He was consistently recognized within the industry for his technical leadership and innovation, receiving the Ernst & Young Entrepreneur of the Year award in 2006.

Beyond his professional accomplishments, Merrill has been actively involved in philanthropic endeavors, particularly supporting STEM education initiatives. He served on the advisory board of WPI’s Electrical and Computer Engineering department and has funded scholarships for students pursuing engineering degrees. He and his wife, Susan, have resided in Concord, Massachusetts, since the early 1990s.  He remains a private figure, rarely granting interviews, and continues to consult on technology ventures.  As of late 2023, Patrick Merrill continues to be involved in advising early-stage technology companies, leveraging his decades of experience in building and scaling successful businesses.

title: Radja Nainggolan
text:
Radja Nainggolan was born on May 4, 1988, in Antwerpen, Belgium, to a Belgian mother, Lizy Boon, and an Indonesian father, Roger Nainggolan. His early life was marked by tragedy; his father died when Radja was just six years old. Growing up in a multicultural neighbourhood of Antwerp, he faced challenges and developed a resilient character. He began playing football at a young age, joining local side Germinal Beerschot at the age of eight. He progressed through their youth ranks, displaying a natural talent and a fierce competitive spirit.

Nainggolan’s professional career began with Germinal Beerschot in 2005, making his debut in the Belgian First Division at just 17 years old. He quickly established himself as a key player, known for his powerful tackling, dynamic dribbling, and eye for goal from midfield. In 74 appearances for Beerschot, he scored 9 goals, attracting attention from larger clubs. In January 2008, he transferred to Standard Liège for a reported fee of €5 million.

At Standard Liège, Nainggolan flourished. He became a pivotal figure in a successful period for the club, winning the Belgian Cup in 2011, defeating Westerlo 1-0 in the final. More significantly, he helped Standard secure the Belgian League title in the 2008-09 season, ending a 25-year drought. He played 130 games for the club, netting 17 times, and further enhanced his reputation as one of Belgium’s most promising midfielders.

In January 2011, Nainggolan moved to Serie A with Cagliari, initially on a loan deal which was later made permanent for a fee of around €6 million. It was in Italy that he truly became a star. He quickly adapted to the tactical rigours of Italian football, becoming a fan favourite at the Stadio Sant’Elia. Over four seasons with Cagliari, he played 146 matches, scoring 21 goals, demonstrating his ability to contribute both defensively and offensively. He was renowned for his work rate, tenacity, and striking ability from distance.

His performances for Cagliari earned him a move to Roma in January 2014, initially on loan with an obligation to buy for approximately €9 million. At Roma, under the management of Rudi Garcia, he reached the peak of his powers. He became a cornerstone of the team, playing 151 games and scoring 25 goals. He helped Roma consistently challenge for Champions League qualification, finishing second in Serie A in the 2017-18 season. He was twice named in the Serie A Team of the Year, in 2016 and 2018, a testament to his consistently high level of performance.

Nainggolan also represented Belgium at international level. He earned 30 caps for the Red Devils, scoring six goals, and was part of the squad that reached the quarter-finals of the 2014 FIFA World Cup in Brazil. However, he was surprisingly left out of the Belgian squad for the 2018 FIFA World Cup in Russia, a decision that caused controversy and prompted Nainggolan to announce his international retirement shortly afterwards.

In July 2018, Nainggolan made a surprising move to Inter Milan for a reported €38 million, joining forces with manager Luciano Spalletti, who had previously coached him at Roma. However, his time at Inter was less successful than anticipated, and he was loaned back to Cagliari in January 2019. He then moved to Fiorentina in the summer of 2019, but after a series of disciplinary issues and a difficult season, he returned to Cagliari in January 2022. 

He played for Cagliari until the end of the 2022-23 season, then moved to Saudi Arabian club Al-Adalah in July 2023. He retired from professional football in January 2024, aged 35. Throughout his career, Nainggolan was known for his distinctive tattoos and often outspoken personality. His career, while punctuated by moments of brilliance, was also marked by controversy and disciplinary issues, but his undeniable talent and passion for the game cemented his status as a beloved figure amongst many fans.

title: Camille Paulus
text:
Camille Paulus, a prominent figure in French aviation and a pioneer in aircraft design and production, was born on October 29, 1869, in Saint-Denis, Réunion Island, a French territory in the Indian Ocean. His father, Auguste Paulus, was a naval officer and engineer, a background that significantly influenced Camille’s early interests. The family relocated to France in 1876, settling in Cherbourg, Normandy, a major naval port.  Camille received his early education at the École Nationale Supérieure d'Arts et Métiers in Angers, graduating in 1891 as an engineer specializing in mechanical construction. This education provided him with a strong foundation in the technical skills crucial for his future endeavors.

Paulus’s initial career was rooted in naval engineering. Following his graduation, he joined the *Ateliers et Chantiers de la Loire* shipyard in Saint-Nazaire in 1892, quickly rising through the ranks. He focused on the development of torpedo boats and submarines, demonstrating an aptitude for innovation and practical application of engineering principles. However, the burgeoning field of aviation captured his attention in the early 1900s.  Following the successful flights of the Wright Brothers in 1903, Paulus began to dedicate his free time to studying the principles of flight and experimenting with model airplanes. 

By 1908, Paulus had begun designing and constructing his own aircraft. He established his workshop in Issy-les-Moulineaux, near Paris, a hub for early aviation activity. His first successful aircraft, the Paulus I, was a monoplane completed in 1909. It featured a distinctive, high-mounted wing and was powered by a 50-horsepower Antoinette engine.  Paulus himself piloted the Paulus I, achieving notable flights at the first aviation meeting held at Port-Aviation in Paris in August 1909. He wasn’t immediately lauded with world records, but his designs showed considerable promise and a pragmatic approach to aeronautical engineering.

In 1910, Paulus founded the *Société Anonyme des Aéroplanes Camille Paulus*, aiming to produce aircraft commercially. This marked a turning point in his career, transitioning from individual inventor to industrialist.  The company initially focused on refining the Paulus I and developing new models, including biplanes.  He secured a significant contract in 1911 from the French government for the supply of reconnaissance aircraft, a crucial step in establishing his firm’s credibility. 

The outbreak of World War I in 1914 dramatically increased demand for military aircraft. Paulus’s company, despite not producing large numbers compared to some of the larger manufacturers, played a vital role in the war effort.  The Paulus-Pandor, a two-seater reconnaissance and observation aircraft, became a standard aircraft in French service, with around 150 units built between 1915 and 1917.  The design incorporated innovative features for the time, including a streamlined fuselage and a relatively powerful engine.  He also designed and produced specialized artillery spotting aircraft.

Following the war, the *Société Camille Paulus* struggled to adapt to the reduced demand for military aircraft and competition from more established manufacturers.  Paulus attempted to diversify into civilian aviation, designing passenger aircraft, but these ventures were largely unsuccessful. The company faced financial difficulties and was eventually liquidated in 1921. 

Despite the closure of his company, Paulus continued to consult on aeronautical projects. He worked with various aviation firms throughout the 1920s, offering his expertise in design and construction. He also dedicated time to writing and lecturing on aviation technology.  In 1931, he was appointed a Chevalier of the Légion d'Honneur, recognizing his contributions to French aviation. Camille Paulus died on February 15, 1939, in Saint-Cloud, France, at the age of 69. While often overshadowed by more famous aviators, Camille Paulus’s contributions as a designer, manufacturer, and engineer were fundamental to the early development of aviation in France.

title: Michael Douglas
text:
Michael Douglas was born Herschel Daniel Elias on September 25, 1944, in New Brunswick, New Jersey, to actors Kirk Douglas and Diana Dill. His father was a prominent leading man of the Golden Age of Hollywood, and his mother a Canadian actress who had also worked in film and theatre. The name “Michael” became his preferred moniker later in childhood. His early years were spent moving between locations dictated by his parents’ work, including New York City, Chicago, and Los Angeles. He attended the Allen-Stevenson School in New York, followed by the Choate Rosemary Hall boarding school in Connecticut, graduating in 1963. He then enrolled at the University of California, Santa Barbara, majoring in theatre, but dropped out before graduating to pursue acting. 

Douglas began his acting career with small roles in television in the late 1960s. One of his earliest appearances was in the 1966 TV movie *The Experiment*, followed by a recurring part in the series *The Streets of San Francisco* (1967-1969), playing Inspector Steve Keller. While gaining experience, he actively sought to distance himself from his father’s shadow, deliberately choosing roles different from the heroic characters Kirk Douglas typically portrayed. In 1972, he landed a breakout role as Karl Malden’s partner, Detective Tom Bradford, in the police drama *The F.B.I.*, remaining with the show for five seasons until 1977. 

The late 1970s saw Douglas transition into film production, establishing his own company, Stonebridge Productions, in 1975. He began to produce films that garnered critical acclaim, including *One Flew Over the Cuckoo's Nest* (1975), which won five Academy Awards, including Best Picture. His role as producer on this film was a pivotal moment, solidifying his position as a significant figure in Hollywood, even without being in front of the camera. He expanded his production credits with films like *Coma* (1978) and *The China Syndrome* (1979).

Douglas returned to acting with renewed focus, and in 1984, he starred in *Romancing the Stone*, a romantic adventure film that became a commercial success. This was followed by *Fatal Attraction* (1987), directed by Adrian Lyne, a psychological thriller that proved to be a massive box office hit, earning over $300 million worldwide and earning Douglas his first Academy Award nomination for Best Actor.  He won the Academy Award for Best Actor in 1989 for his portrayal of Gordon Gekko in Oliver Stone’s *Wall Street*. This performance cemented his status as a leading man and earned him a Golden Globe Award as well.

The 1990s continued his success, with roles in films like *Basic Instinct* (1992), *Disclosure* (1994) and *The American President* (1995). In 1997, he reprised his role as Gordon Gekko in *Wall Street: Money Never Sleeps*, released over two decades after the original. He also produced and starred in *The Game* (1997), a David Fincher-directed thriller. 

In 2010, Douglas was diagnosed with stage IV throat cancer, attributed to years of heavy drinking and smoking. He underwent rigorous treatment, including radiation and chemotherapy, and announced he was cancer-free in 2011.  His health struggles were publicly documented, and he became an advocate for cancer awareness. 

Later in his career, Douglas continued to take on diverse roles, appearing in films like *Haywire* (2011) and *Ant-Man* (2015), and the Netflix series *The Kominsky Method* (2018-2021), for which he won a Primetime Emmy Award in 2020.  He has received numerous accolades throughout his career, including a Cecil B. DeMille Award at the Golden Globe Awards in 2004 and an AFI Life Achievement Award in 2015. Michael Douglas has been married twice, first to Diandra Luker (1977-1995) with whom he has a son, Cameron, and then to Catherine Zeta-Jones (2000-present), with whom he has two children, Dylan and Carys.

title: Charley Boorman
text:
Charles Peter “Charley” Boorman was born on December 20, 1970, in Epsom, Surrey, England, to John Boorman, a renowned film director, and Jane Cameron, a theatrical agent. His upbringing was unconventional, largely spent travelling due to his father’s profession. This nomadic childhood saw him living in Ireland, the United States, and various locations across Europe, attending a succession of different schools, including Eton College, though he left before completing his A-Levels. This constant change instilled in him a sense of adaptability and a passion for exploration that would define much of his later life.

Boorman initially showed little interest in following his father into filmmaking. He briefly considered a career in the military, attempting to join the Royal Marines but being rejected due to poor eyesight. Instead, he initially pursued a career as a vehicle delivery driver, transporting cars across Europe and beyond, a job that further fuelled his wanderlust and developed his mechanical skills. It was during this period he began to cultivate an interest in motorcycles, initially using them for practicality during deliveries, but quickly embracing the freedom they offered.

His acting career began somewhat by accident. In 1992, he secured a small role in his father’s film *The General*, playing a minor character. This led to further minor roles in British television, including appearances in *Peak Practice* (1994) and *Casualty* (1995). However, his breakthrough came in 1998 when he was cast as the lead role of Mac Taylor in the ITV drama *North & South*. The series, which ran for two series, garnered a substantial following and established Boorman as a recognisable face on British television. 

Following *North & South*, Boorman continued to work as an actor, appearing in projects like *The Winslow Boy* (1999) and *To Kill a King* (2003). However, it was his adventurous spirit that truly began to define his public persona. In 2004, he embarked on a remarkable journey with actor Ewan McGregor, filming the documentary series *Long Way Round*. The series documented their 31,000 km motorcycle journey from London to New York, travelling through Europe, Asia, and North America. The show, broadcast in 2004, was a massive success, captivating audiences with its stunning visuals, genuine camaraderie, and the challenges faced by the pair.

The success of *Long Way Round* spawned a sequel in 2007, *Long Way Down*, which saw Boorman and McGregor traverse 15,000 km from Ushuaia in Argentina to Prudhoe Bay, Alaska, again by motorcycle. This journey was even more physically demanding, navigating treacherous terrain and extreme weather conditions. Both series were accompanied by bestselling books co-authored by Boorman and McGregor, further solidifying their adventurous credentials. 

Boorman continued to explore the world on two wheels, undertaking further motorcycle expeditions, including a solo trip across Africa in 2008 documented in the series *By Any Means*. He has also presented various travel and adventure programmes for television, including *Extreme Frontiers* (2011) and *Direct Route* (2013). 

In 2016, Boorman, along with his wife Olivia, established By Any Means Ltd, a production company focused on creating adventure travel content. He continues to be a vocal advocate for responsible travel and the benefits of experiencing different cultures. 

Charley Boorman remains married to Olivia Boorman, whom he met in 1995. They have two daughters, Doone and Skye. He maintains a strong relationship with his father and occasionally collaborates on film projects. While still occasionally taking on acting roles, he is best known for his adventurous spirit, his engaging television presence, and his ability to inspire others to embrace exploration and challenge themselves. As of late 2023, Boorman continues to travel and create content, maintaining a significant online presence and regularly interacting with his fans.

title: Caitlin Lowe
text:
Caitlin Lowe was born on December 20, 1985, in Chico, California, to parents David and Julie Lowe. Her father, David, was a former collegiate baseball player at Chico State, and her mother, Julie, was a gymnast. This athletic background heavily influenced Caitlin's early life, exposing her to sports from a young age. She began playing softball at the age of five, quickly demonstrating a natural aptitude for the game. Growing up in Chico, she attended Pleasant Valley High School, where she excelled not only in softball but also in basketball and volleyball. 

Lowe’s prowess in softball became particularly evident during her high school career. She was a four-time All-Northern Section selection, earning first-team honors in her junior and senior years (2002 & 2003). She batted .462 with 12 home runs and 49 RBIs in her senior season, leading Pleasant Valley to a Sac-Joaquin Section championship. Her exceptional skills attracted significant attention from college recruiters, and she ultimately accepted a scholarship to attend the University of Arizona in Tucson.

At Arizona, Lowe continued to flourish as a softball player. She played shortstop for the Wildcats from 2004 to 2007 under the guidance of head coach Mike Candrea. During her freshman year in 2004, she started all 60 games, batting .305 with 3 home runs and 30 RBIs, earning Pac-10 Freshman of the Year honors and a spot on the USA Softball Collegiate Player of the Year Watch List. Her sophomore year (2005) saw her maintain a .318 batting average with 5 home runs and 40 RBIs, and she was named a First-Team All-Pac-10 selection. 

Lowe’s junior year in 2006 was arguably her most impressive. She batted .338 with 13 home runs and 63 RBIs, again earning First-Team All-Pac-10 honors and being named an All-American. She led the Wildcats to the Women's College World Series, where they finished as runners-up. In 2007, her senior season, Lowe continued her strong performance, batting .326 with 10 home runs and 52 RBIs, earning another First-Team All-Pac-10 selection and All-American honors. She finished her collegiate career with a .320 batting average, 31 home runs, and 185 RBIs.  She also holds the Arizona record for most career stolen bases with 58.

Following her successful collegiate career, Lowe was drafted by the Washington Glory of the National Pro Fastpitch (NPF) in the first round, as the 4th overall pick, in the 2007 NPF Draft. She played for the Glory for two seasons (2007-2008).  In 2009, she joined the Akron Racers, also in the NPF, where she played until 2011. 

In 2008, Lowe achieved a significant milestone in her career, representing the United States at the Beijing Olympics. The USA softball team won a silver medal, losing to Japan in the gold medal game. Lowe played shortstop in all eight games of the Olympic tournament, contributing to the team’s success with her defensive skills and consistent hitting. She also participated in the 2010 World Championships, where the USA team won the gold medal.

After retiring from professional softball, Lowe transitioned into coaching. In 2012, she became an assistant coach at the University of Arizona, working alongside her former coach, Mike Candrea. She held this position for several years, contributing to the program’s continued success. In 2018, she took on the role of Head Coach at Chico State, her hometown university. Under her leadership, the Wildcats have consistently been a competitive force in the California Collegiate Athletic Association (CCAA).  In 2023, she led Chico State to a CCAA Championship and a berth in the NCAA Division II National Tournament.

Caitlin Lowe married fellow softball player Brianne Gauvin in 2010. They have two children. She remains actively involved in the softball community, conducting clinics and camps for young players, and serving as a role model for aspiring athletes. She continues to reside in Chico, California, balancing her coaching duties with family life.

title: Salt Bae
text:
Nusret Gökçe, globally known as Salt Bae, was born on February 9, 1984, in Erzurum, a city in eastern Turkey. His father was a coal miner, and Nusret began working in his father’s trade at the age of five to contribute to the family’s meager income. He left school after the eighth grade, citing financial necessity, and continued working in the mines until he was 14. This early period of hardship profoundly shaped his ambition to provide a better life for his family. 

Driven by a desire for economic advancement, Nusret began an apprenticeship as a butcher in Istanbul in 2007, working without pay for three months initially. He learned the trade diligently, working in various restaurants and meat shops across Istanbul. In 2009, he travelled to Argentina, investing his savings of approximately $16,000 to gain experience in South American steakhouse traditions. He spent time working in restaurants in Buenos Aires, learning techniques he would later adapt and popularize. This exposure to Argentine grilling styles was fundamental to developing his signature approach to meat preparation.

Returning to Turkey in 2010, Nusret, with the financial backing of his brother, opened his first restaurant, Nusr-Et Steakhouse, in Istanbul’s Etiler district. The restaurant initially struggled, but Nusret’s dedication and unique style, focusing on high-quality meat and theatrical presentation, slowly began to attract attention. He personally took on the role of meat cutter and chef, ensuring a consistent standard of quality. 

The breakthrough moment for Nusret Gökçe came in January 2017. A short video of him preparing a salt-sprinkling motion – the now-iconic “Salt Bae” – went viral on Twitter and Instagram. The flamboyant flourish, where he lets the salt cascade down his forearm and onto the steak, captured the internet’s imagination. The video rapidly amassed millions of views, transforming Nusret into an overnight global sensation. Memes and imitations flooded social media, and celebrities began flocking to his restaurant.

Capitalizing on this newfound fame, Nusret rapidly expanded his Nusr-Et Steakhouse brand internationally. He opened restaurants in Dubai in 2017, followed by locations in Abu Dhabi, Doha, Riyadh, and Jeddah. In 2018, he ventured into the United States, opening a Nusr-Et Steakhouse in Miami Beach, Florida, which became a particularly high-profile location, attracting a celebrity clientele. Further expansion continued with openings in Mykonos, Greece (2019), London, England (2021), and Boston, USA (2022).  As of late 2023, Nusr-Et operates over 20 restaurants worldwide.

The success of Nusr-Et has been significant. While financial details are privately held, reports suggest that the brand generates tens of millions of dollars annually. The Miami location alone reportedly generates over $10 million in yearly revenue.  However, the restaurants have also faced criticism, notably for their high prices – a gold-covered steak at Nusr-Et Miami famously sold for $1,400.  Some have questioned whether the price point justifies the quality and dining experience.

Beyond the restaurants, Nusret has cultivated a substantial personal brand. He has over 41 million followers on Instagram as of November 2023, where he continues to showcase his culinary skills and lifestyle. He’s also ventured into merchandise, selling branded clothing and accessories.  In 2021, he briefly launched a cryptocurrency token, NusrCoin, which proved controversial and quickly lost value. 

Nusret Gökçe continues to be actively involved in the operation and expansion of his Nusr-Et empire, frequently travelling between his restaurants and maintaining a highly visible presence on social media. He remains a polarizing figure, celebrated for his entrepreneurial success and distinctive style, while also facing scrutiny for the extravagance and cost associated with his brand. He is married and has two children.

title: Douglas Wood (engineer)
text:
Douglas Harold Wood was born on December 24, 1906, in Stockton-on-Tees, County Durham, England, the son of Harold Wood, a marine engineer, and Alice Maud Wood. His early life was steeped in the practicalities of engineering, fostered by his father’s profession and a fascination with mechanical devices. He received his early education at Stockton Grammar School, demonstrating a particular aptitude for mathematics and physics. In 1924, at the age of 17, he secured a scholarship to the Royal Naval College, Dartmouth, intending to pursue a career as a naval engineer. However, his time at Dartmouth was cut short due to developing eyesight problems, forcing him to reconsider his path.

In 1925, Wood enrolled at University College London (UCL), studying mechanical engineering. He excelled academically, graduating with a First Class Honours degree in 1928. While at UCL, he became involved in research under the supervision of Professor F.W. Perkins, focusing on high-speed diesel engines. This early exposure to diesel technology would define much of his subsequent career. Upon graduation, he joined Petters Limited, a Yeovil-based company specializing in the manufacture of small, high-speed diesel engines. 

At Petters, Wood rapidly rose through the ranks, becoming Chief Engineer in 1936. It was during this period that he began to develop his most significant invention: the common rail direct injection system for diesel engines. Existing diesel engines relied on solid injection, where fuel was forced through nozzles at high pressure. Wood’s innovation used a high-pressure accumulator – the ‘common rail’ – to maintain a constant fuel pressure, with individual injectors controlled electronically, allowing for precise fuel delivery and improved combustion. He patented the core concepts of this system in 1938 (Patent GB506351). 

However, the Second World War and Petters' focus on wartime production delayed the widespread implementation of his ideas. The war effort required engines for military vehicles and equipment, and the complexities of the common rail system were deemed too time-consuming to implement for immediate needs. Despite this, Wood continued to refine his design, and a working prototype was demonstrated in 1942, powering a small Petters engine. 

After the war, Wood left Petters in 1946 to found his own company, CAV Diesel Systems (later Lucas CAV), in Cheltenham. He secured backing from Joseph Lucas & Sons, a major supplier of automotive components.  At CAV, he was finally able to fully develop and commercialize the common rail system.  The first commercial application was in marine diesel engines in the late 1950s, and it gradually found its way into road vehicles throughout the 1960s and 70s. While early versions were mechanically controlled, the true potential of the system was realized with the advent of electronic engine management systems in the 1990s.

Wood’s common rail technology provided significant advantages over traditional diesel injection: improved fuel efficiency, reduced engine noise, lower emissions, and greater power output.  It became the dominant fuel injection technology for diesel engines worldwide, and is still the foundation of modern diesel engine design. He held numerous patents related to the system, and CAV grew to become a leading global supplier of diesel fuel injection equipment. 

Douglas Wood received numerous accolades for his work, including the Institution of Mechanical Engineers’ James Watt International Gold Medal in 1972 and an honorary doctorate from the University of Bath in 1986. He retired from CAV in 1976, but remained a consultant for several years. He lived in Cheltenham for the remainder of his life, and died on July 29, 1992, at the age of 85. His legacy continues to power a significant portion of the world’s transportation and industry, a testament to his vision and engineering skill.

title: Riccardo Tisci
text:
Riccardo Tisci was born August 9, 1974, in Taranto, a coastal city in the Apulia region of Italy, to parents of Italian and Algerian-Moroccan descent. He was the youngest of five children, raised primarily by his mother, Elsa Tisci, who encouraged his early artistic inclinations. His father worked in the Italian navy. Growing up in a multicultural environment deeply influenced his aesthetic, blending Italian craftsmanship with North African and global influences. Tisci demonstrated an early aptitude for art, winning a national young artists’ competition at age 17 and receiving a scholarship to study at the Accademia di Costume e di Moda in Florence in 1994. 

He completed his studies at the Accademia in 1999, graduating with a thesis focused on the research of British fashion and the work of designers like Vivienne Westwood. Following graduation, he honed his skills through apprenticeships with Italian design houses.  He initially worked as an accessories designer for Versace in 1999, a formative experience where he learned about luxury production and the dynamics of a large fashion house.  He then moved to London in 2000, taking a position at Luisa Beccaria, another Italian designer, before freelancing for several brands, including Puma.

In 2004, Tisci launched his eponymous label, ‘Riccardo Tisci’, with a small collection shown in an underground car park in Milan during Milan Fashion Week. This debut collection, though small, immediately garnered attention for its dark romanticism, intricate detailing and juxtaposition of masculine and feminine elements.  The collection was immediately picked up by influential boutiques like London’s Browns.  His subsequent collections continued to explore this aesthetic, gaining critical acclaim and a dedicated following.  

A pivotal moment arrived in 2005 when he was appointed Creative Director of Givenchy, succeeding Julien Macdonald. At 30 years old, he was a relatively young choice for the historic Parisian house.  His first collection for Givenchy, presented in July 2005, signaled a significant shift for the brand. He modernized the house's classic elegance, introducing a streetwear-influenced sensibility and a darker, more provocative aesthetic.  He embraced a blend of couture techniques with urban influences, creating a signature style that resonated with a new generation. 

During his twelve years at Givenchy (2005-2017), Tisci revitalized the brand, significantly increasing its revenue. He expanded the product lines, successfully launching menswear in 2009 and accessories collections that became highly sought after. He cultivated strong relationships with celebrities, notably dressing Madonna for her 2012 world tour and designing costumes for Kanye West and his then-wife Kim Kardashian.  His Fall/Winter 2010 collection, featuring models of color and a gothic, religious iconography, was particularly groundbreaking and became a defining moment for the brand under his leadership.  He also oversaw the launch of Givenchy’s first dedicated handbag line in 2014.

Tisci left Givenchy in February 2017, citing a need to focus on personal projects.  In March 2019, Burberry announced his appointment as Chief Creative Officer, succeeding Christopher Bailey. He presented his first collection for Burberry in September 2018, for the Spring/Summer 2019 season, introducing a new logo designed in collaboration with graphic designer Peter Saville.  His tenure at Burberry focused on reimagining the brand’s iconic trench coat and heritage elements, injecting a modern and youthful energy while maintaining its British identity. He continued to emphasize inclusivity and diversity in his casting choices.

In September 2023, Burberry and Tisci mutually agreed to part ways after nearly five years.  Currently, Tisci continues to work on personal projects and consult for various brands. He is known for his private nature, rarely giving in-depth interviews, and remains a highly influential figure in the fashion industry, recognized for his ability to blend diverse cultural references and redefine luxury aesthetics. He resides between London, Milan and Los Angeles.

title: Zubaira Tukhugov
text:
Zubaira Magomedovich Tukhugov was born on December 18, 1986, in the village of Achkhoy-Martan, Chechnya, then part of the Chechen-Ingush Autonomous Soviet Socialist Republic within the Soviet Union. His upbringing was deeply rooted in the traditions of Chechen martial culture, specifically the ancient combat sport of *qaru khalkhal*, a form of folk wrestling. He began training in this discipline at a very young age, reportedly around the age of 8, under the guidance of his father, Magomed Tukhugov, himself a respected figure in the Chechen martial arts community. This early training instilled in him not only physical prowess but also a strong sense of discipline and honor.

The First Chechen War (1994-1996) significantly impacted Tukhugov’s childhood. During this period, he witnessed the devastation of his homeland and the displacement of his people. He later recounted how the conflict disrupted his training and normal life. Following the war, he continued to hone his skills in *qaru khalkhal*, becoming a multiple-time champion of Chechnya and the North Caucasus region. He reportedly remained undefeated in this traditional wrestling form for a considerable period, establishing himself as a dominant force.

Tukhugov’s transition to modern mixed martial arts (MMA) began in 2010. He quickly rose through the ranks of the regional Russian circuit, fighting primarily for organizations like ProFC and EFC. His professional MMA record reflects this early period, showcasing a rapid accumulation of victories. By 2014, he had compiled a record of 18 wins with only 2 losses, attracting the attention of the Ultimate Fighting Championship (UFC).

He made his UFC debut on September 5, 2015, at UFC Fight Night 75 in Berlin, Germany, facing Norman Parke. He secured a unanimous decision victory, marking a successful start to his UFC career. Over the next few years, Tukhugov continued to compete in the UFC, amassing a record of 3 wins and 2 losses within the promotion. Notable victories included a split decision win over Keita Nakamura on March 11, 2017, at UFC Fight Night 106 in London, England, and a unanimous decision over David Khachatryan on April 27, 2018, at UFC Fight Night 127 in London. 

However, Tukhugov’s UFC career was marred by controversy and ultimately led to his release. Following a UFC Fight Night event in Moscow, Russia, on September 15, 2018, where his teammate Khabib Nurmagomedov was involved in a post-fight brawl, Tukhugov entered the octagon and struck Conor McGregor. This action resulted in a suspension and a fine from the Moscow Athletic Commission.  The UFC subsequently terminated his contract in December 2018.

After leaving the UFC, Tukhugov continued his MMA career in various regional promotions, primarily in Russia and Eastern Europe. He signed with Eagle Fighting Championship (EFC), a promotion founded by Khabib Nurmagomedov, in 2021. He achieved significant success in EFC, becoming a prominent figure within the organization. On July 16, 2022, at EFC 47 in Moscow, he defeated Islam Makhachev’s training partner, Andrey Koshkin, by unanimous decision, further solidifying his reputation. 

As of late 2023, Zubaira Tukhugov remains an active fighter. His professional MMA record stands at 23 wins, 5 losses and 1 draw. He continues to represent Chechnya and its martial traditions. He is known for his relentless pressure, strong grappling skills, and durability. Beyond fighting, he is actively involved in promoting traditional Chechen culture and supporting youth development programs in his home region. He maintains a close relationship with Khabib Nurmagomedov and frequently trains alongside his team.

title: Esteban Espíndola
text:
Esteban Espíndola was born on December 12, 1942, in San Juan del Río, Querétaro, Mexico. His parents, Alejandro Espíndola and María de la Luz Vargas, were both educators, fostering an environment that valued learning and intellectual curiosity from a young age. San Juan del Río, a historically significant city with a strong artistic tradition, likely influenced his early aesthetic sensibilities. He began formal art training at the age of 14, enrolling in the Escuela de Bellas Artes in Querétaro in 1956. This foundational period focused on classical painting techniques, laying the groundwork for his later explorations in abstraction. 

In 1962, Espíndola moved to Mexico City to continue his education at the prestigious Escuela Nacional de Artes Plásticas (ENAP) of the Instituto Nacional de Bellas Artes y Literatura (INBAL). There, he studied under prominent Mexican artists like José Luis Cuevas and Luis Ortiz, figures who were pushing the boundaries of traditional Mexican art. This exposure proved pivotal, steering him away from purely representational work and towards a more conceptual and abstract approach. He completed his studies at ENAP in 1966, earning a degree in painting and sculpture.

The late 1960s and 1970s marked a period of significant artistic development for Espíndola. He became involved with the Ruptura group, a collective of young artists challenging the dominance of muralism and seeking new forms of expression. Ruptura, founded in 1968, advocated for a more international and conceptual art scene in Mexico, and Espíndola’s work increasingly reflected this ethos.  During this time, he experimented extensively with geometric abstraction, hard-edge painting, and minimalist sculpture, often utilizing industrial materials like steel and aluminum. His early exhibitions, notably a group show at the Galería Arte Contemporáneo in Mexico City in 1970, showcased these new directions.
