In 1943, at the age of 18, Cogan volunteered for the Women Accepted for Volunteer Emergency Service (WAVES), the women’s branch of the U.S. Naval Reserve. She completed basic training at Hunter College, which had been converted into a WAVES training facility, and was then assigned to the Naval Intelligence Office in Washington D.C. Her linguistic abilities, particularly her fluency in Spanish learned from neighbors in her diverse Bronx neighborhood, proved invaluable. Cogan worked as an interpreter and translator, analyzing intercepted enemy communications during the latter stages of the war. She held the rank of Seaman First Class when discharged in 1946.

Cogan’s wartime experience profoundly shaped her post-war career path. She returned to Hunter College and earned a Bachelor of Arts degree in Spanish in 1948. She then pursued a Master of Arts degree in Latin American Studies from Columbia University, completing it in 1950.  This education led her to a career with the United States Foreign Service, beginning in 1951.  

Her initial assignment was as a consular officer in Mexico City, where she served until 1954.  She then held a series of increasingly prominent positions, including postings in Guatemala City (1954-1957), San Salvador (1957-1959), and Buenos Aires, Argentina (1959-1961). In 1961, Cogan became the first female American diplomat to hold the position of Principal Officer, leading the U.S. Consulate in Antofagasta, Chile. This was a significant breakthrough for women in the Foreign Service, traditionally a male-dominated field. 

In 1965, Cogan was appointed as the United States Ambassador to the Federated States of Micronesia, a newly formed Trust Territory administered by the United States. This appointment, confirmed by the Senate, made her the first female career Foreign Service officer to become an ambassador. She served in this role until 1969, navigating the complex political landscape as the territory prepared for independence. During her ambassadorship, she focused on promoting economic development, education, and self-governance within Micronesia. 

Following her service in Micronesia, Cogan returned to Washington D.C. and held various senior positions within the State Department. She served as Deputy Assistant Secretary of State for Inter-American Affairs from 1970 to 1973, and subsequently as the Coordinator for Population Affairs from 1973 to 1977. She played a key role in shaping US policy on population issues globally.  

Maggie Cogan retired from the Foreign Service in 1978 after 27 years of service.  She continued to be involved in international affairs, serving on several boards and advisory committees related to Latin America and Micronesia. She frequently lectured on foreign policy and the role of women in diplomacy.  

In her later life, Cogan remained a strong advocate for education and cross-cultural understanding. She moved to a retirement community in Bethesda, Maryland. Maggie Cogan passed away on February 1, 2023, at the age of 98, leaving behind a legacy of dedicated service and pioneering achievement. She never married and had no children, dedicating her life to her career and public service. Her contributions were recognized with numerous awards and commendations throughout her career, including the Distinguished Service Award from the American Foreign Service Association.

title: Marcel Hernández
text:
Marcel Hernández was born on October 23, 1967, in Santiago de Cuba, a city steeped in musical tradition. His full name is Marcel Hernández Rodríguez. From a very young age, he was immersed in the world of *son cubano*, the foundational genre of much Cuban music, through his family. His father, Rafael Hernández, was a professional *tresero* (player of the Cuban tres guitar) and instilled in Marcel a deep appreciation and technical understanding of the instrument. His mother, Caridad Rodríguez, was a vocalist who further nurtured his musical ear.  Marcel didn’t initially pursue the *tres*; instead, he began studying classical guitar at the age of eight at the Escuela Provincial de Música in Santiago de Cuba, completing his studies there in 1985. 

While excelling in classical guitar, Marcel remained drawn to the sounds of his heritage. He began to seriously dedicate himself to the *tres* around 1987, seeking out and learning from older masters like Eusebio Delfín, considered a pivotal figure in the modern revival of the instrument.  He quickly developed a distinctive style, blending the technical precision of his classical training with the rhythmic complexity and improvisational spirit of *son*. 

In 1991, Hernández joined the renowned Grupo Folklórico y Experimental Nuevayorkino, led by Orlando “Cachao” López, a legendary bassist and innovator of *mambo*. This marked a significant turning point in his career, exposing him to a broader international audience and solidifying his reputation as a virtuoso *tresero*. He toured extensively with the group, performing at major venues and festivals across the United States, Europe, and Japan.  His playing on several of Nuevayorkino’s albums, including “20 Años” (1993) and “Légate” (1994), brought him considerable recognition. 

Following his time with Cachao, Hernández embarked on a solo career, releasing his debut album, “Son Tresero,” in 1997 on the Corazon label. The album showcased his mastery of the *tres* and featured a diverse repertoire of traditional *son* pieces and original compositions. It was critically acclaimed and earned him a nomination for a Latin Grammy Award in 1998. He followed this with “Tradiciones” in 2001, further establishing his position as a leading interpreter of Cuban traditional music.  

Throughout the 2000s, Hernández continued to record and perform as a soloist, while also collaborating with numerous other artists. He appeared on albums by Rubén González, another prominent Cuban pianist, and worked with vocalists like Omara Portuondo, a celebrated figure of *Buena Vista Social Club* fame. He consistently toured internationally, frequently appearing at prestigious festivals such as the Montreal Jazz Festival, the Newport Jazz Festival, and the Festival de Jazz de Havana.  

In 2006, he released “El Tres Cubano,” a project specifically designed to demonstrate the versatility of the instrument and its role within different Cuban musical styles. He explored arrangements ranging from *son* to *bolero* to *guaracha*.  He also dedicated himself to education, holding workshops and masterclasses around the world, aiming to pass on his knowledge and passion for the *tres* to a new generation of musicians.  

His album “Sabor Cubano” (2010) featured a broader ensemble and showcased his arranging skills alongside his instrumental prowess. In 2016, he released "Raíces," a return to more traditional *son* arrangements, receiving positive reviews for its authenticity and heartfelt performance. 

Marcel Hernández continued to be an active performer and educator until his death on December 22, 2023, in Miami, Florida, at the age of 56.  The cause of death was complications from a prolonged illness. He leaves behind a legacy as one of the most important *treseros* of his generation, a musician who successfully bridged the gap between tradition and innovation, and a dedicated advocate for the preservation of Cuban musical heritage. His discography consists of six studio albums and numerous collaborations, and his influence can be heard in the playing of countless musicians worldwide.

title: Abdelhamid Shabana
text:
Abdelhamid Shabana (Arabic: عبد الحميد شعبان‎; born February 26, 1938, in Cairo, Egypt) was a prominent Egyptian football player and coach, widely regarded as one of the greatest midfielders in Egyptian history. His career spanned from the late 1950s to the early 1980s, leaving an indelible mark on Egyptian football and contributing significantly to its golden era. 

Shabana’s football journey began in the streets of Cairo before attracting the attention of Al Ahly Sporting Club, one of Egypt’s most successful teams. He joined Al Ahly in 1956 at the age of 18, quickly establishing himself as a key player in midfield. He possessed exceptional vision, passing ability, and tactical intelligence.  His debut in the Egyptian League occurred in 1957, marking the start of a career that would last nearly two decades with the Red Devils. 

Throughout his playing career with Al Ahly, Shabana participated in numerous championships. He was instrumental in Al Ahly’s dominance in the Egyptian Premier League, winning titles in 1958–59, 1960–61, 1962–63, 1964–65, 1966–67, 1968–69, 1970–71, and 1974–75.  His consistency in performance earned him widespread recognition.  He was also vital in Al Ahly’s Egyptian Cup victories in 1959, 1963, 1965, 1967, 1970, and 1975.  Beyond domestic success, Shabana played a crucial role in Al Ahly’s continental achievements. He was a key member of the team that won the African Champions League (now CAF Champions League) in 1966 and 1977.  He was particularly noted for his performance in the second leg of the 1966 final against Asante Kotoko of Ghana in Accra, where he scored a crucial goal.  He also played in the African Cup Winners’ Cup, winning it in 1976. 

Shabana was also a regular member of the Egyptian national team. He earned his first international cap in 1959, representing Egypt in over 60 international matches. He participated in three Africa Cup of Nations tournaments: 1959 in Sudan (where Egypt won), 1962 in Ethiopia, and 1970 in Sudan.  He was also part of the Egyptian squad in the 1968 Olympic Games in Mexico City. While Egypt didn't achieve significant success in these tournaments, Shabana consistently displayed his skill and leadership.  He retired from international football in 1973.

Beyond his playing abilities, Shabana was known for his sportsmanship and ethical conduct. He rarely received disciplinary action throughout his career. His elegant playing style and fair play earned him respect from opponents and fans alike.  He was admired not only for his footballing prowess but also for his character.

Following his retirement from playing in 1979, Shabana transitioned into coaching. He initially worked as an assistant coach with Al Ahly, contributing to their continued success.  He then took on head coaching roles in several clubs in Egypt and abroad. He managed clubs like Al Masry in Port Said, Ismaili in Suez, and even had a stint in Libya in the early 1980s.  He never reached the same level of success in coaching as he did in playing, but he continued to contribute to the development of Egyptian football.  He was known as a disciplinarian who emphasized tactical awareness in his coaching approach. 

In his later years, Shabana lived a relatively quiet life in Cairo. He occasionally appeared in television interviews reflecting on his illustrious career. He passed away on December 15, 2012, in Cairo, aged 74.  His death was mourned throughout Egypt, and he was remembered as a true legend of the game.  Numerous tributes were paid to him in the Egyptian media, recognizing his significant contribution to Egyptian football history. His legacy continues to inspire generations of Egyptian footballers.

title: Ryan Brasier
text:
Ryan Brasier was born on April 22, 1988, in Hartford, Connecticut, the son of John and Nancy Brasier. He grew up in Crestwood, Illinois, a suburb of Chicago, and attended Victor J. Andrew High School in Tinley Park, Illinois. A three-sport athlete, Brasier excelled in baseball, basketball, and football, ultimately focusing on baseball as his primary pursuit. He primarily played as a shortstop and pitcher during his high school career, showcasing a strong arm that would define his professional path. He was drafted by the Cincinnati Reds in the 16th round of the 2006 Major League Baseball draft, with the 468th overall pick. 

Brasier initially attended College of DuPage in Glen Ellyn, Illinois for a year before transferring to Jacksonville State University in Jacksonville, Alabama, where he continued his collegiate baseball career. He pitched for the Jacksonville State Gamecocks from 2008 to 2009. His success at Jacksonville State drew further attention from scouts, and he was again drafted, this time by the Los Angeles Angels of Anaheim in the 6th round of the 2009 MLB draft, the 188th overall pick. 

He began his professional career in 2009 with the Cedar Rapids Kernels, the Angels’ Class A affiliate, pitching in 15 games with a 4.20 ERA. He steadily worked his way through the Angels’ minor league system, progressing through the Inland Empire 66ers (Class A Advanced) in 2010 and the Salt Lake Bees (Triple-A) in 2011 and 2012. His time in the minor leagues was marked by inconsistency and struggles with control, often battling high walk rates. In 2011, he underwent Tommy John surgery on his right elbow, sidelining him for the majority of the season and significantly impacting his development.

Brasier finally made his Major League debut with the Angels on May 11, 2013, pitching one inning in relief against the Texas Rangers and allowing one hit. He appeared in 23 games for the Angels in 2013, posting a 6.84 ERA over 27.2 innings. Despite flashes of potential, his control issues continued to plague him, and he was designated for assignment in February 2014.

He was claimed off waivers by the New York Yankees in February 2014.  However, he only pitched in one game for the Yankees’ Triple-A Scranton/Wilkes-Barre RailRiders before being released in May 2014.  He then spent the remainder of the 2014 season and the entire 2015 season pitching in the independent Atlantic League for the Bridgeport Bluefish, working to refine his mechanics and rediscover his form. 

A turning point came in 2016 when he signed with the Hiroshima Toyo Carp of the Nippon Professional Baseball (NPB) league in Japan. He spent two seasons in Japan, where he flourished as a setup man, significantly improving his control and command. In 2017, he recorded a remarkable 0.68 ERA in 28 appearances, saving 14 games. This success reinvigorated his career and drew the attention of Major League teams once again.

In December 2017, Brasier signed a two-year, $2 million contract with the Boston Red Sox. He became a key component of the Red Sox bullpen in 2018, posting a stellar 1.60 ERA in 30 appearances and contributing to the team’s World Series championship. He pitched in two games of the World Series against the Los Angeles Dodgers.  He continued to be a reliable reliever for the Red Sox in 2019, recording a 3.74 ERA in 41 games. 

He became a free agent after the 2019 season and signed a one-year, $2 million deal with the Philadelphia Phillies in January 2020. However, he opted out of the 2020 season due to concerns surrounding the COVID-19 pandemic. He signed a minor league deal with the Los Angeles Dodgers in February 2021, and was later released. He then rejoined the Boston Red Sox on a minor league contract in May 2021, and was called up to the major league roster shortly after. He pitched for the Red Sox through the 2022 season before becoming a free agent again.



As of late 2023, Ryan Brasier remains a free agent. Throughout his career, he has appeared in 223 Major League games, accumulating a 4.14 ERA and 226 strikeouts over 258.1 innings pitched. He is known for his impressive fastball and the resilience he demonstrated in rebuilding his career after facing early setbacks.

title: Ricky Martin
text:
Enrique Martín Morales, known globally as Ricky Martin, was born on December 24, 1971, in San Juan, Puerto Rico. He was the youngest of six children born to Nereida Morales, a schoolteacher, and José Enrique Martín, a social worker. His upbringing was marked by financial hardship and a somewhat turbulent family life, with his parents separating when he was young. He spent much of his childhood moving between his father’s home in Puerto Rico and his maternal grandmother’s house. From a young age, Martin displayed a strong passion for performing, influenced by American artists like Michael Jackson and imitating them for family and friends. 

His introduction to the entertainment industry came at age nine, when he began appearing in Puerto Rican television shows, including “Por Encima de tus Manos” in 1980. He quickly gained recognition and secured roles in several other programs and commercials. A pivotal moment arrived in 1988 when he successfully auditioned for the boy band Menudo, a Latin American sensation. He joined the group at the age of 16, replacing a member who had aged out. Menudo’s strict contract dictated that members would be replaced when they turned 16 or reached a certain height, a system designed to maintain a youthful image.

Martin toured extensively with Menudo for five years, recording eleven albums with the group that sold over 20 million records worldwide. While the experience provided invaluable stage presence and a massive international fanbase, Martin felt creatively stifled by the band’s limitations. He left Menudo in 1991, initiating a legal battle to secure the rights to his own image and future recordings. He subsequently moved to New York City, studying acting at the Neighborhood Playhouse and taking various odd jobs to support himself.

His solo career officially launched in 1991 with the self-titled album *Ricky Martin*. The album, and its follow-up *Me Amarás* in 1993, achieved moderate success in Latin America, establishing him as a rising star. However, it was his 1995 album, *A Medio Tiempo*, that began to garner significant attention, incorporating a blend of ballads and dance tracks. The breakthrough came in 1998 with *Vuelve*. The album’s lead single, “La Copa de la Vida” (“The Cup of Life”), became a global anthem, particularly after being chosen as the official song for the 1998 FIFA World Cup in France. 

*Vuelve* sold over 22 million copies worldwide, cementing Martin’s status as a Latin crossover artist. He followed this success in 1999 with the English-language album *Ricky Martin*, which featured the hugely popular single “Livin' la Vida Loca.” The album became a blockbuster, selling over 30 million copies globally and earning him numerous awards, including Grammy and Latin Grammy Awards. He continued to release successful albums throughout the 2000s, including *Sound Loaded* (2000) and *Life* (2005).

Throughout the 2010s, Martin continued to tour and release music, though with a slightly reduced mainstream profile. He ventured into television, appearing as a coach on *The Voice Australia* in 2013 and *The Voice US* in 2016. In 2018, he released the collaborative EP *Pa’lla Voy*, and in 2020, he released his eleventh studio album, *Movimiento*. 

In 2010, Martin publicly came out as gay, a decision he described as liberating.  He began a relationship with Jwan Yosef, a Swedish-Syrian painter, in 2016. They married in a private ceremony in 2018 and have four children together: Matteo and Valentino (born via gestational surrogacy in 2008), Lucia (born in 2018), and Renn (born in 2019).  Throughout his career, Ricky Martin has sold over 100 million records worldwide, making him one of the best-selling Latin music artists of all time. His influence extends beyond music; he is also a philanthropist and advocate for human rights, particularly focusing on LGBTQ+ rights and ending human trafficking through his Ricky Martin Foundation, established in 1995.

title: Dana Ashbrook
text:
Dana Ashbrook was born on September 24, 1961, in Marshalltown, Iowa, to Donald and Patricia Ashbrook. His father was a marketing executive and his mother a homemaker. He spent his early childhood in Marshalltown before the family relocated to Bellflower, California, when he was ten years old. This move was spurred by his father’s job transfer and proved pivotal as it brought young Dana closer to the entertainment industry. He attended Mayfair High School in Lakewood, California, graduating in 1979. His early interests leaned towards athletics, particularly football, but he also participated in drama club and discovered a passion for acting. 

Ashbrook’s initial foray into acting occurred through school productions, but his professional career began to take shape in the early 1980s with minor roles in television. He landed a small part in an episode of “Diff’rent Strokes” in 1982, followed by appearances in “Silver Spoons” and “Hotel” in 1983. These early roles, though brief, provided valuable on-set experience and allowed him to learn the mechanics of television production. A more substantial role came in 1985 with a recurring part as Brad in the CBS sitcom “Charles in Charge,” appearing in 25 episodes over two seasons. This marked a significant step in his career, increasing his visibility and establishing him as a recognizable face on television.

However, it was his portrayal of Bogey Lowenstein in the groundbreaking television series “Twin Peaks,” created by David Lynch and Mark Frost, that cemented his place in television history. He joined the cast in 1990, initially for a planned three-episode arc, but his character’s popularity with audiences led to him becoming a regular for the show’s second season, appearing in 23 episodes. “Twin Peaks,” which premiered in 1990, became a cultural phenomenon, and Ashbrook's portrayal of the troubled, musically inclined Bogey resonated with viewers. The role earned him a devoted fanbase and critical acclaim, despite the show’s controversial and often surreal nature. 

Following the cancellation of "Twin Peaks" in 1991, Ashbrook continued to work in television and film, though he rarely achieved the same level of recognition. He took on guest roles in shows like “Beverly Hills, 90210” (1992), "Melrose Place" (1994), and “Diagnosis: Murder” (1999). He also appeared in a number of made-for-television movies, including "Moment of Truth" (1993) and "A Deadly Silence" (1998). Film roles were less frequent but included appearances in "Surf II" (1987) and "Getting Personal" (1999).

Throughout the 1990s and 2000s, Ashbrook also pursued his musical interests, performing as a singer-songwriter in various venues. He formed a band called “The Dana Ashbrook Band” and released several independent albums, often incorporating the themes and atmosphere of "Twin Peaks" into his music. He maintained a close relationship with the "Twin Peaks" fanbase, attending conventions and actively engaging with fans online.

In 2017, Ashbrook reprised his role as Bogey Lowenstein in the highly anticipated revival of “Twin Peaks,” titled “Twin Peaks: The Return,” directed by David Lynch. This offered him a chance to revisit the character that had defined his career and brought him renewed attention from both critics and fans. He appeared in six episodes of the limited series.

As of late 2023, Dana Ashbrook continues to be active in the entertainment industry, performing music with his band and making occasional appearances at fan events. He resides in California. While he has never reached the same mainstream success as some of his contemporaries, his iconic role in “Twin Peaks” has ensured his legacy as a significant figure in television history, and he remains a beloved actor amongst a dedicated and passionate fanbase. He has consistently credited the show and its fans for providing him with a fulfilling and enduring career.

title: Kathinka Pasveer
text:
Kathinka Pasveer was born on August 22, 1920, in Bussum, Netherlands, to Willem Pasveer, a painter, and Johanna Margaretha van Hall. Her upbringing was deeply immersed in the arts, significantly shaping her future trajectory. From a young age, she demonstrated a talent for drawing and painting, encouraged by her father who provided her with early artistic training. She initially studied at the Rijksnormaalschool voor Tekenonderwijs in Amsterdam from 1938 to 1942, qualifying as an art teacher. However, the outbreak of World War II and the subsequent Nazi occupation dramatically altered her life and artistic development.

During the war, Pasveer became involved in the Dutch Resistance, utilizing her artistic skills to create forged identity papers and documents for Jewish people and resistance members.  This dangerous work, carried out between 1943 and 1945, required meticulous attention to detail and a steady hand, skills honed through her art education.  She worked primarily with a group in Hilversum, forging documents under the direction of Johan van Hulst, a prominent figure in the local resistance.  This period profoundly influenced her, instilling a strong sense of social responsibility that would later become central to her artistic themes.

Following the war, Pasveer dedicated herself fully to her art. She initially experimented with various styles, including realism and expressionism, but gradually developed her signature style – a distinctive form of Constructivism and Concrete art.  She became a founding member of the Dutch Concrete Art Group, *Concrete Inducties*, in 1958, alongside artists such as Ger van Elk, Jan Schoonhoven, and Armando. This group advocated for a purely abstract art, devoid of representation and focused on the inherent properties of materials and form.

Pasveer’s work is characterized by precise geometric shapes, often squares and rectangles, arranged in carefully balanced compositions. She primarily worked with acrylic paint on canvas and wood, meticulously applying layers of color to achieve subtle tonal variations and visual effects.  Her early work from the 1950s and 60s featured bolder, brighter colors, but she gradually transitioned to a more restrained palette of muted tones and greys in the 1970s and 80s.  A key element of her work is the manipulation of perception; her paintings often create illusions of depth and movement, challenging the viewer’s understanding of space.

Throughout her career, Pasveer exhibited extensively, both nationally and internationally.  She had her first solo exhibition in 1966 at Galerie Witteveen in Amsterdam.  Significant group exhibitions included shows at the Stedelijk Museum Amsterdam (1963, 1978, 1983), the Kröller-Müller Museum in Otterlo (1969), and numerous international Concrete Art exhibitions.  In 1978, she received the prestigious Sandberg Prize, a highly regarded award for Dutch artists.  She was made a Knight of the Order of Orange-Nassau in 1989, recognizing her contributions to Dutch art and culture.

While never seeking widespread fame, Pasveer steadily gained recognition as a significant figure in post-war Dutch abstract art.  Her work is held in the collections of major museums, including the Stedelijk Museum Amsterdam, the Kröller-Müller Museum, the Van Abbemuseum in Eindhoven, and the Rijksmuseum in Amsterdam.  

Kathinka Pasveer continued to paint and exhibit her work well into her later years. She lived and worked in Bussum for nearly her entire life, maintaining a dedicated studio space. She passed away on February 4, 2010, in Bussum, at the age of 89. Her legacy endures through her meticulously crafted paintings, which continue to be admired for their intellectual rigor, visual subtlety, and enduring relevance in the realm of abstract art.

title: Abdul Halik Hudu
text:
Abdul Halik Hudu was born on October 27, 1922, in Wa, in the then Gold Coast (now Ghana), to Amidu Hudu and Ayishetu Kanton. His father was a prominent local chief and a key figure in the Wala traditional area. This lineage significantly shaped Halik Hudu’s early life, exposing him to traditional governance and the complexities of colonial rule from a young age. He received his initial education at the local primary school in Wa, and subsequently attended Tamale Middle School from 1935 to 1938. Recognizing his potential, his father ensured he continued his education at Achimota College, a prestigious boarding school near Accra, from 1939 to 1942. Achimota, known for its pan-Africanist ideals and focus on developing future African leaders, proved formative for Hudu, and he excelled academically and in extracurricular activities. 

Following Achimota, Hudu pursued further studies in the United Kingdom, attending the University of Birmingham from 1947 to 1950, where he earned a Bachelor of Commerce degree. He then proceeded to the London School of Economics and Political Science, completing a Master of Science degree in Economics in 1952. These qualifications were relatively rare for Ghanaians at the time, positioning him for a significant role in the nascent post-colonial nation.

Upon returning to the Gold Coast, Hudu entered public service in 1953, joining the Colonial Civil Service as an Administrative Officer. He quickly rose through the ranks, demonstrating administrative acumen and a commitment to national development. In 1957, with the Gold Coast achieving independence and becoming Ghana, he transitioned into the newly formed Ghana Civil Service. He held various positions, including Assistant Secretary to the Ministry of Finance from 1957 to 1959 and Secretary to the Ministry of Food and Agriculture from 1959 to 1961. 

His career took a pivotal turn in 1961 when he was appointed Governor of the Bank of Ghana, a position he held for an unusually long period, until 1969. During his tenure, he oversaw significant growth in the Ghanaian economy, particularly in the cocoa sector, which remained a vital export commodity. He navigated the financial challenges of a newly independent nation, establishing policies aimed at stabilizing the cedi and attracting foreign investment. He was instrumental in the development of Ghana's financial infrastructure, including the expansion of the banking sector and the promotion of local entrepreneurship.  A key achievement during his governorship was the establishment of the Agricultural Development Bank (ADB) in 1965, specifically designed to provide financial support to the agricultural sector, reflecting his understanding of the importance of agriculture to the Ghanaian economy.

The political landscape in Ghana underwent significant upheaval with the 1966 coup d'état that overthrew President Kwame Nkrumah. Hudu, despite not being directly involved in the coup, remained in his position as Governor of the Bank of Ghana under the new military government, the National Liberation Council (NLC), led by General Joseph A. Ankrah. However, he eventually resigned from the governorship in 1969, citing differences in policy direction with the ruling NLC.

After leaving the Bank of Ghana, Hudu remained active in public life, serving as a consultant on economic and financial matters to various organizations.  He was appointed Chairman of the Ghana Cocoa Marketing Board from 1971 to 1972, again demonstrating his expertise in a crucial sector of the Ghanaian economy.  He also served as a member of the Council of State, an advisory body to the President, during the 1970s. 

In his later life, Abdul Halik Hudu dedicated himself to philanthropic activities and remained a respected elder statesman. He actively supported educational initiatives in his home region of Wa and across the country. He received an honorary doctorate from the University of Ghana in 1999 in recognition of his contributions to the nation’s development. Abdul Halik Hudu passed away on August 26, 2000, at the Korle-Bu Teaching Hospital in Accra, at the age of 77, leaving behind a legacy of dedicated public service and economic leadership. He was survived by his wife, Hajia Mariama Hudu, and several children.

title: Cha Eun-woo
text:
Lee Dong-min, more widely known as Cha Eun-woo, was born on March 30, 1997, in Anyang, Gyeonggi Province, South Korea. He is the younger of two sons; his older brother, Lee Dong-hyeon, is also a public figure, working as a doctor and gaining recognition through appearances on the Korean reality television show “Master in the House.” Eun-woo’s father, Lee Chang-hoon, is a professor of physical education at Hanyang University. His mother’s profession is less publicly discussed. He attended Surigo High School in Seongnam, Gyeonggi, graduating in February 2016. 

Even during his high school years, Eun-woo demonstrated a strong interest in the performing arts. He was a popular figure in school, known for his good looks and participation in a band. However, his path towards becoming an entertainer began more concretely in 2014, when he was scouted by Fantagio entertainment during a school festival. He signed with them as a trainee and began intensive training in singing, dancing, and acting.  This period of training lasted approximately a year, and involved rigorous schedules alongside future ASTRO members.

Eun-woo officially debuted as a member of the six-member boy group ASTRO on February 23, 2016, under Fantagio. The group’s debut mini-album, “Spring Part. 0.2,” was released alongside the music video for their title track, “Hide & Seek.” While ASTRO initially faced challenges gaining widespread recognition, they steadily built a fanbase through consistent releases and promotions.  Eun-woo's visual appeal quickly became a significant part of ASTRO's public image. 

Concurrent with his group activities, Eun-woo began to pursue acting. His first acting role was a cameo appearance in the 2015 KBS2 drama “The Producers.”  His first proper acting role came in 2016 with a supporting part in the historical drama “Moon Lovers: Scarlet Heart Ryeo,” where he played the 13th Prince, Baek Ah. Though the drama didn’t achieve high ratings domestically, it garnered significant international attention, particularly in China, boosting Eun-woo’s recognition.

His breakthrough role arrived in 2018 with the JTBC school romance drama "My ID is Gangnam Beauty," where he played Do Kyung-seok, a popular and seemingly perfect university student. This drama was a commercial and critical success, and catapulted Eun-woo to leading man status.  He followed this with roles in the 2019 tvN fantasy romance “Rookie Historian Goo Hae-ryung” and the 2020 KBS2 drama “True Beauty”, which further solidified his popularity. "True Beauty" achieved peak ratings of 8.5% nationwide and consistently trended on social media.

Beyond dramas, Eun-woo has also been active in variety shows. He became a fixed cast member of the popular SBS variety show "Master in the House" in April 2019, remaining until December 2020, showcasing a more playful and relatable side of his personality.  He hosted the 2021 Mnet Asian Music Awards (MAMA) alongside Jeon Hyun-moo and Lee Hyori, demonstrating his ability to command a large stage. In 2022, he took on the lead role in the historical drama “The King’s Affection,” portraying the Crown Prince Lee Hwi. 

As of late 2023, Eun-woo has continued to expand his acting portfolio. He starred in the fantasy romance drama “Wonderful Life” (also known as “A Good Day to Be a Dog”) in late 2023. In February 2024, he signed an exclusive contract with HighZium Studio, a production company known for dramas like "Crash Landing on You" and "Twenty-Five Twenty-One,” signaling a focus on further developing his acting career. 

Throughout his career, Eun-woo has received numerous accolades, including Best New Actor awards at the 2018 KBS Entertainment Awards and the 2019 The Fact Music Awards. He consistently ranks high in brand reputation rankings for individual celebrity members, demonstrating his enduring popularity and influence within the Korean entertainment industry. He is also known for philanthropic work, having been involved in various charitable activities and donating to causes such as disaster relief.

title: Worranit Thawornwong
text:
Worranit Thawornwong, often known simply as “Daeng,” was a prominent Thai activist and founder of the Community Organization Development Institute (CODI), a key organization in securing land rights and improving the living conditions of Thailand’s urban poor. She was born on January 27, 1936, in Ban Na, Nakhon Ratchasima Province, northeastern Thailand, to a farming family. Her early life was marked by the economic hardships and social inequalities prevalent in rural Thailand during that period. Witnessing the struggles of her community fuelled a lifelong commitment to social justice. She completed her secondary education at Nakhon Ratchasima Witthayalai School before moving to Bangkok to pursue higher education.

Worranit earned a Bachelor of Arts degree in Sociology from Thammasat University in 1960. This academic foundation provided her with a critical framework for understanding the systemic issues facing marginalized communities.  Following graduation, she initially worked as a social worker with the Department of Public Welfare, gaining valuable experience in direct community engagement.  However, she quickly became frustrated by the limitations of bureaucratic processes and the lack of genuine empowerment for the people she was trying to assist. 

This frustration led her to leave the Department of Public Welfare in 1976 and dedicate herself to grassroots organizing. She began working with slum dwellers in Bangkok, initially focusing on issues of eviction and inadequate housing.  Recognizing the need for a more coordinated and sustainable approach, Worranit, along with a small group of dedicated colleagues, established the Community Organization Development Institute (CODI) in 1984.  CODI’s initial work centered on providing legal assistance and advocacy for communities facing forced eviction, often due to large-scale development projects. 

Worranit’s leadership at CODI was characterized by a participatory approach, emphasizing the importance of empowering communities to identify their own needs and solutions. She championed the concept of “land tenure security” as fundamental to improving the lives of the urban poor.  CODI developed innovative strategies, including community mapping, negotiation with government agencies, and the creation of community-managed funds. A pivotal moment came in 1992 with the establishment of the Baan Mankong program, a nationwide initiative that provided financial assistance and technical support to slum communities to upgrade their own housing and infrastructure.  The program, initially funded with a loan of 800 million baht from the Thai government and later supported by the World Bank, enabled over 68,000 families in 800 communities to improve their living conditions by 2012. 

Worranit’s work wasn’t without challenges. She faced resistance from powerful interests, including property developers and corrupt officials, who benefited from the displacement of vulnerable communities.  She skillfully navigated these obstacles through strategic advocacy, building alliances with sympathetic government officials, and mobilizing public opinion.  Her tireless efforts earned her numerous awards and accolades, including the 1999 Ramon Magsaysay Award for Community Leadership, often considered Asia’s Nobel Prize.  In 2002, she received an honorary doctorate from Rangsit University.  

Throughout her career, Worranit consistently stressed the importance of community ownership and self-reliance.  She believed that sustainable development could only be achieved when communities were empowered to control their own destinies.  She mentored a new generation of community leaders and activists, ensuring the continuation of CODI’s work.  

Worranit Thawornwong retired from her position as Director of CODI in 2006, but remained actively involved in social justice issues as a consultant and advisor. She passed away on November 28, 2018, at the age of 82, after a prolonged illness. Her legacy continues to inspire community organizers and advocates across Thailand and beyond, and the Baan Mankong program remains a model for participatory urban development.  Her work fundamentally changed the landscape of land rights and housing policy in Thailand, leaving an indelible mark on the lives of countless marginalized citizens.

title: Sila María Calderón
text:
Sila María Calderón Alfonso was born on September 19, 1942, in San Juan, Puerto Rico, into a prominent political family. Her father, Juan Antonio Calderón, was a lawyer and served as a Senator in the Puerto Rican legislature for 16 years, and her mother, Sila Alfonso, was a teacher and active in civic organizations. This environment deeply instilled in her a sense of public service and a keen awareness of Puerto Rico’s political landscape. She received her early education at the Colegio Sagrado Corazón de Jesús in San Juan, a Catholic school for girls, graduating in 1960. She then pursued higher education at the University of Puerto Rico, earning a Bachelor of Arts in Education in 1964. Furthering her studies, she obtained a Master’s degree in Education from the same institution in 1970. 

Calderón's professional life began in education. Following her graduation, she worked as a teacher at the Luis Muñoz Marín School in San Juan, dedicating herself to elementary education for several years. However, her ambitions extended beyond the classroom. In 1972, she transitioned into the public sector, joining the staff of Governor Rafael Hernández Colón as an advisor on education issues. This marked the start of a long and influential career in government, initially focused on shaping education policy. 

Over the next two decades, she steadily climbed the ranks within the New Progressive Party (PNP), advocating for statehood for Puerto Rico. She served as the Executive Director of the Puerto Rico Tourism Company from 1985 to 1989, under Governor Hernández Colón, during which time she focused on promoting the island as a tourist destination and boosting the economy. In 1988, she was elected as a Senator for the District of San Juan, a position she held until 1992. During her time in the Senate, she focused on issues related to education, women's rights, and economic development, becoming a respected voice in the legislative process.

A pivotal moment in her career came in 1996 when she ran for and won the mayorship of San Juan. She became the first woman to hold the office, serving three consecutive terms from 1997 to 2001, 2001 to 2005, and 2005 to 2009. As mayor, Calderón implemented numerous urban renewal projects, revitalizing historic districts like Old San Juan and focusing on improving infrastructure. She prioritized cultural initiatives, transforming San Juan into a vibrant center for the arts and tourism. She also spearheaded efforts to address social issues, including homelessness and crime.  Her administration was marked by substantial budgetary investments in public safety, leading to a decrease in crime rates during her tenure. 

In 2000, Sila Calderón ran for Governor of Puerto Rico, facing off against incumbent Pedro Rosselló. She won the election with approximately 49.6% of the vote, becoming the first female governor of Puerto Rico. Her term, from 2001 to 2005, was challenging. She inherited a significant fiscal deficit and faced increasing public debt. She focused on improving public education, healthcare, and public safety, attempting to implement reforms to address the island’s economic woes. However, her administration was also plagued by accusations of corruption and mismanagement, and a controversial sales tax increase, known as the Value Added Tax (VAT), proved deeply unpopular. 

After leaving office in 2005, Calderón remained active in public life, though she stepped back from seeking elected office. She established the "Fundación Sila M. Calderón," dedicated to promoting education, leadership, and community development. She has also served on various boards and commissions. In 2016, she publicly endorsed Hillary Clinton during the U.S. presidential election. In recent years, she has frequently commented on Puerto Rico’s political and economic situation, advocating for responsible fiscal management and a resolution to the island’s status issue. As of 2023, Sila María Calderón continues to reside in San Juan, remaining a respected, if sometimes controversial, figure in Puerto Rican politics and a symbol of female leadership in the Caribbean.

title: Pratibha Patil
text:
Pratibha Devisingh Patil, born on December 19, 1934, in the village of Ralegaon, Jalgaon district, Maharashtra, was the 12th and first female President of India. Her parents, Vishnu Bhaskar Patil and Shramishtabai Patil, belonged to a politically active family with a background in cooperative movements. Vishnu Patil was a schoolteacher and later involved in local politics, serving as the President of the Jalgaon District Congress Committee. Pratibha Patil received her early education at a local primary school and then attended Sir S. Sassoon Jain Girls' High School in Jalgaon. She completed her Bachelor of Arts degree in Political Science and Economics from Government Arts College, Jalgaon, in 1954, followed by a law degree from the Government Law College, Bombay (now Mumbai) in 1962. 

Patil’s entry into politics was gradual, building on her family’s established base. She married Devendra Singh Shekhawat, a lawyer, in 1965, and they had one son, Rajsingh Devisingh Shekhawat. She began her political career by being elected to the Jalgaon Municipal Council in 1964.  She then successfully contested and became a Member of the Maharashtra Legislative Assembly (MLA) representing the Muktainagar constituency in 1967. She won this seat continuously for five terms – 1967, 1972, 1978, 1980 and 1985.  During her time as an MLA, Patil held various ministerial portfolios in the Maharashtra state government.  She served as Minister of Irrigation from 1979 to 1980, Minister of Urban Development from 1980 to 1983, and Minister of Education from 1983 to 1985. 

In 1986, she was elected to the Rajya Sabha, the upper house of the Indian Parliament, and served for one term until 1992.  Following a break from parliamentary politics, she was appointed as the Governor of Rajasthan on November 8, 2004, becoming the first woman to hold that constitutional post. During her tenure as Governor, she focused on promoting education, particularly for girls, and addressing social issues.  She also actively involved herself in initiatives related to water conservation and rural development.

In 2007, Patil was nominated as the candidate of the United Progressive Alliance (UPA), the ruling coalition led by the Indian National Congress, for the presidential election. Her nomination came somewhat unexpectedly, as she wasn't widely considered a frontrunner. She contested against Bhairon Singh Shekhawat, the then Vice President and candidate for the National Democratic Alliance (NDA).  The election, held on July 10, 2007, resulted in a victory for Patil, securing 658,096 electoral votes against Shekhawat’s 352,884.  She was sworn in as the President of India on July 25, 2007, making history as the first woman to hold the highest office in the country.

As President, Patil focused on a pro-people agenda, emphasizing inclusive growth and social justice. She travelled extensively across India, addressing public gatherings and interacting with citizens.  During her five-year term, she commuted the death sentences of 35 convicts, a point of some controversy. She also signed the Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act in 2009, a landmark legislation guaranteeing free education for children between the ages of six and fourteen.  Patil’s presidency was largely ceremonial, as India follows a parliamentary system where the President’s role is largely symbolic.

Following the completion of her term on July 25, 2012, Pratibha Patil retired from active politics. She has since largely remained out of the public eye, occasionally making appearances at public functions.  She authored an autobiography titled *My Life: An Autobiography*, published in 2014, detailing her journey and experiences in politics.  She continues to reside in Pune, Maharashtra, and remains a notable figure in Indian political history as a pioneer for women in leadership roles.

title: Carl Braun (obstetrician)
text:
Carl August Braun was born on November 16, 1886, in Freiberg, Saxony, Germany, the son of a mining engineer, Wilhelm Braun, and his wife, Marie (née Schubert). His early education took place in Freiberg, culminating in his Abitur (university entrance qualification) in 1904. He initially pursued studies in mining, honoring his father’s profession, enrolling at the Technical University of Dresden. However, a strong interest in the natural sciences, particularly biology, quickly steered him towards medicine. He transferred to the University of Leipzig in 1905 and completed his medical studies there in 1911, receiving his doctorate in medicine (Dr. med.) with a dissertation on the topic of artificial pneumothorax in the treatment of tuberculosis.

Following his doctorate, Braun began his residency in obstetrics and gynecology, initially working at the University Women's Hospital in Leipzig under Professor Wilhelm Schüchle. He then spent time at the municipal hospital in Zwickau, gaining practical experience in the complexities of childbirth.  The outbreak of World War I interrupted his career progression. He served as a medical officer in the German army from 1914 to 1918, stationed primarily in field hospitals in Belgium and France. This experience, while undeniably traumatic, further honed his surgical skills and exposed him to a wider range of medical emergencies. 

After the war, Braun returned to Leipzig and qualified as a specialist in obstetrics and gynecology (Facharzt für Geburtshilfe und Gynäkologie) in 1919.  He quickly established himself as a highly skilled and innovative practitioner. In 1926, he was appointed *Privatdozent* (unsalaried lecturer) at the University of Leipzig, a position he held for over two decades. He began to focus his research on pelvic presentation and breech births, areas where mortality rates were particularly high. 

Braun’s defining achievement was the development of the “Braun maneuver,” a technique for safely delivering babies in breech presentation.  Prior to its introduction, internal podalic version (manually turning the baby in the womb) was the primary method, often risky and requiring significant skill.  The Braun maneuver, meticulously documented and published in 1929 in the journal *Zeitschrift für Geburtshilfe und Gynäkologie*, involved a carefully orchestrated sequence of external manipulation – applying pressure to the baby’s buttocks to rotate it into a cephalic (head-down) presentation *without* internal intervention.  This significantly reduced the risks associated with breech deliveries, lowering both maternal and infant mortality. The maneuver wasn't universally adopted immediately, requiring careful training and understanding, but it gradually became a cornerstone of obstetric practice worldwide.

Throughout the 1930s, Braun continued to refine his technique and disseminate his knowledge through publications and teaching.  The political climate in Germany under the Nazi regime presented challenges. While he wasn’t a politically active individual, the increasing restrictions and ideological pressures impacted academic freedom. He remained at his post in Leipzig, focusing on his medical work.

World War II brought further disruption.  The University of Leipzig suffered significant damage during bombing raids, and Braun’s hospital faced increasing strain. After the war and the subsequent division of Germany, Leipzig fell under Soviet control. In 1949, Braun was offered a professorship and directorship of the Department of Obstetrics and Gynecology at the University of Tübingen in West Germany. He accepted, and remained there until his retirement in 1956. 

During his time in Tübingen, he continued to mentor students and contribute to advancements in obstetric care. Though he formally retired, he maintained an active interest in the field, attending conferences and following developments in obstetrical techniques. Carl Braun died on February 22, 1962, in Tübingen, Baden-Württemberg, West Germany, at the age of 75.  His legacy persists through the continued use of the Braun maneuver, a testament to his dedication to improving the safety of childbirth. He received numerous honors during his career, including the honorary doctorate from the University of Marburg in 1950.

title: Shawn Ashmore
text:
Shawn Ashmore was born on October 20, 1979, in Brampton, Ontario, Canada, to parents Linda and Rick Ashmore. He is the elder of two sons; his brother, Aaron Ashmore, is also an actor. Growing up in a household with a father working as a publisher and a mother as a homemaker, Ashmore’s initial interest wasn’t explicitly focused on acting. He enjoyed sports, particularly hockey, and initially envisioned a career in that field. However, at the age of eight, he was encouraged by his mother to attend an audition for a role in the Canadian television series “The Mighty Ducks” (1992), a live-action adaptation of the popular film. He secured the part of Dale Appleton, a young hockey player, launching his professional acting career.

Ashmore continued to balance school with acting throughout his childhood and adolescence. He attended Turner Fenton Secondary School in Brampton, graduating in 1998. While working on “The Mighty Ducks”, he appeared in several television guest roles, including episodes of “Are You Afraid of the Dark?” (1993) and “Family Affair” (1995). He also landed minor roles in films like “Executive Decision” (1996) alongside Kurt Russell and Halle Berry, and “Murder in a Small Town” (1997) with Frances Fisher. 

The late 1990s and early 2000s saw Ashmore transition into more prominent roles. He gained recognition for his recurring role as Jimmy Olsen in the WB’s “Smallville” (2001-2011), a modern reimagining of the Superman story. While initially appearing in only a few episodes during the first season, his portrayal of the inquisitive reporter became a fan favorite, and he ultimately appeared in 25 episodes across the show’s ten-season run. His performance as Olsen earned him a nomination for a Gemini Award in 2003 for Best Supporting Actor in a Dramatic Series. 

Concurrent with “Smallville”, Ashmore actively sought out film roles. He appeared in “The Sum of All Fears” (2002) with Ben Affleck and Morgan Freeman, playing a Navy lieutenant, and played a key role in the horror film “Along Came the Spider” (2001) opposite Morgan Freeman again. He also showcased his versatility in independent films like “Loyal” (2001) and “Eager Beaver” (2003).  A significant role came in 2004 with “Cadet Kelly”, a Disney Channel original movie where he starred alongside Hilary Duff.

Ashmore’s career continued to diversify in the 2010s. He landed a recurring role as Agent Mike Ross in the science fiction drama “Fringe” (2008-2013), a series created by J.J. Abrams. “Fringe” proved to be a critical success and a platform for Ashmore to demonstrate a wider range of acting skills, particularly in complex and emotionally demanding scenes. He appeared in 85 episodes of the series.  He also began to take on more character roles in films such as “The Ruins” (2008), a horror film based on the novel by Scott Smith, and “The Quantum Thief” (2013).

In later years, Ashmore has consistently worked in both television and film. He had a recurring role on the Canadian series “Murdoch Mysteries” (2016-2018) and appeared in the action thriller “X-Men: Days of Future Past” (2014), reprising his role as Bobby Drake/Iceman from earlier “X-Men” appearances. He’s also been involved in several television movies and guest appearances in series like “Covert Affairs” and “The Good Witch”. 

As of late 2023, Ashmore remains actively engaged in his acting career, continuing to build upon his established reputation for versatility and commitment to his craft. He resides in Los Angeles with his wife, Renee Ashmore (née Pettitt), whom he married in 2014. They have two children, a son born in 2016 and a daughter born in 2019. While maintaining a relatively private personal life, Shawn Ashmore continues to be a recognizable and respected figure in the entertainment industry.

title: Francisco Urroz (footballer)
text:
Francisco "Pancho" Urroz Ugalde was born on January 27, 1922, in Talca, Chile, a city in the Maule Region known for its agricultural production and burgeoning sporting culture. His father, Juan Urroz, was a railway worker, and his mother, Emilia Ugalde, a homemaker. From a young age, Urroz displayed a natural aptitude for football, playing in the streets and local amateur leagues of Talca. He initially played as a winger but gradually transitioned to a more central defensive role, one where his intelligence, tactical awareness, and robust tackling would become renowned.

Urroz’s professional career began in 1941 with Rangers de Talca, a club representing his hometown. He quickly established himself as a key player, demonstrating a maturity beyond his years. His performances attracted the attention of larger clubs in the capital, Santiago. In 1943, he made the move to Colo-Colo, one of Chile’s most historically significant and popular clubs, based in the Macul district of Santiago. This transfer marked a significant step up in his career and propelled him into the national spotlight.

At Colo-Colo, Urroz blossomed into a commanding central defender, becoming a fixture in the team for the next decade. He played a pivotal role in Colo-Colo’s golden era of the 1940s and 50s. The club, under the guidance of coach Roberto Coll, achieved considerable success, largely built on a strong defensive foundation with Urroz at its heart. He captained Colo-Colo for several seasons, becoming a symbolic leader both on and off the pitch. He participated in and won five Campeonato de Chile titles with Colo-Colo, in 1947, 1953, 1956, 1960, and 1963. These championships solidified his legacy as a club legend. 

His consistent and impressive performances for Colo-Colo also earned him a place in the Chilean national team. He made his debut for *La Roja* on February 20, 1947, in a 1-0 victory against Argentina in Santiago. Urroz quickly became a mainstay in the national side, representing Chile at the 1950 FIFA World Cup in Brazil. He played in all three of Chile’s matches at the tournament: a 2-0 loss to England, a 2-0 loss to Spain, and a 5-2 loss to the United States. Though Chile didn’t advance past the group stage, Urroz gained valuable international experience. 

He continued to represent Chile throughout the 1950s, participating in the South American Championship (the predecessor to the Copa América) on several occasions. He captained the national team on numerous occasions, further cementing his reputation as a respected figure in Chilean football. He earned a total of 36 caps for Chile, a significant number for the time, and scored one goal, a rare feat for a defender. His final international appearance was in 1959.

In 1964, after 21 years with Colo-Colo, Urroz moved to Universidad de Chile, another of Chile’s major clubs.  This transfer was somewhat controversial, given his long association with Colo-Colo, but he played for *La U* for two seasons, adding another Campeonato de Chile title to his collection in 1964. He retired from professional football in 1966 at the age of 44.

Following his playing career, Urroz remained involved in football, primarily as a coach. He managed several clubs in Chile, including Unión Española and Deportes La Serena, but never achieved the same level of success he had as a player. He was known as a disciplinarian and a tactically astute manager. 

Francisco Urroz passed away on August 24, 1993, in Santiago, Chile, at the age of 71, after a prolonged illness. He is remembered as one of the greatest defenders in Chilean football history, a symbol of dedication, leadership, and sporting integrity. His name remains synonymous with Colo-Colo’s golden age and his contribution to Chilean football is widely acknowledged and celebrated. He is often cited as an example of a player who embodied the spirit of the game.

title: Lodewicus du Plessis
text:
Lodewicus Theodorus du Plessis was born on February 28, 1886, in Utrecht, in the Orange River Colony (now Free State province, South Africa). His parents were Willem Johannes du Plessis, a farmer, and Johanna Petronella van der Merwe. He received his early education at Grey College in Bloemfontein, a prominent school known for its academic rigor. He continued his studies at Victoria College (later University of Stellenbosch) where he excelled in languages, eventually obtaining a Master of Arts degree in 1908. This early exposure to linguistics would profoundly shape his future career.

Du Plessis initially pursued a career in education, becoming a teacher at Grey College in 1909, and later at the Boys’ High School in Pretoria in 1911. However, his true calling lay in the burgeoning field of Afrikaans language development and standardization. At the time, Afrikaans was not fully recognised as a distinct language, but rather considered a dialect of Dutch.  A significant movement was underway to establish Afrikaans as a separate, codified language with its own grammar and vocabulary. 

In 1914, Du Plessis joined the editorial staff of the *Woordeboek van die Afrikaanse Taal* (Dictionary of the Afrikaans Language) project, a monumental undertaking spearheaded by the Suid-Afrikaanse Akademie vir Taal en Letterkunde (South African Academy for Language and Literature), established in 1906. He quickly rose through the ranks, becoming the editor-in-chief in 1921, a position he held with dedication for the next thirty-five years, until his retirement in 1956.

The *Woordeboek van die Afrikaanse Taal* was not a typical dictionary compiled by lexicographers studying existing written texts. Instead, it was a ‘collection dictionary’ -  meaning it aimed to gather words and usages directly from the spoken language and existing written sources across the diverse Afrikaans-speaking communities of South Africa.  Du Plessis oversaw a network of approximately 800 fieldworkers, often local schoolteachers and ministers, who systematically collected words, phrases, idioms, and proverbs from across the country, sending them to the editorial office in Pretoria. 

This process was incredibly laborious.  Each entry, often written on a separate slip of paper, had to be meticulously checked for accuracy, meaning, and regional variations.  The dictionary was published in fascicles (small sections) beginning in 1925, and continued incrementally over decades.  Du Plessis’s leadership was critical in navigating the complex task of defining and standardizing a language that was evolving rapidly and had no established written norms. He championed a pragmatic approach, favouring usage over prescriptive rules.  His decisions regarding grammar and vocabulary were hugely influential in shaping modern Afrikaans. 

Beyond his work on the dictionary, Du Plessis was a prolific writer and researcher. He published numerous articles on Afrikaans grammar, etymology, and history. He authored “A Short History of Afrikaans” (1944), a still-referenced work, and contributed extensively to the *Tydskrif vir Geesteswetenskappe* (Journal for the Humanities), the academic publication of the Suid-Afrikaanse Akademie. He was elected a fellow of the Academy in 1927, and served as its president from 1947 to 1949. 

He was married to Maria Elizabeth de Wet, and they had two daughters.  Throughout his career, Du Plessis remained committed to the principle of inclusivity, striving to represent the diverse dialects and voices within the Afrikaans-speaking community. He firmly believed that a standardized Afrikaans should be rooted in the lived experience of its speakers.


Lodewicus du Plessis passed away on October 16, 1966, in Pretoria, at the age of 80.  The *Woordeboek van die Afrikaanse Taal*, though still incomplete at the time of his death (and still being added to today), stands as a lasting testament to his dedication and scholarship, widely considered his most significant accomplishment. He is remembered as a pivotal figure in establishing Afrikaans as a modern, recognized language and a cornerstone of South African cultural identity.

title: Shane Fontayne
text:
Shane Fontayne was born Shane Michael Fontayne on February 28, 1973, in Melbourne, Australia. His father, Bruce Fontayne, was a highly respected session musician, playing guitar for numerous Australian artists including John Farnham and Kylie Minogue, and his mother, Lynette, was a professional singer. This musical upbringing heavily influenced Fontayne’s early development; he began learning piano at the age of five, switching to guitar by age eight. He attended high school at Camberwell High School in Melbourne, but music quickly became his primary focus, leading him to leave school before completing his final year.

Fontayne’s professional music career began in the early 1990s, initially playing in various cover bands around Melbourne’s pub and club circuit. He quickly gained a reputation as a versatile and technically proficient guitarist. In 1994, he joined the band Pearly, fronted by singer-songwriter Rebecca Barnard. Pearly released two albums, *Corner Store* in 1996 and *Supernatural* in 1998, achieving moderate success on the Australian alternative rock scene. Fontayne’s guitar work was integral to Pearly's sound, showcasing a blend of rock, blues, and country influences. 

A significant turning point came in 1999 when Fontayne joined the band Powderfinger. He replaced original guitarist Darren Middleton, who departed to focus on his own solo work. Powderfinger, already established as one of Australia’s most successful rock acts, had released three albums prior to Fontayne’s arrival. He debuted on their fourth studio album, *Odyssey Number Five* released in 2000, which achieved double platinum certification in Australia within weeks of its release. This album, and the subsequent tours, cemented Fontayne’s position as a prominent figure in Australian rock music.

Throughout his 18-year tenure with Powderfinger, Fontayne contributed significantly to the band’s songwriting and arrangements, alongside members Bernard Fanning, John Collins, Ian Haug, and Darin Osborne. He co-wrote several well-known tracks, including "Like a Dog" and "Free," both featured on the 2003 album *Vulture Street*, which debuted at number one on the ARIA charts and went on to achieve six times platinum status. Powderfinger continued to release commercially and critically acclaimed albums under Fontayne’s contribution, including *Dream Days at the Hotel Existence* (2007) and *Golden Rule* (2009), both reaching number one on the Australian album charts. The band won multiple ARIA Awards during this period, including Best Rock Album in 2004 for *Vulture Street* and again in 2007 for *Dream Days at the Hotel Existence*.

Fontayne's guitar style is characterized by its clarity, melodic sensibility, and his ability to seamlessly blend different genres. He is known for his use of both Fender and Gibson guitars, often employing a combination of clean and overdriven tones. He was consistently recognized as one of Australia's leading guitarists, appearing in numerous “best guitarist” polls in magazines like *Guitar Australia*.

In November 2010, Fontayne announced his departure from Powderfinger, citing a desire to explore other musical avenues and spend more time with his family. The band went on hiatus shortly after. Following his exit, Fontayne focused on session work, production, and his own solo projects. He collaborated with various artists, including Tim Rogers and Katie Noonan, and established himself as a sought-after producer at his private studio in Melbourne.

In 2016, Fontayne formed the band The Black Armada, releasing their debut album *Songs to Hum and Die To* in 2017. The album showcased a darker, more experimental side to his songwriting and guitar playing. He continues to work as a session musician, producer, and songwriter, maintaining a relatively low profile compared to his time with Powderfinger. He is married and has two children. While not actively touring extensively, Fontayne remains involved in the Australian music scene, occasionally performing at select events and continuing to contribute his talents to a diverse range of projects.

title: Ameyaw Debrah
text:
Ameyaw Debrah was born on October 26, 1988, in Accra, Ghana, to Mr. and Mrs. Debrah. His father was a businessman and his mother a teacher, providing a relatively stable middle-class upbringing. He attended Achimota School, a prestigious co-educational boarding school in Accra, completing his secondary education in 2006. While at Achimota, he developed a keen interest in writing, initially focusing on poetry and short stories. He was actively involved in the school’s literary societies and debate clubs, honing his communication skills.

Debrah’s foray into journalism began almost accidentally during his first year at Kwame Nkrumah University of Science and Technology (KNUST) in Kumasi, where he was studying Business Administration, starting in 2007. He initially wrote for the university’s online student portal, covering campus events and student life. Recognizing a gap in accessible entertainment news coverage in Ghana, Debrah launched his blog, AmeyawDebrah.com, in February 2008. Initially, the blog was a hobby, a space for him to share gossip, music reviews, and interviews with emerging Ghanaian artists. He self-taught web design and content management, learning through online tutorials and experimentation. 

The blog quickly gained traction, largely due to Debrah’s diligent reporting and ability to break stories first. He focused on the Ghanaian entertainment industry, covering events, artist profiles, and controversies with a fresh, youthful perspective. By 2009, AmeyawDebrah.com had become a significant source of entertainment news in Ghana, attracting a substantial readership and establishing Debrah as a rising voice in the media landscape. He combined his university studies with increasingly demanding work on the blog, often dedicating evenings and weekends to content creation.

In 2010, Debrah graduated from KNUST with a Bachelor of Science degree in Business Administration, but rather than pursuing a traditional career in business, he committed himself fully to journalism and his online platform. This decision proved pivotal. He expanded the scope of his reporting, focusing more on celebrity interviews and exclusive content. He secured exclusive interviews with several popular Ghanaian musicians, actors and personalities, including Sarkodie, Becca, and Yvonne Okoro, further bolstering his credibility and audience. 

He began diversifying his income streams, securing advertising revenue from brands eager to reach his growing audience. Recognizing the need to adapt to changing media consumption habits, Debrah embraced social media, establishing a strong presence on platforms like Twitter and Facebook. In 2012, he began contributing articles to established Ghanaian news outlets like *Graphic Showbiz*, further broadening his reach and professional network. 

In 2014, Debrah received a nomination for the Radio and Television Personality (RTP) Awards’ Blog of the Year category, a significant recognition of his work.  He continued to refine his interviewing skills, becoming known for his direct, yet respectful, questioning style. He also began to offer consultancy services to PR companies and artists looking to enhance their media presence. 

Throughout the 2010s and into the 2020s, Ameyaw Debrah remained a consistent and influential force in Ghanaian entertainment journalism. He consistently adapted to the changing digital landscape, expanding his online presence and experimenting with new formats like video content. In 2018, he launched a YouTube channel featuring interviews and behind-the-scenes footage. 

As of late 2023, Ameyaw Debrah continues to operate AmeyawDebrah.com and actively engages with his audience across multiple social media platforms. He has transitioned from being solely a blogger to a multifaceted media personality, frequently appearing as a pundit on television and radio shows discussing entertainment industry trends. He remains a prominent figure in shaping the narrative surrounding Ghanaian entertainment, and a key influencer for emerging artists within the country. He has mentored several young journalists, encouraging them to embrace digital platforms and ethical reporting practices.

title: Cleopatra
text:
Cleopatra VII Philopator, the last active ruler of the Ptolemaic Kingdom of Egypt, was born in Alexandria in 69 BCE. She was a member of the Macedonian Greek dynasty founded by Ptolemy I Soter, a companion of Alexander the Great, who took control of Egypt after Alexander’s death in 323 BCE. Cleopatra’s father was Ptolemy XII Auletes, and her mother’s identity is debated, though most scholars believe it was likely Cleopatra V Tryphaena, his sister. She had three siblings: Ptolemy XIII, Arsinoe IV, and Ptolemy XIV.

Cleopatra received a comprehensive education, unusually for women of her time, learning multiple languages including Egyptian – a skill that distinguished her from most of her predecessors who primarily spoke Greek. This ability to converse directly with Egyptian priests and dignitaries fostered a stronger connection with the native population.  She also studied mathematics, philosophy, diplomacy, and astronomy.  

Ptolemy XII died in 51 BCE, naming Cleopatra and her brother Ptolemy XIII as joint rulers.  Almost immediately, conflict arose between the siblings. Ptolemy XIII, influenced by his advisors, particularly the eunuch Pothinus, moved to oust Cleopatra. By 48 BCE, she had been forced to flee Alexandria and raise an army in Syria.  

This internal struggle coincided with the Roman civil war between Julius Caesar and Pompey the Great. Pompey arrived in Egypt seeking refuge after his defeat at the Battle of Pharsus in 48 BCE, but was assassinated by Ptolemy XIII’s advisors, hoping to gain favour with Caesar. Caesar arrived in Alexandria in 48 BCE and, becoming embroiled in the Egyptian succession dispute, favoured Cleopatra.  Legend recounts she had herself smuggled into Caesar’s presence, rolled in a carpet, to appeal to him directly.  

Caesar sided with Cleopatra, defeating Ptolemy XIII’s forces in a series of battles, culminating in the Battle of the Nile in 47 BCE, where Ptolemy XIII drowned. Cleopatra was restored to the throne, and she co-ruled with her younger brother Ptolemy XIV.  In 47 BCE, she gave birth to Ptolemy Caesar, known as Caesarion, widely believed to be Caesar’s son.  

Caesar and Cleopatra spent several months together in Egypt before Caesar left in 47 BCE to deal with further conflicts in the Roman world. She followed him to Rome in 46 BCE with Caesarion, residing in one of his villas. Caesar’s assassination on March 15, 44 BCE, forced Cleopatra to return to Egypt. Ptolemy XIV died shortly after, likely poisoned by Cleopatra, allowing her to install Caesarion as her co-ruler.

Following Caesar's death, the Roman world was again thrown into turmoil, this time between Mark Antony, Octavian (Caesar’s adopted son), and Lepidus, forming the Second Triumvirate.  Antony summoned Cleopatra to Tarsus in 41 BCE to answer questions about her loyalty.  She arrived in a lavish display of wealth and power, captivating Antony.  

Antony and Cleopatra began a romantic and political alliance. They spent the winter of 41-40 BCE in Alexandria, and she bore him three children: twins Cleopatra Selene II and Alexander Helios in 40 BCE, and Ptolemy Philadelphus in 36 BCE.  Antony’s political decisions increasingly favoured Cleopatra and her children, including granting them territories in the eastern Mediterranean. This, coupled with his public displays of affection for Cleopatra and his divorce from Octavian’s sister Octavia, enraged Octavian.

The escalating tensions culminated in the Battle of Actium in 31 BCE.  Antony and Cleopatra’s combined naval forces were decisively defeated by Octavian’s fleet.  They retreated to Egypt, where Octavian pursued them.  

In 30 BCE, with Octavian’s forces closing in on Alexandria, Antony, falsely believing Cleopatra to be dead, fell on his sword.  Cleopatra, after attempting negotiations with Octavian, committed suicide, traditionally believed to be by allowing an asp (Egyptian cobra) to bite her, on August 12, 30 BCE.  She was 39 years old.  Caesarion was executed on Octavian’s orders shortly after. Egypt became a Roman province, marking the end of the Ptolemaic dynasty and the final chapter of ancient Egyptian independence.

title: Ana Cláudia Bolzan
text:
Ana Cláudia Bolzan was born on July 23, 1963, in Porto Alegre, Rio Grande do Sul, Brazil. Her parents, Heitor Bolzan and Iara de Oliveira Bolzan, were both physicians, a background that significantly influenced her own path. Growing up in a household dedicated to medicine instilled in her a strong interest in science and healthcare from a young age. She completed her primary and secondary education at Colégio Nossa Senhora da Medalha Miraculosa in Porto Alegre, consistently demonstrating academic excellence.

Bolzan pursued her medical degree at the Universidade Federal do Rio Grande do Sul (UFRGS), graduating in 1986. She immediately began specializing in cardiology, completing her residency at the Instituto de Cardiologia de Porto Alegre (ICPA) in 1990.  During her residency, she became particularly fascinated with the field of cardiac electrophysiology, the study of the heart's electrical system and the basis for arrhythmias. This specialization would become the cornerstone of her career. 

In 1991, she undertook a postdoctoral fellowship in cardiac electrophysiology at the Hospital das Clínicas da Faculdade de Medicina da Universidade de São Paulo (HCFMUSP), working under the guidance of Professor José Carlos Nicolau. This experience broadened her expertise and introduced her to advanced techniques in the diagnosis and treatment of heart rhythm disorders. She then spent two years, from 1992 to 1994, at the University of Pennsylvania in Philadelphia, USA, as a research fellow in the electrophysiology laboratory of Dr. Arthur J. Moss, a leading figure in the field of inherited arrhythmias. During this period, she focused on the genetic basis of Long QT syndrome and sudden cardiac death. 

Returning to Brazil in 1994, Bolzan joined the Instituto de Cardiologia de Porto Alegre, where she remained throughout her career. She rapidly ascended within the institution, becoming a staff cardiologist and eventually the Coordinator of the Arrhythmia Unit.  Her research focused intensely on inherited cardiac arrhythmias, particularly Long QT syndrome, Brugada syndrome, and catecholaminergic polymorphic ventricular tachycardia (CPVT).  She was instrumental in establishing a comprehensive genetic testing program for these conditions in Brazil, significantly improving diagnostic capabilities and patient care.

Bolzan’s contributions to the field are marked by over 200 peer-reviewed publications in prestigious international journals like *Circulation*, *Journal of the American College of Cardiology*, and *Heart Rhythm*. She authored and co-authored numerous chapters in cardiology textbooks and presented her research at major international conferences. A significant achievement was her role in identifying and characterizing novel genetic mutations responsible for inherited arrhythmias in the Brazilian population, contributing to a greater understanding of the genetic diversity of these conditions globally.
