In 2008, she was elected to the Brazilian National Academy of Medicine, a prestigious honor recognizing her scientific achievements.  She also served as President of the Brazilian Society of Cardiology (SBC) from 2017 to 2019, the first woman to hold the position in the society’s history. During her presidency, she championed initiatives to improve cardiovascular health across Brazil, focusing on preventative measures and access to advanced cardiac care.  She was a passionate advocate for women in cardiology, actively promoting mentorship and leadership opportunities for female colleagues.

Beyond her clinical and research work, Ana Cláudia Bolzan was a dedicated educator, mentoring numerous young cardiologists and researchers. She held a professorship at UFRGS, lecturing on cardiology and electrophysiology.  She also supervised countless medical students and residents. 

Ana Cláudia Bolzan passed away unexpectedly on November 26, 2023, in Porto Alegre, at the age of 60, following a sudden illness. Her death was met with widespread grief within the Brazilian cardiology community and internationally. She left behind a legacy of scientific innovation, clinical excellence, and dedication to improving the lives of patients with heart rhythm disorders. She is survived by her husband, Dr. Eduardo Krieger, also a cardiologist, and their two children.

title: Evgeny Shalunov
text:
Evgeny Nikolaevich Shalunov was born on April 17, 1940, in the village of Plotnikovo, Kirov Oblast, Russian SFSR, then part of the Soviet Union. His father, Nikolai Pavlovich Shalunov, worked as a mechanic, and his mother, Klavdiya Ivanovna Shalunova, was a collective farm worker. This rural upbringing significantly influenced his later artistic themes, frequently depicting the lives and landscapes of the Russian countryside. He demonstrated artistic talent from a young age, sketching and drawing constantly, and received initial artistic instruction at a local art school in Kirov.

In 1957, Shalunov moved to Leningrad (now Saint Petersburg) and entered the Leningrad Higher School of Industrial Art, studying decorative and applied arts for three years. This foundational training provided him with skills in design and craftsmanship, which would later inform his painting style. However, he soon felt a pull towards fine art, specifically painting, and in 1960, he successfully transferred to the Leningrad Institute of Painting, Sculpture and Architecture named after Ilya Repin, the leading art school in the Soviet Union. He studied under prominent instructors like Boris Ioganson and Yuri Neprin-Repin, focusing on easel painting. 

Shalunov graduated from the Repin Institute in 1966, presenting his graduation work, a painting titled “Evening in the Village,” which immediately garnered attention. He joined the Leningrad Union of Artists in the same year, becoming a professional artist and embarking on a career dedicated to depicting the realities of Soviet life, albeit with a growing emphasis on lyrical landscapes and scenes of rural existence. 

Throughout the 1970s and 1980s, Shalunov became a recognized figure within the Leningrad artistic community. He participated in numerous prestigious exhibitions, including the “Autumn” exhibition, considered one of the most important displays of contemporary Soviet art, from 1967 onwards, exhibiting consistently until the late 1980s. He also showed his work in numerous national and international exhibitions, including shows in Bulgaria (1976), Hungary (1979), and East Germany (1981).  His style evolved during this period, moving away from strict socialist realism towards a more nuanced and emotionally resonant portrayal of the Russian landscape and its people. He frequently depicted the Kirov region, returning regularly to paint *en plein air*, capturing the changing seasons and the everyday lives of villagers.  

Shalunov’s work is characterized by a muted palette, often dominated by grays, browns, and ochres, reflecting the often-harsh realities of rural life. He was a master of light and shadow, creating atmospheric scenes that evoke a sense of quiet contemplation. He was particularly adept at depicting water, often featuring rivers and lakes in his paintings.  He wasn't prolific, producing around 150 paintings during his career, but each work demonstrates meticulous attention to detail and a deep emotional connection to his subjects. 

In 1983, Shalunov was awarded the prestigious State Prize of the Russian SFSR for his series of paintings dedicated to the Kirov region. This recognition solidified his position as a leading landscape painter in the Soviet Union.  He was also awarded the title of People’s Artist of the Russian Federation in 1994, a testament to his significant contribution to Russian art.

Following the dissolution of the Soviet Union, Shalunov continued to paint, though his output slowed. He remained committed to his realistic style, resisting the more avant-garde trends emerging in post-Soviet Russia. He devoted time to mentoring young artists, sharing his knowledge and experience.  Evgeny Shalunov died on December 27, 2005, in Saint Petersburg, aged 65. His works are held in numerous museums and private collections throughout Russia and internationally, including the State Russian Museum in Saint Petersburg and regional art museums across Russia.  His legacy rests on his sensitive and evocative portrayals of the Russian countryside and the enduring spirit of its people.

title: Cris Cyborg
text:
Cristiane Justino Venâncio, better known as Cris Cyborg, was born on July 19, 1985, in Curitiba, Paraná, Brazil. Her early life was marked by a significant focus on athleticism, initially pursuing handball and volleyball. However, after witnessing her mother taking self-defense classes, she became interested in martial arts around the age of 15. Initially drawn to kickboxing, she trained under Evandro Whatsappen, quickly demonstrating natural talent. This led to her competing in and winning local kickboxing tournaments. 

By 2005, Justino transitioned to mixed martial arts, training with renowned coaches such as Rudimar Fedrigo. She made her professional MMA debut on September 26, 2005, in Brazil, defeating Eliza Silva via first-round TKO. Her early career saw a rapid ascent with dominant victories in smaller Brazilian promotions like Show Fight and Ring Girls, largely punctuated by her powerful striking and aggressive style. She amassed a record of 12-1, with 11 wins by knockout, before significantly expanding her reach.

In 2008, Cyborg moved to the United States and signed with Strikeforce, a prominent promotion at the time. It was here her career truly began to gain international recognition. She quickly became a force in the women’s featherweight division. On August 15, 2009, she challenged Gina Carano for the inaugural Strikeforce Women's Featherweight Championship. Cyborg defeated Carano via second-round TKO in a highly anticipated matchup, becoming the first female Strikeforce champion. This victory propelled her to mainstream attention, though it was also shadowed by post-fight controversy regarding the weight difference between the two fighters. 

Cyborg continued to defend her Strikeforce title, defeating Jan Finney on June 26, 2010, and Hitomi Akano on December 18, 2010, both by TKO.  A planned fight against Ronda Rousey, which would have been a highly publicized and potentially groundbreaking women's MMA bout, never materialized due to disagreements over weight class and fight terms. 

In 2013, Strikeforce was acquired by the UFC, but a women’s featherweight division did not immediately exist. Cyborg initially competed at bantamweight (135lbs) in the UFC, but struggled to make the weight consistently. After a win over Leslie Smith on May 14, 2016, the UFC created a women’s featherweight division, and Cyborg was crowned the inaugural UFC Women's Featherweight Champion. She solidified her position with a first-round TKO victory over Tonya Evinger on July 29, 2017. She defended the title successfully against Evinger again on September 23, 2017, and Holly Holm on December 30, 2017, both via TKO.

Her reign as UFC champion ended on January 25, 2018, when she lost to Amanda Nunes via unanimous decision in a highly competitive fight at UFC 232. This marked her first defeat since 2005. Following this loss, Cyborg competed in Bellator MMA, signing with the promotion in January 2019.  She quickly captured the Bellator Women's Featherweight Championship on January 25, 2020, defeating Julia Budd via TKO. In a historic cross-promotional fight on November 20, 2021, she faced Arlene Blencowe, winning by first-round TKO, and becoming the only MMA fighter to simultaneously hold championship titles in both the UFC and Bellator.  

Cyborg continued to defend her Bellator title, most recently defeating Sinead Kavanagh on April 22, 2023.  As of late 2023, her professional MMA record stands at 26-2, with 20 wins by knockout.  Throughout her career, Cyborg has been known not only for her striking prowess but also for her advocacy for fighter pay and fair treatment within the sport.  Beyond fighting, she has engaged in various business ventures and remains a prominent figure in the MMA world, continuing to train and compete while advocating for the athletes who follow in her footsteps.

title: Jean Muir (actress)
text:
Jean Muir, born Jessie Marlene Weir on February 8, 1902, in Visalia, California, was an American actress whose career spanned from the silent film era through television in the 1960s. Her parents, James and Mary Weir, were farmers, and Jean was the youngest of three children, with an older brother, James Jr., and sister, Anna. Her early life was marked by a nomadic existence following her father’s agricultural pursuits as the family moved between various Californian towns, including Long Beach and Arcadia. She received her education in public schools and displayed a talent for dramatic performance early on, participating in school plays and amateur theatrical productions. 

Muir’s professional acting career began in 1922, after winning a local beauty contest that led to bit parts and extra work in Hollywood films. Initially, she was under contract with Universal Studios, appearing in uncredited roles in numerous productions. Her early work was largely in Westerns and comedies, and she adopted the stage name Jean Muir, a suggestion from a studio executive who felt her given name lacked memorability. A significant early role came in 1929 with a part in *The Black Pirate*, a swashbuckler starring Douglas Fairbanks, though again, her name wasn’t prominently featured in the credits.

The advent of sound film proved beneficial to Muir. She possessed a clear, articulate speaking voice, which distinguished her from many silent film stars. Throughout the 1930s, she secured increasingly important roles in a variety of genres. She worked steadily for major studios including Paramount, Warner Bros., and RKO, frequently cast as the charming, often sophisticated, “other woman.” Notable films from this period include *The Public Enemy* (1931) alongside James Cagney, *Broadway Bad* (1933) with Joan Blondell, and *Born Reckless* (1933) with John Gilbert.  She appeared in 54 films during the 1930s alone.

Muir’s career reached a peak in the late 1930s and early 1940s. She starred alongside Cary Grant in the screwball comedy *Holiday* (1938), a performance widely considered one of her best. She also appeared in *The Lady in Question* (1940) with Rita Hayworth and *They Dare to Dream* (1941) with Robert Paxton. However, her career suffered a significant setback in 1947 when she was accused of communist sympathies during the Red Scare.  She testified before the House Un-American Activities Committee (HUAC), vehemently denying any involvement in communist organizations. Despite her denials and lack of concrete evidence, she was effectively blacklisted from the film industry. 

The blacklist severely curtailed her film opportunities. She continued to work sporadically in theatre, appearing in regional productions and summer stock.  In the 1950s, she found some work in television, making guest appearances on shows like *Schlitz Playhouse of Stars* and *The Loretta Young Show*.  She returned to feature films in 1964 with a role in *The Americanization of Emily*, her last credited movie appearance. 

Beyond acting, Muir was an accomplished author. In 1970, she published her autobiography, *My Life with Archie*, detailing her marriage to actor Archie Leach, better known as Cary Grant. The book revealed details of their tumultuous relationship, including Grant's struggles with mental health and drug use, causing considerable controversy.  It became a bestseller, offering a candid look behind the glamorous facade of Hollywood.

Jean Muir spent her later years relatively secluded. She married three times – first to writer Robert Riskin in 1932 (divorced 1935), then to Cary Grant in 1942 (divorced 1945), and finally to Walter Leopold in 1947, remaining with him until his death in 1979. She died of cancer on January 24, 1996, at her home in Santa Barbara, California, aged 93.  Her contributions to early Hollywood, and her willingness to speak frankly about her life, left a lasting, if often overlooked, legacy.

title: Deyverson
text:
Deyverson Fernando de Souza, commonly known as Deyverson, was born on February 10, 1991, in Belo Horizonte, Minas Gerais, Brazil. His early life was marked by challenges, growing up in the Vila Pinho neighborhood, an area known for its socio-economic difficulties. Football offered an escape, and he began his youth career at local club Minas Cruiseiro in 2006, demonstrating promising attacking ability from a young age. He remained with Minas Cruiseiro for two years before moving to Ipatinga in 2008, continuing his development in the youth setup.

Deyverson’s professional debut arrived in 2009 with Ipatinga, making his senior appearance in the Campeonato Mineiro. He quickly established himself as a key player for the club, scoring 8 goals in 21 appearances. This attracted the attention of larger clubs, and in January 2010, he transferred to Tombense, also in Minas Gerais. His time at Tombense was relatively short, lasting only a season, but he continued to showcase his goal-scoring prowess, netting 12 goals in 30 games.

A significant step in his career came in 2011 when he signed with Náutico, a club based in Recife, Pernambuco. Here, he played in the Série B, Brazil’s second tier, and contributed 10 goals in 33 appearances, helping Náutico secure promotion to the Série A for the 2012 season. However, his time in the top flight with Náutico was less impactful, and he was loaned out to Portuguesa in São Paulo in January 2013. 

At Portuguesa, Deyverson found a resurgence in form, becoming a prolific scorer in the Série A. He scored 14 goals in 32 matches during the 2013 season, attracting the interest of Palmeiras, one of Brazil’s most prominent clubs. He officially joined Palmeiras in December 2013, marking a high point in his career thus far.

His initial years at Palmeiras were characterized by inconsistency and loan spells. He was loaned back to Portuguesa in 2014, then to Ponte Preta in 2015, where he scored 8 goals in 27 games.  Returning to Palmeiras in 2016, under coach Cuca, Deyverson finally cemented his place in the first team. He played a crucial role in Palmeiras’s successful 2016 campaign, scoring 13 goals in 32 appearances across all competitions, including the winning goal in the Copa do Brasil final against Santos on December 4, 2016, securing Palmeiras's fourth Copa do Brasil title. 

This victory made him a hero amongst the Palmeiras faithful. He continued with Palmeiras until January 2019, accumulating a total of 52 goals in 167 games for the club.  He then transferred to fellow Série A side, Cruzeiro, but his time there was troubled by financial issues at the club and his own disciplinary problems. He scored only 4 goals in 25 appearances for Cruzeiro.

In July 2019, Deyverson moved to Japan, joining J1 League club Kashima Antlers. He played for Kashima Antlers for a year, scoring 5 goals in 19 matches.  He returned to Brazil in August 2020, signing with Ceará.  He had a productive spell with Ceará, scoring 14 goals in 48 appearances.

In December 2022, Deyverson joined Paysandu, a club in the Série C, with the goal of helping them achieve promotion. He was instrumental in their promotion to Série B in 2023, finishing as the top scorer of the Série C with 13 goals.  He continued with Paysandu into the Série B in 2024, but was released in April 2024 following incidents of alleged misconduct and disciplinary issues.  As of late 2024, Deyverson’s future in football remains uncertain, with his career often overshadowed by on-field altercations and disciplinary problems alongside his undeniable goalscoring ability.

title: Charles Allen (jurist)
text:
Charles Allen was born on February 22, 1833, in New Orleans, Louisiana, to Charles and Eliza (née Winston) Allen. His father was a prominent attorney and judge who significantly influenced his early life. The Allen family had deep roots in Louisiana, with ancestors involved in the state’s legal and political history since its early days under French and Spanish rule. Charles Allen’s early education took place in New Orleans, initially under private tutors due to the disruption caused by yellow fever epidemics common in the city. He later attended Jefferson College in St. Louis, Missouri, graduating in 1851. 

Following his college education, Allen returned to New Orleans and began studying law under his father’s tutelage. He was admitted to the Louisiana bar in 1853 at the age of 20 and immediately began practicing law, quickly establishing a reputation for diligence and legal acumen. His practice initially focused on commercial law and maritime cases, reflecting the importance of commerce in New Orleans. The outbreak of the American Civil War in 1861 profoundly impacted Allen’s career. He served as an aide-de-camp to Confederate General David Porter DeLeon during the conflict, although his contributions were largely logistical and administrative rather than directly combat-related. 

After the war, Allen returned to New Orleans to rebuild his legal practice amidst the challenging Reconstruction era. He became involved in the efforts to revise Louisiana’s legal code, heavily influenced by the Napoleonic Code due to the state’s French heritage. In 1879, he was elected as a judge of the District Court for the Parish of Orleans, a position he held for six years. During this time, he became known for his fairness and efficiency, navigating the often-turbulent legal environment of post-Reconstruction Louisiana. 

In 1885, Allen was elevated to the Louisiana Supreme Court, serving as an Associate Justice. He quickly distinguished himself as a leading voice on the bench, particularly in cases involving property rights, contracts, and constitutional law. His opinions were noted for their clarity, thoroughness, and adherence to legal principles. He served as Chief Justice of the Louisiana Supreme Court from 1896 until his retirement in 1911. During his tenure as Chief Justice, he oversaw significant reforms to the court's procedures, aiming to reduce backlogs and improve the administration of justice. He played a key role in establishing a standardized system for reporting court decisions, making Louisiana jurisprudence more accessible.

Allen was also actively involved in legal scholarship. He authored “Louisiana Civil Law,” a comprehensive treatise published in 1892, which became a standard reference work for lawyers practicing in Louisiana. The book meticulously detailed the state’s unique civil code, blending French and common law traditions. This work cemented his status as the foremost authority on Louisiana civil law at the time. He was a member of the Louisiana Law Institute, contributing to the ongoing efforts to modernize and codify the state’s laws.

Beyond his judicial and scholarly pursuits, Allen was a respected figure in New Orleans society. He was a member of several historical and literary societies, including the Louisiana Historical Society. He was also a trustee of Tulane University, supporting its growth as a leading institution of higher learning. 

Charles Allen retired from the bench in 1911 at the age of 78, having served Louisiana’s legal system for over 58 years. He continued to live in New Orleans, remaining active in legal circles and offering counsel to younger attorneys until his death on January 24, 1918, at the age of 84. He is buried in Metairie Cemetery in New Orleans. Allen never married and left no direct descendants. His legacy rests on his significant contributions to Louisiana law, his commitment to judicial integrity, and his enduring scholarship.

title: Ruth Fischer
text:
Ruth Fischer was born Rutha (later Ruth) Weiss on August 26, 1892, in Warsaw, Congress Poland, then part of the Russian Empire. Her parents, Jacob and Miriam Weiss, were both Jewish and politically active, involved in the socialist Bund movement. This early exposure profoundly shaped her life. The family moved to Vienna, Austria-Hungary, in 1905, fleeing increasing political repression in Poland. In Vienna, Ruth quickly became involved in youth socialist organizations, demonstrating a remarkable aptitude for languages and political organization. She mastered German, Yiddish, Polish, Russian, and later English and French. 

By 1912, at age 20, Fischer had joined the Social Democratic Workers’ Party of Austria (SDAPÖ) and became a prominent figure within its youth wing, known as the “Red Guards.” She was a gifted orator and writer, contributing frequently to socialist publications. She became increasingly critical of the party’s moderate leadership, aligning herself with the radical left and advocating for a more revolutionary approach. This led to friction within the party. 

The outbreak of World War I in 1914 significantly altered the political landscape. Fischer opposed the war and actively participated in anti-war activities, facing arrest and imprisonment multiple times. Following the collapse of the Austro-Hungarian Empire in 1918 and the subsequent Austrian Revolution, she played a crucial role in establishing a workers’ council system in Vienna, mirroring the soviets in Russia. She was elected to the Provisional National Assembly in November 1918, becoming one of the first women in Austrian parliament. 

However, Fischer, along with Otto Bauer and Karl Renner, found herself increasingly at odds with the more radical socialist elements, particularly those influenced by the Bolshevik revolution in Russia. In 1919, she became a founding member of the Communist Party of Austria (KPÖ), breaking from the SDAPÖ.  She quickly rose to prominence within the KPÖ, becoming its leading theoretician and spokesperson.  In March 1919, she was a key figure in the short-lived, but significant, Vienna Uprising – an attempt to establish a communist government. The uprising was brutally suppressed by the Austrian government, and Fischer was forced to flee Austria.

Following the suppression of the uprising, Fischer spent the next several years in exile, largely in Germany. She became a leading figure in the Communist Party of Germany (KPD), working closely with Rosa Luxemburg and Karl Liebknecht. After their assassination in January 1919, Fischer became a vocal critic of the KPD’s increasingly dogmatic and Moscow-directed policies, particularly the “March Action” of 1921, which she believed was premature and disastrous. This independent thinking brought her into conflict with the party leadership, especially Ernst Thälmann, who was becoming increasingly loyal to the Comintern under Grigory Zinoviev. 

In 1925, Fischer was expelled from the KPD, accused of “deviationism” and “social-democratic tendencies.” This marked a turning point in her life. She subsequently joined the Left Communist Party of Germany, a small group critical of both social democracy and the Comintern.  She continued to write and analyze political developments, but her influence significantly diminished.  

With the rise of Nazism in Germany, Fischer emigrated to the United States in 1933. She initially struggled to find stable employment, working as a translator and freelance writer.  She eventually found a position as a research associate at the Hoover Institution on War, Revolution and Peace at Stanford University in 1954, where she remained until her retirement in 1967. During her time at the Hoover Institution, she meticulously researched and wrote her magnum opus, *The Struggle for Power in Europe, 1917-1918,* published in 1979, which offered a nuanced and critical analysis of the revolutionary period following World War I. 

Ruth Fischer never returned to Europe. She died on January 27, 1985, in Palo Alto, California, at the age of 92. Despite her early prominence and intellectual contributions to the socialist and communist movements, her independent spirit and willingness to challenge dogma led to her marginalization.  Her work, however, continues to be studied by historians seeking a more complex understanding of the revolutionary era and the internal dynamics of communist movements.

title: Yuyan
text:
Yuyan, born as Shen Shouchun on April 21, 1909, in Nanjing, Jiangsu province, was a prominent Chinese painter renowned for her depictions of horses and landscapes in the traditional *guohua* (national painting) style. Her life spanned a period of immense social and political upheaval in China, significantly influencing both her artistic development and her eventual fate. She was the youngest of five children born to Shen E, a well-respected official in the Qing dynasty government, and Lady Wu, a woman known for her own artistic talents in calligraphy and painting. This upbringing immersed Yuyan in a cultured environment from a young age, fostering her early artistic inclinations.

Yuyan began her formal art training at the age of nine, studying under the tutelage of her mother.  However, a pivotal moment came in 1918 when she became a student of the celebrated painter and calligrapher, Wu Changshuo. Wu, a master of the ‘Jin-Stone School’, profoundly impacted her technique and aesthetic sensibilities, emphasizing bold brushwork and a mastery of ink wash.  She studied with Wu for seven years, developing a deep understanding of traditional Chinese painting principles.  Following Wu’s guidance, she also learned from other masters like Qi Baishi, though her association with him was briefer. 

By the 1930s, Yuyan had begun to establish herself as a professional artist, exhibiting her work in Shanghai and other major cities. Her paintings, particularly those of horses, quickly gained recognition for their dynamic energy and precise anatomical detail.  She moved to Shanghai in 1935, and began teaching art at the Xinhua Academy of Fine Arts, a position she held until 1937. This period also saw her marry Zhang Yuren, a scholar and collector of ancient bronzes, in 1936.  Their marriage provided both emotional and intellectual support throughout her career.

The outbreak of the Second Sino-Japanese War in 1937 forced Yuyan and her husband to flee Shanghai, relocating to the countryside of Sichuan province.  This period, spanning eight years until the end of the war in 1945, proved to be intensely productive. Living amidst the natural beauty of the Sichuan landscape inspired a new focus in her work, alongside the continued depiction of horses.  She extensively studied the local horse breeds, capturing their unique characteristics and spirit.  During the war, she also took on teaching positions to support herself and her husband, further disseminating her artistic knowledge. 

After the war, Yuyan and Zhang Yuren returned to Shanghai. She continued to paint prolifically, holding solo exhibitions in Shanghai (1948) and Beijing (1954).  However, the political climate in China following the Communist Revolution in 1949 significantly impacted her life.  Initially, her art was still appreciated, and she was employed as a professional artist.  However, during the Cultural Revolution (1966-1976), Yuyan, along with many other artists and intellectuals, became a target of persecution.  

Her work was labelled as ‘bourgeois’ and ‘reactionary’, and she was publicly denounced.  She was forced to cease painting and endured significant hardship, including public humiliation and forced labor.  Her husband, Zhang Yuren, died in 1968, a devastating loss that compounded her suffering. The destruction of many of her paintings during this period represents a significant cultural loss.

Following the end of the Cultural Revolution in 1976 and the subsequent rehabilitation of wrongly accused individuals, Yuyan was gradually restored to some degree of recognition.  However, the years of persecution had taken a heavy toll on her health.  She resumed painting, but her output was limited.  Yuyan passed away on November 21, 1993, in Shanghai, at the age of 84.  Today, her surviving works are highly valued by collectors and museums, and she is rightfully remembered as one of the most important Chinese painters of the 20th century, celebrated for her masterful technique and her passionate portrayal of the horse as a symbol of strength and freedom.

title: Joe McGinniss
text:
Joe McGinniss Jr. was born on January 25, 1942, in Scranton, Pennsylvania, the son of Joseph McGinniss Sr., a railway mail clerk, and Mary McGinniss. He grew up in a working-class Irish Catholic family, attending West Scranton High School where he was a standout basketball player, earning a scholarship to Bucknell University in Lewisburg, Pennsylvania. He graduated from Bucknell in 1964 with a Bachelor of Arts degree in English. Following graduation, he served in the U.S. Navy for two years, spending much of his service as a journalist aboard the USS Intrepid, an aircraft carrier. 

McGinniss began his professional journalism career in 1966 at the *Scranton Times*. Within a year, he moved to the *Philadelphia Inquirer*, where he covered the 1968 presidential campaign of Richard Nixon. This experience proved formative, sparking an interest in political reporting and in-depth narrative journalism. In 1970, he joined *Newsday*, quickly becoming a national political reporter. He covered the Watergate scandal extensively, and in 1974, published his first book, *Fatal Vision*, a meticulously researched account of the 1970 murders of the Proctor family in Oshkosh, Wisconsin, committed by Jeffrey MacDonald, a Green Beret doctor. 

*Fatal Vision* was a massive success, spending 35 weeks on the *New York Times* bestseller list and winning the Edgar Award for Best Fact Crime in 1984. The book’s detailed reconstruction of the events and its questioning of MacDonald’s innocence led to a highly publicized legal battle. MacDonald sued McGinniss for libel, a case that lasted for over a decade and ultimately ended with a jury finding McGinniss had not acted with “actual malice” – a key requirement for a successful libel suit by a public figure. The trial, however, significantly impacted McGinniss’s career and finances.

During the 1980s, McGinniss continued writing, publishing *Heroes* (1981), a look at Vietnam veterans, and *Going to Extremes* (1984), detailing his experiences living with a remote Alaskan family. He also taught journalism at Northwestern University and the University of Iowa.  In 1988, he published *Cruel Doubt*, another true crime book focusing on the case of the Menendez brothers, Lyle and Erik, who were convicted of murdering their parents. 

A significant turning point came in 1992 when McGinniss began work on a book about then-Governor of Alaska, Bill Sheffield. Sheffield withdrew his cooperation, and McGinniss then shifted his focus to Sarah Palin, then the mayor of Wasilla, Alaska. He spent three years meticulously researching Palin, culminating in the 2011 publication of *The Rogue: Searching for the Real Sarah Palin*. The book was controversial, presenting a critical and often unflattering portrait of Palin, particularly concerning allegations of past drug use and marital issues. Palin vehemently denied the claims and accused McGinniss of invading her privacy. 

The publication of *The Rogue* was accompanied by further controversy regarding McGinniss’s methods. It was revealed he had created a fictitious persona online, using the name “Joe Sixpack,” to communicate with Palin’s associates and gather information. This raised ethical questions about journalistic practice.  

In his later years, McGinniss continued to write, publishing *Presidential Leadership: Politics and Power, 1956-2008* in 2012 and *Colin Powell: A Political Biography* in 2014. He also maintained a blog where he continued to comment on political and social issues.  Throughout his career, McGinniss was known for his immersive reporting style, often spending extended periods living within the communities he wrote about. 

Joe McGinniss Jr. died on March 9, 2023, at his home in Falmouth, Massachusetts, at the age of 81. He left behind a complex legacy as a groundbreaking, yet controversial, figure in the field of narrative journalism, remembered for his meticulously researched, often provocative, and frequently litigated works.

title: Eric Winter
text:
Eric Winter was born on July 28, 1978, in Laurel, Maryland, to parents Dan and Carol Winter. His father was a former Marine, and his mother worked as a real estate agent. He is of German, English, Irish, and Native American descent. Winter spent his early childhood in Laurel before his family relocated to Orange County, California, when he was ten years old. He attended Villa Park High School in Villa Park, California, graduating in 1996. During his high school years, he was a competitive swimmer and considered pursuing a collegiate athletic career, but ultimately decided to focus on performing arts.

Winter’s initial interest in acting led him to take classes at the Orange County Performing Arts Center. He began his professional career with small roles in television, appearing in episodes of “Days of Our Lives” in 1996, marking his first credited screen appearance. He followed this with guest spots on shows like "Buffy the Vampire Slayer" (1997) and “7th Heaven” (1999). He also secured minor roles in television films, including “The Luck of the Irish” (2001) for Disney Channel, where he played Kyle Johnson, and "The Hot Chick" (2002), though his role was uncredited.

A significant early role came in 2003 when Winter was cast as Rex Brady on “Days of Our Lives,” a character he portrayed on a recurring basis until 2008, appearing in over 200 episodes. This role provided him with consistent work and increased visibility within the television industry. While continuing with "Days of Our Lives," he also took on other projects, including a role in the film “West Side Story” (2003) as a member of the Jets gang. 

The year 2005 saw him appear in the film “Dirty Sexy Boy.”  His career began to broaden in 2008 when he was cast as Liam Moretti in the short-lived ABC drama “Cashmere Mafia.” Though the series was cancelled after one season, it exposed Winter to a wider audience. He then landed a key role as Craig Briggs in the NBC drama “Parenthood” (2010-2011), joining the cast in its second season and appearing in 27 episodes. 

Winter's profile continued to rise with his portrayal of Detective Mark Callan in the Lifetime television film series “The Pregnancy Pact” (2010) and its sequel, “The Pregnancy Pact 2” (2011). He also began to secure more substantial roles in television movies, solidifying his presence as a reliable leading man. 

From 2012 to 2016, Winter played Nash Miranda in the Hallmark Channel series "Witches of East End," a role that allowed him to explore more complex and dramatic material. This series proved to be a significant turning point in his career.  He continued to appear in television films, with projects like “A Christmas Detour” (2015) and “A Christmas Melody” (2017) showcasing his appeal in the holiday movie genre.

In 2018, Winter joined the cast of “Rosewood” as the recurring character of Dr. Sam Kincaid, appearing in 12 episodes.  He has consistently worked in television since, with guest appearances on shows such as “Hawaii Five-0” and “NCIS.” More recently, he took on a recurring role as Roger Grant in the Freeform series "Good Trouble" (2019-2021) and played Detective Jake Morales in the series “The Good Doctor” (2023).

On December 28, 2009, Eric Winter married Roselyn Sánchez, a Puerto Rican actress and model. They have two children: a daughter, Sebella Rose Winter, born in January 2017, and a son, Dylan Heywood Winter, born in December 2019. The family currently resides in Los Angeles, California. Throughout his career, Winter has maintained a consistent work ethic, transitioning successfully between network television, cable, and made-for-television films, establishing himself as a recognizable and versatile actor.

title: Maxime Masson
text:
Maxime Masson was born on February 28, 1886, in Nantes, France, to a family with a strong artistic inclination. His father, Fernand Masson, was a painter and engraver, and his mother, Marie-Rose, was also an artist. This early exposure to the creative world profoundly shaped his life. He received his initial artistic training from his father, learning foundational skills in drawing and painting. He attended the École des Beaux-Arts in Nantes, then moved to Paris in 1908 to further his studies at the Académie Julian, a renowned private art school. However, he quickly became disillusioned with the traditional academic approach, finding it restrictive and unsuited to his emerging artistic vision.

By 1909, Masson was gravitating towards more avant-garde circles in Paris, frequenting artist gatherings and becoming fascinated by the work of artists like Henri Matisse and Pablo Picasso. He was particularly drawn to Fauvism, the bold use of colour and expressive distortion that characterized the movement. In 1910, he exhibited with the Salon d'Automne, a significant milestone marking his entry into the Parisian art scene. This period saw him experimenting with various styles, including Cubism, though he never fully adhered to any single movement, preferring to synthesize elements from different sources.

World War I significantly impacted Masson’s life and art. He was mobilized in 1914 and served as a stretcher-bearer, experiencing the horrors of trench warfare firsthand. These experiences profoundly affected him, instilling a deep sense of trauma and influencing the dark, often disturbing imagery that would appear in his later work. He was severely wounded in 1916, and his convalescence marked a turning point in his artistic development. 

Following the war, in 1919, Masson co-founded the influential art journal *La Liberté*. It became a platform for disseminating Dadaist and Surrealist ideas, and he became increasingly involved with the Surrealist movement, officially joining in 1924 under the guidance of André Breton.  He contributed to several key Surrealist texts and exhibitions, experimenting with automatic drawing – a technique aimed at accessing the subconscious mind – and developing a unique style characterized by biomorphic forms and a sense of psychological turbulence.  His artwork from this period often explored themes of violence, sexuality, and the anxieties of the modern age.

Throughout the 1930s, Masson continued to develop his distinct style, moving away from the strict tenets of Surrealism while retaining its emphasis on the subconscious. He began to incorporate more mythological and historical references into his work, often depicting scenes of violent conflict and human suffering.  In 1940, with the outbreak of World War II and the Nazi occupation of France, Masson fled to the United States, settling in New York City.

In America, he taught at several institutions, including the New School for Social Research from 1941 to 1943, and Black Mountain College in North Carolina from 1948 to 1951. He exerted a considerable influence on a generation of American artists, including Jackson Pollock and Willem de Kooning, introducing them to Surrealist techniques and encouraging experimentation with abstract expressionism.  His influence is often cited as a crucial element in the development of Abstract Expressionism.

Masson’s later years were spent traveling and working in various locations, including Mexico and Italy. He received significant recognition for his contributions to modern art, with major exhibitions of his work held in museums around the world. He remained a prolific artist until his death on April 14, 1973, in Paris, aged 87. His legacy lies in his powerful and often unsettling imagery, his contribution to the Surrealist movement, and his important role in fostering the development of American Abstract Expressionism.  His work can be found in prominent collections including the Museum of Modern Art in New York, the Tate Modern in London, and the Centre Pompidou in Paris.

title: Bobby Thomson
text:
Robert Paul Thomson was born on October 31, 1923, in Jacksonville, Florida, the youngest of five children born to Scottish immigrants, William and Margaret Thomson. His father worked as a boilermaker, and the family moved to Staten Island, New York City, when Bobby was still a young boy, settling in the West Brighton neighborhood. Though small in stature, standing only 5’9” and around 160 pounds, Thomson displayed a natural athletic ability, initially excelling in basketball and baseball at Port Richmond High School. He didn’t begin to focus seriously on baseball until his junior year, but quickly became a standout player, attracting the attention of major league scouts.

Thomson signed with the New York Giants in 1942, receiving a bonus of $100, though his professional debut was delayed due to World War II. He served in the U.S. Navy from 1943 to 1945, spending much of his time at the Norfolk Naval Training Station, where he also played baseball with a service team alongside future stars like Yogi Berra. Upon his discharge in January 1946, he joined the Jersey City Giants, a Giants farm club in the International League, where he honed his skills. 

He made his Major League debut with the Giants on April 23, 1946, at the age of 22, playing third base. However, it took a few years for Thomson to establish himself as a regular. He bounced between positions - third base, shortstop, and the outfield – before finding a consistent role in center field.  He was a consistent, if not spectacular, hitter in his early years, displaying a good eye and solid contact. His breakout season came in 1948, when he batted .292 with 22 home runs and 82 RBIs, establishing him as a key player for the Giants.

Over the next few years, Thomson became a cornerstone of the Giants’ lineup, known for his clutch hitting and competitive spirit. He averaged over 25 home runs a season from 1949-1953. He was a five-time All-Star (1949-1953) and finished in the top ten of the National League MVP voting three times (1949, 1951, 1953).  However, his career is overwhelmingly defined by a single moment: "The Shot Heard 'Round the World."

On October 3, 1951, during a National League playoff game against the Brooklyn Dodgers at the Polo Grounds, Thomson hit a three-run home run in the bottom of the ninth inning off Ralph Branca, dramatically winning the pennant for the Giants. The score was tied 4-4, with two runners on base.  The home run instantly became one of the most iconic moments in baseball history, securing the Giants’ place in the World Series against the New York Yankees.  The Giants would lose the World Series to the Yankees in six games.

Thomson continued to play for the Giants until June 1956, when he was traded to the Kansas City Athletics. He played with the Athletics for a season and a half before being traded to the Chicago White Sox in December 1957. He finished his major league career with the White Sox in 1958. Over his 15-year career, he batted .275 with 264 home runs and 873 RBIs in 1,533 games.

After retiring as a player, Thomson pursued a career in broadcasting. He worked as a color commentator for the New York Yankees (1960-1966) and the Montreal Expos (1972-1973). He also spent time as a scout for the Giants.  

Throughout his life, Thomson remained a popular figure, frequently appearing at baseball events and signing autographs.  He battled throat cancer in the 1990s, but continued to make public appearances.  He was inducted into the New York State Baseball Hall of Fame in 1987.  Bobby Thomson passed away on August 16, 2010, in Mentor, Ohio, at the age of 86. His legacy remains inextricably linked to that monumental home run, forever etching his name in baseball lore.

title: Hoshiar Singh Dahiya
text:
Hoshiar Singh Dahiya was born on February 17, 1927, in Kharkhari village, Sonipat district, Haryana, India, to Chhotu Ram Dahiya and Muskan Devi. His family belonged to the Dahiya Khap, a prominent Jat community known for its agricultural background and historical warrior traditions. Kharkhari, at the time of his birth, was a relatively small village under British rule, and Hoshiar Singh’s early life was deeply rooted in the rural customs and challenges of pre-independence India. He received his primary education in Kharkhari and later attended the Jat High School in Gohana, completing his matriculation in 1944. Even as a young man, he demonstrated a strong physique and a natural aptitude for wrestling, a popular sport in the region. 

Dahiya’s formal training in wrestling began under the tutelage of Master Chandiram, a renowned guru in the Gohana area. He quickly excelled, demonstrating exceptional strength, agility, and a strategic approach to the sport. However, his wrestling career was interrupted by the political upheaval surrounding India’s independence in 1947. He briefly joined the Indian National Army (INA) led by Subhas Chandra Bose, though his involvement was short-lived due to the INA’s disbandment. 

Following independence, Dahiya joined the Punjab Police in 1948, initially as a constable. He continued to hone his wrestling skills alongside his police duties, participating in and winning numerous local and regional competitions. Recognizing his potential, the Punjab Police encouraged his participation in national and international events. His breakthrough came in 1955 when he won the Bharat Kesari title, a prestigious national wrestling championship, held in Delhi. This victory significantly raised his profile and opened doors for further opportunities.

Dahiya’s international career began in 1957, when he was selected to represent India at the World Wrestling Championships in Istanbul, Turkey. He competed in the freestyle wrestling category (79 kg) and secured a silver medal, becoming the first Indian wrestler to win a medal at a World Championship. This achievement was a watershed moment for Indian wrestling, inspiring a new generation of athletes. He followed this success with a gold medal at the 1958 Asian Games in Tokyo, Japan, again in the 79 kg freestyle category. This victory cemented his status as a leading wrestler on the Asian continent.

The pinnacle of Dahiya’s career arrived at the 1960 Summer Olympics in Rome, Italy. Competing in the 79 kg freestyle wrestling, he fought valiantly, defeating several formidable opponents. In the final bout, he faced Musaev of the Soviet Union, a highly regarded wrestler. Dahiya lost the final match, but his performance was enough to earn him the silver medal, making him the first Indian Olympic medalist in wrestling. This was a momentous occasion for India, marking the country’s first individual Olympic medal since independence.

Throughout his career, Dahiya was known for his strong grip, powerful takedowns, and unwavering determination. He remained an active competitor until 1963, winning numerous national and international accolades.  In 1963, he was awarded the Arjuna Award, India's second-highest sporting honour, recognizing his contribution to Indian sports.  

After retiring from competitive wrestling, Hoshiar Singh Dahiya remained connected to the sport. He served as a wrestling coach with the Punjab Police and dedicated himself to promoting wrestling among young people. He also engaged in social work, focusing on the development of his village and the welfare of the farming community. He was deeply respected within the Jat community for his achievements and his commitment to his roots.  Hoshiar Singh Dahiya passed away on July 23, 2018, in Kharkhari village at the age of 91, leaving behind a legacy as a pioneering wrestler and a national hero. His achievements continue to inspire generations of Indian wrestlers and remain a source of pride for his community and the nation.

title: James Tyrrell
text:
James Tyrrell was born around 1474, likely at Gipping, Suffolk, England, though precise records of his birth are scarce. He came from a family with established, though not particularly high-ranking, connections within East Anglian society. His father, Sir John Tyrrell of Gipping, was a landowner and served as a Member of Parliament for Suffolk in 1491. James’s mother was Joan, daughter of Sir Thomas Playters, another Suffolk gentleman. This lineage provided James with a solid grounding in local politics and access to opportunities within the Tudor court.

Tyrrell’s early education remains largely undocumented, but it is presumed he received training in arms and courtly manners befitting his status. By the late 1490s, he was in the service of Edward Stafford, 3rd Duke of Buckingham. Buckingham was a powerful and ambitious figure, a cousin of King Henry VII and a potential rival for the throne. Tyrrell quickly became a trusted member of Buckingham’s household, managing his estates and acting as his military captain. He was appointed Constable of Windsor Castle in 1501, a significant position indicating Buckingham’s favour and Tyrrell’s administrative capabilities. 

Buckingham’s ambition ultimately led to his downfall. In 1521, he was accused of treason, specifically plotting to overthrow Henry VII. The evidence against him was largely based on the testimony of informers, and the precise nature of the alleged plot remains debated by historians. However, Tyrrell became a central figure in the accusations. He was alleged to have contracted with Dominican friars to use necromancy to predict Buckingham’s future reign, and crucially, to have ordered the murder of the Duke’s young ward, Henry Stafford, 1st Earl of Wiltshire, in 1509.  The death of Henry Stafford removed a legitimate male heir who could challenge Buckingham’s claims. 

Tyrrell vehemently denied the charges, maintaining his loyalty to the crown. However, his close association with Buckingham and the damning testimony proved insurmountable. He was arrested and tried for treason in May 1521. The trial, held at Westminster Hall, was swift. The prosecution presented witnesses claiming Tyrrell had actively participated in the conspiracy and had commissioned the murder of the Earl of Wiltshire, suggesting he had paid a sum of £800 (a substantial amount at the time) for the deed.  Despite his defence, Tyrrell was found guilty. 

On May 26th, 1521, James Tyrrell was executed on Tower Hill, London. He was beheaded, a method reserved for those of noble birth. Before his execution, he reportedly maintained his innocence, proclaiming he would rather die than falsely accuse another. His attainder, passed by Parliament shortly after his death, stripped him of his lands and titles.

The legacy of James Tyrrell is inextricably linked to the Buckingham conspiracy. For centuries, he was largely remembered as a ruthless murderer and a traitor. However, historical interpretations have shifted. Modern historians question the validity of the evidence presented against him, suggesting he may have been a scapegoat used by Henry VII to eliminate a powerful rival and consolidate his own power. Some scholars argue the accusations were fabricated or exaggerated to justify Buckingham’s execution and eliminate potential claimants to the throne. 

Following his execution, Tyrrell’s lands were confiscated by the crown. His family attempted to petition for the restoration of their estates, but were largely unsuccessful. The Tyrrell family continued to reside in Suffolk, though their influence and wealth were significantly diminished.  The events surrounding Tyrrell’s life and death continue to be a subject of historical debate, highlighting the complexities of power, ambition, and justice in the early Tudor period. His story serves as a cautionary tale about the dangers of association with powerful figures and the precariousness of favour within the royal court.

title: Blanca Errázuriz
text:
Blanca Errázuriz Richards, a prominent Chilean architect, was born in Santiago, Chile on February 28, 1928, into a family deeply rooted in Chilean history and politics. Her father, Jorge Errázuriz Alderete, was a lawyer and diplomat, and her mother, Blanca Richards Lyon, came from a family involved in mining. This background instilled in her a sense of social responsibility and a connection to the nation’s development which would heavily influence her professional life. She received her early education at the Liceo Javiera Carrera, a prestigious girls’ school in Santiago, and later entered the Pontificia Universidad Católica de Chile in 1946 to study architecture. 

Errázuriz was one of only three women in a class of over sixty students, facing considerable prejudice in a field largely dominated by men. She completed her degree in 1952, graduating with honors and receiving the prestigious Municipal Award for her final thesis project.  Immediately following graduation, she began working with the renowned architect Ricardo Tironi, a pivotal figure in the modernization of Chilean architecture and a proponent of integrating local materials and traditions. This apprenticeship, lasting until 1956, proved foundational to her developing design philosophy.

In 1956, Errázuriz established her own architectural practice, initially focusing on residential commissions. However, her career trajectory quickly expanded.  She became deeply involved in the national housing program initiated under President Jorge Alessandri Rodríguez in the early 1960s, known as the *Comité de Mejoramiento Urbano* (Committee for Urban Improvement). This program aimed to address the severe housing shortages in rapidly urbanizing Chile. Errázuriz didn't simply design houses; she pioneered a participatory approach, working directly with the future residents to understand their needs and integrate them into the design process. 

Her work during this period, particularly the *Villa San Rafael* in Peñalolén, Santiago (completed 1964), became a landmark example of socially conscious housing.  The project, encompassing 160 houses, was innovative for its use of prefabricated concrete panels – a cost-effective solution – and its emphasis on creating community spaces and fostering a sense of ownership amongst the residents.  It was significantly more than just providing shelter; she aimed to build neighborhoods.  

During the government of Salvador Allende (1970-1973), Errázuriz’s commitment to social housing intensified.  She served as Director of Housing and Urban Planning (SERVIU) for the Metropolitan Region of Santiago from 1971 to 1973.  In this role, she oversaw the construction of thousands of housing units, prioritizing affordable and dignified dwellings for the working class.  She also championed innovative financing mechanisms and community-based construction techniques. This period saw the initiation of several large-scale housing projects, including the *Unidad Vecinal El Volcán* in La Granja, which, though not fully completed due to the 1973 coup, remains a testament to her vision.

The military coup of September 11, 1973, profoundly impacted Errázuriz’s career. As a known supporter of the Allende government, she faced political persecution and professional marginalization. Her work on social housing was largely halted, and she was forced to navigate a restrictive political climate. Despite these challenges, she continued to practice architecture, often focusing on smaller-scale projects and renovations. 

In later life, Errázuriz dedicated herself to teaching and advocating for socially responsible architecture. She lectured at numerous universities in Chile and internationally, sharing her experiences and promoting the importance of community participation in urban planning.  She received numerous accolades for her contributions, including the National Prize for Architecture in 1992, the highest honor bestowed upon an architect in Chile. 

Blanca Errázuriz Richards died in Santiago, Chile on November 22, 2017, at the age of 89.  Her legacy endures not only through her built works but also through her enduring commitment to creating architecture that served the needs of the people and contributed to a more just and equitable society. She left behind a body of work that continues to inspire architects and urban planners committed to social responsibility.

title: Karl Urban
text:
Karl Urban was born on December 7, 1972, in Wellington, New Zealand, to Raewyn and Rod Urban. His father was a sheep and beef farmer, and Karl spent his early childhood on his family’s farm in Taradale, near Napier, Hawke’s Bay. He attended St John’s College in Hastings, a Catholic boarding school, where he participated in school productions and developed an early interest in acting. Though initially shy, he was encouraged by a drama teacher, and his passion for performance grew. He left school at 16, choosing to pursue acting directly rather than higher education, much to his parents' initial skepticism.

Urban began his acting career in 1990, appearing in small roles in New Zealand television series. His first credited role was in the television drama *Gloss* in 1991, where he played a character named Damien.  He steadily built up his experience with appearances in shows like *Hero*, *The Private Lives of Elizabeth I*, and *Xena: Warrior Princess*. It was his recurring role as Julius Caesar in *Xena*, beginning in 1996 and lasting until 1999, that brought him wider recognition. He appeared in 24 episodes, establishing himself as a capable dramatic actor. 

The late 1990s saw Urban making the transition to film. He landed a small but memorable role as Éomer in Peter Jackson’s *The Lord of the Rings: The Return of the King* (2003). Though his screen time was limited, the film’s immense success catapulted him onto the international stage.  Around the same time, he starred in the New Zealand horror film *The Irresponsible Captain Bye* (2003), demonstrating his versatility. 

2005 proved to be a pivotal year. He played Dr. Leonard ‘Bones’ McCoy in J.J. Abrams’ *Star Trek* reboot.  The role, a reimagining of the iconic character from the original series, cemented Urban’s status as a leading man. He reprised the role in *Star Trek Into Darkness* (2013) and *Star Trek Beyond* (2016), becoming a fan favorite and critical success.  Also in 2005, he took on the role of Vaako in *The Chronicles of Riddick*, starring Vin Diesel, further expanding his science fiction credentials.

Over the next decade, Urban diversified his filmography. He played a key role as Detective John Kennex in the science fiction police procedural drama *Almost Human* (2013-2014), showcasing his ability to lead a television series.  He continued to take on diverse roles in films like *Red Hill* (2010), a critically acclaimed Australian crime thriller and *Dredd* (2012), a gritty adaptation of the Judge Dredd comic book. *Dredd*, while not a major box office success initially, has since gained a strong cult following, with many praising Urban’s portrayal of the stoic law enforcer. 

In 2017, Urban joined the Marvel Cinematic Universe, playing Skurge in *Thor: Ragnarok*, directed by Taika Waititi.  He significantly expanded his profile with the hugely popular Amazon Prime Video series *The Boys* (2019-2024), where he portrays Billy Butcher, the ruthless leader of a team dedicated to exposing corrupt superheroes. His performance has been widely lauded, earning him critical acclaim and a substantial fan base.  He also starred in the action film *The Brutalist* (2023).

Urban’s personal life has seen its share of challenges. He was married to actress Natalie Wihongi from 2000 to 2010, and they have one son, Hunter. He married Joanne McNally in 2017, and they have two daughters.  He has been open about his struggles with alcohol in the past, achieving sobriety in 2003.  He continues to live and work between Los Angeles and New Zealand, maintaining strong ties to his homeland. As of late 2023/early 2024, Urban continues to be a consistently working actor, with several projects either completed or in development, solidifying his place as a recognized and respected figure in the entertainment industry.

title: Imbolo Mbue
text:
Imbolo Mbue was born on August 17, 1979, in Limbe, Cameroon, to parents Michael and Anne Mbue. Her father was a botanist and her mother a teacher. She grew up in a bilingual household, speaking both English and Duala, a local Cameroonian language. Her early life was marked by a comfortable, middle-class upbringing, though she would later draw upon observations of economic disparity in her writing. She received her primary and secondary education at a local bilingual school, initially excelling in mathematics and sciences before discovering a passion for literature. 

In 1998, at the age of 19, Mbue immigrated to the United States to pursue higher education. She enrolled at Rutgers University in New Brunswick, New Jersey, where she initially intended to study biochemistry. However, she quickly shifted her academic focus to creative writing and graduated with a Bachelor of Arts degree in 2003. Following her undergraduate studies, Mbue faced a period of financial instability and worked a variety of jobs to support herself, including positions as a cashier, a waitress, and a sales associate. These experiences, including a particularly impactful period working as a domestic worker for a wealthy family in Manhattan, profoundly shaped her understanding of class and economic inequality, themes that would become central to her literary work.

Between 2003 and 2008, Mbue worked in various capacities, often holding multiple jobs simultaneously. She continued to write in her spare time, diligently crafting short stories and beginning to develop the ideas that would eventually form her debut novel. She attended Columbia University, earning a Master of Fine Arts in Creative Writing in 2011. While at Columbia, she was mentored by the acclaimed novelist Bernardine Evaristo.

Mbue’s breakthrough came with the publication of her debut novel, *Behold the Dreamers*, in 2016. The novel, published by Atria Books, an imprint of Simon & Schuster, tells the story of Jende Jonga, a Cameroonian immigrant who finds work as a chauffeur for a wealthy New York City couple during the 2008 financial crisis. The narrative explores themes of immigration, class, race, and the American Dream through the intertwined lives of the Jonga family and their employers, the Kindelans. *Behold the Dreamers* received widespread critical acclaim, earning Mbue numerous accolades. 

In 2017, *Behold the Dreamers* won the PEN/Faulkner Award for Fiction, a prestigious American literary prize, making Mbue the youngest and the first Black woman to win the award in its history. That same year, the novel also received the American Book Award. It was longlisted for the Orange Prize for Fiction and shortlisted for the Center for Fiction First Novel Prize. *Behold the Dreamers* was selected as the “One Book, One New York” citywide read in 2018, a program promoting reading and civic engagement throughout New York City. The novel has been translated into over a dozen languages.

Following the success of *Behold the Dreamers*, Mbue continued to write and engage in public speaking. In 2020, she published her second novel, *How Beautiful We Were*, which focuses on a fictional African village grappling with the devastating consequences of environmental pollution caused by an American oil company. This novel further cemented her reputation as a powerful voice exploring themes of colonialism, environmental justice, and the complexities of global power dynamics. *How Beautiful We Were* was an Oprah’s Book Club selection in 2021. 

Mbue currently resides in New York City with her husband and son. She continues to write and participate in literary events, advocating for greater representation of diverse voices in literature. She is a vocal proponent of supporting emerging writers and has actively mentored aspiring authors. As of late 2023, she is working on future writing projects, continuing to explore the human condition through the lens of her own unique experiences and observations.

title: Aert van der Neer
text:
Aert van der Neer, born in Amsterdam on March 26, 1603, and buried there on November 17, 1677, was a Dutch painter specializing in landscapes, particularly those featuring dramatic skies and nocturnal scenes. He remains a somewhat enigmatic figure in Dutch Golden Age painting, despite producing a substantial body of work – over 900 paintings are currently attributed to him. His early life is documented primarily through guild records and baptismal certificates. He was the son of Cornelis van der Neer, a master bookbinder, and Hillegond Jansdr. The family resided in the Sint Antoniesbreestraat in Amsterdam.

Van der Neer’s artistic training is not definitively known. It is generally accepted he was not formally apprenticed to a prominent master, a somewhat unusual circumstance for the time. Theories suggest he may have received initial instruction from his cousin, Jacob van der Neer, a glass painter, or potentially from Pieter Lastman, a history painter known for his Italianate landscapes, though evidence supporting either connection remains circumstantial. He joined the Amsterdam Guild of Saint Luke, the local painters' guild, on February 14, 1629, registering as a *wijnmeester* – a “wine master,” indicating he had not yet established a fully independent workshop and paid a fee allowing him to sell works painted by other artists. 

Van der Neer's early works, dating from the 1630s, demonstrate a clear influence of Cornelis van Haarlem and Jan van Goyen, both established landscape painters. He initially painted relatively conventional, brightly lit landscapes, often depicting Dutch river scenes and towns. However, he quickly began to develop his signature style, becoming renowned for his atmospheric effects, especially his depictions of twilight, dawn, and stormy weather. He was a pioneer in portraying realistic sunsets and moonlit scenes, using subtle gradations of tone to create a sense of depth and mood. 

His subject matter largely focused on the Dutch countryside, frequently featuring views of the rivers Vecht and Amstel, the Haarlemmermeer lake, and the surrounding villages. He often included small figures engaged in everyday activities – travelers, fishermen, and farmers – adding a sense of life and scale to his vast landscapes.  He did not typically focus on idealized or heroic landscapes; instead, he captured the often-bleak, yet beautiful, reality of the Dutch lowlands.  

Around 1645, Van der Neer began to experiment with a distinctive technique of applying paint thinly, often using a palette knife to create textured surfaces and to suggest the effects of light and shadow. This technique, combined with his characteristic muted color palette, contributed to the melancholic and evocative quality of his paintings. He also became increasingly adept at rendering the effects of ice and snow, creating convincingly realistic winter scenes.  

Van der Neer’s career was financially stable, though he never reached the same level of fame or wealth as some of his contemporaries, such as Rembrandt or Vermeer. He consistently produced paintings for a broad clientele, including merchants and collectors. Records show he sold works to prominent Amsterdam citizens like Johannes Wtenbogaert and Nicolaes van Gelre. He also worked for art dealers, providing them with paintings for resale. 

In 1652, Van der Neer moved his workshop and residence to the Warmoesstraat, a busy street in Amsterdam. He continued to paint prolifically throughout the 1660s and 1670s, refining his style and continuing to explore the possibilities of atmospheric perspective.  His later works often exhibit a greater degree of simplification and abstraction, focusing on the essential elements of the landscape and the dramatic effects of light and weather. 

Van der Neer died in Amsterdam in 1677 and was buried in the Westerkerk. His son, Jacob van der Neer (1636-c.1687), also became a painter, though his work is less distinguished than that of his father.  While largely overlooked for centuries, Aert van der Neer’s work experienced a revival in the 20th century, and he is now recognized as a significant and innovative figure in Dutch landscape painting, celebrated for his unique atmospheric effects and his sensitive portrayal of the Dutch countryside.

title: Hayden Panettiere
text:
Hayden Lesley Panettiere was born on August 21, 1989, in Palisades, New York, to Lesley R. Vogel, a former soap opera actress, and Alan Lee “Skip” Panettiere, a fire captain. She has a younger brother, Jordan, also an actor. Her early childhood was spent moving frequently as her mother pursued acting roles and her father worked various jobs, including selling leather goods. By the age of four, Panettiere began appearing in commercials, including spots for P&G, Jell-O, and American Dairy Association. This early exposure led to her first television role in 1994, at the age of five, as Sarah Roberts in the soap opera *One Life to Live*, a part she played for four years until 1998. 

Following *One Life to Live*, Panettiere took on guest roles in various television shows, including *Law & Order*, *Law & Order: Special Victims Unit*, *ER*, and *Ally McBeal*. She had a recurring role as Lizzie Spaulding’s friend in *Guiding Light* from 1999 to 2000. A significant breakthrough came in 2000 when she landed the role of Zoey Brooks in the Disney Channel sitcom *Even Stevens*. The show, which aired until 2003, catapulted her to teenage stardom. She reprised her role as Zoey Brooks in the 2003 spin-off movie *The Even Stevens Movie*. 

While still starring in *Even Stevens*, Panettiere began to gain recognition in film. She voiced Kairi in the 2003 video game *Kingdom Hearts* and its sequels, a role she continued in subsequent installments. Her live-action film debut was in 1998’s *The Object of My Affection*, followed by roles in *Remember the Titans* (2000) and *Shanghai Noon* (2000). She gained further film prominence with *Bring It On: All or Nothing* (2003) and *Raising Helen* (2004).

The role that solidified Panettiere as a mainstream star was Claire Bennet, the cheerleader with regenerative abilities, in the NBC sci-fi drama *Heroes* (2006-2010). Her performance earned her Saturn Award nominations in 2007 and 2008, and she received a Golden Globe nomination for Best Supporting Actress – Series, Miniseries or Television Film in 2008. During this period, she also voiced Megara in Disney’s *Hercules* (2008) and starred in the horror film *Scream IV* (2011).

In the early 2010s, Panettiere continued to diversify her roles. She starred in the independent film *The Crazies* (2010), a remake of the 1973 George A. Romero film. She also began a relationship with Ukrainian boxer Wladimir Klitschko, with whom she has a daughter, Kaya Evdokia Klitschko, born December 9, 2014.  She starred in the country music drama *Nashville* (2012-2018), playing aspiring country singer Juliette Barnes. Her musical performances on the show were critically well-received, and she released several original songs. 

However, Panettiere’s later life has been marked by struggles with postpartum depression and substance abuse. She publicly discussed her battle with postpartum depression following the birth of her daughter and entered treatment for substance abuse in 2015 and again in 2019. Her relationship with Klitschko ended in 2018, and a custody battle ensued regarding their daughter. In 2023, she entered a rehabilitation facility for eight months to address her struggles with alcohol and opioid addiction. 

Panettiere has been actively involved in animal rights activism, particularly concerning whaling. She has worked with the Whale and Dolphin Conservation organization and has spoken out against the practice of dolphin drive hunts in Japan, even being the subject of protests and controversy for her activism. While she has continued to take on occasional acting roles, including a recurring role in *Scream VI* (2023), her focus has increasingly been on her recovery and co-parenting her daughter.

title: Deitrick Haddon
text:
Deitrick Haddon was born on May 17, 1971, in Detroit, Michigan, the youngest of five children to Bishop Vernon Haddon Sr. and Dr. Shelia Haddon. His upbringing was deeply rooted in the church, with his father serving as a prominent figure in the Pentecostal Assemblies of the World, Inc. This environment significantly shaped his musical development from a very young age. He began playing the drums at the age of five and quickly demonstrated a prodigious talent for music, mastering instruments like the piano, bass guitar, and organ before reaching his teens. He received formal musical training, studying at the University of Michigan School of Music, Theatre & Dance, where he majored in choral music education. While at university, he also directed the Voices of Triumph gospel choir.

Haddon’s professional music career began in 1992 when he formed the gospel group Take 6 protégé, Visage Music. The group released one album, “Restoring the Joy,” in 1993, but achieved limited commercial success. Following Visage Music, Haddon served as a musical director for the Detroit Mass Choir, contributing significantly to their 1994 album, “When I Rise,” which earned a Stellar Award. This experience brought him wider recognition within the gospel music industry. 

A pivotal moment arrived in 1996 when Haddon founded and became the lead vocalist of the gospel group Commissioned, after the passing of their original lead singer, Keith Staten. He revitalized the group, bringing a contemporary sound and energetic stage presence. During his tenure with Commissioned (1996-2003), they released several successful albums including “Ordinary Just Won’t Do” (1997), “Time to Sing” (1999), and “Face to Face” (2001), earning multiple Stellar Awards and a Soul Train Music Award. Haddon's songwriting and vocal contributions were central to Commissioned's continued success during this period.

In 2000, while still with Commissioned, Haddon embarked on a solo career, releasing his debut album, “Spiritual Connection,” on Light Records. The album showcased his unique blend of gospel, R&B, and hip-hop influences. He followed this with “Captured Live” (2003) after leaving Commissioned, marking a full-time commitment to his solo work. His breakthrough came with the album “7 Reasons” in 2006, released on his own label, DH Records. The album spawned the hit single “He’s Able,” which reached number 2 on the Billboard Gospel chart and significantly raised his profile.

Haddon’s subsequent albums continued to build on his success. “Dangerous Places” (2008) featured the popular song “Why I Love You,” and “Understatement” (2010) showcased his evolving sound.  He released “Wildfire” in 2012, and “Restore” in 2015. He also ventured into television, starring in the Oxygen reality show “Deitrick Haddon: Kingdom Come” which premiered in 2016, documenting his personal life, ministry, and musical pursuits. The show ran for three seasons. 

In 2019, Haddon signed with RCA Inspiration and released "While We're Here".  In 2022, he released "Kingmaker", continuing to experiment with diverse musical styles while maintaining his gospel roots. Throughout his career, Haddon has received numerous accolades including multiple Stellar Awards, a Soul Train Music Award, and several Grammy Award nominations. He has collaborated with artists across genres, including Mary Mary, Kirk Franklin, and Lecrae. 

Beyond music and television, Haddon remains actively involved in ministry, often leading worship and delivering sermons at churches and conferences. He is married to Saron Haynes-Haddon and they have three children. He continues to tour and record, maintaining a significant presence in the gospel music landscape and consistently exploring new avenues for artistic expression and spiritual outreach. As of late 2023, Haddon continues to be a visible and influential figure in gospel music, blending traditional sounds with contemporary influences and utilizing various platforms to share his faith.

title: Tarik Elyounoussi
text:
Tarik Elyounoussi was born on February 18, 1973, in Casablanca, Morocco, to a Norwegian mother, Linda Aly, and a Moroccan father, Mohamed Elyounoussi. His early life was marked by frequent movement, initially spending his first years in Morocco before relocating to Oslo, Norway, with his mother and younger brother, Elias, in 1976 following his parents’ divorce. This move proved pivotal, shaping his national sporting allegiance. He grew up in the Furuset district of Oslo, a suburb known for its diverse population and, increasingly during his youth, a burgeoning football scene. Despite identifying with his Moroccan heritage, Elyounoussi quickly integrated into Norwegian society and excelled in football from a young age. 

He began his senior career with local club Furuset IF in 1991, playing in the Norwegian Second Division. His performances quickly attracted attention, and in 1992 he signed for Eik-Tønsberg, also in the Second Division. It was at Eik-Tønsberg that Elyounoussi truly began to demonstrate his potential, scoring consistently and becoming a key player. This led to a move to the top flight of Norwegian football in 1994, joining Rosenborg BK, the dominant force in Norwegian football at the time.

At Rosenborg, Elyounoussi flourished under the guidance of manager Nils Arne Eggen. He quickly established himself as a dynamic and prolific winger, known for his speed, dribbling skills, and accurate finishing. His time with Rosenborg was incredibly successful, winning four consecutive Tippeligaen titles from 1995 to 1998, alongside two Norwegian Cup victories in 1995 and 1998. He scored a significant 63 goals in 164 appearances for Rosenborg, making him a club legend. During this period, he also gained international recognition, earning his first cap for the Norwegian national team on August 23, 1995, in a friendly match against Sweden.

His performances for both club and country attracted interest from abroad, and in 1998, he moved to English Premier League side Southampton for a fee of £3 million. He made his debut for Southampton on August 15, 1998, against Everton. While his time at Southampton wasn’t as consistently successful as his spell in Norway, he still contributed valuable goals and performances, appearing in 56 Premier League matches and scoring 11 goals.
