He became a popular figure amongst the Southampton faithful, known for his exciting attacking play.

Following Southampton’s relegation from the Premier League in 2005, Elyounoussi returned to Norway, signing for Aalesunds FK. He spent two seasons with Aalesunds, again demonstrating his goalscoring ability, scoring 26 goals in 55 league appearances.  In 2007, he moved to Fredrikstad FK, where he played for a further two seasons, adding another 17 league goals to his tally. He retired from professional football in 2009 after a brief spell back at Rosenborg, making a final appearance for the club on November 1, 2009, against Strømsgodset.

Throughout his international career, Elyounoussi earned 66 caps for Norway, scoring 16 goals. He represented his country at the 1998 FIFA World Cup in France, playing in all three of Norway’s group stage matches. He also featured in several European Championship qualifying campaigns, though Norway failed to qualify for the tournament during his tenure. 

After retiring from playing, Elyounoussi transitioned into coaching. He held various roles within the Norwegian football system, including youth coaching positions. He became an assistant coach at Rosenborg in 2014, working alongside head coach Kåre Ingebrigtsen, contributing to another league title win in 2016. He later took on head coaching roles at lower league clubs, including Asker Fotball and Kolbotn.  He has also worked as a football commentator and pundit for Norwegian television.  As of late 2023, Elyounoussi continues to be involved in football, focusing on coaching and analysis. His son, Mohamed Elyounoussi, is also a professional footballer, currently playing for Copenhagen and also representing the Norwegian national team, continuing the family’s legacy in the sport.

title: Andreas Ivanschitz
text:
Andreas Ivanschitz was born on November 8, 1983, in Sankt Pölten, Lower Austria, to a Croatian father and an Austrian mother. His father, Josip Ivanschitz, was a professional footballer himself, playing as a defender for various clubs in Austria and Croatia, providing an early and influential role model. Andreas began his footballing journey at the age of six with local club SK St. Pölten, following in his father’s footsteps. He quickly displayed a natural talent, particularly a refined left foot and exceptional passing range, attracting attention from larger clubs. 

By 1998, at the age of 15, Ivanschitz had been scouted by Rapid Wien, one of Austria’s most successful football clubs. He joined their youth academy and continued to develop his skills, progressing rapidly through the ranks. He made his professional debut for Rapid Wien on May 16, 2000, in a Bundesliga match against FC Tirol Innsbruck, becoming, at 16 years and 186 days old, the youngest player to ever feature in the Austrian top flight at the time – a record later broken. He scored his first professional goal on November 4, 2000, against SV Austria Salzburg.

Ivanschitz quickly established himself as a key player for Rapid Wien, showcasing his playmaking abilities from midfield. He spent five seasons with the club, becoming a fan favorite and amassing 148 appearances, scoring 32 goals. He won the Austrian Bundesliga title with Rapid Wien in the 2001-02 season and the Austrian Cup in 2002, contributing significantly to the team’s successes. His performances earned him a move to international football, joining Belgian side Lierse SK in January 2006 for a reported fee of €2.5 million.

His time at Lierse was relatively short, lasting just one season. He made 17 appearances, scoring 4 goals, before attracting the attention of Red Bull Salzburg, then known as FC Red Bull Salzburg. He transferred to Salzburg in July 2006 for around €3 million. At Salzburg, he continued to demonstrate his creative flair, playing a pivotal role in their attacking play. He played 72 games for the club, netting 15 times and winning the Austrian Bundesliga and Austrian Cup double in the 2006-07 season.

In January 2008, Ivanschitz made a move to the German Bundesliga, signing for Alemannia Aachen. He became a regular in the Aachen midfield, making 56 appearances and scoring 8 goals over two seasons, but the club struggled and eventually suffered relegation in 2009. He then transferred to Mainz 05 in July 2009, where he enjoyed arguably the most successful period of his club career. 

He quickly became a key figure for Mainz, known for his set-piece expertise and ability to unlock defenses. He played 164 Bundesliga matches for Mainz, scoring 31 goals. During his time there, he captained the side and led them to their highest ever Bundesliga finish, fifth place in the 2010-11 season, securing qualification for the UEFA Europa League. He also scored a memorable free-kick against Liverpool in the Europa League group stage in November 2011.

After leaving Mainz in 2013, Ivanschitz spent a season in China with Shanghai SIPG, before returning to Austria in 2014 to join his boyhood club, Rapid Wien, for a second spell. He played 66 times in his second stint, adding 13 goals, before moving to the Austrian Second League with FC Liefering in 2017 as a player-coach. He retired from professional football in 2018.

Internationally, Ivanschitz represented Austria at various youth levels before making his senior debut on March 31, 2006, in a friendly match against Croatia. He earned 69 caps for the Austrian national team, scoring 10 goals, and captained the side on numerous occasions. He participated in the UEFA Euro 2008, which Austria co-hosted, and the UEFA Euro 2016. 

Following retirement, Ivanschitz transitioned into coaching. He held coaching positions at Liefering and later became an assistant coach at Rapid Wien, returning to the club where his professional career began. As of late 2023, he is working as a youth coach within the Austrian Football Association, focusing on developing the next generation of Austrian talent.

title: Gopi Sundar
text:
Gopi Sundar Govindan Nair, born November 28, 1977, in Thiruvananthapuram, Kerala, India, is a prominent Indian film composer and singer known for his distinctive blend of electronic music, traditional Kerala instruments, and contemporary arrangements. His career spans over two decades, marked by innovative soundscapes and collaborations with leading figures in Malayalam cinema.

Gopi Sundar’s early life was steeped in music. His father, Govindan Nair, was a Carnatic vocalist and introduced him to classical music from a young age. He began learning Carnatic music at the age of four and later pursued a degree in music from the University of Kerala in Thiruvananthapuram. While formally trained in classical music, Gopi Sundar also developed a keen interest in Western musical styles, particularly electronic music. This fusion of influences would become a hallmark of his later work. He also holds a Bachelor of Technology degree in Electronics from College of Engineering, Thiruvananthapuram, showcasing his academic versatility. 

His professional journey began in 1999, initially working as a keyboard programmer in Chennai. He collaborated with several composers like A.R. Rahman, Harris Jayaraj, and Vidyasagar, honing his skills in sound design and arrangement. This experience proved invaluable in shaping his own musical identity. He contributed significantly to Rahman’s *Alaipayuthey* (2000) as a programmer.  He then moved to Dubai in 2001 where he worked independently for a few years before returning to India.

Gopi Sundar made his debut as an independent composer in Malayalam cinema with *Flash* in 2007, directed by Rony Mathew.  However, it was *Notebook* (2006) directed by Venu Nagavally that truly showcased his potential.  The album featured the popular song "Pattampoochi," sung by Vineeth Sreenivasan, which became a chartbuster. This marked the beginning of his successful collaboration with Vineeth, who also became a frequent lyricist in his films.  

Over the next few years, Gopi Sundar rapidly established himself as a leading composer in Malayalam cinema. *Poppins* (2008), directed by Venu Nagavally, further cemented his reputation. He composed scores for *Yodha* (2009), *Cocktail* (2010), *China Town* (2011), *Run Baby Run* (2012) and *Drishyam* (2013) - all commercially successful films. *Drishyam*, directed by Jeethu Joseph, won him the Kerala State Film Award for Best Music Director in 2013.  The songs "Dimaak Khara" and "Unne Nee Ennale" became hugely popular.  He also ventured into Tamil cinema in 2014 with *Idhu Enna Maayai*, directed by Sudha Kongara.

His most acclaimed work arguably came with *Bangalore Days* (2014), directed by Anjali Menon.  The soundtrack received widespread critical acclaim, featuring songs like "Njan Eesho", "Aarum Kayyarinje", and "Little Girl". It won him another Kerala State Film Award for Best Music Director in 2015.  He continued to deliver popular soundtracks in films like *Oru Vadakkan Selfie* (2015), *Paavada* (2016), *Jomonte Suvishesham* (2017), *Liger* (2017), *Aadhi* (2018) and *Lucia* (2019).  He also composed music for *Marakkar: Arabikadlinte Simham* (2021), directed by Priyadarshan, starring Mohanlal.  This epic historical drama featured a grand orchestral score.

Beyond film music, Gopi Sundar has also released independent albums and collaborated with several musicians. He has also sung numerous songs in his own compositions. His work often incorporates traditional Kerala instruments like the veena, chenda, and mridangam, blended seamlessly with electronic elements.  This unique approach has garnered him a devoted fan base.  He has composed over 200 songs in Malayalam and Tamil films.  He has also been involved in several live concerts and musical tours.  

In recent years, Gopi Sundar continues to be highly sought after in the Malayalam film industry, consistently delivering innovative and memorable soundtracks. He remains one of the most influential figures in contemporary Indian film music, celebrated for his ability to blend tradition with modernity in a uniquely captivating style.

title: Clancy Brown
text:
Clarence J. Brown III, known professionally as Clancy Brown, was born on March 5, 1959, in Newport News, Virginia, to Clarence J. Brown Jr., a career United States Navy officer, and Joyce Brown, a high school English teacher. His father’s military postings meant the family moved frequently during Clancy’s childhood, living in locations including Washington D.C., the Philippines, and Hawaii. This nomadic upbringing instilled in him a degree of adaptability and a self-described “outsider” perspective. He attended several high schools, graduating from Governor Dummer Academy in Byfield, Massachusetts, in 1977. 

Brown’s interest in performing arts began in high school, participating in theatrical productions. He continued his education at the University of Southern California, studying acting and graduating with a Bachelor of Fine Arts degree in 1983. While at USC, he actively participated in stage productions and honed his craft. His early professional work centered around theatre, notably with the Los Angeles Shakespeare Festival.

His film debut came in 1983 with a small role in *Bad Dreams*, but it was his portrayal of the villainous Kurt Brennan in *Extreme Prejudice* (1987), alongside Nick Nolte and Powers Boothe, that first garnered him wider attention. This role established a pattern in his early career – frequently being cast as imposing, often menacing, characters. A significant break arrived in 1990 with his role as Captain Byron Hadley in *Hunt for Red October*, directed by John McTiernan and starring Sean Connery and Alec Baldwin. This performance cemented his reputation for playing authoritative and physically imposing figures.

The 1990s saw Brown working steadily in both film and television. He appeared in *Mo’ Money* (1992) with Damon Wayans, *Starship Troopers* (1997) as Sergeant Zim, and *Thor* (2011) as Odin’s father, Bor. However, it was his voice work that began to significantly expand his career. He first lent his distinctive baritone to the animated series *Batman: The Animated Series* in 1992, voicing the villain Mr. Freeze. This performance is widely considered a definitive interpretation of the character, influencing subsequent depictions in comics and films. 

Brown continued to be a prominent voice actor throughout the late 1990s and 2000s, taking on roles in *Superman: The Animated Series*, *Justice League*, and *Invader Zim*. He became a go-to voice for powerful and often villainous characters. He notably voiced Lex Luthor in multiple DC animated projects, including *Superman/Batman: Public Enemies* (2009) and *Justice League: Doom* (2012).  His work extends beyond superheroes, including roles in *SpongeBob SquarePants* where he voices Mr. Krabs since 1999, a role for which he remains highly recognizable. He has voiced Mr. Krabs in over 200 episodes.

In live-action television, Brown had recurring roles in *Carnivàle* (2003-2005) as the enigmatic religious figure Justin Crowe, and *Lost* (2010) as the manipulative and dangerous Zalin.  He played Howard Stark, father of Tony Stark, in *Agents of S.H.I.E.L.D.* (2013-2014) and reprised the role in *Captain America: Civil War* (2016). More recently, he appeared in *Billions* (2016-2023) as the powerful and ruthless Walter “Bobby” Axelrod, a role that earned him critical acclaim.

Throughout his career, Brown has accumulated over 200 acting credits, spanning film, television, animation, and video games. He has received several awards and nominations for his voice work, including Daytime Emmy Awards for his role as Mr. Krabs. 

Clancy Brown resides in California with his wife, Jeanne Marie Schultz, a businesswoman, whom he married in 1993. They have three children. He continues to be actively involved in acting and voice acting, demonstrating a remarkably enduring and versatile career spanning four decades. As of late 2023, he continues to be a sought-after performer, consistently delivering memorable performances across a wide range of media.

title: Jesse Chacón
text:
Jesse Manuel Chacón was born on December 19, 1936, in El Paso, Texas, to Manuel and Emilia Chacón, Mexican immigrants who instilled in him a strong sense of social justice and a deep connection to his cultural heritage. His father worked as a railroad worker and his mother as a homemaker, and they raised Jesse and his seven siblings in a working-class neighborhood. He attended El Paso High School, graduating in 1954, and then briefly attended Texas Western College (now the University of Texas at El Paso) before enlisting in the United States Army in 1956.

Chacón served in the Army for two years, stationed primarily in Germany. Following his military service, he returned to El Paso and completed his Bachelor of Arts degree in Government at Texas Western College in 1960. He then pursued a Juris Doctor degree at Georgetown University Law Center in Washington, D.C., earning his law degree in 1963. 

Returning again to El Paso, Chacón began his legal career as a staff attorney for the Mexican American Legal Defense and Educational Fund (MALDEF) in 1964. This role proved formative, exposing him to the legal battles surrounding civil rights for Mexican Americans. He quickly rose within the organization, becoming the regional counsel for MALDEF’s Southwest regional office in 1966, a position he held for eight years. During this time, he litigated numerous landmark cases concerning voting rights, employment discrimination, and educational equality, significantly impacting the legal landscape for Hispanic communities in Texas and New Mexico. 

In 1974, Chacón transitioned from direct legal advocacy to public service, successfully running for District Attorney of El Paso County. He served three terms, from 1975 to 1987, becoming the first Hispanic District Attorney in the county’s history. As DA, he focused on improving the administration of justice, increasing the number of Hispanic attorneys in the office, and addressing issues of police misconduct. He also prioritized community-based crime prevention programs.

His political ambitions continued to grow, and in 1987, Chacón was appointed by Governor William Clements to the Texas Railroad Commission, a powerful state agency regulating the oil and gas industry. He served on the Commission from 1987 to 1995, becoming the first Hispanic commissioner in its history. During his tenure, he advocated for responsible energy development, environmental protection, and fair pricing for consumers. He was involved in navigating the complexities of the oil bust of the late 1980s and early 1990s. 

In 1995, President Bill Clinton nominated Chacón to serve as the United States Ambassador to Guatemala. He was confirmed by the Senate and served in this role from 1996 to 1999. He played a vital role in the implementation of the Guatemalan peace accords, which formally ended a 36-year civil war. He worked to strengthen bilateral relations between the United States and Guatemala, promoting economic development, democracy, and human rights. He was lauded for his diplomatic skills and his understanding of the socio-political complexities of the region.

Following his ambassadorship, Chacón returned to El Paso and resumed the practice of law, joining the firm of McCall, Chalberg & Wells. He remained active in civic and community affairs, serving on various boards and commissions. Throughout his career, he received numerous awards and recognitions for his contributions to law, public service, and the Hispanic community, including honorary degrees from multiple universities. 

Jesse Chacón passed away on November 23, 2023, in El Paso, Texas, at the age of 86. He is survived by his wife, Maria Elena Alvarez Chacón, whom he married in 1962, and their three children, Elena, Manuel, and Marcos. His legacy is one of pioneering leadership, dedicated public service, and a lifelong commitment to social justice and the advancement of the Hispanic community.

title: Cicero
text:
Marcus Tullius Cicero was born on January 3, 106 BC in Arpinum, a Volscian hill town about 70 miles southeast of Rome. His father, also named Marcus Tullius Cicero, was a wealthy equestrian, a social class below the patrician aristocracy but still possessing considerable means. Though not of noble birth, his family possessed Roman citizenship for generations, and Cicero always valued this heritage. His mother, Helvia, is noted for her attentive care of her son’s education. Unlike many Roman youths, Cicero was not raised in Rome itself, a factor he believed instilled in him a certain detachment from the intense political factionalism of the city.

Cicero received a rigorous education, first from his father and then from the leading Roman orators and philosophers of the time. He studied rhetoric under Lucius Licinius Crassus, and philosophy with Philo of Larissa, the head of the New Academy, who resided in Rome from 88 BC. He also travelled to Greece in 79-77 BC to further his studies in Athens, immersing himself in the philosophical traditions of the region. Military service was a common expectation for aspiring politicians, and Cicero served a brief period in the Social War (91-88 BC), gaining practical experience despite not participating in major battles. 

Cicero began his public career as a lawyer in 81 BC with the defense of Sextus Roscius of Ameria, accused of parricide. This case, detailed in his early work *Pro Roscio Amerino*, immediately brought him to attention, although it also incurred the displeasure of the powerful Lucius Cornelius Sulla, whose associate had been the actual perpetrator.  He deliberately delayed his ascent through the *cursus honorum* (the sequential order of public offices) due to political instability and his concern for personal safety. 

He served as quaestor in Sicily in 75 BC, a position that involved financial administration. He rose through the ranks, becoming an aedile in 69 BC, responsible for public works and festivals, and then praetor in 66 BC, a judicial magistrate. It was during his praetorship that he gained considerable renown for his legal skills, notably in the prosecution of Gaius Verres, a corrupt former governor of Sicily, in 73 BC. His speeches against Verres, *Verrines*, are considered masterpieces of Roman oratory. 

In 63 BC, Cicero was elected consul, the highest office in the Roman Republic. This was a remarkable achievement for a *novus homo* – a man who was the first in his family to attain such high office.  His consulship was dominated by the Catiline Conspiracy, a plot led by Lucius Sergius Catilina to overthrow the Roman government. Cicero skillfully exposed the conspiracy through a series of fiery speeches delivered to the Senate – the *Catilinarian Orations* – and ultimately secured the Senate’s authority to execute several of the conspirators without trial, a controversial decision that would later haunt him.

Following his consulship, Cicero experienced a period of political exile.  Publius Clodius Pulcher, a tribune of the plebs, politically targeted Cicero for his actions during the Catiline affair. In 58 BC, Clodius successfully passed a law condemning Cicero and he was forced into exile. He spent thirteen months in Thessalonica and Dyrrhachium, continuing to write and correspond with friends. He was recalled to Rome in 57 BC thanks to the efforts of Pompey and Crassus, who needed his support. 

Cicero largely withdrew from active politics after his return, dedicating himself to writing on philosophical and rhetorical topics. He produced numerous treatises, including *De Oratore*, *De Republica*, *De Legibus*, and *Tusculanae Disputationes*, which significantly influenced Western thought. The end of the Republic, marked by the rise of Julius Caesar, deeply troubled Cicero, a staunch defender of the traditional republican system. 

After Caesar’s assassination in 44 BC, Cicero re-entered public life, hoping to restore the Republic. He delivered the *Philippics*, a series of scathing speeches against Mark Antony, who he saw as a dangerous threat to Roman liberty. However, the Second Triumvirate, formed by Antony, Octavian, and Lepidus, proscribed Cicero. He was hunted down and murdered on December 7, 43 BC, at his villa in Formiae. His head and hands were displayed in the Roman Forum by Antony’s orders, a grim testament to his unwavering opposition.

title: Roman Pavlyuchenko
text:
Roman Sergeyevich Pavlyuchenko was born on December 21, 1981, in Krasnodar, Russia, then part of the Russian Soviet Federative Socialist Republic. His early footballing education began at the age of seven with a local sports school in his hometown. He showed promise early on, but faced initial setbacks, being deemed too small for the demanding physicality of the game. He persevered, however, and continued his development, eventually joining the youth academy of FC Chernomorets Novorossiysk in 1995 at the age of 14. 

Pavlyuchenko made his professional debut for Chernomorets in the Russian First Division on August 16, 1998, against FC Lokomotiv Nizhny Novgorod. He quickly established himself as a key player, demonstrating a powerful shot and a knack for scoring goals. Over four seasons with Chernomorets, appearing in 126 league matches, he scored 64 goals, averaging over a goal every two games. This prolific form attracted the attention of larger clubs.

In July 2003, Pavlyuchenko transferred to FC Spartak Moscow for a reported fee of $3.5 million.  His time at Spartak further cemented his reputation as one of Russia’s most exciting strikers.  He formed a potent attacking partnership with Dmitri Alenichev, and in the 2005 season, he was the Russian Premier League's top scorer with 18 goals, leading Spartak to a second-place finish.  He also won the Russian Cup with Spartak in 2003 and 2005. During his four seasons with the Moscow club, he played 132 league games and scored 68 goals.

Pavlyuchenko’s international career began with the Russian national team on November 19, 2003, in a friendly match against Estonia. He quickly became a regular, representing Russia at Euro 2004, where he scored one goal in three appearances. He was a pivotal figure in Russia’s qualifying campaign for the 2006 World Cup, scoring nine goals, and was subsequently included in the squad for the tournament in Germany. He scored a crucial penalty against Sweden in the group stage.  He continued to be a mainstay in the national team, participating in Euro 2008, where he scored three goals, including two penalties against Sweden, and the 2010 World Cup qualification campaign. He earned a total of 51 caps for Russia, scoring 21 goals, retiring from international football in 2011.

In August 2008, Pavlyuchenko moved to Tottenham Hotspur in the English Premier League for a reported £13.9 million. He scored on his debut against Manchester City on August 23, 2008.  While he showed flashes of brilliance, including scoring the winning goal in a League Cup final against Chelsea in 2008, his time at Tottenham was largely inconsistent. He struggled to fully adapt to the physicality and pace of the Premier League, and faced competition for a starting position.  He played 113 games for Tottenham across all competitions, scoring 42 goals. 

After four seasons with Tottenham, Pavlyuchenko returned to Russia in February 2012, joining Lokomotiv Moscow on loan for the remainder of the season. He made the move permanent in July 2012. He spent two seasons at Lokomotiv, scoring 11 goals in 48 league appearances. In August 2014, he signed for Kuban Krasnodar, playing for a single season, making 26 appearances and scoring 8 goals. 

Pavlyuchenko finished his professional career with FC Dynamo Stavropol in the Russian Football National League 2, joining in June 2016 and retiring in December 2016. He made 15 appearances for the club, scoring 3 goals. 

Since retirement, Pavlyuchenko has largely remained out of the public eye. He has occasionally been involved in football-related events as a guest or commentator. He has also reportedly pursued business interests in Krasnodar.  He is known to enjoy fishing and hunting in his free time. As of late 2023, he maintains a relatively private life, focusing on family and personal endeavors.

title: Kelli White
text:
Kelli Ann White was born on April 29, 1970, in Phoenix, Arizona, to parents Donald and Patricia White. Her father was a retired Air Force veteran and her mother worked as a secretary. Growing up in a musical household, White began singing at a young age, participating in school choirs and local talent shows. She showed early aptitude for vocal performance, studying classical voice throughout her childhood and adolescence. She attended Camelback High School in Phoenix, graduating in 1988. While still in high school, she began performing professionally in local bands, honing her skills in diverse genres including rock, pop, and R&B.

White’s initial foray into the national music scene came in 1990 when she joined the all-female rock band, XYZ. The band, based in Los Angeles, released their self-titled debut album on Capitol Records in 1992. The album achieved moderate success, charting at number 61 on the Billboard 200 and yielding the single “Good Thing,” which reached number 68 on the Billboard Hot 100. XYZ toured extensively in support of the album, opening for acts like Bon Jovi and Warrant. Despite the initial momentum, internal creative differences led to the band’s disbandment in 1994.

Following XYZ, White pursued a solo career, relocating to Nashville, Tennessee in 1996. She initially worked as a songwriter, penning songs for other artists while simultaneously developing her own unique country sound. This period saw her co-writing the song “Heartache” which was recorded by Clay Walker and reached number 22 on the Billboard Hot Country Singles & Tracks chart in 1997. 

Her breakthrough came in 1999 with the release of her debut solo album, *No Fair Warning*, on Warner Bros. Records. The album, produced by Mark Wright, blended pop sensibilities with a strong country foundation. The title track, “No Fair Warning,” became her signature song, reaching number 17 on the Billboard Hot Country Songs chart and establishing her as a rising star in the country music world. The album itself peaked at number 43 on the Billboard Top Country Albums chart.

White followed up with her second studio album, *Honest to Goodness*, in 2001, also on Warner Bros. While the album showcased her vocal versatility and songwriting prowess, it didn’t achieve the same commercial success as her debut. The lead single, “Wish I Could Be You,” reached number 33 on the country charts. Despite a dedicated fanbase, she faced challenges navigating the evolving landscape of country music. 

During the early 2000s, White became increasingly involved in animal welfare activism, particularly focused on rescuing and rehabilitating abused and neglected dogs. This passion led her to establish the “Kelli White’s Angels Among Us” animal rescue organization, which successfully rehomed hundreds of dogs. She also became a vocal advocate for responsible pet ownership and spay/neuter programs.

In 2005, White largely stepped away from recording and touring to dedicate herself full-time to her animal rescue work. She continued to perform sporadically at charity events and private functions. She also began offering vocal coaching, sharing her expertise with aspiring singers. In 2010, she released a digital EP titled *Time Flies* featuring previously unreleased material and new recordings, primarily as a fundraiser for her animal rescue. 

In recent years, White has remained actively involved in animal rescue, continuing to run “Angels Among Us.” She maintains a low public profile but occasionally performs at local venues in the Nashville area. She has also embraced social media to connect with fans and promote her advocacy work. As of 2023, Kelli White resides in Tennessee and continues to dedicate her life to music and animal welfare. She has never married and has no children.

title: Melvin Van Peebles
text:
Melvin Van Peebles, born Melvin Purvis Peebles on August 22, 1932, in Chicago, Illinois, was a pioneering African-American filmmaker, actor, and musician who fundamentally altered the landscape of American cinema. His early life was marked by a diverse educational and geographical journey. His mother, Augustama, was a seamstress, and his father, Robert Peebles, was a Pullman porter. He attended DuSable High School in Chicago, a historically Black high school known for producing accomplished alumni. Following high school, Van Peebles briefly attended West Virginia State University before transferring to Ohio Wesleyan University, where he earned a Bachelor of Arts degree in English in 1954. He then served in the United States Air Force from 1954 to 1957, stationed in France, where he also developed a passion for painting and began writing. 

Following his military service, Van Peebles moved to Mexico City in 1958 and then to Paris in 1959, immersing himself in the European art scene. He worked as a journalist, painter, and street performer, even appearing in French theater productions. He also began writing novels, publishing “The Big Four” in 1963, followed by “Les Aventuriers” (The Adventurers) in 1964, which became a bestseller in France and was adapted into a 1967 film starring Burt Lancaster, though Van Peebles had little creative control over the adaptation.

Returning to the United States in 1968, Van Peebles dedicated himself to filmmaking, motivated by a desire to create stories that reflected the Black experience authentically and challenged existing Hollywood norms. He founded Melvin Van Peebles Productions and secured funding—a relatively small $50,000—to produce his groundbreaking film, *Sweet Sweetback’s Baadasssss Song* (1971).  Shot in just 19 days in the Mojave Desert, the film was a defiant response to the Blaxploitation genre that was beginning to emerge, but aimed to be more politically charged and stylistically innovative.  *Sweet Sweetback* deliberately eschewed conventional narrative structure, employing fragmented scenes, poetic dialogue, and a focus on Black male empowerment. Though controversial, the film grossed over $15 million and became a cult classic, influencing a generation of Black filmmakers.

The success of *Sweet Sweetback* allowed Van Peebles to continue making films, though with varying degrees of commercial success. He directed *Watermelon Man* (1972), a satirical comedy about a white insurance investigator who inexplicably turns Black, which earned him a Writers Guild of America Award nomination.  He followed with *Posse* (1973), a Western featuring an all-Black cast.  Throughout the 1970s and 1980s, Van Peebles continued to direct, write, and occasionally act in films, including *Greased Lightning* (1977) and *Identity Crisis* (1989). He also worked in theater, directing and choreographing productions on and off Broadway.

His son, Mario Van Peebles, followed in his footsteps, becoming a successful actor and director in his own right. They collaborated on several projects, including the 1992 film *Posse*, a remake of Melvin's 1973 film, and the HBO series *Baadasssss!* which chronicled Melvin's life and career. 

In his later life, Van Peebles remained a vocal advocate for independent filmmaking and Black representation in the arts. He received an Honorary Palme d'Or at the 2021 Cannes Film Festival, recognizing his lifetime achievement.  In September 2021, shortly before his death, the American Film Institute presented him with the AFI Life Achievement Award, recognizing his outstanding contributions to the art of motion pictures.  Melvin Van Peebles died on September 24, 2021, in New York City, at the age of 89, leaving behind a legacy as a fearless innovator and a crucial figure in the history of American cinema. He is survived by his three children: Mario, Dedra and Robin.

title: 14th Dalai Lama
text:
Tenzin Gyatso, the 14th Dalai Lama, was born Lhamo Dhondup on July 6, 1935, in Taktser village, Amdo province, northeastern Tibet. His parents, Sonam Phuntsok and Dechen Dolma, were farmers. The search for the 14th Dalai Lama began after the death of the 13th Dalai Lama, Thubten Gyatso, in 1933. Guided by oracles and the interpretation of signs, a search party eventually identified Lhamo Dhondup as the reincarnation. He was formally recognized on February 22, 1939, at the age of four. 

The young Dalai Lama was brought to Lhasa, the Tibetan capital, in 1940 and installed as the supreme political and spiritual leader of Tibet on February 22, 1940, in the Potala Palace. His monastic education commenced immediately, studying Buddhist philosophy, logic, Sanskrit, medicine, and the arts. He began his Geshe Lharampa degree – the highest level of Buddhist scholarship – in 1959, though the Chinese invasion disrupted his studies. His principal tutors included Ling Rinpoche, Trijang Rinpoche, and Penchen Lobsang Yeshe.

The political landscape of Tibet dramatically altered with the Chinese invasion in 1950. Initially, the Dalai Lama attempted to work with the Chinese government, hoping to secure genuine autonomy for Tibet. He met with Mao Zedong in Beijing in 1954 and 1955, but these discussions ultimately failed to produce a satisfactory agreement. Increasing repression and unrest within Tibet led to the 1959 Tibetan uprising, beginning on March 10th in Lhasa.  Fearing for his life, the Dalai Lama fled Lhasa on March 17, 1959, accompanied by a small entourage, crossing the border into India.

He established a government-in-exile in Dharamsala, India, in 1960, which remains the center of the Tibetan exile community today, housing approximately 80,000 Tibetans.  Here, he focused on preserving Tibetan culture, religion, and identity. He oversaw the establishment of schools, monasteries, and cultural institutions to ensure the continuation of Tibetan traditions. 

Throughout the 1960s and 70s, the Dalai Lama advocated for a peaceful resolution to the Tibetan issue, consistently rejecting calls for independence and instead proposing a ‘Middle Way’ approach, advocating for genuine autonomy within the People’s Republic of China. He drafted a memorandum outlining this proposal in 1963, which was presented to the United Nations.  

From the 1980s onwards, the Dalai Lama embarked on numerous international tours, engaging with political leaders, academics, and the public, raising awareness about the situation in Tibet and promoting his message of peace, compassion, and universal responsibility. He has met with numerous heads of state, including Pope John Paul II (1980, 1982, 1988, 1995, 2006), President George H.W. Bush (1987), and President Barack Obama (2010, though in a non-official capacity).

In 1989, he was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize for his consistent advocacy of peaceful solutions based on non-violence in the struggle for the liberation of Tibet. The Nobel Committee specifically recognized his practical efforts to create peace and reconciliation between Tibet and China. He received the US Congressional Gold Medal in 2006, the highest civilian honor awarded by the US Congress.

In 2011, the Dalai Lama formally relinquished his political authority, transferring it to a democratically elected leadership within the Tibetan exile community, marking a significant transition towards a secular political system. He continues to serve as a spiritual leader. He has authored over 100 books, translated into numerous languages, covering Buddhist philosophy, ethics, and his personal experiences.  

Now in his 80s, Tenzin Gyatso continues to travel and teach, promoting interreligious harmony and environmental responsibility. He is known for his engaging personality, sense of humor, and unwavering commitment to non-violence.  He remains a globally recognized figure, advocating for a more peaceful and compassionate world.

title: Arthur Wakefield
text:
Arthur Wakefield was born on 17th April 1888 in Lambton Quay, Wellington, New Zealand, the third son of Edward Gibald Wakefield and his wife, Elizabeth (née Haggard). His family was deeply connected to the early colonial history of New Zealand; his grandfather, William Wakefield, was a key figure in the New Zealand Company and its land settlements. This familial legacy significantly shaped Arthur's early life and future trajectory. He received his education at Wanganui Collegiate School, a boarding school established by his uncle, and later at Cambridge University in England, attending St John's College from 1908 to 1911, where he studied law but did not complete a degree. 

Upon returning to New Zealand in 1912, Wakefield initially worked as a sheep farmer in the Wairarapa region, attempting to establish himself in the traditional rural economy. However, this proved unsatisfactory and he soon turned towards a career in public service, beginning as a clerk in the Department of Lands and Survey in Wellington in 1913. His legal background, even without a formal degree, proved beneficial, and he quickly progressed. He served during World War I with the New Zealand Expeditionary Force, holding the rank of Captain and serving in France and Italy from 1916 to 1919. This experience, like many returning soldiers, profoundly influenced his post-war outlook.

Wakefield’s career truly blossomed in the interwar period. He became a key figure in the development of New Zealand’s social welfare system. In 1926, he was appointed to the position of Director of Social Services under Sir Frederick Langstone, then Minister of Health. He played a pivotal role in the creation of the Social Security Act 1938, often considered the cornerstone of the modern New Zealand welfare state.  Wakefield wasn't merely an administrator; he was a driving force behind the Act’s conception, advocating for a comprehensive system encompassing health, unemployment, and old-age benefits.  He meticulously researched social welfare models in countries like the United Kingdom, Australia, and Canada, incorporating best practices into the New Zealand framework. 

The 1938 Act introduced universal healthcare, unemployment benefits, and a national superannuation scheme – radical changes for New Zealand at the time. Wakefield’s practical and pragmatic approach was crucial in navigating the political complexities and ensuring the Act’s successful implementation. He believed strongly in preventative social policy, aiming to address the root causes of poverty and hardship rather than simply providing relief.  He championed the establishment of state housing, recognising the link between housing conditions and public health.

Following the implementation of the Social Security Act, Wakefield continued to serve in key administrative roles. He was appointed as Secretary of the Department of Social Security in 1941, a position he held until his retirement in 1950. During this period, he oversaw the expansion of the social security system to meet the demands of wartime and post-war reconstruction. He was made a Companion of the Order of the British Empire (CBE) in 1946 for his services to the state.

Throughout his life, Wakefield remained a committed advocate for social justice and a strong believer in the power of government to improve the lives of its citizens. He was known for his meticulous attention to detail, his strong organisational skills, and his ability to build consensus among diverse stakeholders.  He wasn’t a flamboyant public figure, preferring to work behind the scenes, shaping policy through careful analysis and persuasive advocacy.

Arthur Wakefield died on 27th August 1961, in Wellington, at the age of 73. He was survived by his wife, Margaret (née Richmond), whom he married in 1921, and their two daughters. His contribution to the development of New Zealand’s social welfare system is enduring, and he is widely recognised as one of the key architects of the country's modern social safety net. While not always in the spotlight, his influence remains deeply embedded in the fabric of New Zealand society.

title: Carrie Ann Inaba
text:
Carrie Ann Inaba was born Carrie Ann Dickenson on January 18, 1968, in Honolulu, Hawaii. Her father, Rodney Dickenson, was a Japanese American veteran of World War II who worked as a tour bus driver, and her mother, Jeannette (née Miyake) Dickenson, was of Okinawan descent. Carrie Ann’s early life was marked by frequent moves due to her father's profession. She spent her childhood in Hawaii, California, and Japan, attending numerous schools. This nomadic upbringing instilled in her a sense of adaptability and independence. Her parents divorced when she was eleven years old, after which she lived primarily with her mother in California. She attended McKinley High School in Van Nuys, California, graduating in 1986. 

Inaba began her dance training at age three, initially studying hula. Later she focused on jazz, ballet, and hip-hop. While still in high school, she earned a scholarship to UCLA but deferred entry for a year to pursue professional dancing. She joined the "The Grind," a popular dance show in Los Angeles, in 1988. This led to appearances in several music videos throughout the early 1990s, including Paula Abdul's “Straight Up,” Janet Jackson’s “That’s the Way Love Is,” and Madonna’s “In This Bed.” She also performed as a dancer on *In Living Color* from 1990 to 1993, showcasing her versatility. 

Inaba transitioned into acting in the mid-1990s. She secured recurring roles in television series like *Saved by the Bell: The New Class* (1993-1994), *Sunset Beach* (1996-1997), *One World One Heart* (1997), and *Two Guys, A Girl and A Pizza Place* (1998-1999).  She also had a main role in *Felicity* (1998-1999) as Ava Moore. During this period, she also hosted *The American Music Awards* in 1997 alongside Queen Latifah. 

Inaba’s career took a significant turn in 2005 when she became a permanent judge on *Dancing With the Stars* (DWTS). She remained on the show for seventeen seasons, becoming known for her critiques delivered with a signature combination of encouragement and directness. Her scoring system, often favoring artistry over technical perfection, frequently sparked debate among viewers. She judged alongside figures like Bruno Tonioli and Len Goodman for many years. She took a break from DWTS in 2017 due to health issues but returned in later seasons. She also served as a judge on *So You Think You Can Dance* in 2013.

In addition to her judging roles, Inaba has continued to pursue acting opportunities. She starred in the Syfy series *Shark Tank Without Sharks* in 2011 and appeared in episodes of *Castle* in 2015. She also co-hosted *The Talk* from 2017 until February 2022, providing commentary on current events and celebrity news. Her tenure on *The Talk* was occasionally marked by controversy related to her perspectives on racial issues. 

Inaba’s personal life has been marked by health challenges. She has publicly discussed her struggles with Crohn’s disease, lupus, fibromyalgia, rheumatoid arthritis, and Sjögren’s syndrome – conditions she was diagnosed with over a period of years. She underwent multiple surgeries including a total knee replacement in 2023. Inaba married actor Ross Thomspon in May 2019 in Hawaii. In February 2024, they welcomed their first child, a son named Hudson via surrogate. She is also an advocate for autoimmune disease awareness and supports several charitable organizations.  Inaba has authored two books: *Dancing in the Dark* (2011), detailing her battle with autoimmune diseases, and *The Silver Lining* (2017), focusing on her experiences navigating life and love.  She maintains an active presence on social media, sharing insights into her life, health journey, and career.

title: Rui Campos
text:
Rui Manuel da Silva Campos was born on September 27, 1936, in Lisbon, Portugal, to Manuel and Maria da Silva Campos. His father was a lawyer and his mother a homemaker, and Rui was raised in a middle-class environment that valued education and cultural pursuits. He attended the Liceu Camões, a prestigious secondary school in Lisbon, demonstrating early aptitude in languages and literature. He then enrolled at the Faculty of Law of the University of Lisbon in 1954, completing his law degree in 1959. However, despite following his father’s profession initially, Campos’s true passion lay in journalism and writing.

Campos began his journalistic career in 1960, joining the news agency Agência Nacional do Notícias (National News Agency). This provided him with foundational experience in news gathering and reporting, but his ambitions extended beyond simple reporting. In 1962, he moved to the daily newspaper *Diário de Lisboa*, quickly ascending to a position of prominence as a commentator and columnist. It was during this period that he began to develop his distinctively critical and often provocative writing style, frequently challenging the authoritarian Estado Novo regime then governing Portugal. 

The repressive political climate of the 1960s and 70s significantly impacted Campos’s career. He faced censorship and periodic harassment from the PIDE (Polícia Internacional e de Defesa do Estado - the Portuguese secret police) for his outspoken views. Despite this, he continued to write, becoming a key voice for democratic ideals within Portugal’s constrained public sphere.  In 1966, he joined the newspaper *Expresso*, a publication known for its independent stance, and remained there for the next three decades, solidifying his reputation as one of Portugal’s leading journalists. 

Campos’s influence extended beyond daily journalism. He published his first book, *A Arte de Fugir* (The Art of Escaping), a collection of essays, in 1969. This was followed by several other acclaimed works, including *O Crime do Padre Amaro* (The Crime of Father Amaro) in 1975, a critical analysis of the famous novel by José Maria de Eça de Queirós, and *Portugal: O Estado e o Poder* (Portugal: The State and Power) in 1978, a detailed examination of the Portuguese political system. He was a prolific essayist, publishing over twenty books throughout his career, often focusing on Portuguese society, politics, and culture. 

A pivotal moment in his career arrived with the Carnation Revolution of April 25, 1974, which overthrew the Estado Novo dictatorship. Campos actively supported the revolution and the subsequent democratic transition, using his platform at *Expresso* to advocate for political reform and social justice.  Following the revolution, he became a frequent commentator on television and radio, further broadening his audience and influence. He was known for his sharp intellect, eloquent delivery, and willingness to engage in rigorous debate.

In 1996, Campos received the Grand Cross of the Order of Public Instruction, Portugal’s highest honour for services to education and culture. He continued to write and comment on current affairs well into his seventies, remaining a respected and influential figure in Portuguese public life.  He also served as a visiting professor at several universities, including the University of Coimbra and the New University of Lisbon.

Rui Campos suffered a stroke in December 2008, which significantly impacted his health and ability to write. He passed away on May 22, 2011, in Lisbon, at the age of 74.  His death was widely mourned in Portugal, with tributes pouring in from across the political spectrum. He left behind a substantial body of work that continues to be read and studied, and is remembered as a courageous journalist, a gifted essayist, and a staunch defender of democratic values. His collected works, numbering in the dozens of volumes, remain a significant contribution to Portuguese intellectual history.

title: Christian Almeida
text:
Christian Almeida was born on October 12, 1978, in São Paulo, Brazil, to parents José Almeida, a civil engineer, and Ana Maria Almeida, a schoolteacher. He was raised in a middle-class family in the Vila Mariana district of the city, attending the Escola Britânica de São Paulo, a bilingual school that fostered his early interest in both the arts and technology. From a young age, Almeida displayed a talent for drawing and a keen aptitude for computers, skills he would later combine in his professional life. He began experimenting with digital art and basic coding in his early teens, building simple websites and creating pixel art. 

Almeida’s formal education continued at the Universidade de São Paulo, where he enrolled in a Bachelor of Science program in Computer Science in 1996. He focused his studies on computer graphics and interactive media, graduating with honors in 2000. During his university years, he began freelancing as a web designer and developer, building websites for local businesses and contributing to small independent game projects. This practical experience solidified his desire to pursue a career in the burgeoning field of visual effects.

In 2001, Almeida relocated to Vancouver, Canada, a growing hub for the visual effects industry. He initially took a position as a runner at Rainmaker Visual Effects, a relatively small studio at the time. He quickly proved his technical skills and artistic eye, transitioning into a junior compositor role within six months. Over the next five years, he steadily climbed the ranks, becoming a senior compositor and working on projects like the animated film *Sky Captain and the World of Tomorrow* (2004) and the live-action *Fantastic Four* (2005). 

A pivotal moment in his career came in 2006 when he was recruited by Industrial Light & Magic (ILM), the visual effects company founded by George Lucas. At ILM, Almeida worked as a Senior Digital Artist, contributing significantly to large-scale projects including *Pirates of the Caribbean: At World’s End* (2007), for which he specialized in complex water simulations and environment work. He was then a crucial part of the team that brought *Star Trek* (2009) to life, handling extensive digital matte painting and set extensions. 

His work on *Inception* (2010), directed by Christopher Nolan, earned him significant recognition. Almeida was responsible for creating several of the film's most iconic and challenging visual effects, including the rotating corridor sequence and the collapsing cityscapes. This work was acknowledged with a nomination for the Academy Award for Best Visual Effects in 2011, shared with Paul Franklin, Christopher Nolan, and Peter Chiaramonte. 

In 2012, Almeida joined Weta Digital in Wellington, New Zealand, as a Visual Effects Supervisor. This marked a significant shift in his career, taking on a leadership role overseeing entire sequences and teams of artists. He quickly became an integral part of Peter Jackson’s *The Hobbit* trilogy (2012-2014), where he supervised the creation of digitally-enhanced environments and creature effects, notably the Smaug the dragon sequences. He subsequently served as a VFX Supervisor on *War for the Planet of the Apes* (2017) and *Alita: Battle Angel* (2019).

Throughout his career, Almeida has consistently pushed the boundaries of visual effects technology. He is credited with developing several innovative techniques for creating realistic simulations of natural phenomena, particularly water and fire. He has also been a vocal advocate for the importance of artistic collaboration within the VFX pipeline. 

In 2020, Almeida stepped away from full-time studio work to establish his own independent visual effects consultancy, Almeida Studios. Based in Los Angeles, the company focuses on providing high-end visual effects services for feature films and television, as well as offering training and mentorship programs for aspiring artists. As of 2023, he continues to work on select projects and frequently lectures at industry conferences, sharing his expertise and insights with the next generation of visual effects professionals. He is married to artist Isabella Rossi and they have two children.

title: Joseph A. Lopez
text:
Joseph Anthony Lopez was born on July 28, 1917, in the small farming community of Bluff, Utah, to parents of Mexican and Native American descent. His father, Francisco Lopez, was a sheep herder and his mother, Maria Sanches Lopez, managed their household and worked seasonally in agricultural labor. Growing up, Lopez experienced the hardships of a marginalized community, facing both economic disadvantage and racial prejudice. He attended public schools in Moab, Utah, but left after the eighth grade to help support his family, working primarily in mining and ranching. Despite limited formal education, Lopez was a voracious reader and self-taught, developing a strong understanding of history and political theory. 

Lopez enlisted in the United States Army on January 26, 1942, shortly after the attack on Pearl Harbor. He was assigned to the 104th Infantry Division, nicknamed the “Timberwolves,” and shipped to Europe in August 1944. The 104th was involved in some of the fiercest fighting of World War II, particularly in the Hürtgen Forest and during the Battle of the Bulge. It was during the assault on the Siegfried Line near the village of Kalenborn, Germany, on November 29, 1944, that Lopez performed the actions for which he would ultimately be recognized. 

Facing intense enemy fire, Lopez single-handedly attacked and neutralized two machine gun nests, allowing his company to advance. He then located and destroyed a third machine gun position, again under heavy fire. After his company had successfully taken the hill, he again volunteered to scout for enemy positions. He discovered a heavily defended area with two 88mm guns, which were causing significant casualties.  Lopez, armed only with a carbine and grenades, launched a one-man assault, destroying one gun and forcing the crew of the other to abandon their position. This sustained, exceptional bravery earned him the Distinguished Service Cross, the nation’s second-highest military honor. 

However, the official citation for his bravery was initially flawed. In 1997, research by historian Doug Sterner revealed that Lopez’s Distinguished Service Cross was awarded for actions that, according to the standards of the time, should have warranted the Medal of Honor. Sterner’s research involved detailed analysis of after-action reports, witness statements, and comparisons to other Medal of Honor citations.  He argued that Lopez’s courage exceeded the criteria for the Distinguished Service Cross.

Following a lengthy review process, the Army officially upgraded Lopez’s Distinguished Service Cross to the Medal of Honor on February 9, 2014. The ceremony took place at the Pentagon, and Lopez, then 96 years old, was presented with the medal by President Barack Obama. He was the oldest living Medal of Honor recipient at the time.  This delay of over 70 years in recognizing his heroism was widely noted and attributed to racial bias within the military's award system during and after World War II.  

After the war, Lopez returned to Utah and resumed ranching and mining, remaining largely out of the public eye. He married Maria Esther Lucero in 1946, and they raised five children – Joseph Jr., Manuel, Richard, Robert, and Esther.  He was a devout Catholic and active in his local church. Despite his wartime heroism, he rarely spoke about his experiences, preferring to live a quiet life focused on his family and community. 

Lopez received numerous accolades in his later years, including honorary degrees from Utah State University (2014) and Weber State University (2015). He became a symbol of overlooked valor and a champion for recognizing the contributions of minority veterans. He passed away on July 24, 2016, just four days before his 99th birthday, at his home in Dolores, Colorado, surrounded by family. He is buried at Fort Logan National Cemetery in Denver, Colorado.

title: Marty Mayberry
text:
Marty Mayberry, born Martin Lee Mayberry on October 26, 1956, in Benton, Illinois, is a retired American professional rodeo cowboy who specialized in bull riding. His career spanned nearly two decades and culminated in a world championship, solidifying his place as a legend in the sport. He was the son of Gene and Betty Mayberry, and grew up on a family farm where he began riding horses at a very young age. This early exposure to livestock and rural life proved crucial in developing the skills and tenacity needed for a career in rodeo. 

Mayberry’s interest in bull riding began in his teenage years, initially competing in local rodeos and high school events around Southern Illinois. He quickly excelled, demonstrating a natural aptitude for the sport and an unusually calm demeanor for someone facing a 2,000-pound animal. After graduating from Benton High School in 1974, he bypassed traditional college plans, opting instead to pursue rodeo full-time. He initially traveled the circuit independently, relying on winnings and the support of his family. 

His professional rodeo career officially began in 1975 with the Rodeo Cowboys Association (RCA), which would later become the Professional Rodeo Cowboys Association (PRCA). The early years were characterized by consistent, though not spectacular, performance. He steadily climbed the rankings, earning enough to sustain his lifestyle but lacking the breakthrough wins needed to become a top contender. He spent considerable time honing his technique, working with experienced bull riders and learning from both successes and failures. 

The turning point came in the late 1980s. Mayberry’s dedication and refined skills began to translate into significant victories. In 1987, he finished 8th in the world standings, a considerable improvement. 1989 was his banner year. He won the National Finals Rodeo (NFR) in Las Vegas, Nevada, with an impressive cumulative score of 438 points on 10 bulls. This win, combined with consistent performance throughout the year, earned him the 1989 PRCA World Championship in Bull Riding. He earned $128,793 in that championship year, a substantial amount at the time. Throughout his career, he consistently rode for renowned stock contractors like Beutler & Son and Frontier Rodeo, often drawing some of the most challenging bulls in the business.

Mayberry was known for his smooth, balanced style and his ability to “stay centered” on the bull, absorbing the animal’s movements. He wasn’t a flashy rider known for high-risk maneuvers, but rather one who focused on consistency and control. He was also respected for his sportsmanship and calm demeanor, even in the face of danger. This earned him the admiration of fellow competitors and fans alike. 

He continued to compete at a high level through the early 1990s, though injuries began to take their toll. He suffered numerous concussions and broken bones, typical consequences of a bull riding career. He officially retired from professional rodeo in 1994 at the age of 37, acknowledging the physical demands and the need to protect his long-term health.

Following his retirement, Mayberry remained involved in the rodeo world, though in a less physically demanding capacity. He spent several years working as a stock contractor, providing bulls for rodeo events. He also became a popular rodeo clinician, sharing his knowledge and experience with aspiring bull riders.  He moved back to his hometown of Benton, Illinois, and remained active in the local community. 



In 2018, Marty Mayberry was inducted into the National Cowboy & Western Heritage Museum’s Rodeo Hall of Fame in Oklahoma City, Oklahoma, further cementing his legacy as one of the great bull riders of his era. As of late 2023, Mayberry resides in Illinois and enjoys spending time with his family. He is considered a quiet, humble icon of the sport, remembered not only for his championship but also for his grace and dedication to the cowboy way of life.

title: Andry Rajoelina
text:
Andry Nirina Rajoelina was born on February 22, 1974, in Antananarivo, Madagascar. His father, Colonel Hyppolite Rajoelina, was a military man and his mother, Any Rasoamanarivo, worked in education. He spent his early years in the Andohimampy neighbourhood of the capital, attending primary school at the École Publique d'Andohimampy and continuing his secondary education at the Collège Saint-Michel and the Lycée Technique d'Antananarivo, graduating in 1993. Though he initially enrolled in medicine at the University of Antananarivo, he dropped out after only a year to pursue a career in business.

Rajoelina’s entrepreneurial path began in the mid-1990s, focusing on advertising and event management. He established a company called "Show Business," which quickly gained prominence organizing concerts and promotional events, becoming a key player in Madagascar’s entertainment industry. His success led him to invest in radio and television. In 1999, he founded Radio Feon’ny Merina, a popular radio station, and in 2002, he launched Television Plus, a private television channel. These media ventures allowed him to cultivate a significant public profile and influence, particularly among younger Madagascans.

His foray into politics began in 2007 when he was appointed as Mayor of Antananarivo by then-President Marc Ravalomanana. Initially seen as a technocratic appointment, Rajoelina quickly proved a popular leader, implementing reforms aimed at improving traffic management and urban cleanliness. He became a prominent figure challenging Ravalomanana’s administration, particularly regarding concessions granted to foreign companies, notably a controversial lease of farmland to South Korean firm Daewoo Logistics. 

The political climate in Madagascar became increasingly volatile in early 2009. Protests erupted, fueled by public discontent over Ravalomanana’s governance and Rajoelina’s growing popularity. On January 26, 2009, clashes between protesters and presidential guards resulted in fatalities, further escalating tensions. Rajoelina, backed by the military, declared himself head of a transitional government on February 7, 2009, effectively ousting Ravalomanana, who fled the country. 

This transition was widely condemned internationally as an unconstitutional coup d'état. The African Union suspended Madagascar’s membership, and many countries imposed sanctions. Rajoelina headed the High Transitional Authority (HTA) for five years, overseeing a period marked by political instability and economic hardship. A new constitution was adopted in 2010 through a controversial referendum, further solidifying his position.  

After years of international pressure and negotiations, elections were finally held in 2013. Rajoelina did not participate directly, as international agreements stipulated he could not run. Instead, he supported Hery Rajaonarimampianina, who won the presidential election.  However, Rajaonarimampianina’s presidency was also marked by political challenges and allegations of mismanagement.

Rajoelina re-entered the presidential race in 2018. The first round of voting on November 16, 2018, saw him facing Rajaonarimampianina in a runoff election. On December 19, 2018, Rajoelina defeated Rajaonarimampianina, winning the presidency with approximately 55.69% of the vote. He was inaugurated on January 19, 2019. 

His second term as president has focused on economic development, infrastructure projects, and combating corruption. He initiated a national overhaul of infrastructure, including road construction and improvements to the Antananarivo airport. He has also faced continued challenges relating to poverty, political polarization, and allegations of authoritarian tendencies. In December 2023, he secured re-election in a vote marred by low turnout and accusations of irregularities, winning with 58.95% of the vote, extending his time in office and solidifying his position as a dominant figure in Madagascan politics. He remains a controversial figure, both lauded for his modernization efforts and criticized for his methods of achieving and maintaining power.

title: Sheldon T. Mills
text:
Sheldon Theodore Mills, a prominent figure in American finance and a trailblazer for African Americans in the investment banking world, was born on November 29, 1956, in New York City. He was raised in the St. Albans neighborhood of Queens, a middle-class Black community that fostered a strong sense of achievement. His father, Theodore Mills, was a postal worker, and his mother, Vivian Mills, was a school teacher. This background instilled in him a strong work ethic and the importance of education. Mills attended Archbishop Molan High School in Queens, graduating in 1974. He then pursued higher education at Stanford University, earning a Bachelor of Arts degree in Economics in 1978. He continued his studies at Harvard Business School, graduating with a Master of Business Administration degree in 1981.

Mills’s career began on Wall Street at Goldman Sachs in 1981, joining as an associate in the Corporate Finance department. This was a significant achievement, as African Americans were vastly underrepresented in the high-finance world at the time. He quickly distinguished himself through his analytical skills and dedication, steadily climbing the ranks. He became a Vice President in 1987, and a Partner in 1990, making him one of the first African American partners in the firm’s history. During his 21-year tenure at Goldman Sachs, he specialized in mergers and acquisitions, advising companies on deals totaling billions of dollars. He was instrumental in several high-profile transactions, including the $10.3 billion merger of Bell Atlantic and NYNEX in 1997, and the $5.3 billion acquisition of Quaker Oats by PepsiCo in 2001. 

Beyond his deal-making prowess, Mills was a committed advocate for diversity within the firm and the broader financial industry. He actively mentored young professionals from underrepresented backgrounds and championed initiatives to increase recruitment and retention of minority employees. He served as the head of Goldman Sachs’ Pine Street leadership program, designed to cultivate future leaders within the company. 

In 2002, Mills left Goldman Sachs to join Wasserstein Perella & Co., a boutique investment bank, as a Managing Director. He was brought in specifically to build and lead the firm’s financial sponsors group, focusing on private equity clients. He successfully expanded the group’s business, forging strong relationships with prominent private equity firms.  

In 2006, Mills transitioned to a new phase of his career, becoming a Senior Advisor to Apollo Global Management, a leading alternative investment firm. He provided strategic advice on investments and played a key role in the firm’s expansion. Simultaneously, he became a member of the Board of Directors for several public companies, including Hess Corporation, where he served on the Audit Committee, and Viacom, now Paramount Global. He also served on the Board of Trustees for his alma mater, Stanford University, from 2008 to 2016, contributing to the university's financial oversight and strategic direction.

Throughout his career, Mills was recognized for his leadership and contributions to the financial community. He was consistently listed among the “100 Most Influential Black Executives in America” by *Savoy Magazine*. He was also a frequent speaker at industry events, sharing his insights on finance, diversity, and leadership. 

Sheldon T. Mills passed away on March 17, 2023, in New York City, at the age of 66, following a battle with cancer. His death was widely mourned throughout the financial world. He is remembered not only for his impressive career achievements but also for his commitment to mentoring and paving the way for future generations of diverse leaders in finance. He left behind his wife, Dr. Deborah C. Mills, and two daughters, Stephanie and Alexandra. His legacy continues to inspire those seeking to break barriers and create a more inclusive financial landscape.

title: Hu Qili
text:
Hu Qili (胡启立, born November 25, 1926, in Wujin County, Jiangsu Province, died February 23, 2016, in Beijing) was a prominent Chinese Communist Party (CCP) official who served as Vice Chairman of the National People’s Congress Standing Committee and played a key role in economic reforms during the 1980s. His career was marked by both significant advancement and a dramatic fall from grace following the Tiananmen Square protests of 1989.

Hu’s revolutionary roots were firmly established early in life. He joined the New Fourth Army, a communist guerrilla force operating in Japanese-occupied China, in 1940 at the age of 14, serving as a messenger and later a fighter. He participated in numerous campaigns against the Japanese and later against the Kuomintang forces during the Chinese Civil War. He officially joined the CCP in November 1944. Following the establishment of the People’s Republic of China in 1949, Hu remained in the People's Liberation Army (PLA), holding various positions within the logistics and political branches. 

His career trajectory took a significant turn in 1958 when he was transferred to Anhui Province and began a long career in provincial administration. He served as Deputy Secretary of the Anhui Provincial Party Committee from 1978 to 1981, a period witnessing the initial phases of Deng Xiaoping’s economic reforms. This provincial experience proved crucial, as it allowed him to gain practical knowledge of the challenges and opportunities presented by the shift from a centrally planned economy to a more market-oriented system. 

In 1981, Hu Qili moved to Beijing and entered the central government, becoming a member of the CCP Central Committee. He quickly rose through the ranks, becoming a Secretary of the Central Committee in 1982 and a member of the Politburo in September 1985.  Crucially, he was appointed as a Vice Premier in charge of economic planning, overseeing key areas like agriculture, finance, and trade. He worked closely with Zhao Ziyang, another key reformer, and became a leading figure in implementing the “two-tier pricing system” and other policies designed to stimulate production and consumer demand.  These reforms, introduced in 1984, allowed factories to sell a portion of their output on the open market at prices determined by supply and demand alongside state-controlled prices. 

Hu was considered a pragmatic and relatively liberal voice within the CCP, advocating for a gradual and cautious approach to economic liberalization. He played a significant role in the establishment of special economic zones and the opening up of China to foreign investment. His influence was visible in the rapid economic growth China experienced throughout the 1980s. He also championed increased autonomy for local enterprises and a reduction in bureaucratic control. 

However, Hu’s career was abruptly derailed during the 1989 Tiananmen Square protests. While not considered directly responsible for the crackdown, he was perceived as sympathetic to the students and had argued for a more conciliatory approach to the demonstrations. He was accused of “serious mistakes” in handling the situation, specifically of failing to adequately control the growing unrest and of being insufficiently supportive of hardline policies. 

In May 1989, shortly after the military suppression of the protests, Hu Qili was stripped of all his positions within the CCP and government. He was formally removed from the Politburo and the State Council. This dismissal marked a dramatic end to a promising career and signaled a turn towards a more conservative political climate. 

Following his removal, Hu lived a largely quiet and secluded life for the next two decades. He remained a member of the CCP, but held no official positions. He did, however, continue to write and publish articles on economic issues.  He was eventually reinstated as a member of the National People's Congress Standing Committee in 1998.  He retired in 2003. Hu Qili died in Beijing on February 23, 2016, at the age of 89, leaving behind a complex legacy as a reformer who fell victim to the political turmoil of the late 1980s.

title: James Franco
text:
James Edward Franco was born on April 19, 1978, in Palo Alto, California, to Douglas Eugene Franco, a businessman, and Betsy Lou Franco, a writer. He grew up in a Portuguese-American family with two siblings, older brother Dave Franco, also an actor, and younger sister Annabel, who pursued a career in art. His mother’s side traces back to Portugal, and his father has Swedish and English ancestry. Franco’s childhood was somewhat nomadic, spending time in various locations in California, including Concord and Preston School of Industry, a juvenile detention facility, due to instances of substance use and disruptive behavior during his teenage years. Despite these challenges, he excelled academically, graduating from Palo Alto High School in 1996. He initially enrolled at the University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA), intending to pursue a degree in English, but left after his sophomore year to pursue acting.

Franco’s acting career began with small roles in television in the early 2000s. He appeared in single episodes of shows like “Pacific Blue” (2000) and “Freaks and Geeks” (1999-2000), the latter being a significant early role that showcased his comedic timing. His breakthrough came with the role of Daniel Desario in the short-lived but critically acclaimed teen drama “Freaks and Geeks,” created by Paul Feig and Seth Rogen. This role established him as a rising talent.

He gained wider recognition playing the title role in the 2002 made-for-television biographical film “James Dean,” earning him a Golden Globe Award and a Screen Actors Guild Award nomination. This performance led to more substantial film roles. He appeared in films like “Spider-Man” (2002) as Harry Osborn, a role he reprised in “Spider-Man 2” (2004) and “Spider-Man 3” (2007), and “Annapolis” (2006).  

Franco’s career diversified significantly in the late 2000s and 2010s. He began directing and producing independent films, including “Good People” (2010), which he co-wrote, directed, and starred in alongside his brother Dave. He also took on more challenging and experimental roles, notably in Gus Van Sant’s “Milk” (2008), portraying Scott Smith, a gay rights activist.  He received an Academy Award nomination for Best Actor for his performance in Danny Boyle’s “127 Hours” (2010), where he played Aron Ralston, a mountain climber who amputates his own arm after becoming trapped by a boulder. 

Franco’s ambition extended beyond acting and filmmaking. He simultaneously pursued multiple degrees at UCLA, earning a Bachelor of Arts in Creative Writing in 2008. He continued his education, attending Columbia University’s MFA film program, New York University’s MFA writing program, and eventually obtaining a PhD in Literature from Yale University in 2016. During this period, he published collections of short stories, including “Palo Alto” (2010) and “Hollywood A-List” (2015). He also taught film courses at UCLA and New York University.

However, in 2018, allegations of sexually exploitative behavior towards his acting students at his Studio 4 acting school surfaced, leading to significant backlash and effectively halting his career momentum. Lawsuits were filed alleging coercion and manipulation.  He settled two of these lawsuits in 2021 for a reported $2.2 million.  Following the allegations, many of his projects were shelved, and he faced widespread condemnation. 

Since the allegations, Franco has largely remained out of the public eye. He has expressed remorse for his behavior and sought treatment for issues related to addiction.  In 2023, he appeared in the independent film "Mace," marking a return to acting, though his comeback has been met with continued scrutiny. As of late 2023, he continues to work intermittently in independent films, but his reputation remains significantly tarnished.

title: George VI
text:
Albert Frederick Arthur George, later known as George VI, was born on December 14, 1895, at York Cottage in Sandringham, Norfolk, the third son of the Duke and Duchess of York (later King George V and Queen Mary). His early life was marked by a perceived lack of academic ability and a stammer, which caused him considerable distress. He was a left-handed child forced to write with his right, a practice thought to improve his speech, though it proved largely ineffective. His education began with private tutors, followed by naval training at the Royal Naval College, Osborne, in 1909, and then Dartmouth Naval College in 1911. 

His naval career, though initially promising, was cut short by ill health. He served during World War I as a sub-lieutenant aboard HMS Collingwood, participating in the Battle of Jutland in 1916. Suffering from persistent stomach problems, he was discharged from the navy in 1919. This unexpected turn of events dramatically altered the course of his life. With his older brother, Edward, Prince of Wales, unmarried, and his second brother, Prince Albert, also without issue, Albert became a more prominent figure in line to the throne.

On April 23, 1923, at Westminster Abbey, he married Lady Elizabeth Bowes-Lyon, the daughter of the Earl of Strathmore and Kinghorne. The marriage proved a remarkably successful and supportive partnership, producing two daughters: Princess Elizabeth (later Queen Elizabeth II), born on April 21, 1926, and Princess Margaret, born on August 21, 1930.
