She meticulously collected and cataloged testimonies, photographs, and artifacts related to the bombing, becoming a crucial figure in preserving the historical record. Her dedication extended beyond simply archiving materials; she actively sought out hibakusha and encouraged them to share their experiences, recognizing the powerful impact of first-person accounts.

Kuroki’s work at the museum led to her involvement in international peace initiatives.  In 1975, she became actively involved with the Women’s International League for Peace and Freedom (WILPF), a global organization advocating for peace and disarmament.  She travelled extensively, representing the organization and sharing her experiences as a hibakusha with audiences around the world.  These speaking engagements took her to countries including the United States, Canada, various European nations, and Australia. She consistently emphasized the human cost of nuclear weapons and the urgent need for their abolition. 

A defining achievement of Kuroki’s career was her role in the creation of the "Hiroshima Appeals," a series of statements issued by the city of Hiroshima calling for nuclear disarmament. Beginning in 1985, Kuroki was deeply involved in drafting and disseminating these appeals, which were presented to the United Nations and other international bodies. She was particularly instrumental in ensuring the appeals reflected the voices and perspectives of hibakusha.  Over the years, the Hiroshima Appeals were presented to numerous world leaders and organizations, becoming a significant component of Hiroshima’s peace advocacy.

Kuroki retired from the Hiroshima Peace Memorial Museum in 1992 after 28 years of service, but continued her peace work with undiminished passion. She established the “Hiroshima Interpreters for Peace” organization, training volunteers to effectively communicate the stories of hibakusha to international audiences.  She also remained actively involved with WILPF, serving on various committees and continuing to travel and speak. 

In 2003, Kuroki received the Pax Christi Peace Award, a prestigious international recognition for her tireless efforts in promoting peace and disarmament. She was also a recipient of the Hiroshima Peace Culture Award in 1994.  

Kaoru Kuroki passed away on October 22, 2023, in Hiroshima, at the age of 91.  Her death was widely mourned by peace activists and those who had been touched by her story. She left behind a legacy of unwavering commitment to peace, a detailed archive of hibakusha testimonies, and a lasting impact on the global movement for nuclear disarmament. Her life served as a powerful reminder of the human cost of war and the importance of striving for a world free of nuclear weapons.

title: Jackson Martínez
text:
Jackson Martínez was born on October 14, 1986, in Béguilas, a small rural town in the Bolívar Department of Colombia. His childhood was marked by significant hardship; his father was murdered when Jackson was just four years old, forcing his mother, Mercedes González, to work tirelessly selling lottery tickets and empanadas to support him and his siblings. Football offered an escape from this difficult reality, and he began playing organized football with a local team, Estrella Roja, at the age of 12. He quickly demonstrated a natural talent, excelling as a striker despite his slight build. 

His early career took shape in 2004 when he joined the youth academy of Unión Magdalena in Santa Marta. He didn't remain long in the youth system, making his professional debut for the club in the Categoría Primera A, Colombia’s top football league, on March 13, 2005, in a match against Envigado. He scored his first professional goal shortly after, on March 27, 2005, against Atlético Bucaramanga. He spent two seasons with Unión Magdalena, appearing in 42 matches and scoring 13 goals, attracting attention from larger clubs.

In 2006, Jackson Martínez moved to Once Caldas in Manizales. This proved to be a pivotal moment in his career. He played a key role in Once Caldas' successful 2006 Apertura campaign, scoring 12 goals in 18 appearances and helping the team secure the league title. More importantly, he was instrumental in their Copa Sudamericana triumph that same year, scoring the winning goal in the second leg of the final against Fluminense on December 13, 2006, at the Palogrande Stadium. This victory marked the first international title for a Colombian club in 26 years.

His performances earned him a move to Mexican side Club América in January 2010 for a reported fee of around $4 million. In Mexico, Martínez flourished. He quickly became a prolific goalscorer, netting 32 goals in 39 league games during the 2010 Apertura and Clausura seasons, becoming the league’s top scorer. He continued his impressive form in subsequent seasons, accumulating a total of 75 goals in 115 appearances for Club América across all competitions.  

In August 2012, Martínez joined Portuguese giants FC Porto for a transfer fee of €11.2 million. He continued his goalscoring prowess in Portugal, forming a potent attacking partnership with Hulk. In the 2012–13 season, he scored 31 goals in 30 league matches, winning the Bola de Prata (Portuguese Golden Boot) as the league’s top scorer. He also played a crucial role in Porto's league title win that season and reached the Europa League final, losing to Sevilla. He contributed 13 goals in the Europa League campaign, finishing as the competition's top scorer. He totaled 67 goals in 90 appearances for Porto.

His consistent performance attracted the attention of Atlético Madrid, who signed him in July 2014 for €35 million. However, his time in Spain was less successful. He struggled to adapt to Diego Simeone's tactical system and was hampered by injuries. He scored only three goals in 22 La Liga appearances for Atlético.

In February 2016, he moved to Chinese Super League side Guangzhou Evergrande for a reported €42 million, becoming one of the highest-paid players in the world at the time. He scored 36 goals in 53 league appearances for Guangzhou, winning the Chinese Super League title in 2017. 

After three seasons in China, Martínez returned to Colombia in July 2019, signing for Atlético Nacional in Medellín. His return was met with enthusiasm, but he faced challenges with form and injuries. He retired from professional football in April 2023, citing ongoing knee problems that had plagued the latter part of his career. 

Jackson Martínez earned 45 caps for the Colombia national team, scoring 17 goals. He represented his country at the 2010 and 2014 FIFA World Cups, and the Copa América tournaments in 2007, 2011, 2015 and 2016.

title: Margaret Rose Vendryes
text:
Margaret Rose Vendryes was born on August 22, 1930, in Baltimore, Maryland, the only child of William Vendryes, a postal worker, and Rose Thompson Vendryes, a seamstress. Her early life was shaped by the vibrant, yet segregated, community of West Baltimore. She attended Frederick Douglass High School, a historically Black institution renowned for its academic rigor, graduating in 1948. From a young age, Vendryes demonstrated a keen interest in history and a dedication to academic excellence, fostered by her mother who emphasized education as a path to opportunity. 

Vendryes’ higher education began at Morgan State College (now Morgan State University) in 1948, where she initially intended to study pre-med. However, inspired by her history teachers and a growing awareness of the limitations placed upon African Americans in the medical field at the time, she switched her major to history, earning a Bachelor of Arts degree in 1952. She continued her studies at the University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, and in 1956, became one of the first African American women to earn a doctorate in history from that institution. Her dissertation, completed under the direction of Professor Wilma King, focused on the social and economic history of free Black people in Baltimore during the antebellum period.

Following her doctoral studies, Vendryes embarked on a distinguished academic career. In 1956, she accepted a position at Howard University in Washington D.C., initially as an instructor and quickly rising through the ranks to become a full professor in 1968. She remained at Howard for over three decades, becoming a cornerstone of the university’s history department. She specialized in African American history, with a particular focus on the experiences of free Black communities in the 19th century, slavery, and the history of Baltimore. 

Vendryes’ scholarship significantly contributed to reshaping historical narratives. Her 1986 publication, *Free Black People of Maryland, 1693-1860: A Demographic Study*, published by Johns Hopkins University Press, was a landmark work. Based on meticulous research in county court records, wills, and other primary sources, it provided a detailed quantitative analysis of the free Black population in Maryland, challenging prevailing assumptions about their economic status, social mobility, and familial structures. The book demonstrated that free Black people were not simply a marginal group, but a dynamic and resourceful population actively building lives and communities despite the constraints of slavery and racial prejudice. It remains a foundational text for scholars of African American history. 

Beyond *Free Black People of Maryland*, Vendryes published numerous articles and book chapters and presented her research at conferences nationally and internationally. She served as a mentor to generations of students, many of whom went on to become prominent historians themselves. She was deeply committed to public history and engaged in extensive community outreach, giving lectures and presentations to local organizations and contributing to historical preservation efforts in Baltimore. In 1992, she received an honorary Doctor of Humane Letters from Morgan State University in recognition of her contributions to scholarship and the community.

Margaret Rose Vendryes retired from Howard University in 1993, but continued her research and writing. She returned to Baltimore and devoted much of her later life to researching the history of the Black elite in the city. In 2000, she established the Vendryes Family Research Institute, dedicated to the preservation and study of African American genealogical and historical records. She passed away on January 7, 2016, in Baltimore, Maryland, at the age of 85. Her legacy continues through her scholarship, the researchers she mentored, and the enduring impact of her work on the field of African American historical studies. The Margaret Rose Vendryes Papers are held at the Moorland-Spingarn Research Center at Howard University, providing scholars with access to her extensive research materials.

title: G. Venugopal
text:
G. Venugopal, a highly respected Indian nuclear scientist and the former Director of the Indira Gandhi Centre for Atomic Research (IGCAR), was born on December 11, 1943, in Chennai, Tamil Nadu. His father, G. Krishnamurthy, was a physics professor, instilling in Venugopal a foundational interest in science from a young age. He received his early education at P.S. High School, Chennai, demonstrating an aptitude for mathematics and physics. He went on to pursue a Bachelor of Engineering in Mechanical Engineering from the College of Engineering, Guindy, Chennai, graduating in 1965 with a first-class honors degree.

Venugopal’s academic journey continued with a Master of Technology in Nuclear Engineering from the Indian Institute of Technology, Madras, in 1967. He then embarked on a doctoral degree, earning his Ph.D. in Fast Reactor Physics from the same institution in 1971. This period was pivotal, as it cemented his specialization in the complex field of fast breeder reactor technology – a crucial component of India’s three-stage nuclear power program. 

He joined the Bhabha Atomic Research Centre (BARC), Trombay, in 1967 as a Scientific Officer, beginning his long and distinguished career within India’s Department of Atomic Energy. Initially, his work focused on reactor physics calculations and the development of computational tools for analyzing fast reactor behavior.  Over the next two decades, he progressively took on roles of increasing responsibility within BARC, contributing significantly to the design and safety analysis of the Fast Breeder Test Reactor (FBTR), India’s first fast reactor which achieved first criticality in 1985.  He was instrumental in the validation of critical experiments and the development of sophisticated computer codes essential for reactor operation and safety.

In 1988, Venugopal was transferred to the newly established IGCAR in Kalpakkam, Tamil Nadu, and played a central role in the development of the Advanced Heavy Water Reactor (AHWR) and, crucially, the Fast Breeder Reactor (FBR) program. He led numerous teams involved in the design, construction, and commissioning of critical facilities and experimental loops.  His expertise in neutronics, thermal-hydraulics, and reactor safety was widely recognized.  He was appointed as the Director of IGCAR on January 1, 2001, succeeding P. K. Iyengar.

During his five-year tenure as Director, from 2001 to 2006, Venugopal oversaw significant advancements in the FBR program. The Bharatiya Nabhikiya Vidyut Shakti Nigam Limited (BHAVINI), the company responsible for building India’s first commercial FBR, the Prototype Fast Breeder Reactor (PFBR) at Kalpakkam, was under his direct purview. He championed indigenous technology development and focused on enhancing the safety and reliability of the FBR system.  He actively promoted collaboration with other national laboratories and academic institutions to accelerate the progress of the program.  Under his leadership, IGCAR also made considerable progress in areas like accelerator-driven systems and advanced fuel cycle technologies.

Venugopal retired from IGCAR in January 2006, but continued to contribute to the Department of Atomic Energy as a senior advisor. He served on numerous national and international committees related to nuclear energy and safety.  He was a Fellow of the Indian National Academy of Engineering and the Indian Society for Nuclear Energy.  He received several awards and recognitions for his contributions to the field, including the Homi Bhabha Science and Technology Excellence Award in 2004. 

Beyond his professional life, Venugopal was known for his modest and unassuming personality and his dedication to mentoring young scientists.  He was a keen follower of Carnatic music and enjoyed spending time with his family. G. Venugopal passed away on November 27, 2023, in Chennai, leaving behind a legacy of dedicated service and significant contributions to India’s nuclear energy program. He is survived by his wife and two daughters.

title: Lionel Messi
text:
Lionel Andrés Messi Cuccittini was born on June 24, 1987, in Rosario, Argentina, the third of four children to Jorge Messi, a steel factory manager, and Celia María Cuccittini, a part-time cleaner. His siblings are Rodrigo, Matías, and María Sol. From a young age, Messi displayed a prodigious talent for football, playing for Grandoli, a local club coached by his father, and later for Newell’s Old Boys, one of Rosario’s most prominent clubs. However, at age 11, Messi was diagnosed with growth hormone deficiency, a condition requiring expensive medical treatment. Newell's Old Boys promised to contribute to the costs, but later reneged, and River Plate, another Argentine powerhouse, showed interest but also hesitated due to the financial burden. 

In September 2000, at the age of 13, Messi and his father travelled to Barcelona, Spain, for a trial with FC Barcelona. Carles Rexach, the club’s sporting director, was immediately impressed, famously offering Messi a contract written on a paper napkin. Barcelona agreed to pay for Messi’s medical treatment, and he joined their youth academy, La Masia. He quickly progressed through the ranks, playing in various youth teams. He was initially homesick and struggled to adapt to life away from his family, but his talent shone through.

Messi made his official debut for Barcelona’s first team on November 16, 2003, in a friendly match against Porto. His La Liga debut followed on October 16, 2004, against Espanyol. While initially a substitute player, his skill and dribbling ability became increasingly apparent. The 2005-06 season saw a breakthrough, as he scored six league goals and helped Barcelona win La Liga and the Champions League. 

Over the next decade and a half, Messi became the focal point of Barcelona’s success. He won ten La Liga titles (2005-06, 2008-09, 2009-10, 2010-11, 2012-13, 2014-15, 2015-16, 2017-18, 2018-19, 2020-21), seven Copa del Rey titles (2008-09, 2011-12, 2014-15, 2015-16, 2016-17, 2017-18, 2020-21) and four Champions League titles (2005-06, 2008-09, 2010-11, 2014-15). Individually, he achieved unprecedented success. He won the Ballon d’Or – awarded to the world’s best player – a record eight times (2009, 2010, 2011, 2012, 2015, 2019, 2021, 2023). He also holds the record for most goals scored in La Liga (474) and most goals scored for a single club (672 for Barcelona).

For the Argentina national team, Messi's career initially lacked the same level of success. He participated in the 2006, 2010, 2014 and 2018 FIFA World Cups, reaching the final in 2014, where Argentina lost to Germany. He also featured in several Copa América tournaments, suffering defeats in the finals in 2007, 2015 and 2016, leading to considerable criticism from fans and media. However, he finally broke this drought by captaining Argentina to victory in the 2021 Copa América, defeating Brazil 1-0 in the final at the Maracanã Stadium. 

His long-awaited World Cup triumph came in December 2022, when he led Argentina to victory over France in a thrilling penalty shootout in the final held in Doha, Qatar. Messi scored twice in the match and was awarded the Golden Ball as the tournament’s best player. He currently holds the record for most appearances (180) and goals (106) for Argentina.

In August 2021, due to Barcelona's financial difficulties, Messi left the club after 21 years, signing for Paris Saint-Germain (PSG) on a two-year contract. He won two Ligue 1 titles with PSG (2021-22, 2022-23) before joining Inter Miami of Major League Soccer (MLS) in July 2023. He instantly impacted the league, leading Inter Miami to victory in the Leagues Cup in August 2023. 

Messi married Antonela Roccuzzo, his childhood sweetheart, in Rosario on June 30, 2017. They have three sons: Thiago, Mateo, and Ciro. He continues to be a global icon, admired for his exceptional footballing ability, humility, and dedication to the sport.

title: Terrence Romeo
text:
Terrence Romeo Villanueva, born July 17, 1992, in Cavite City, Philippines, is a professional basketball player widely regarded as one of the most exciting and prolific scorers in Philippine Basketball Association (PBA) history. His journey to becoming a household name began with humble beginnings, shaped by a single-parent household and a fervent passion for the sport. Raised by his mother, Violeta Villanueva, Terrence faced early challenges, often relying on basketball as an escape and a means to provide for his family. He honed his skills on the streets and in local tournaments of Cavite, quickly gaining recognition for his dazzling ball-handling, creative shot-making, and competitive fire.

Romeo’s formal basketball career took root at Far Eastern University (FEU), where he played for the FEU Tamaraws from 2009 to 2013. He wasn’t immediately a star, spending his freshman year largely on the bench. However, his dedication and relentless practice paid off.  He blossomed into a dominant force in the UAAP (University Athletic Association of the Philippines), showcasing a unique scoring ability that captivated audiences. In his final season, 2012-2013, Romeo truly cemented his legend, averaging a league-leading 18.3 points per game and leading FEU to the UAAP championship, earning him the Most Valuable Player (MVP) award. This championship marked FEU’s first title in 18 years.  

Capitalizing on his collegiate success, Romeo declared for the 2013 PBA draft and was selected 5th overall by the GlobalPort Batang Pier. His arrival in the PBA was met with excitement, and he quickly lived up to the hype. He immediately became the focal point of the Batang Pier’s offense, averaging 11.8 points in his rookie season.  Over the following years, Romeo consistently improved his game, showcasing a wider range of offensive skills. 

His breakthrough season came in 2016, where he averaged a career-high 18.8 points per game and earned his first All-Star selection.  He also participated in the 2016 PBA All-Star Game Slam Dunk Contest, putting on a show with his explosive athleticism.  In 2017, Romeo was traded to the San Miguel Beermen in a blockbuster deal that sent him, along with Chris Lutz, to the powerhouse team.  This move significantly elevated his career, allowing him to compete for championships alongside established stars like June Mar Fajardo. 

With San Miguel, Romeo won two PBA championships: the 2018 Commissioner’s Cup and the 2019 Philippine Cup.  He played a crucial role in both title runs, often delivering clutch performances. In the 2018 Commissioner's Cup Finals against TNT KaTropa, he averaged 23.8 points per game and was named Finals MVP.  He also became a consistent member of the Philippine national basketball team, Gilas Pilipinas, representing his country in international competitions like the FIBA Asia Cup and the Southeast Asian Games. He played a pivotal role in the 2019 SEA Games, helping the Philippines secure a gold medal on home soil.

In 2023, Romeo was traded to the Terrafirma Dyip, a move that surprised many in the PBA community. While his scoring numbers remained impressive, averaging 16.2 points, the team struggled to achieve success. In February 2024, Romeo was again traded, this time to the Phoenix Super LPG Fuel Masters. He currently continues to play for Phoenix, showcasing his scoring prowess and veteran leadership.  

Throughout his career, Romeo has consistently been recognized for his scoring ability, having won multiple scoring titles. As of late 2023, he holds the record for the most three-pointers made in a single PBA game, netting 11 against the Alaska Aces in 2019. Beyond the statistics, Terrence Romeo is remembered for his charismatic personality, his dedication to the game, and his impact on the popularity of basketball in the Philippines. He remains a fan favorite and a symbol of hard work and perseverance for aspiring basketball players in the country.

title: Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva
text:
Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, commonly known as Lula, was born on October 27, 1945, in Garanhuns, Pernambuco, Brazil, to humble beginnings. His parents, Aristides Inácio da Silva and Euraci Correia de Barros, were rural migrants seeking economic opportunity. The family moved to São Paulo in 1952, settling in the Brás district, where Lula experienced poverty and hardship. Formal education was limited; he completed only two years of primary school, but became largely self-educated through reading and political engagement. 

Lula began working at age 12, first as a shoeshine boy and then in various factory jobs, including as a metalworker. It was during his time at the Villares metalworks factory in São Bernardo do Campo, a major industrial hub, that he became involved in the labor movement. He rose through the ranks of the São Bernardo do Campo Metalworkers’ Union, becoming its president in 1975. This period saw Brazil under a military dictatorship, and Lula’s leadership of strikes in 1978 and 1980, demanding better wages and workers’ rights, brought him national attention and resulted in imprisonment for 560 days, beginning in May 1980. 

Upon his release, Lula became a key figure in the formation of the Partido dos Trabalhadores (Workers’ Party or PT) in 1980, a left-wing political party advocating for social justice and the rights of the working class. He ran for president in 1989, 1994, and 1998, losing each time to Fernando Collor de Mello, Itamar Franco, and Fernando Henrique Cardoso respectively. Despite these defeats, Lula significantly increased the PT’s representation in Congress and solidified his position as a leading voice for the poor and marginalized.

Lula finally won the presidency in 2002, defeating José Serra in a runoff election with 61.3% of the vote. He took office on January 1, 2003. His first term focused on social programs aimed at reducing poverty and inequality. The most notable of these was *Bolsa Família*, a conditional cash transfer program providing financial aid to impoverished families, which reached over 12 million families by 2010. Other key initiatives included *Fome Zero* (Zero Hunger) and programs to expand access to education and healthcare. Economically, Brazil experienced a period of growth during his presidency, fueled by a commodities boom and increased foreign investment. 

He was re-elected in 2006, again defeating Serra in a runoff, with 58.3% of the vote.  His second term continued the social programs of the first, and Brazil saw further economic progress, including paying off its debt to the International Monetary Fund (IMF) in 2008.  He also championed South-South cooperation, strengthening ties with other developing nations, particularly through the BRICS economic grouping (Brazil, Russia, India, China, and South Africa). Lula left office on December 31, 2010, with an approval rating of 80%, one of the highest for any outgoing Brazilian president.

Following his presidency, Lula remained politically active, and in 2017, he was convicted on charges of corruption and money laundering related to the *Lava Jato* (Car Wash) scandal, a sprawling investigation into corruption within Petrobras, the state-owned oil company. He was sentenced to 12 years and one month in prison. This conviction initially barred him from running in the 2018 presidential election, which was won by Jair Bolsonaro. 

After serving 19 months in prison, the Supreme Federal Court overturned his convictions in 2019, citing procedural errors, but he remained ineligible to run for office due to the *Lei da Ficha Limpa* (Clean Slate Law).  In 2021, the Supreme Court fully annulled his convictions, restoring his political rights. He then ran for and won the 2022 presidential election, defeating Bolsonaro in a close runoff on October 30, 2022, with 50.9% of the vote.  Lula was inaugurated for a third term on January 1, 2023, at the age of 77, promising to rebuild Brazil’s social safety net and address environmental concerns.

title: Juan Nepomucino Goetz
text:
Juan Nepomucino Goetz was born on February 13, 1775, in Prague, Bohemia (present-day Czech Republic), then part of the Habsburg monarchy. His father, Johann Goetz, was a skilled instrument maker, specifically specializing in the construction of mechanical musical instruments, particularly musical clocks and orchestrions. This familial profession heavily influenced Juan’s early life. He received his initial training in his father’s workshop, demonstrating a natural aptitude for mechanics and music. By age 14, he was already actively involved in the family business, learning the intricacies of clockwork, bellows systems, and the precise crafting of musical components.

In 1794, at the age of 19, Juan Goetz left Prague and traveled to Vienna, seeking to expand his knowledge and opportunities. He initially worked for a clockmaker named Joseph Riegl, but quickly moved on to collaborate with the renowned organ builder Joseph Rieger, gaining experience in larger-scale musical mechanisms. This period was crucial in broadening his understanding of acoustics and musical engineering beyond the smaller, self-contained world of musical clocks. 

Around 1800, Goetz accepted a position with the French firm of Panormo & Sons, instrument makers based in London. This move marked a significant shift in his career. He spent approximately seven years with Panormo, becoming a key figure in their production of mechanical musical instruments, including elaborate automata and large-scale orchestrions. It was during his time in London that Goetz began to develop his own innovative designs and refinements, moving beyond simply replicating existing models.

In 1807, Goetz established his own workshop in London, at 21 Cecil Street, Strand. He quickly gained a reputation for building exceptionally high-quality and complex musical automata and orchestrions. His instruments were renowned for their intricate craftsmanship, realistic figures, and the breadth of their musical capabilities. He employed a team of skilled artisans, including wood carvers, painters, and mechanics, to bring his ambitious designs to life. 

Goetz’s work was highly sought after by wealthy patrons and royalty. He produced instruments for King George IV, the Duke of Wellington, and various European nobility. His orchestrions, which could simulate the sound of a full orchestra, were particularly popular. A particularly famous example, completed in 1816, was a large orchestrion featuring a complex arrangement of automated figures performing various musical pieces. He consistently pushed the boundaries of the technology, incorporating new mechanisms and improving the quality of sound reproduction. 

He patented several inventions related to musical mechanisms, including improvements to the barrel organ and methods for controlling the dynamics and expression of automated instruments.  His instruments often featured multiple musical movements, including flutes, drums, bells, and stringed instruments, all powered by a sophisticated system of bellows and rotating cylinders.  He also became known for his ‘Singing Birds’ – complex automata housed in ornate cages, featuring intricately carved and animated birds that sang realistic melodies.

Goetz’s success continued throughout the 1820s and 1830s.  His workshop expanded and he took on increasingly complex commissions.  However, the rise of cheaper, mass-produced musical instruments, coupled with changing musical tastes, began to impact the demand for his highly specialized and expensive creations in the late 1830s.

Juan Nepomucino Goetz died on August 15, 1858, in London, at the age of 83. He left behind a legacy of exceptional craftsmanship and innovation in the field of mechanical music.  While the number of his surviving instruments is relatively small, those that remain are considered masterpieces of their time and are highly valued by collectors and museums worldwide.  His work is preserved in institutions such as the British Museum, the Musée des Arts Décoratifs in Paris, and the Kunsthistorisches Museum in Vienna, serving as a testament to his skill and ingenuity.

title: Ian Khama
text:
Ian Seretse Khama was born on February 23, 1953, in Chinchin, Serowe, Bechuanaland Protectorate (now Botswana). He is the son of Seretse Khama, who would become Botswana’s first president, and Ruth Williams Khama, a British woman of Welsh descent. His early life was marked by both privilege as the son of a prominent chief and considerable disruption. Due to political sensitivities surrounding his father’s marriage to a white woman – a situation that led to exile for Seretse Khama from 1962 to 1966 due to pressure from the British government and neighbouring South Africa – Ian spent much of his childhood in boarding schools in the United Kingdom. He attended Queen’s College, Taunton, Somerset, followed by The Royal Military Academy Sandhurst, graduating in 1971. 

Following Sandhurst, Khama embarked on a distinguished military career, primarily within the Botswana Defence Force (BDF). He was commissioned as a Second Lieutenant in 1971 and quickly rose through the ranks. He received further military training at the Defence Staff College in Wellington, England, in 1978. Throughout the 1980s, he held various command positions, including Commander of the Botswana Mobile Police Unit and Deputy Commander of the BDF. A pivotal moment in his military career came in 1998 when he became the Commander of the BDF, a position he held until his retirement in 2001 with the rank of Lieutenant General. His leadership was instrumental in developing the BDF into a professional and well-respected force, and he oversaw its modernization and expansion. His military service spanned 30 years.

Khama’s transition to politics began with his election as a Member of Parliament for Serowe North West in 1999, representing the Botswana Democratic Party (BDP), which his father founded. He was immediately appointed as Assistant Minister to the President, initially overseeing Presidential Affairs and Public Administration. In 2002, he became Minister of Works and Transport, and then, in 2003, he was appointed as Vice President of Botswana by then-President Festus Mogae. He also retained the portfolio of Presidential Affairs and Public Administration. 

Following Mogae’s decision to step down after two terms, Ian Khama became President of Botswana on April 1, 2008. He won the subsequent general elections in October 2009 with a landslide victory, securing 53 out of 63 parliamentary seats for the BDP. He was re-elected in 2014, again with a significant majority, though with a reduced margin of victory. 

During his presidency, Khama focused on economic diversification, infrastructure development, and combating corruption. He presided over a period of continued economic growth, largely driven by the diamond industry, although efforts were made to bolster other sectors like tourism and financial services. He implemented policies aimed at improving education and healthcare, and oversaw significant investments in infrastructure projects, including the expansion of Sir Seretse Khama International Airport and the construction of new roads and power plants. Khama was also known for his strong stance against poaching, increasing penalties and deploying the military to combat wildlife crime, particularly involving elephants. Botswana’s elephant population, although facing ongoing challenges, remained relatively stable during his tenure. 

Khama stepped down as President on April 1, 2018, after serving the maximum of two terms allowed by the Botswana constitution. His successor was Mokgweetsi Masisi. Following his departure from office, Khama became increasingly critical of the BDP and the Masisi administration, alleging corruption and a departure from the principles of good governance. This led to a public falling out and a period of political tension. He eventually left the BDP in 2019 and has been a vocal advocate for alternative political forces in Botswana. He resides primarily in his rural home in Serowe and continues to be a significant, though controversial, figure in Botswana’s political landscape. He has faced accusations of undue influence and attempts to undermine the current government, which he denies.

title: Sam Michael
text:
Samuel Michael was born on December 28, 1972, in High Wycombe, Buckinghamshire, England. His early life wasn’t steeped in motorsport; his father was a chartered accountant and his mother a teacher. However, a fascination with engineering and a keen interest in motorsport began early, fueled by watching Formula 1 on television and building model cars. He excelled in mathematics and physics at the Royal Grammar School in High Wycombe, demonstrating a natural aptitude for problem-solving that would become a hallmark of his career. He went on to study Mechanical Engineering at the University of Cambridge, graduating with a First-Class Honours degree in 1994. 

Rather than immediately pursuing a traditional engineering role, Michael sought practical experience within motorsport. He began as a data engineer with the McLaren Formula 1 team in 1995, a relatively junior position involving the collection, analysis, and interpretation of telemetry from the cars during testing and races. He quickly proved himself capable, demonstrating an ability to identify performance trends and communicate them effectively to engineers and drivers. This analytical skillset, coupled with a relentless work ethic, propelled his rapid ascent within McLaren. 

By 1998, Michael had become a race engineer, initially working with Mika Häkkinen. This role involved direct responsibility for the setup and performance of Häkkinen’s car on race weekends, a position of significant pressure and influence. He remained Häkkinen’s race engineer through the Finn’s consecutive World Championship wins in 1998 and 1999, contributing significantly to McLaren’s success during that period. He was instrumental in refining the car's setup to suit Häkkinen’s driving style, particularly focusing on braking and aerodynamic balance.

In 2001, Michael moved to WilliamsF1 as Chief Race Engineer, a more senior role overseeing the entire race engineering department. This was a challenging time for Williams, as the team was experiencing a decline in competitiveness following the dominant years of the 1990s.  He worked closely with drivers like Ralf Schumacher and Juan Pablo Montoya, attempting to extract maximum performance from often-underperforming machinery.  He spent six years at Williams, navigating a period of significant technical and organizational restructuring. 

A significant turning point came in 2006 when Michael joined Toyota Racing as a Technical Director. He was tasked with leading the team's technical direction and spearheading their efforts to become a consistent front-running contender. Despite investment and some promising results, Toyota never achieved a Grand Prix victory under Michael’s leadership. He held the position for three seasons, overseeing the development of the TF106, TF107, and TF108 chassis.

In 2009, Michael unexpectedly joined the newly formed Brawn GP team, initially as a consultant before becoming Sporting Director. This was arguably the most successful period of his career. Brawn GP, formed from the ashes of Honda Racing, defied expectations by winning both the Drivers' Championship with Jenson Button and the Constructors' Championship in their debut season. Michael played a vital role in maximizing the performance of the innovative "double diffuser" concept that gave Brawn GP a significant aerodynamic advantage. He was lauded for his calm demeanor under pressure and his ability to make quick, effective decisions.

Following Mercedes-Benz’s acquisition of Brawn GP at the end of 2009, Michael remained with the team, now as Executive Director. He oversaw the integration of the team into the Mercedes structure, a complex process involving significant organizational changes.  He left Mercedes in 2013, citing a desire to pursue other opportunities.

After leaving Formula 1, Michael transitioned into a consultancy role, offering his expertise to various motorsport teams and organizations. He also became involved in the development of electric vehicle technology and sustainable motorsport initiatives. He joined the Extreme E electric off-road racing series in 2021 as a technical consultant, contributing to the development of the series’ electric powertrain and overall technical regulations.  He currently continues to work in a consultancy capacity within the motorsport industry, leveraging his extensive experience and analytical skills. He remains a highly respected figure within the paddock, known for his technical acumen and pragmatic approach.

title: Henry VII of England
text:
Henry Tudor, later known as Henry VII, was born on January 28, 1457, at Pembroke Castle in Wales. His father, Edmund Tudor, 1st Earl of Richmond, was a distant relative of the English royal family through his mother, Margaret Beaufort, and a key supporter of Henry VI during the Wars of the Roses. His mother, Margaret Beaufort, was only thirteen years old at the time of his birth and a crucial figure in securing his future claim to the throne. Edmund Tudor died in November 1456, just three months before Henry's birth, leaving the young Henry as a precarious heir. 

Henry’s childhood was largely spent under the guardianship of his uncle, Jasper Tudor, Earl of Pembroke, who moved him between various estates in Wales and England to avoid the conflict between the Houses of York and Lancaster. The Yorkists, led by Edward IV, came to power in 1461, and Henry, being a Lancastrian, was constantly in danger. He received a humanist education, likely influenced by his mother’s piety and connections with scholars such as John Havyng. Following Edward IV’s death in 1483, his brother Richard III seized the throne, further complicating Henry’s position. 

In 1483, Henry fled to Brittany, France, under the protection of Duke Francis II. He spent the next fourteen years in exile, carefully cultivating alliances and planning his attempt to claim the English throne. He received financial support from his mother and explored potential marriage alliances to bolster his claim.  Crucially, he secured a promise of support from Charles VIII of France, although the assistance ultimately proved limited.

The death of Richard III at the Battle of Bosworth Field on August 22, 1485, marked a turning point. Henry landed at Milford Haven in Wales with a small army of around 5,000 men, primarily French mercenaries and Welsh supporters. He defeated Richard III, ending the Wars of the Roses.  Richard III was the last Plantagenet king of England.  Henry, though his claim through his mother was somewhat tenuous, established his legitimacy by pledging to marry Elizabeth of York, daughter of Edward IV, uniting the warring houses. 

Henry and Elizabeth married on January 18, 1486, at Westminster Abbey. This union, symbolized by the Tudor rose combining the red rose of Lancaster and the white rose of York, was instrumental in bringing stability to England.  Over his 23-year reign, Henry VII focused on consolidating royal power and restoring the finances of the crown. He established a new council, the Privy Council, to administer the country and curtailed the power of the nobility through laws like the Statute of Livery and Maintenance (1487), which restricted noblemen from maintaining armed retainers. 

Henry was a shrewd financial administrator.  He aggressively pursued those who had illegally obtained royal lands and imposed harsh penalties for rebellion, resulting in significant increases in royal revenue. He utilised legal mechanisms like the Court of Star Chamber to enforce law and order, often bypassing traditional legal processes.  During his reign, England’s revenue increased from approximately £12,000 to £26,000 annually. He also actively promoted trade and exploration, commissioning John Cabot to explore North America in 1497. 

Henry also pursued a cautious foreign policy, seeking to maintain peace with France and Scotland through diplomacy and strategic marriages. He signed the Treaty of Perpetual Peace with France in 1489, and his daughter Margaret married James IV of Scotland in 1503, attempting to create a lasting peace between the two nations. He built a strong navy, recognizing its importance for trade and defense. 

In later life, Henry became increasingly preoccupied with securing the succession. He faced challenges with the premature deaths of his first son, Arthur, Prince of Wales, in 1502, and his daughter Margaret. His second son, Henry, eventually succeeded him as Henry VIII.  Henry VII died on April 21, 1509, at Richmond Palace, Surrey. He was buried in Westminster Abbey, leaving behind a financially stable and politically secure England, setting the stage for the Tudor dynasty’s golden age.

title: Virginia Christine
text:
Virginia Christine Kraft was born on March 5, 1925, in Milwaukee, Wisconsin, to German-American parents, George and Ida Kraft. Her father was a tool and die maker, and her mother a homemaker. From a young age, Virginia displayed a talent for mimicry and voices, often entertaining family and friends with impressions. She attended West Division High School in Milwaukee, graduating in 1943. Initially aiming for a career in nursing, she enrolled at Marquette University, but quickly shifted her focus to drama, participating in university productions and radio work while supporting herself as a model.

Christine’s professional career began in radio. In 1944, at age 19, she landed a role on the nationally syndicated radio program *The Jack Benny Program*, playing various small parts and quickly becoming adept at character voices. This experience proved invaluable, honing her skills and exposing her to a large audience. She continued working in radio throughout the late 1940s and early 1950s, contributing to shows like *Fibber McGee and Molly* and *The Aldrich Family*. 

Her transition to television came in the early 1950s with appearances on shows like *I Love Lucy* (1951) and *The Abbott and Costello Show* (1952-1954). However, she remained largely a character actress, playing bit parts and often uncredited roles. Her breakthrough came in 1954 when she was cast as Miss Lily Cactus, a recurring character on the CBS western *Gunsmoke*. She appeared in 19 episodes between 1954 and 1961, portraying the proprietor of the local saloon and delivering lines with a distinctive, slightly nasal voice and a dry wit. This role significantly raised her profile, but it was her work in advertising that would ultimately define her career.

In 1963, Virginia Christine began her long association with Max Factor, becoming the face – and more specifically, the voice – of the Max Factor makeup commercials. She didn’t *become* the “Max Factor Woman” immediately; initially, other actresses appeared on camera while Christine provided the voiceover. However, her delivery – a sophisticated, confident tone suggesting transformation and glamour – proved so effective that Max Factor eventually put her *on* screen, showcasing her applying the makeup and delivering the iconic line, “Now you’ve never looked lovelier.”  

The “Max Factor Woman” campaign, running from 1963 to 1972, was exceptionally successful. Christine's voice became synonymous with the brand, and the commercials were instantly recognizable. She wasn’t just selling makeup; she was selling aspiration and self-confidence. The campaign generated an estimated $50 million in sales annually during its peak. She received an estimated $75,000 annually for her work with Max Factor, a substantial sum at the time. 

Throughout the 1960s and 1970s, Christine continued to work in television and film, often taking on character roles. She appeared in episodes of *The Twilight Zone* (1963), *Bewitched* (1969), *The Mary Tyler Moore Show* (1970), and *Police Woman* (1974). She also had small roles in films like *Palm Springs* (1962) and *Airport 1975* (1974). Despite her success, she consistently expressed frustration at being typecast, desiring more dramatic roles.

In 1972, Max Factor discontinued the "Max Factor Woman" campaign, a decision Christine reportedly took hard.  She continued to work, but found it difficult to escape the association with the commercials.  She made guest appearances on shows like *Charlie's Angels* (1976) and *The Love Boat* (1977).  She also did voice work for animated series, including *The New Scooby-Doo Movies* (1972).

Virginia Christine married Jack Goodman, a television writer, in 1947. They divorced in 1964. In 1966, she married Edwin “Ed” Nathan, a marketing executive.  The couple remained married until her death. 

Virginia Christine died on July 24, 1996, at the age of 71, at a hospital in Los Angeles, California, after a short illness. The cause of death was reported as lung cancer. She left behind a legacy not just as a versatile actress, but as the voice that helped define a generation's idea of beauty and glamour.

title: A. K. Ramanujan
text:
Attipat Krishnaswami Ramanujan was born on June 16, 1929, in Mysore, Karnataka, India, to Attipat Krishnaswami and his wife, Ghantimathi. His father was a lawyer and amateur astronomer, and his mother a homemaker with a strong interest in Kannada poetry. Ramanujan was the youngest of three children, having an older brother and sister. His early education took place at Bishop Cotton Boys’ School in Bangalore, and later at The Hindu High School, Mysore. He demonstrated an early aptitude for languages, though initially showed more interest in botany and zoology. He began writing poetry in English during his teenage years, significantly influenced by the poetry of W. B. Yeats. 

Ramanujan completed his B.A. in English Literature from the University of Mysore in 1950, graduating with honors. He then pursued an M.A. in English and a diploma in Journalism, both also from the University of Mysore, finishing in 1951 and 1952 respectively. Following his studies, he worked briefly as a lecturer in English at the University of Mysore (1952-1953) and then as a government college teacher in Karnataka (1953-1958). This period saw the beginnings of his serious engagement with translation, particularly of classical Tamil poetry, initially as a personal exploration sparked by a chance encounter with a collection of poems.

A pivotal moment arrived in 1959 when Ramanujan received a fellowship from the Ford Foundation to study creative writing at the University of Iowa, in Iowa City, Iowa, USA. He arrived in the US with his wife, Kamala, and their two children. He completed his MFA in Creative Writing in 1962 and continued at Iowa, earning a Ph.D. in Linguistics in 1964 with a dissertation titled “The Structure of Meaning in Selected Tamil Poems.”  This marked a shift in his academic focus, blending his literary sensibilities with a rigorous linguistic approach.

Ramanujan began his academic career as an assistant professor of English at the University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, in 1965. He remained there for nearly two decades, becoming a full professor in 1973.  During this time, he cemented his reputation as a major poet and translator. His first book of poems, *Poems* (1965), received the PEN/Oakland Josephine Miles Award.  His subsequent poetry collections, including *Relations* (1971), *The Striders* (1976), and *Second Sight* (1986), garnered widespread critical acclaim for their innovative use of language, their exploration of Indian-American identity, and their unique blend of personal and cultural experience.

However, Ramanujan’s most significant contribution arguably lies in his translations of classical Tamil poetry.  He published *The Interior Landscape* (1966), a groundbreaking collection of translations of Sangam poems (circa 300 BCE to 300 CE), introducing this ancient literary tradition to a Western audience.  He followed this with *Poems of Love and War from the Soongam* (1985), a more extensive and rigorously annotated selection.  These translations were not literal renderings but poetic re-creations, informed by his linguistic expertise and a deep understanding of the cultural context. 

In 1992, Ramanujan moved to the University of Chicago as a professor in the Committee on Southern Asian Studies and the Department of Comparative Literature.  He continued to publish and teach, focusing on Indian languages and literature, translation theory, and the relationship between language and culture. A controversial incident occurred in 1994 when the Indian government rejected several of his essays for inclusion in a collection to be published by the Sahitya Akademi (India’s National Academy of Letters), citing their perceived negative portrayal of Indian culture. This sparked a significant debate about academic freedom and censorship in India.

A. K. Ramanujan died on July 13, 1996, in Chicago, Illinois, at the age of 67, after a long battle with illness. His posthumous collections, *Collected Poems* (1997) and *The Black Helicopter* (2000), further solidified his legacy. He left behind a substantial body of work that continues to be studied and celebrated for its intellectual rigor, poetic beauty, and profound exploration of identity, belonging, and the complexities of translation.

title: Ramkumar Mukhopadhyay
text:
Ramkumar Mukhopadhyay, a pivotal figure in the development of Indian statistical methodology and a dedicated educator, was born on December 22, 1908, in the village of Talitpur, in the Nadia district of West Bengal, India. His father, Radhakrishna Mukhopadhyay, was a schoolteacher and his mother, Charubala Devi, instilled in him a strong emphasis on education and cultural values. He received his early education at the Talitpur High English School, consistently demonstrating exceptional aptitude in mathematics. He continued his studies at Presidency College, Calcutta, graduating with a Bachelor of Science in Physics in 1930, securing first class honours. 

While initially focused on physics, Mukhopadhyay’s academic path dramatically shifted after being introduced to the nascent field of statistics by Professor P.C. Mahalanobis at Presidency College. He joined the Indian Statistical Institute (ISI), founded by Mahalanobis in 1932, becoming one of its earliest recruits and a foundational pillar of its growth. He initially worked as a research assistant, quickly proving his talent for statistical analysis and contributing to early ISI projects focused on agricultural statistics and the analysis of monsoon rainfall patterns.

In 1938, Mukhopadhyay travelled to the London School of Economics, studying under the renowned statistician Karl Pearson, and earned a Sc.D. degree in Statistics in 1941. His doctoral dissertation, focused on sequential analysis, showcased his innovative thinking and laid the groundwork for much of his future research. He returned to India in 1942, amidst the complexities of World War II, and resumed his work at ISI, now facing challenges of wartime resource constraints and the need to contribute to national planning.

Mukhopadhyay’s contributions to statistical theory and application are substantial. He is particularly renowned for his work on sequential analysis, specifically the development of Sequential Probability Ratio Test (SPRT) designs and their application to industrial quality control and clinical trials. He published extensively on this topic, with key papers appearing in journals like *Biometrika* and *The Annals of Mathematical Statistics* throughout the 1940s and 50s.  He also made significant contributions to the theory of estimation, hypothesis testing, and design of experiments. Beyond purely theoretical work, he spearheaded the application of statistical methods to diverse fields including demography, economics, and public health. 

He held various key positions at ISI throughout his career. He became a Professor in 1946 and served as the Director of the Statistics Department. From 1954 to 1956, he was the Deputy Director of ISI, assisting Mahalanobis in the Institute’s administrative and research activities. He played a critical role in establishing ISI’s postgraduate programs and shaping the curriculum, fostering a generation of Indian statisticians.  He was elected a Fellow of the Royal Statistical Society in 1952 and a Fellow of the American Statistical Association in 1956, recognizing his international stature in the field. 

Mukhopadhyay was also deeply involved in national planning and policy-making. He served on numerous government committees, advising on statistical aspects of the Five-Year Plans and contributing to the development of national sample surveys. His expertise was instrumental in establishing robust statistical infrastructure for India’s economic development. He was a member of the Planning Commission's Statistical Sub-Committee for a considerable period, contributing significantly to the statistical framework used for national planning. 

In his later life, Mukhopadhyay continued his research and teaching at ISI, focusing increasingly on the philosophical foundations of statistics and the ethical considerations in its application. He retired from ISI in 1972, but remained actively engaged in scholarly pursuits until his health declined. He received the Padma Bhushan, one of India’s highest civilian awards, in 1973, acknowledging his lifetime contributions to the field of statistics and to national development. Ramkumar Mukhopadhyay passed away on November 23, 1981, in Calcutta, leaving behind a legacy as a pioneering statistician, a dedicated teacher, and a key architect of India's statistical capabilities.

title: Carlos Ghosn
text:
Carlos Ghosn was born on March 9, 1954, in Porto Velho, Brazil, to Lebanese parents, Jorge and Rose Ghosn. His father, a businessman, ran a network of distribution companies in South America, and his mother was involved in activism, particularly regarding Lebanese independence. Ghosn’s early life was marked by frequent relocation across South America as his father’s business expanded, including stops in Brazil, Argentina, and Venezuela. He is fluent in Portuguese, Spanish, English, French, and Arabic. He received his primary and secondary education in Lebanon, attending the Collège Notre-Dame de Jamhour, a Jesuit school. 

In 1974, Ghosn moved to France to study at École Polytechnique, graduating as an engineer in 1978. He then attended École des Mines de Paris, earning an advanced engineering degree in 1980. He began his career at Michelin in France in 1981, holding various manufacturing and engineering positions. By 1985, he had risen to become head of Michelin’s audit department. 

A pivotal shift came in 1996 when Ghosn joined Renault, the French automobile manufacturer. He quickly ascended the ranks, becoming Chief Operating Officer in 1999 and then President and CEO in 2000 following the appointment of Louis Schweitzer as Chairman.  Renault was facing significant financial difficulties at the time, and Ghosn implemented a radical restructuring plan known as the “Renault Revival Plan.” This plan, announced in 2002, involved cost-cutting measures, plant closures, and a focus on profitability.  It successfully returned Renault to profitability, earning Ghosn the nickname “Le Cost Killer.”

In 2005, Nissan Motor Co. of Japan, then struggling with debt and declining market share, entered into an alliance with Renault.  Ghosn was appointed Chief Operating Officer of Nissan in June 2005 and, in 2008, became President and CEO. He implemented a similar restructuring plan to the one he used at Renault, dubbed “Nissan Revival Plan,” which focused on cost reduction, product innovation, and expanding into new markets, particularly China. Nissan experienced a dramatic turnaround under his leadership, becoming one of the most profitable automakers globally.

Ghosn simultaneously held the positions of Chairman and CEO of both Renault and Nissan, as well as Chairman of Mitsubishi Motors (following Nissan’s acquisition of a controlling stake in 2016). He was widely credited with forging a powerful automotive alliance, the Renault-Nissan-Mitsubishi Alliance, which became one of the largest automotive groups in the world, selling over 10 million vehicles annually by 2017.  

However, Ghosn’s career took a dramatic turn in November 2018. He was arrested in Tokyo on allegations of underreporting his income and violating Japan’s Financial Instruments and Exchange Act.  He was subsequently removed as Chairman of Nissan, Renault, and Mitsubishi.  The charges revolved around discrepancies in his compensation, allegedly underreporting income by billions of yen over several years. 

Ghosn maintained his innocence, claiming the allegations were part of a conspiracy by Nissan executives to prevent him from further integrating the companies.  He was released on bail in March 2019, but faced further charges. In December 2019, Ghosn fled Japan, reportedly hidden in a large instrument case, and arrived in Lebanon, which has no extradition treaty with Japan. 

Since then, Ghosn has remained in Lebanon.  Interpol issued a red notice for his arrest, but he has not been apprehended.  In 2022, the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission charged Ghosn with fraud, alleging he concealed over $100 million in compensation.  He has consistently denied wrongdoing and continues to argue his case through legal challenges and public statements. As of late 2023, Ghosn continues to live in Beirut, Lebanon, and remains a controversial figure in the automotive industry.

title: Stephanie Beatriz
text:
Stephanie Beatriz Bush, known professionally as Stephanie Beatriz, was born on July 14, 1982, in San Jose, California, to a Colombian mother, Deyanira Hardison, and a Bolivian father, David Bush. Her parents were both social workers, and she was raised in Needham, Massachusetts, after her family moved there when she was a young child. She has a younger brother, Michael Bush. Growing up, Beatriz was a self-described “tomboy” and initially hesitant about pursuing acting, preferring athletics like soccer and field hockey at Needham High School, where she graduated in 2000. However, a high school drama class, taken on a whim to fulfill an arts requirement, sparked a passion for performance. 

Beatriz attended Tulane University in New Orleans, Louisiana, graduating in 2004 with a Bachelor of Fine Arts degree in Acting. During her time at Tulane, she was actively involved in the university’s theatre program, honing her skills in various productions. Following graduation, she moved to New York City to pursue a professional acting career, supporting herself with various jobs including waitressing and working as a nanny. She quickly became involved in the off-Broadway theatre scene, appearing in numerous productions.

Her early television credits include guest appearances on shows like "All My Children" in 2006, “The Closer” in 2007, and "Numbers" in 2008. She had a recurring role as Gloria’s sister, Sofia, in the ABC comedy “Modern Family” between 2009 and 2011, appearing in 12 episodes. This role brought her increased visibility, but it was her casting as Detective Rosa Diaz in the critically acclaimed NBC/later Peacock comedy series “Brooklyn Nine-Nine” in 2013 that truly launched her into mainstream recognition. 

“Brooklyn Nine-Nine,” which premiered on September 17, 2013, ran for eight seasons, concluding on September 16, 2021. Beatriz’s portrayal of the stoic, sardonic, and fiercely independent Rosa Diaz garnered significant praise and earned her numerous accolades. She was part of the ensemble cast that won a Screen Actors Guild Award for Outstanding Performance by an Ensemble in a Comedy Series in 2019. Throughout the series’ run, she became a vocal advocate for LGBTQ+ representation, and in 2017, her character, Rosa Diaz, came out as bisexual, a storyline Beatriz actively collaborated on with the show's writers to ensure authentic and sensitive representation. 

Beyond "Brooklyn Nine-Nine," Beatriz has continued to work consistently in both television and film. She voiced Mirabel Madrigal’s Tia Pepa in Disney’s animated musical fantasy film “Encanto,” released in November 2021, which became a global phenomenon.  She also voiced a character, Detective Loretta Duran, in the animated series “Harley Quinn” beginning in 2019. Film credits include roles in “The Heat” (2013) alongside Sandra Bullock and Melissa McCarthy, “Champaign Ill” (2014), “Happy Christmas” (2014), and “Candy Jar” (2018).

In 2022, Beatriz published her memoir, “The Stress Test: How Pressure Can Make You Perform at Your Best,” which details her journey with anxiety and the techniques she learned to manage it, including taking a Yale course on the science of well-being. The book became a New York Times bestseller.

On June 21, 2022, Beatriz welcomed her first child, a daughter named Rosaline, with her husband, actor Justin Feldman, whom she married in 2018. The couple resides in Los Angeles. She continues to be an active voice for representation and inclusivity in the entertainment industry, and remains a sought-after actress with a diverse and growing body of work. In 2023, she starred in the Apple TV+ series “High Desert” alongside Patricia Arquette, further demonstrating her range as a performer.

title: Anurag Kashyap
text:
Anurag Kashyap was born on September 10, 1972, in Gorakhpur, Uttar Pradesh, India, to a middle-class family. His father, Bhagat Kashyap, was a government employee, and his mother, Chhaya Kashyap, was a homemaker. The family relocated to Gonda, Uttar Pradesh, during his early childhood, and later to Delhi when he was around eleven years old. Kashyap’s early education took place in Delhi Public School, Mathura Road, where he was reportedly a disruptive student, more interested in cinema than academics. After completing his schooling, he enrolled in Delhi University to study zoology, but dropped out after a year, realizing his passion lay elsewhere.

Driven by a fervent love for film, Kashyap moved to Mumbai in 1993 with the intention of becoming a filmmaker. This period was marked by significant hardship. He worked various odd jobs to sustain himself, including assisting with stage productions and doing menial tasks on film sets. A crucial early influence was his association with Rajiv Rai, for whom he worked as an assistant director on the 1994 film *Guddu*. This experience, despite not being creatively fulfilling, provided him with a firsthand understanding of the technical aspects of filmmaking. 

Kashyap's initial attempts at directing were largely unsuccessful. He wrote the screenplay for Ram Gopal Varma’s *Satya* (1998), a landmark film in Indian cinema that is widely credited with ushering in a new wave of neo-noir gangster films. Though a critical and commercial success, Kashyap received only ₹5,000 for his work. He then penned the screenplay for *Shool* (1999), also directed by Varma, and *Kaun* (1999), directed by Ram Madhavani. While these projects established him as a talented writer, his ambition remained focused on directing.

His directorial debut, *Paanch* (2003), a raw and gritty portrayal of youth culture in Mumbai, faced severe censorship issues and was only granted a limited theatrical release. Despite its critical acclaim, its limited reach hampered its impact.  He followed this with *Black Friday* (2004), a powerful and realistic depiction of the 1993 Bombay bombings, based on S. Hussain Zaidi's book of the same name.  The film faced significant delays due to legal concerns and censorship, finally releasing after a protracted battle. 

The turning point in Kashyap’s career arrived with *Gangs of Wasseypur – Part 1* and *Gangs of Wasseypur – Part 2* (2012), a sprawling, multi-generational crime saga set in Wasseypur, Jharkhand.  The film, produced by Sunil Bohra, was a massive critical and commercial success, establishing Kashyap as a prominent auteur.  He continued to explore dark and unconventional themes with films like *Ugly* (2014), a psychological thriller, *Raman Raghav 2.0* (2016), a neo-noir crime thriller inspired by the life of serial killer Raman Raghav, and *Mukkabaaz* (2018), a sports drama with social commentary.

Kashyap has also been instrumental in launching the careers of numerous actors, including Nawazuddin Siddiqui, Richa Chadha, and Huma Qureshi, often casting relative newcomers in challenging roles. He has consistently championed independent cinema and provided a platform for emerging talent. He ventured into digital platforms with *Sacred Games* (2018-2019), a Netflix original series based on Vikram Chandra’s novel, which garnered international acclaim.  He also directed the anthology film *Ghost Stories* (2018) for Netflix. 

In later years, Kashyap has continued to produce and direct films, including *Choked: Paisa Bolta Hai* (2020), a dark comedy released on Netflix, and *Almost Pyaar with DJ Mohabbat* (2023).  He has also been involved in controversies, notably a #MeToo allegation in 2018 which he denied and which led to a police investigation that ultimately found no evidence of wrongdoing. Kashyap remains a significant and influential figure in contemporary Indian cinema, known for his unique storytelling, gritty realism, and willingness to push boundaries.

title: Angela Bairstow
text:
Angela Bairstow was born on 17th February 1949 in Bradford, Yorkshire, England, to parents Arthur and Margaret Bairstow. Her father worked as a textile mechanic and her mother was a homemaker. From a young age, Bairstow demonstrated a strong aptitude for mathematics and science, excelling in these subjects at Bradford Girls’ Grammar School, where she was a student from 1960 to 1967. She achieved top marks in her ‘A’ Levels, securing her a place to read mathematics at Newnham College, Cambridge University in 1967. 

At Cambridge, Bairstow thrived in a stimulating academic environment, completing her Bachelor of Arts degree in Mathematics in 1970, achieving a First Class Honours. She continued her studies at Cambridge, undertaking research in fluid dynamics under the supervision of Professor Sir James Lighthill, a prominent figure in the field. This led to the award of a PhD in Aeronautics in 1973. Her doctoral thesis was specifically focused on the study of turbulent boundary layers, a complex area of fluid mechanics with applications in aerodynamics and engineering.

Following her PhD, Bairstow embarked on a postdoctoral research fellowship at the California Institute of Technology (Caltech) in Pasadena, California, from 1973 to 1975. This period provided her with valuable experience in a different academic setting and allowed her to broaden her research interests, working with leading experts in the field of turbulence. Returning to the United Kingdom in 1975, she accepted a position as a Research Fellow at the University of Manchester’s Institute of Science and Technology (UMIST). 

Bairstow’s career at UMIST spanned over three decades. She quickly progressed through the ranks, becoming a lecturer in 1977, a senior lecturer in 1988, and finally, a professor of fluid mechanics in 1992. Her research at UMIST focused on a wide range of fluid dynamics problems, including turbulence, aerodynamics, and computational fluid dynamics. She was particularly known for her work on the development and application of Large Eddy Simulation (LES), a technique used to model turbulent flows. 

Throughout her career, Bairstow published over 100 peer-reviewed scientific papers in prestigious journals, including the *Journal of Fluid Mechanics* and *Physics of Fluids*. Her work garnered significant recognition within the scientific community. She was elected a Fellow of the Royal Society in 1998, a particularly significant honour recognizing her substantial contribution to science, and a Fellow of the Royal Aeronautical Society in 1991. In 2003, she was awarded the Heitor Gatto Belluzo Medal by the International Council of Aeronautical Sciences, acknowledging her outstanding contributions to aeronautical science.

Bairstow was not only a dedicated researcher but also a committed educator. She supervised numerous PhD students, many of whom went on to successful careers in academia and industry. She was known for her supportive mentoring style and her ability to inspire the next generation of fluid dynamicists. She also actively participated in outreach activities, promoting science and engineering to a wider audience.  

Beyond her academic pursuits, Angela Bairstow served on several national and international committees, providing expert advice on science and technology policy. She was a member of the Engineering and Physical Sciences Research Council (EPSRC) from 2000 to 2004, and served as Vice-President of the Royal Aeronautical Society from 2002 to 2004.

Angela Bairstow retired from her position as professor at the University of Manchester in 2009.  She lived in Cheshire with her husband, Dr. David Holmes, a specialist in biomedical engineering whom she married in 1973. Sadly, Angela Bairstow died on 20th December 2018, aged 69, after a long illness. Her legacy continues through her extensive research contributions and the many students she mentored, leaving a lasting impact on the field of fluid dynamics.

title: Mateo Correa Magallanes
text:
Mateo Correa Magallanes was born on December 30, 1863, in Concepción, Chile, to José María Correa and Margarita Magallanes. His father was a railway worker, and the family experienced a degree of economic hardship during his childhood, a circumstance that would later influence his dedication to social issues. He received his primary education in Concepción, attending the School of the Sacred Heart, run by the French Brothers of the Holy Cross. Even at a young age, Mateo displayed a keen intellect and a strong sense of justice. 

In 1878, at the age of 15, he began his formal medical training at the University of Concepción, enrolling in the School of Medicine. He excelled in his studies, demonstrating a particular aptitude for anatomy and physiology. However, his education was interrupted in 1883 when he was forced to abandon his studies due to the severe economic crisis that affected the country and his family. He then took up work as a teacher, first in Penco, a coastal town near Concepción, and later in Tomé, a rural area south of the city. It was during this period, witnessing the precarious health conditions and lack of medical care in rural communities, that his commitment to public health truly solidified. 

Correa Magallanes returned to his medical studies in 1888, resuming at the University of Concepción. He graduated as a surgeon in 1891 with a thesis titled “Higiene Pública” (Public Hygiene), a clear indication of his burgeoning focus. Immediately after graduation, he joined the Chilean Public Health Service, beginning his career as a sanitary doctor in the province of Ñuble. He quickly rose through the ranks, becoming the provincial sanitary chief in 1893. 

His career was marked by relentless dedication to improving public health, particularly focusing on preventative medicine and combating infectious diseases. In 1897, he was appointed Director of Public Health for the province of Biobío, a region grappling with outbreaks of typhus and other diseases. He implemented innovative sanitary measures, including widespread disinfection campaigns, improved water supplies, and public education programs focused on hygiene. He was particularly successful in controlling an outbreak of yellow fever in Valdivia in 1901, utilizing mosquito control measures, a relatively novel approach at the time.

Correa Magallanes's most significant contribution came during his tenure as General Director of Public Health, a position he held from 1919 until his retirement in 1931.  During this period, he spearheaded the national vaccination campaign against smallpox, a disease that had plagued Chile for centuries.  He organized a nationwide network of vaccination centers, utilizing mobile units to reach remote communities and ensuring free access to the vaccine for all citizens.  By 1924, the campaign had effectively eradicated smallpox from Chile, a monumental public health achievement.  He also implemented measures to control tuberculosis, a leading cause of death, establishing sanatoriums and promoting early detection.  

Beyond vaccination, he championed improvements in maternal and infant health, advocating for the establishment of maternal centers and providing training for midwives. He understood the link between social conditions and health, and consistently pushed for policies that addressed poverty and improved living standards. Correa Magallanes was a prolific writer and speaker, publishing numerous articles and delivering lectures on public health issues.  He founded the “Revista Chilena de Salud Pública” (Chilean Journal of Public Health) in 1922, providing a platform for the dissemination of research and best practices. 

Mateo Correa Magallanes retired from his position as General Director in 1931, but continued to advocate for public health initiatives. He was honored with numerous awards and recognitions throughout his career, including the Order of Public Health from the Chilean government. He died on October 14, 1937, in Santiago, Chile, at the age of 73.  His legacy remains strong, remembered as a pioneering figure in Chilean public health and a champion of social justice who significantly improved the health and well-being of the Chilean population. His work laid the foundation for modern public health systems in Chile and continues to inspire public health professionals today.

title: R. Selvaraj (politician)
text:
R. Selvaraj was an Indian politician and trade union leader, primarily known for his significant role in the Dalit movement and his long association with the Communist Party of India (Marxist), or CPI(M). He was born on February 12, 1934, in Melakkarai, a village in the Tirunelveli district of Tamil Nadu, to Rathinathurai and Lakshmi Ammal, belonging to the Pallar caste, a sub-caste within the broader Dalit community. His early life was marked by the socio-economic hardships and systemic discrimination prevalent against Dalits in rural India. He received his primary education at the local elementary school in Melakkarai, and continued to the Government Higher Secondary School in Nanguneri, completing his secondary education in 1952. 

Selvaraj's political awakening began during his student days, influenced by the burgeoning Dalit political movements and the broader communist ideology gaining traction in Tamil Nadu. He joined the All India Youth Federation (AIYF), the youth wing of the CPI, in 1953, and quickly became involved in organizing agricultural labourers and advocating for their rights. He actively participated in land struggles and protests against feudal practices, focusing particularly on issues impacting Dalit communities. This early activism led to several arrests and periods of imprisonment, solidifying his commitment to social justice.

In 1964, following a split within the Communist Party of India, Selvaraj joined the newly formed CPI(M). He dedicated himself to strengthening the party’s base amongst agricultural labourers, particularly Dalits, in Southern Tamil Nadu. He rose through the ranks, becoming a key organizer and strategist for the party in the region.  He was elected as the Secretary of the Tamil Nadu State Kisan Sabha (farmers' wing of the CPI(M)) in 1976, a position he held for a remarkable 22 years, until 1998. This role was central to his influence, allowing him to mobilize farmers, negotiate for their rights, and represent their concerns before the government.

Selvaraj’s influence extended beyond agricultural labour. He played a crucial role in establishing and leading numerous trade unions, particularly those representing workers in the beedi (cigarette) industry and the construction sector across Tamil Nadu. He became a prominent voice for unorganized labour, demanding fair wages, safe working conditions, and social security benefits. He was instrumental in organizing several large-scale protests and strikes that led to improvements in the lives of these workers.  

He was first elected to the Tamil Nadu Legislative Assembly in 1989, representing the Nanguneri constituency. He successfully retained this seat in the 1991 and 1996 elections. As a Member of the Legislative Assembly (MLA), Selvaraj focused on advocating for policies aimed at uplifting Dalits and other marginalized communities. He consistently raised issues related to land rights, education, employment, and social discrimination within the assembly.
