He actively participated in debates and committees, pushing for increased budgetary allocations for welfare programs targeted towards vulnerable sections of society. 

Throughout his career, Selvaraj maintained a strong focus on Dalit empowerment. He consistently emphasized the need for political representation and participation of Dalits in all spheres of life. He actively campaigned against caste-based discrimination and violence, and advocated for the implementation of affirmative action policies. He was a vocal critic of the Varna system and its continued influence on Indian society.

After stepping down as Secretary of the Tamil Nadu State Kisan Sabha in 1998, Selvaraj remained actively involved in CPI(M) politics and continued to mentor younger leaders. He remained a respected figure within the Dalit movement, often sought after for his counsel and guidance. He authored several pamphlets and articles on Dalit issues and the need for social transformation. R. Selvaraj passed away on November 23, 2010, at the age of 76, leaving behind a legacy of tireless advocacy for the rights of the marginalized and a significant contribution to the communist movement in Tamil Nadu. His work continues to inspire activists and politicians working for social justice in the region.

title: Mindy Smith
text:
Mindy Smith was born on November 10, 1971, in Asheville, North Carolina, to parents Jack and Susan Smith. Her upbringing was steeped in music, particularly gospel and country, as her father was a choir director and her mother a church pianist. She grew up singing in church choirs and performing in local musical theatre productions, developing a strong vocal foundation early on. Smith attended Asheville High School, graduating in 1990, and continued her education at Belmont University in Nashville, Tennessee, majoring in music business. While at Belmont, she honed her songwriting skills and began performing in local clubs, often playing covers alongside her original material.

After graduating from Belmont in 1994, Smith worked a variety of jobs to support herself while pursuing her music career. She held positions as a wedding singer, a session vocalist, and even a bicycle messenger. This period of relative obscurity and hard work lasted for several years as she navigated the competitive Nashville music scene. Her persistence eventually led to a showcase performance at the Bluebird Cafe in 1997, a renowned venue for aspiring songwriters, which garnered attention from industry representatives. 

This performance led to a development deal with Giant Records in 1998.  However, the label folded before she could release a full album, leaving her in limbo.  She persevered and signed with Warner Bros. Records in 2000. Her debut album, *Lean Into the Light*, was released on August 7, 2001. The album, a blend of country, folk, and pop influences, was critically acclaimed for its honest lyrics and Smith’s distinctive, emotive vocals. The single "Come to Jesus" became a crossover hit, reaching number 42 on the Billboard Hot 100 chart and achieving significant airplay on Adult Contemporary and Christian radio stations.  *Lean Into the Light* was certified Gold by the RIAA in 2002, signifying sales of over 500,000 copies in the United States.

Smith followed up with her second album, *Long Story Short*, released on September 23, 2003. While critically respected, it did not achieve the same commercial success as her debut. The album showcased a more polished sound, incorporating elements of pop and rock.  She toured extensively to support both albums, opening for artists like Sheryl Crow and John Mellencamp.

In 2006, Smith parted ways with Warner Bros. Records and decided to take a different path, focusing on independent releases. She released *My Holiday*, an album of Christmas songs, in 2006.  This was followed by *Devil’s Advocate* in 2009, and *Snowglobe* in 2011, both released on her own label, Pomegranate Records.  These albums demonstrated a willingness to explore different musical styles, including more Americana and singer-songwriter influences. She also began to embrace a more intimate and direct connection with her fanbase through online platforms.

Throughout the 2010s, Smith continued to record and tour, releasing albums like *Living Proof* in 2014 and *Jupiter* in 2018.  She also became increasingly involved in songwriting for other artists and developed a strong community through online teaching, offering vocal coaching and songwriting workshops.  In 2023, she released *These Hard Times*, an album reflecting on personal loss and resilience. 

Beyond her musical work, Smith has been an advocate for mental health awareness, openly discussing her own struggles with anxiety and depression. She has used her platform to encourage others to seek help and to destigmatize mental illness. As of late 2023, Mindy Smith continues to tour and write, maintaining a dedicated following and a reputation as a thoughtful and authentic artist. She resides in Nashville with her husband, Kevin Beam, and their two children, born in 2008 and 2011.

title: Raghav Juyal
text:
Raghav Juyal was born on July 4, 1991, in Dehradun, Uttarakhand, India, to a family with a strong connection to the arts. His father, Deepak Juyal, was a choreographer, and his mother, Alka Juyal, taught dance. This early exposure profoundly influenced Raghav, who began dancing at the age of 10, initially learning hip-hop and various other dance forms from his father. He received his early education at St. Joseph’s Academy in Dehradun, and later attended D.A.V. College, also in Dehradun, pursuing a Bachelor of Commerce degree, although he ultimately left before completion to focus on his burgeoning career. 

Raghav’s journey to national recognition began in 2011, at the age of 19, when he auditioned for and was selected as a contestant on the fourth season of the popular dance reality show *Dance India Dance* (DID). Representing the crew ‘Street Maniacs’ alongside teammates Sushant Pujari and Pranav Sachdeva, Raghav quickly gained attention for his unique, fluid dance style, a blend of hip-hop, contemporary, and a distinctive popping and locking technique. While the crew didn’t win the competition, finishing as the second runner-up, Raghav’s individual performances and charismatic stage presence resonated with the audience and judges – Geeta Kapoor, Terence Lewis and Remo D’Souza. He became known for his ‘slow-motion’ style, earning him the nickname “King of Slow Motion.”

Following *Dance India Dance*, Raghav’s career took off. He was immediately offered opportunities in the entertainment industry. In 2012, he appeared as a stage performer in the film *Son of Sardaar*, directed by Indra Kumar. This was followed by hosting duties on several television shows. From 2014 to 2016, he hosted *India's Dancing Superstar* alongside Lauren Gottlieb, and then *The Stage*, a live music reality show, from 2016 to 2017. He continued to host youth-centric shows, including *Dil Hai Hindustani* in 2017-2018, co-hosting with Karan Kundra, and *Sa Re Ga Ma Pa Little Champs* in 2019.

Raghav’s versatility extended into acting. He debuted in a lead role in the 2018 film *Babumoshai Bandookbaaz*, directed by Kushan Nandy, alongside Nawazuddin Siddiqui and Bidita Bag. Though a smaller role, it marked his entry into feature film acting. He subsequently appeared in *Abhi Toh Party Shuru Hui Hai*, a comedy released in 2018.  He had a more substantial role in the 2019 dance film *Street Dancer 3D*, directed by Remo D'Souza, where he played the character of Pop, showcasing his established dance skills on the big screen. 

Beyond television and film, Raghav has been actively involved in music videos. He featured in several popular music videos, including “Naach Baby” with Jasmine Anmolani in 2017, and “Kyon Karle Tu” with Tiffany Bartell in 2019. He also ventured into singing, releasing his first single, “Kya Zindagi Hai,” in 2020 which garnered over 10 million views on YouTube.  In 2021, he released “Tum Jo Milte Ho,” demonstrating a further expansion of his artistic range. 

Throughout his career, Raghav has been recognized with several awards, including the Zee Gold Awards for ‘Best Debut Host’ in 2015 for *India’s Dancing Superstar*. He maintains a significant social media presence, with millions of followers across platforms like Instagram and YouTube, where he regularly shares dance routines, music, and glimpses into his personal life.  As of late 2023, Raghav continues to be a prominent figure in Indian entertainment, balancing hosting duties, acting projects, and musical pursuits. He frequently collaborates with other artists and remains a popular choice for brand endorsements, solidifying his position as a multi-talented personality in the Indian media landscape. He is currently focused on expanding his musical repertoire and exploring opportunities within the film industry.

title: Ernestine Eckstein
text:
Ernestine Eckstein was born on December 23, 1893, in Vienna, Austria-Hungary, to Jewish parents, Jakob and Rosa Eckstein. Her father was a successful businessman involved in the wholesale trade of textiles. Ernestine was the youngest of three children, with an older brother, Wilhelm, and an older sister, Elsa. She grew up in a comfortable, intellectually stimulating environment in a large apartment on the prestigious Ringstraße boulevard. From a young age, Ernestine displayed a marked intelligence and a strong inclination towards academic pursuits, uncommon for girls of her time. She received a comprehensive education, attending the Lyzeum, a secondary school for girls that prepared students for university entrance, graduating in 1912.

Ernestine’s ambition led her to the University of Vienna, where she began studying medicine in the winter semester of 1912/1913. This was a significant step, as women faced considerable barriers to entry and acceptance in the medical profession. She initially studied with professors like Hans Hörbiger, known for his glacial cosmogony, but quickly gravitated towards the burgeoning field of psychoanalysis. In 1918, she became a member of the Vienna Psychoanalytic Society (WPS), a crucial turning point in her life. Crucially, she underwent psychoanalysis herself with Sigmund Freud between 1919 and 1921, a particularly intense and documented analysis that would later become a subject of scholarly debate. 

Her training analysis with Freud was unusually lengthy and fraught with transference issues, documented extensively in their correspondence, published in 1985 as *The Complete Letters of Sigmund Freud to Ernestine von Freud-Eckstein*. The analysis was complicated by the fact that Freud was also analyzing her husband, Felix Eckstein, a wealthy industrialist whom she married in 1916.  Despite the complexities, she successfully completed her medical degree in 1923, specializing in neurology and psychiatry.  

Ernestine quickly distinguished herself as a dedicated and insightful psychoanalyst. In 1926, she became a training analyst with the WPS, a testament to her competence and standing within the psychoanalytic community. She focused her practice on the treatment of neuroses, particularly those affecting women.  She delivered influential papers at psychoanalytic congresses, notably presenting “On the Social and Psychological Significance of Female Chastity” at the 1928 International Psychoanalytic Congress in Prague. This paper demonstrated her engagement with feminist thought and her willingness to challenge conventional societal norms. 

As the political climate in Austria deteriorated in the 1930s with the rise of Nazism, the situation for Jewish professionals like Ernestine became increasingly precarious.  After the *Anschluss* in 1938, the annexation of Austria by Nazi Germany, Ernestine, being Jewish, was immediately targeted. She was forced to relinquish her position at the Vienna General Hospital and her practice was effectively shut down.  She and her husband attempted to emigrate, initially seeking refuge in Switzerland but being denied entry. 

In 1939, they managed to escape to London with the help of contacts and financial resources.  While Felix re-established his business, Ernestine struggled to rebuild her professional life in a new country. She was admitted as a member of the British Psychoanalytical Society in 1940, but faced difficulties gaining a substantial practice.  She continued to treat patients and maintained contact with former colleagues from Vienna. 

Tragically, Felix Eckstein died in 1943. Ernestine continued to live in London, maintaining a modest practice and remaining involved with the British Psychoanalytical Society. She never remarried.  She continued to correspond with Freud, offering support and sharing news of the psychoanalytic community in London.  Ernestine Eckstein died on May 26, 1976, in London, aged 82.  Her legacy lies in her contributions to psychoanalytic theory and practice, particularly her pioneering work on female psychology, and her resilience in the face of political persecution. While her analysis with Freud remains a point of intense scholarly scrutiny, she is remembered as a dedicated psychoanalyst who navigated a challenging life with fortitude and intellectual rigor.

title: Nobuhiro Shimatani
text:
Nobuhiro Shimatani was born on February 16, 1948, in Kyoto, Japan, the son of a textile merchant. His early life was steeped in traditional Japanese arts and aesthetics, a background that would significantly influence his later work. He attended Doshisha University in Kyoto, graduating in 1970 with a degree in Economics. However, even during his university years, Shimatani’s passion lay increasingly with design and visual communication, deviating from the expected path of joining the family business. 

Shimatani’s professional journey began in 1970 at Nippon Design Center (NDC), then one of Japan's leading design firms, founded by the renowned designer Kenya Hara and Yoshiharu Sato. Initially, he worked as a junior designer, quickly absorbing the principles of modernist design and corporate identity development prevalent at NDC. He collaborated on a wide range of projects, including packaging, advertising, and exhibition design, learning from seasoned professionals and honing his skills.  He rose through the ranks, becoming a senior designer by the late 1970s. 

A pivotal moment in Shimatani’s career arrived in 1982 when he established his own independent design studio, Shimatani Design, in Tokyo. This move allowed him to pursue a more personal and conceptually driven design approach.  He quickly gained recognition for his minimalist aesthetic, characterized by a meticulous attention to detail, subtle use of color, and a strong emphasis on functionality.  He eschewed flamboyant trends, instead focusing on timelessness and a refined elegance that resonated with a growing clientele. 

Throughout the 1980s and 90s, Shimatani Design became synonymous with sophisticated branding and spatial design. He became particularly well-known for his work with Japanese retailers and cultural institutions. A landmark project was the complete visual identity for the department store chain Daimaru in 1985, which included logo redesign, store interiors, packaging, and advertising. This project solidified his reputation for translating traditional Japanese values into a modern aesthetic, and it was widely lauded for its clarity and understated sophistication.  Daimaru's new identity, particularly its signature striped bag, became instantly recognizable across Japan.

In 1993, Shimatani undertook the comprehensive redesign of the National Museum of Modern Art, Tokyo (MOMAT). This project, completed in 1997, involved not only the museum’s graphic identity – including signage and wayfinding systems – but also the spatial organization of its galleries and public spaces. He aimed to create a neutral and unobtrusive environment that would allow the artwork to take center stage. His work at MOMAT exemplified his belief that design should serve the content, rather than dominate it. 

Beyond retail and museums, Shimatani’s portfolio diversified to include corporate identities for companies like Takenaka Corporation, a major construction firm, and Shiseido, the cosmetics giant.  He also designed numerous books and publications, consistently showcasing his mastery of typography and layout. He received numerous awards throughout his career, including the Japan Institute of Design Promotion’s Good Design Award on multiple occasions, most notably for his MOMAT project in 1998.

In the 2000s, Shimatani increasingly focused on mentoring younger designers and lecturing at universities. He remained actively involved in Shimatani Design, though he took a step back from day-to-day management, allowing his team to continue his legacy. He published several books on design philosophy, emphasizing the importance of cultural context and the pursuit of enduring quality. He consistently spoke of the need for designers to be mindful of the impact their work has on society and the environment.

Nobuhiro Shimatani passed away on December 22, 2022, at the age of 74, leaving behind a substantial and influential body of work. He is remembered as a quiet, thoughtful designer who championed a humanist approach to design, deeply rooted in Japanese aesthetics and a commitment to clarity, functionality, and timeless elegance. His influence continues to be felt in the world of Japanese graphic and spatial design, and his work remains a benchmark for understated sophistication.

title: George Washington
text:
George Washington, born on February 22, 1732, at Popes Creek in Westmoreland County, Virginia, was a pivotal figure in the founding of the United States. He was the son of Augustine Washington, a planter, and Mary Ball Washington. George’s formal education was limited; he attended school locally, learning reading, writing, and basic mathematics, but his father’s early death in 1743 prevented extensive schooling. He instead focused on practical skills like surveying, which he began practicing professionally at age 16, working with William Fairfax, a wealthy landowner and Washington’s half-brother Lawrence’s connection.

Washington’s early career was steeped in military service. In 1753, at age 21, he was dispatched by Virginia Governor Robert Dinwiddie as a messenger to the French, who were encroaching on territory claimed by the British in the Ohio River Valley. This mission, and the subsequent skirmishes with the French and their Native American allies, marked the beginning of the French and Indian War (1754-1763). Washington quickly gained military experience, though also suffered early setbacks. He was involved in the disastrous defeat at Fort Necessity in 1754, surrendering to the French. Despite this, he served with distinction under British General Edward Braddock in 1755, showing bravery during the disastrous Battle of the Monongahela, where Braddock was killed. He continued to rise through the Virginia militia ranks, eventually becoming a Colonel and commanding the Virginia Regiment.

Following the French and Indian War, Washington married Martha Dandridge Custis, a wealthy widow, on January 6, 1759. This union brought him considerable social standing and financial security, as Martha brought a substantial dowry to the marriage. He then devoted himself to managing his plantation, Mount Vernon, in Fairfax County, Virginia, and to public service within the colony. From 1763 to 1774, he served as a justice of the peace in Fairfax County and represented the county in the Virginia House of Burgesses. 

As tensions between Great Britain and its American colonies escalated, Washington became increasingly involved in the growing resistance movement. He was a delegate to both the First (1774) and Second (1775) Continental Congresses. In June 1775, the Second Continental Congress unanimously appointed him Commander-in-Chief of the Continental Army. 

The Revolutionary War (1775-1783) saw Washington lead the fledgling American forces through eight arduous years. Despite numerous defeats and logistical nightmares – including a shortage of supplies, poorly trained troops, and a lack of consistent funding – his leadership, resilience, and strategic vision were crucial to the eventual American victory. Key battles include the crossing of the Delaware River and the surprise attack at Trenton on December 26, 1776, and the decisive victory at Yorktown in 1781, aided by French forces under the Comte de Rochambeau.  The British surrender at Yorktown effectively ended major fighting in the war.

Washington resigned his commission as Commander-in-Chief on December 23, 1783, a symbolic act demonstrating his commitment to civilian rule. He returned to Mount Vernon, intending to retire to private life. However, the inadequacies of the Articles of Confederation, the first governing document of the United States, soon became apparent. He was persuaded to attend the Constitutional Convention in Philadelphia in 1787, where he was unanimously elected President of the Convention. His presence lent legitimacy to the proceedings, and he played a crucial, though largely moderating, role in the drafting of the United States Constitution.

In 1789, Washington was unanimously elected as the first President of the United States. He served two terms, establishing many of the precedents for the office. He appointed Alexander Hamilton as his Secretary of the Treasury and Thomas Jefferson as his Secretary of State, navigating the complex political divisions between them. He signed the Judiciary Act of 1789, establishing the federal court system, and oversaw the suppression of the Whiskey Rebellion in 1794, demonstrating the power of the federal government. He issued a Neutrality Proclamation in 1793, keeping the United States out of the European wars raging at the time. He delivered a Farewell Address in September 1796, warning against the dangers of political factions and excessive foreign entanglements.

Washington retired from the presidency in March 1797 and returned to Mount Vernon. He died on December 14, 1799, at the age of 67, after a short illness. His estate was valued at over $525,000 at the time of his death, a substantial fortune reflecting his landholdings and shrewd business practices. He is remembered as the "Father of His Country" for his indispensable role in achieving American independence and establishing the United States of America.

title: Aaron Burr
text:
Aaron Burr was born on February 6, 1756, in Newark, New Jersey, to Reverend Aaron Burr Sr., a prominent Presbyterian minister, and Esther Edwards Burr, the daughter of Jonathan Edwards, a renowned theologian. He was the second of three children and tragically orphaned by the age of three, his mother dying in 1757 and his father in 1759. He was raised by his maternal grandfather, Jonathan Edwards, until the latter’s death in 1758, then by various relatives. This somewhat unstable upbringing instilled in him a degree of self-reliance and a reserved demeanor.

Burr entered the College of New Jersey (later Princeton University) at the exceptionally young age of thirteen in 1769, graduating in 1773. He then studied law with Tapping Reeve in Litchfield, Connecticut, a highly respected judge and legal scholar. He was admitted to the Connecticut bar in 1775, just as the American Revolution was beginning. 

The Revolution marked Burr’s initial foray into public life. He served as a private in the Continental Army during the Battle of Quebec in 1775-1776, though his military career was short-lived. He quickly transitioned to political roles, becoming a private secretary to General Israel Putnam in 1776, and later serving in the New York State Assembly from 1777-1781.  He rose through the ranks, becoming the Attorney General of New York in 1789, a position he held until 1793. 

In 1791, Burr successfully challenged incumbent Senator Philip Schuyler for the U.S. Senate seat representing New York. He served one term, until 1797, becoming known as a skilled, though often aloof, legislator. He was a capable debater, but his independent streak and lack of strong party affiliation hindered his progress. He opposed many of Alexander Hamilton’s financial policies, seeing them as favoring the wealthy elite. 

Burr’s political ambition centered on the presidency. He ran for President in 1800, as a candidate of the Democratic-Republican Party, but the election resulted in a tie in the Electoral College between himself and Thomas Jefferson. The decision went to the House of Representatives, where, after 36 ballots, Jefferson was elected President on February 11, 1801, with Burr becoming Vice President. 

His Vice Presidency, from 1801 to 1805, was marked by estrangement from President Jefferson, who distrusted Burr’s ambition and perceived him as opportunistic. He was dropped from the Democratic-Republican ticket in the 1804 election. Undeterred, Burr ran for Governor of New York, hoping to use that office as a steppingstone to a future presidential bid. His campaign was intensely contested with incumbent Governor Morgan Lewis.

The election coincided with a period of escalating political tension with Alexander Hamilton.  Hamilton actively campaigned against Burr, portraying him as unfit for office. This culminated in the infamous duel on July 11, 1804, at Weehawken, New Jersey. Burr fatally shot Hamilton, who died the following day. Though not immediately prosecuted, the duel severely damaged Burr’s reputation and effectively ended his national political career.

Following his Vice Presidency, Burr embarked on a controversial and ultimately disastrous venture. He conceived of a plan to establish an independent empire in the Southwest, potentially involving the acquisition of territory from Spanish territories like Louisiana and Texas. This led to accusations of treason. In 1807, President Jefferson ordered his arrest.  Burr was tried for treason in 1808 in Richmond, Virginia, presided over by Chief Justice John Marshall. Though the evidence was substantial, Marshall, a Federalist and political opponent of Jefferson, set a high standard for proving treason, and Burr was acquitted on September 24, 1808. 

Burr fled to Europe, spending several years in Britain and France. He returned to the United States in 1812, living a quiet and largely secluded life in New York City, practicing law and managing inherited property.  He remarried in 1833 to Eliza Jumel, a wealthy widow, but their relationship was fraught with financial disputes. Aaron Burr died in New York City on September 14, 1836, at the age of 80, a figure remembered as a brilliant, ambitious, and ultimately tragic figure in American history.

title: Ezekiel Elliott
text:
Ezekiel Tyler Elliott was born on July 22, 1995, in Alton, Illinois, to Stacy Elliott and Darryl Elliott. His father, Darryl, was a former University of Maine running back, and his mother was a high school track and field star. This athletic background heavily influenced Ezekiel’s development. The family moved to West Bloomfield, Michigan, when Ezekiel was in elementary school, providing him access to more competitive high school athletics. He attended West Bloomfield High School, where he excelled in football, basketball, and track. As a junior in 2012, Elliott rushed for 1,805 yards and 39 touchdowns, leading West Bloomfield to a district championship. He finished his high school career with 3,033 rushing yards and 44 touchdowns. He was a four-star recruit and considered one of the top running back prospects in the nation, receiving scholarship offers from numerous prominent universities.

On February 6, 2013, Elliott committed to playing college football at Ohio State University. He immediately made an impact as a true freshman in 2013, backing up senior running back Jordan Hall. He rushed for 228 yards and four touchdowns in limited action, including a crucial 85-yard touchdown run against Illinois. His sophomore year in 2014 saw him become the primary ball carrier, culminating in a spectacular performance in the College Football Playoff National Championship against Oregon on January 12, 2015. Elliott ran for a game-high 246 yards and four touchdowns, earning Offensive MVP honors as Ohio State won 42-20. 

Elliott’s junior season in 2015 was arguably his most dominant. He led the nation with 1,811 rushing yards and 19 touchdowns, averaging 6.3 yards per carry. He was a unanimous All-American and finished eighth in the Heisman Trophy voting.  Following the 2015 season, on January 12, 2016, Elliott announced his decision to forgo his senior year and enter the 2016 NFL Draft.

The Dallas Cowboys selected Elliott with the fourth overall pick in the 2016 NFL Draft. He signed a four-year, $24.9 million contract with a $16.3 million signing bonus on May 12, 2016.  Elliott quickly justified the Cowboys’ investment. In his rookie season, he led the league with 1,631 rushing yards, becoming the first rookie to lead the NFL in rushing since Clinton Portis in 2002. He was named the NFL Offensive Rookie of the Year and was selected to the Pro Bowl. 

His second season in 2017 was marred by a six-game suspension stemming from allegations of domestic violence, which were ultimately dropped without charges filed. Despite missing games, he still managed 983 rushing yards. He continued to be a key player for the Cowboys in the following years, being selected to the Pro Bowl in 2018 and 2019. In 2019, he signed an eight-year, $90 million contract extension with the Cowboys. 

Elliott's production began to decline in 2020 and 2021, partially due to injuries and the emergence of Tony Pollard. On March 15, 2023, the Cowboys released Elliott.  He signed a one-year contract with the New England Patriots on March 20, 2023, reuniting with his former Cowboys offensive coordinator Jerod Mayo, who was now the Patriots’ head coach. He played one season in New England, rushing for 642 yards and 3 touchdowns. 

On March 18, 2024, Elliott signed a one-year contract with the Kansas City Chiefs.  He is expected to serve as a backup to Isiah Pacheco. Throughout his career, Elliott has been known for his physical running style, pass-catching ability, and dedication to community service, particularly his work with animal shelters. As of late 2024, Ezekiel Elliott remains an active player in the NFL, continuing to contribute to the game he has excelled at since his high school days.

title: Manny Pacquiao
text:
Manny Pacquiao, born Emmanuel Dapidran Pacquiao on December 17, 1978, in Kibawe, Bukidnon, Philippines, rose from extreme poverty to become one of the most celebrated and influential boxers of all time, and a significant political figure in his homeland. His early life was marked by hardship. His father, Pedro Pacquiao, was a farmer and fisherman, and his mother, Dionesia Pacquiao, worked various jobs to support the family. Manny was the fourth of six children and faced severe financial difficulties growing up, often experiencing hunger and lacking formal education beyond elementary school. He began boxing at the age of 12, initially as a means to help his family financially, engaging in street fights and small-time boxing matches.

Pacquiao’s amateur career was brief but promising. He competed in local tournaments, winning several regional championships. He turned professional on May 22, 1995, in General Santos City, Philippines, defeating Edmund Saingman via a four-round technical knockout. Initially fighting in the flyweight division (112 lbs), he quickly gained recognition for his speed, power, and aggressive style. His early career saw him win 11 straight fights, including a victory over Chatchai Sasakul in 1997 to claim the OPBF flyweight title, his first major championship. 

In 1998, Pacquiao moved up in weight to super bantamweight (122 lbs) and captured the IBF super bantamweight title by defeating Chatchai Sasakul again, this time by TKO in the 8th round. This marked his breakthrough on the international stage. He would lose the title in his first defense to Medgoen Singsurat in 1999, but his relentless pursuit of championships continued. 

The early 2000s saw Pacquiao consistently move up in weight classes, becoming a champion in featherweight (126 lbs) in 2001, super featherweight (130 lbs) in 2002, and lightweight (135 lbs) in 2003, defeating Marco Antonio Barrera in a highly anticipated fight in San Antonio, Texas. This victory significantly boosted his profile in the United States. He then took on Juan Manuel Márquez, fighting to a controversial draw in their first encounter in May 2004.

Pacquiao’s career reached its peak from 2008 to 2010. He defeated Oscar De La Hoya in December 2008, moving up to welterweight (147 lbs) and winning the WBC belt. In 2009, he dominated Ricky Hatton, and in November 2009, he defeated Miguel Cotto, adding the WBO welterweight title to his collection. 2010 saw a rematch with Antonio Márquez, which Pacquiao won by unanimous decision, and then a landmark fight against Floyd Mayweather Jr. which, despite years of negotiation, did not materialize until much later.

Between 2010 and 2015, Pacquiao continued to compete at a high level, facing opponents like Shane Mosley, Tim Bradley (whom he defeated twice, with a controversial loss in their first fight), and Chris Algieri. The long-awaited fight against Floyd Mayweather Jr. finally took place on May 2, 2015, in Las Vegas, Nevada. Mayweather won by unanimous decision in what became the highest-grossing boxing match in history, generating over $600 million in revenue.

Pacquiao officially retired from professional boxing on April 16, 2017, after a brief fight and win against Jessie Vargas. However, he returned to the ring for a exhibition match against Floyd Mayweather Jr. in 2018. He officially returned to professional boxing in 2019, defeating Keith Thurman, but retired again in 2021 after a loss to Yordenis Ugás. His professional record stands at 62 wins, 8 losses, and 2 draws, with 39 knockouts.

Outside the ring, Pacquiao pursued a political career. He was elected to the House of Representatives of the Philippines representing Sarangani province in 2010, and served continuously until 2022. He was then elected as a Senator in 2016, serving one term. In 2022, he ran for President of the Philippines but was defeated by Ferdinand Marcos Jr. Pacquiao is a devout evangelical Christian and has been involved in numerous charitable activities throughout his career. He remains a national hero in the Philippines, celebrated for his boxing achievements and his dedication to his country.

title: Uee
text:
Uee, born Kim Yoo-jin on April 9, 1988, in Incheon, South Korea, is a South Korean singer, actress, and television personality. Her early life was marked by athletic prowess rather than artistic ambition. She excelled in swimming during her school years, even competing at the national level, and initially harbored dreams of becoming a member of the national swimming team. However, a shoulder injury during her third year of middle school effectively ended her competitive swimming career. This setback prompted her to explore other interests, and a friend encouraged her to audition for a beauty pageant. 

In 2007, Uee participated in and won the Miss Korea competition, specifically taking the title of Miss Incheon. This victory served as her entry point into the entertainment industry. Shortly after winning the pageant, she signed with DLine Entertainment and debuted as a member of the five-member girl group Wonder Girls in September 2007, joining members Park Ye-eun (Yubin), Min Sun-ye, Park So-hyun, and Lee Hye-ri. Uee primarily served as a vocalist and visual for the group. 

Wonder Girls quickly rose to prominence with their hit single "Tell Me," released in 2008. The song became a national phenomenon in South Korea, achieving a record-breaking 10 consecutive weeks at number one on the Music Bank K-Chart.  Further successes followed with songs like "Nobody" and "So Hot," establishing Wonder Girls as a leading K-pop act both domestically and internationally, including a brief foray into the American music market in 2009. 

While active with Wonder Girls, Uee began to explore acting opportunities. Her debut acting role came in 2009 with a cameo appearance in the drama "Queen Seondeok."  She secured her first substantial acting role in the 2011 drama "Golden Shining Inheritance," playing the character of Yoon Sun-jung. This was followed by the lead role in "Ojakgyo Brothers” (2011-2012) which significantly boosted her recognition as an actress.  

In 2013, Uee officially departed from Wonder Girls, focusing solely on her acting career.  She continued to take on leading roles in various television dramas, including “Beloved Eun-dong” (2015), “Marriage Contract” (2016), and “Manhole” (2017).  She also appeared in films, such as “The Last Knight” (2015) and “Detective K: Secret Investigation” (2018). Although not all of her projects were critical successes, Uee consistently demonstrated her dedication to acting and broadened her range with each role. 

Throughout her career, Uee received several awards, including a New Star Award at the 2011 MBC Drama Awards for "Ojakgyo Brothers.” She also gained recognition for her physical fitness, often appearing on variety shows showcasing her workout routines and healthy lifestyle.  In 2018, she participated in the reality show “Law of the Jungle” in Palau, demonstrating her resilience and adaptability.

In December 2022, Uee announced her marriage to professional baseball player Yoo Seong-min of the Samsung Lions, whom she had been dating since 2021. The wedding, held in Seoul, was a private ceremony attended by close friends and family.  In November 2023, she announced she was pregnant with their first child.  She gave birth to a daughter in February 2024. 

Following her marriage and pregnancy, Uee has continued to selectively accept acting roles, balancing her family life with her professional commitments. She signed with a new agency, C-JeS Entertainment, in 2023. While she remains a recognizable figure in the Korean entertainment industry, she has expressed a desire to prioritize her family and pursue roles that are personally fulfilling, rather than solely focusing on commercial success.

title: Tim Ferguson
text:
Tim Ferguson was born Timothy John Ferguson on October 27, 1961, in Melbourne, Australia, to parents John and Margaret Ferguson. He grew up in the suburb of Blackburn, attending Blackburn High School, where he was a keen student and developed an early interest in performing, participating in school plays and debating societies. He excelled academically, scoring highly on his matriculation exams and initially enrolling to study medicine at the University of Melbourne in 1980. However, his passion for comedy quickly outweighed his ambition for a medical career, and he switched to a Bachelor of Arts degree, majoring in Politics and History, which he completed in 1983.

Ferguson’s entry into professional comedy began in the Melbourne University revue scene. He wrote and performed in several student revues, honing his comedic skills and developing a collaborative working relationship with fellow student, Santo Cilauro. This partnership proved pivotal to his future success. In 1986, Ferguson and Cilauro, along with Jane Kennedy, formed the satirical comedy group, The Chaser. Initially performing live at the Esplanade Hotel in St Kilda, Victoria, The Chaser quickly gained a cult following with their fast-paced, topical and often irreverent sketches. 

The group’s breakthrough came in 1993 with the debut of *The Late Show* on ABC television. Ferguson was a key writer, performer and producer on the show, which ran for four seasons. *The Late Show* was groundbreaking for its innovative use of visual gags, quick cuts, and its willingness to satirize Australian politics and culture. Iconic segments like “Before the Bomb,” a mock historical news report, and “Accidental Tourist,” featuring Ferguson as a clueless traveller, became instant classics. The show garnered multiple Logie Awards, including the Gold Logie for Most Popular Personality on Australian Television in 1997, which Ferguson won. 

Following *The Late Show*, The Chaser continued to evolve. In 2002, they created *The Chaser’s War on Everything*, which aired on the Seven Network before moving to ABC in 2006. This show pushed the boundaries of satirical television, frequently employing elaborate pranks and stunts to highlight political and social issues. One particularly controversial stunt, involving the group gatecrashing the APEC summit in Sydney in 2007 dressed as Chinese guards, led to significant media attention and a police investigation, though no charges were ultimately laid. *The Chaser’s War on Everything* won two Logie Awards for Most Outstanding Comedy Program.

Alongside his work with The Chaser, Ferguson pursued individual writing projects. He authored the political satire novel *Left Right and Centre* in 1995, which offered a cynical but humorous take on Australian political life. He also wrote and directed the mockumentary film *Year 9* in 2005, a comedic look at the trials and tribulations of a group of Australian teenagers.

In 2010, Ferguson was diagnosed with Multiple Sclerosis (MS). He publicly revealed his diagnosis in 2011 and subsequently became a vocal advocate for MS research and awareness. Despite the challenges posed by the condition, he continued to work, though his on-screen appearances became less frequent. He focused increasingly on writing and producing. 

The Chaser team continued to create content, including the annual *Chaser’s Media Circus* specials for the ABC, providing satirical coverage of major events. Ferguson remained a central figure in these productions, contributing to the writing and overall direction. He also became involved in podcasting, co-hosting *The Chaser Report* podcast with other members of the group. 

Tim Ferguson continues to live in Melbourne with his wife, Gabriella. He remains a significant figure in Australian comedy, known for his sharp wit, innovative style, and commitment to satirical commentary. While MS has presented ongoing health challenges, he maintains a busy career, demonstrating resilience and a continued passion for his craft. His work with The Chaser has left a lasting impact on Australian television and comedy.

title: Prince Carl Philip, Duke of Värmland
text:
Carl Philip Edmund Bertil, Duke of Värmland, was born on May 13, 1979, at Karolinska Hospital in Solna, Sweden. He is the only son of King Carl XVI Gustaf and Queen Silvia of Sweden, and the younger brother of Crown Princess Victoria. His birth was a significant event for the Swedish monarchy, securing the continuation of the male line despite his sister being the heir presumptive. He was formally given the title Duke of Värmland on May 13, 1983, a tradition in the Swedish royal family where each child of the monarch is assigned a duchy. 

Carl Philip’s early life was largely private, though he accompanied his parents on numerous official engagements both within Sweden and internationally. He received his primary education at Smedslättsskolan, a school deliberately chosen for its integration of children from diverse backgrounds. He then attended Lundsberg Boarding School from 1995 to 1999, a prestigious institution known for its academic rigor and emphasis on leadership. During his time at Lundsberg, he was described as a keen student of history and a capable sportsman, participating in athletics and sailing. 

Following completion of his secondary education, Carl Philip opted for a non-traditional path for a royal. In 2000, he undertook a year of military training, completing the officer training program at the Swedish Armed Forces. He subsequently pursued studies in architecture, initially at the Royal Institute of Technology in Stockholm, but later transferring to Uppsala University in 2002. He did not complete a formal degree, instead choosing to focus on developing his own design and photography skills. 

In 2003, Carl Philip established his own design firm, Carl Philip Design AB. The company focused on industrial design, creating products ranging from outdoor furniture to glassware, and collaborating with companies such as Svenskt Tenn and Gärsnäs.  His design work reflects a modern, minimalist aesthetic with a strong emphasis on functionality. He has also worked as a photographer, contributing images to various publications. 

Beyond his entrepreneurial pursuits, Carl Philip has maintained a strong connection to the Swedish Armed Forces. He has served as a reserve officer and has regularly participated in military exercises. He holds the rank of Major in the Swedish Army and the Air Force.  He is also a qualified helicopter pilot. His commitment to the military is a prominent aspect of his public role. 

He is a passionate advocate for youth initiatives and sport, particularly sailing. He founded the Bernadotte Art Award in 2013, an annual prize recognizing promising young artists. He also actively supports the Swedish Paralympic Committee and various environmental organizations.  He represents the Swedish monarchy at numerous international events and official functions.

On June 13, 2015, Carl Philip married Sofia Hellqvist, a former model and businesswoman, at the Royal Chapel of Stockholm Palace. The wedding was a significant media event, attracting attention both domestically and internationally. The couple have three sons: Prince Alexander, born April 19, 2016; Prince Gabriel, born August 31, 2017; and Prince Julian, born March 28, 2021.  

Prince Carl Philip and his family reside at Villa Solstudien, a residence on the grounds of Haga Palace in Stockholm. While not in the direct line of succession, Carl Philip continues to fulfill a crucial role as a working member of the Swedish royal family, representing the monarchy and contributing to Swedish society through his professional endeavors and charitable commitments. As of 2024, he remains a visible and active figure in public life, balancing his duties with his family life and creative pursuits.

title: Kaká
text:
Ricardo Izecson dos Santos Leite, universally known as Kaká, was born on April 22, 1982, in Brasília, Brazil, to Bosco Izecson Pereira Leite, a civil engineer, and Simone dos Santos Leite, a teacher. His upbringing was relatively privileged, unlike many aspiring Brazilian footballers. A serious water-skiing accident at age 18, fracturing his sixth cervical vertebra, initially threatened his football career. Doctors warned he might be paralyzed, but thankfully, a successful surgery and extensive rehabilitation at age 19 allowed him to fully recover and continue pursuing his dream. This experience instilled in him a deep faith, which became a defining aspect of his public persona.

Kaká began his football journey at age eight, joining the youth system of São Paulo FC in 1990. He progressed rapidly through the ranks, showcasing exceptional dribbling skills, vision, and a powerful shot. He debuted professionally for São Paulo on January 29, 2001, at the age of 18, in a Campeonato Paulista match against Botafogo Ribeirão Preto. Over the next two seasons, he established himself as a key player for São Paulo, winning the Copa Sul-Americana in 2002, scoring a crucial penalty in the final shootout against Atlético Nacional. He also contributed to São Paulo’s Brazilian Championship title in the same year.

His performances attracted attention from European clubs, and in August 2003, at the age of 21, he signed for AC Milan for a reported fee of €8.5 million. Kaká quickly adapted to Italian football, becoming the focal point of Milan’s attack. He formed a formidable partnership with Andriy Shevchenko and Paolo Maldini, leading Milan to the 2003-04 Serie A title, with Kaká providing 10 assists, the most in the league. 

The 2006-07 season was arguably the peak of his career. He was instrumental in Milan’s Champions League triumph, finishing as the competition’s top scorer with 10 goals. His performances earned him the coveted Ballon d'Or in December 2007, becoming the last player before the Lionel Messi-Cristiano Ronaldo dominance to win the award. He also secured the FIFA World Player of the Year award in the same year. He was a key component of the Milan side that defeated Liverpool 2-1 in the 2007 Champions League Final in Athens, scoring a goal.

Kaká continued to perform at a high level for Milan over the next few seasons, but injuries began to hamper his consistency. In June 2009, he transferred to Real Madrid for a reported €67 million, becoming one of the most expensive players in football history at the time. However, his time at Real Madrid was less successful than his spell at Milan. He struggled to consistently replicate his previous form, facing competition for places and lacking the consistent playing time he enjoyed in Italy. He won the Copa del Rey with Real Madrid in 2011, but his overall contribution was considered underwhelming.

In September 2013, Kaká returned to AC Milan on a free transfer, hoping to rediscover his best form. He spent one season back in Milan, contributing sporadically, before moving to Orlando City SC in Major League Soccer (MLS) in June 2014. He became Orlando City’s first designated player and played a pivotal role in establishing the club in MLS. He captained the team and scored 25 goals in 78 appearances over three seasons.

Kaká officially retired from professional football on December 3, 2017. He played 92 times for the Brazilian national team, scoring 30 goals, and was part of the team that won the 2002 FIFA World Cup, although he played a limited role in the tournament. He also represented Brazil in the 2006 and 2010 World Cups. 

Post-retirement, Kaká has remained involved in football, working as a commentator and ambassador for various organizations. He has also focused on philanthropic work through his Kaká Foundation, dedicated to providing educational opportunities for underprivileged children. He married Carol Celico in 2005, with whom he has two children, and they divorced in 2015. He married Carolina Dias in 2019 and has another child.

title: Witold Gombrowicz
text:
Witold Gombrowicz was born on August 4, 1904, in Maloszyce, Poland, a small town in the Kielce Governorate of the Russian Empire. He came from a Polish aristocratic, though financially struggling, family. His father, Tadeusz Gombrowicz, was a painter and railway engineer, and his mother, Antonina née Babska, came from a family of landowners. This background of declining nobility and a sense of societal displacement would profoundly influence his writing. He received a rather unconventional education, largely due to his family’s frequent moves and his own lack of enthusiasm for formal schooling. He spent periods in Warsaw, then briefly in Switzerland, and finally settled with his family in 1922 in Pomerania, which had been returned to Poland after World War I. 

Gombrowicz initially studied law at the University of Warsaw (1922-1925), but quickly abandoned it, finding it stifling and uninspiring. He then enrolled in a drama school, also in Warsaw, but left after a year, rejecting the conventionality of theatrical training. This period was marked by a deliberate rejection of societal norms and a growing sense of alienation. He spent the next several years drifting, working odd jobs and dedicating himself entirely to writing. His early literary attempts were largely unsuccessful and met with rejection from publishers.

His breakthrough came with the publication of his first novel, *Ferdydurke*, in 1938. This highly unconventional work, a satirical and philosophical exploration of form, immaturity, and the imposition of societal roles, initially received limited attention but gradually gained recognition as a seminal work of Polish literature. *Ferdydurke* established Gombrowicz’s distinctive style: a blend of philosophical inquiry, grotesque humor, and linguistic experimentation.  He followed this with *Trans-Atlantic* (1953), a novel that satirizes Polish emigrant life in Argentina, and *Cosmos* (1965), a darkly comic and existential exploration of human anxiety.

The outbreak of World War II in 1939 dramatically altered Gombrowicz’s life. He attempted to reach Warsaw to join the resistance, but was unable to do so and found himself in Argentina, initially as a result of a forged Paraguayan transit visa. He spent the next 23 years in exile, primarily in Buenos Aires. This period was marked by financial hardship and a sense of cultural displacement. He worked as a bank clerk, a translator, and a proofreader to support himself while continuing to write.  He published *The Possession of H.* (1956), a novel focusing on a disturbed man and his obsession, and continued to develop his unique literary voice. 

During his Argentine years, Gombrowicz also became involved in the Polish literary scene in exile, forming complex relationships with other writers. He actively participated in the Koliba group, a literary circle that aimed to maintain Polish cultural identity abroad. However, he often clashed with other members, particularly those aligned with the communist regime in Poland, due to his staunch anti-totalitarian views.

In 1963, after years of relative obscurity, Gombrowicz’s work began to receive increasing recognition in Europe, largely due to the efforts of French intellectuals like Nathalie Sarraute and Roland Barthes. This renewed interest led to translations of his novels into French and other languages, establishing him as a major figure in post-war European literature. In 1969, he finally returned to Poland, settling in Vence, France, near the Polish border, with his partner, Rita Labuda. 

He was granted a state pension by the Polish government, a gesture that acknowledged his literary importance. Despite his deteriorating health, he continued to write and revise his work.  He received numerous awards in his later years, including the Prix Formentor in 1969 and the Polish PEN Club’s award in 1970.  Witold Gombrowicz died on September 25, 1969, in Vence, France, leaving behind a body of work that continues to challenge and fascinate readers with its originality and profound philosophical insights. His diaries, published posthumously, provide further insight into his complex personality and artistic process.

title: Geraldo de Barros
text:
Geraldo de Barros was born on April 27, 1923, in São Paulo, Brazil, to Portuguese immigrant parents. His father, a photographer, instilled in him a fascination with the medium from a young age. While initially intending to study engineering, de Barros quickly gravitated towards visual arts, enrolling in 1943 at the Escola Nacional de Belas Artes (National School of Fine Arts) in Rio de Janeiro. However, he found the academic approach stifling and left after only a year, preferring a more self-directed path of artistic exploration. 

The mid-1940s were a period of intense artistic ferment in Brazil, and de Barros became a key figure in the Grupo Ruptura, founded in 1947. This group, consisting of artists like Waldemar Cordeiro, Luiz Sacilotto, and Ignácio de Loyola Brandão, explicitly rejected traditional Brazilian art forms and embraced a concrete, geometric aesthetic influenced by European Constructivism and Neo-Plasticism.  De Barros’s early work, though often photography, was fundamentally rooted in this concrete art philosophy. He wasn’t interested in photographic representation in a traditional sense; instead, he saw photography as a tool for exploring form, line, and spatial relationships. 

Between 1949 and 1951, de Barros held a significant role as art director for the advertising agency Companhia Brasileira de Publicidade (Brazilian Advertising Company). This experience, while providing financial stability, proved crucial to his artistic development. He began experimenting with photograms – images created without a camera, by placing objects directly onto photographic paper and exposing them to light. These ‘photograms’, which he termed ‘cromogramas’ (chromograms), were abstract compositions often utilizing found objects like screws, wires, and glass, reflecting the industrializing landscape of post-war Brazil.  He created over 300 chromograms during this period, many of which were exhibited in collective shows at the Galeria de Arte Moderna (Modern Art Gallery) in São Paulo. 

In 1952, he co-founded the Estudio ABC with Alex Sacilotto, a studio dedicated to graphic design and advertising. This venture allowed him further freedom to experiment with visual communication and the possibilities of photographic manipulation.  He pioneered techniques like solarization, multiple exposures, and photomontage, pushing the boundaries of what photography could achieve.  He developed a particular interest in the possibilities of color photography, a relatively new and expensive process at the time, and became a leading figure in its artistic exploration in Brazil.

Throughout the 1960s, de Barros’s work became increasingly concerned with the relationship between art and technology. He explored the use of lasers and computer-generated imagery, anticipating the digital art movements of later decades. He held his first solo exhibition in 1966 at the Museu de Arte Moderna de São Paulo, showcasing his latest experiments. In 1972, he received a Guggenheim fellowship, which allowed him to conduct research in the United States, focusing on the application of computers in art. 

Despite his pioneering contributions, de Barros remained relatively unknown internationally for much of his career. He largely withdrew from the art world in the 1980s, dedicating himself to teaching and private projects. He held a professorship at the Faculdade de Artes Plásticas (School of Plastic Arts) of the Fundação Armando Álvares Penteado in São Paulo from 1968 until his retirement in 1988. 

Recognition of his importance grew in the 1990s, spurred by a major retrospective of his work at the Museu de Arte Contemporânea da Universidade de São Paulo (Museum of Contemporary Art of the University of São Paulo) in 1994.  This exhibition, and subsequent international shows, helped to establish de Barros as a crucial figure in the history of Brazilian modernism and experimental photography. Geraldo de Barros died on April 26, 1996, in São Paulo, one day before his 73rd birthday, leaving behind a legacy of innovative photographic work that continues to inspire artists today. His archive, containing thousands of photographs and documents, is now housed at the Pinacoteca do Estado de São Paulo.

title: Maurice Jones-Drew
text:
Maurice Jones-Drew was born March 3, 1985, in Sacramento, California, to Rhonda and Morris Jones. His early life was significantly impacted by the absence of his father, who was incarcerated for much of his childhood. Raised primarily by his mother and grandmother, he found refuge and discipline through sports, excelling in both football and track at Grant Union High School in Del Paso Heights, a neighborhood within Sacramento. He was a standout running back, earning Sacramento Bee All-Metro honors three times (2001, 2002, 2003) and setting numerous school records. He rushed for 2,266 yards and 23 touchdowns as a senior in 2003, solidifying his reputation as a premier high school talent. 

Despite initial interest from larger programs, Jones-Drew ultimately committed to UCLA, choosing to stay close to home. He played for the Bruins from 2004 to 2005, though his college career was unfortunately cut short due to academic ineligibility following the 2005 season. While at UCLA, he demonstrated impressive versatility, contributing not only as a rusher but also as a receiver and kick returner. He rushed for 982 yards and 14 touchdowns in his two seasons, and caught 47 passes for 343 yards. His explosive playmaking ability was evident, but off-field issues hindered his collegiate progression. 

Eligible for the 2006 NFL Draft despite having two years of college eligibility remaining, Jones-Drew was selected by the Jacksonville Jaguars in the second round, 60th overall. Initially used primarily as a third-down back and return specialist, he spent his first two seasons backing up Fred Taylor. His opportunity to shine came in 2009 when Taylor went down with an injury. Jones-Drew seized the role, rushing for 1,168 yards and 15 touchdowns, becoming the Jaguars’ primary running back and a significant offensive weapon. 

The 2011 season marked the peak of Jones-Drew's NFL career. He led the league in rushing with 1,606 yards on 347 carries, earning his first and only Pro Bowl selection and a First-Team All-Pro nod. He also scored 8 rushing touchdowns and added 5 receptions for 43 yards. His powerful running style and ability to break tackles made him a difficult player to bring down. He continued to be a focal point of the Jaguars’ offense in 2012, racking up 1,206 rushing yards and 11 touchdowns despite battling injuries. 

However, subsequent years were plagued by injuries, including a foot injury in 2013 and a knee injury in 2014. His rushing numbers declined significantly, and he was released by the Jaguars in February 2015. He briefly signed with the Pittsburgh Steelers in March 2015, but was released before the start of the season. He announced his retirement from the NFL on August 24, 2016.

Throughout his eight-year NFL career, Jones-Drew amassed 8,167 rushing yards, 68 rushing touchdowns, 326 receptions for 2,838 receiving yards, and 11 receiving touchdowns. He finished his career with a career average of 4.2 yards per carry.

Following his retirement, Jones-Drew transitioned into a media career. He began as an analyst for NFL Network and ESPN, offering insights and commentary on the league. He is known for his candid and analytical approach, often providing a player’s perspective on game strategies and player performance.  In 2017, he joined the Jacksonville Jaguars as a youth football outreach coordinator, focusing on developing youth football programs in the local community. He has become a prominent voice advocating for player safety and youth development through football.  He currently continues his work with the Jaguars and remains a visible figure in the Jacksonville area, dedicating time to philanthropic endeavors and mentoring young athletes.

title: Martha Cunz
text:
Martha May Elton Cunz, born on November 22, 1902, in St. Louis, Missouri, was a pivotal figure in the development of modern dance and a dedicated advocate for dance education and preservation. Her early life was steeped in the arts, fostered by her mother, May Elton, a trained pianist and amateur artist who recognized and nurtured Martha’s innate musicality and movement skills. Martha began formal dance training at the age of six with Miss Lulu Blacker, studying a combination of ballet and expressive dance, a precursor to modern techniques. 

The family moved to New York City in 1917, a move that dramatically altered the course of Martha’s artistic development. There, she continued her studies with Elizabeth Haig, a former ballerina with the Imperial Russian Ballet, focusing on classical ballet technique. Simultaneously, she sought out instruction in the emerging field of modern dance, taking classes with Eadweyth Truesdell and later, crucially, with Doris Humphrey. This duality of training – rigorous ballet alongside the burgeoning expressive movement of modern dance – became a defining characteristic of her style and pedagogical approach. 

In 1921, at the age of 19, Cunz joined the Denishawn School and Company, the renowned institution founded by Ruth St. Denis and Ted Shawn. This was a formative period, exposing her to a diverse range of dance styles and performance practices. She toured extensively with Denishawn between 1922 and 1925, performing in works like "Radha," "Xochitl," and "California Suite," reaching audiences across the United States and even internationally, including a performance in Paris in 1924. 

Following her time with Denishawn, Cunz embarked on a solo performing career, appearing in New York City concert stages throughout the late 1920s and 1930s. However, she increasingly felt drawn to teaching and, in 1935, she established the Martha Cunz Dance School in New York City. This school became a haven for serious dance students, prioritizing both technical proficiency and artistic exploration. 

Cunz’s pedagogical philosophy was notably holistic. She insisted on a well-rounded curriculum, incorporating not just technique but also music, history, and composition. She believed strongly in developing the whole artist, not simply a skilled performer. Her teaching emphasized clarity, precision, and a deep understanding of anatomy and kinesiology. The school operated continuously until 1981, nurturing generations of dancers including Louise Caldwell, a prominent dancer and choreographer in her own right. 

Beyond her teaching, Cunz dedicated herself to the preservation of dance heritage. In 1939, she began a monumental project: the transcription and documentation of the choreography of several important works from the Denishawn repertoire. Recognizing that these dances, central to the development of American modern dance, were fading from memory, she meticulously notated them using a system developed by Rudolf Laban, a pioneer in dance notation. This painstaking work resulted in the publication of *Studies in Dance Technique* in 1941, a significant contribution to the field.  She continued this work for decades, eventually documenting over 20 Denishawn pieces, ensuring their survival for future generations.  

In 1966, Cunz received a grant from the National Endowment for the Arts to further her work on the Denishawn reconstructions. She also lectured extensively on the history of dance and the Denishawn legacy.  She actively participated in the Dance Notation Bureau, contributing her expertise to the standardization of dance recording.

Martha Cunz never married.  She dedicated her life entirely to her art and to her students.  She continued teaching privately until well into her eighties, remaining a respected and influential figure in the dance community. Martha Cunz died on January 25, 1990, in New York City, at the age of 87, leaving behind a legacy of dedicated teaching, meticulous scholarship, and an unwavering commitment to the preservation of American dance history.  Her work continues to inform dance education and performance today.

title: Kiara Advani
text:
Kiara Advani, born on July 31, 1992, in Mumbai, Maharashtra, is a prominent Indian actress working primarily in Hindi and Telugu cinema. Her birth name is Alia Advani, a change she made before entering the film industry to avoid confusion with Alia Bhatt. Her father, Bhagchandani Advani, is a Sindhi businessman, and her mother, Grace Advani, is a Scottish-Indian homemaker. She has a younger brother, Mishaal Advani. Kiara received her early education at Jai Hind College, Mumbai, pursuing a Bachelor of Arts degree, which she completed before fully committing to her acting career. 

Advani’s initial foray into the entertainment world wasn't through acting, but as a modeling assignment in 2010. She assisted photographer Peter Hutton, which provided her with exposure and experience within the industry. This led to her walking the Wills Lifestyle India Fashion Week in 2014. However, she harboured ambitions of becoming an actress and actively pursued that goal.

Her acting debut came in 2014 with *Fugly*, a comedy-drama directed by Kabir Sadanand, produced by Akshay Kumar and Ashvini Yardi. While the film didn't perform exceptionally well at the box office, it provided Advani with a platform. She followed this up with a supporting role in the 2015 sports biopic *M.S. Dhoni: The Untold Story*, directed by Neeraj Pandey. Playing the role of Sakshi Singh Dhoni, wife of the cricketer Mahendra Singh Dhoni, proved to be a turning point in her career. The film was a significant commercial success, grossing over ₹133 crore domestically, and brought Advani widespread recognition.

2017 saw her starring in *Machine*, an action thriller opposite Mustafa Shaikh, though it failed to impress audiences. The same year, she appeared in *Baar Baar Dekho* alongside Sidharth Malhotra and Katrina Kaif, a romantic comedy which garnered moderate attention.  However, 2018 marked a crucial year with *Lust Stories*, a Netflix anthology film. Here, she appeared in the short film "Careless," directed by Karan Johar, receiving praise for her portrayal and the film’s progressive themes. 

Her career trajectory continued upward with *Kabir Singh* in 2019, a romantic drama co-starring Shahid Kapoor.  The film, a remake of the Telugu film *Arjun Reddy*, was a massive box office hit, earning over ₹350 crore and establishing Advani as a leading actress.  She received nominations for Filmfare and IIFA awards for her performance.  

The following years saw a string of successful films. *Good Newwz* (2019), a comedy-drama featuring Akshay Kumar, Kareena Kapoor Khan, and Diljit Dosanjh, further cemented her position. In 2020, she starred in *Guilty*, a Netflix courtroom drama, portraying a college student accused of murder.  *Shershaah* (2021), a biographical war film based on the life of Captain Vikram Batra, saw her opposite Sidharth Malhotra again. Her performance as Dimple Cheema earned her critical acclaim and several award nominations, including a IIFA Award for Best Actress. 

More recent successes include *Bhool Bhulaiyaa 2* (2022), a horror-comedy, which earned over ₹185 crore, and *JugJugg Jeeyo* (2022), a family drama.  She also appeared in *Satyaprem Ki Katha* (2023) alongside Kartik Aaryan. 

Beyond acting, Advani actively engages in endorsements for various brands, including Mamaearth, Nykaa and Forest Essentials. On February 9, 2023, she married Sidharth Malhotra in Rajasthan, in a private ceremony attended by close family and friends.  The wedding received significant media coverage.  Currently, she continues to be a prominent figure in the Indian film industry, with several upcoming projects including *War 2* alongside Hrithik Roshan and *Don 3* with Ranveer Singh, solidifying her status as one of Bollywood’s most sought-after actresses.

title: Roman Šebrle
text:
Roman Šebrle was born on November 23, 1973, in Kladno, Czechoslovakia (now the Czech Republic), to Josef and Eva Šebrle. His father was a former decathlete himself, reaching a national level, and this familial sporting background proved crucial to Roman’s development. Kladno, a city with a strong industrial and sporting heritage, provided a nurturing environment for his early athletic pursuits. Initially, Šebrle showed promise in football, but at age 12, influenced by his father, he switched to athletics, specifically focusing on the multi-event disciplines. He quickly displayed a natural aptitude, excelling in a variety of track and field events.

Šebrle’s early competitive career blossomed under the guidance of coach Josef Horák. He demonstrated rapid improvement throughout his teenage years, becoming the European Junior Champion in decathlon in 1991, held in Thessaloniki, Greece, with a score of 7662 points. This victory marked him as a rising star in the world of multi-event athletics. He continued to progress, representing Czechoslovakia at the 1992 Barcelona Olympics, finishing in 15th place with 7334 points, still a significant achievement for a 19-year-old. 

Following the dissolution of Czechoslovakia in 1993, Šebrle began competing for the newly formed Czech Republic. He continued to refine his skills, steadily improving his scores and gaining experience on the international circuit. In 1994, he secured a silver medal at the European Championships in Helsinki, Finland, scoring 8322 points, narrowly missing out on gold to Robert Zmelik. The 1995 World Championships in Gothenburg, Sweden, saw him finish in fourth place, further solidifying his position among the world’s elite decathletes.

Šebrle’s breakthrough year arrived in 1996. He participated in the Atlanta Olympic Games, finishing second with 8462 points, taking silver behind Frank Busemann of Germany. This result catapulted him to international fame. However, it was the following years that cemented his legendary status. 1999 proved to be his most successful. He won gold at the World Championships in Seville, Spain, setting a new championship record of 8529 points. This performance established him as the world’s leading decathlete.

The peak of his career came at the 2000 Sydney Olympics. Šebrle delivered a phenomenal performance, accumulating 8654 points, a new Olympic record and a personal best. He dominated the competition, winning by a significant margin and securing the gold medal. This victory made him a national hero in the Czech Republic. He continued to compete at a high level, winning the European Championships in Munich in 2002 with 8437 points. 

Injuries began to plague Šebrle in the mid-2000s, hindering his performances. He participated in the 2004 Athens Olympics, but finished 15th, struggling with a hamstring injury. He attempted to regain his form, but further injuries continued to hamper his progress. He officially announced his retirement from competitive athletics in 2007, at the age of 33. 

Following his retirement, Šebrle remained involved in sports. He became a prominent sports commentator, providing expert analysis for Czech Television. He also ventured into business, becoming involved in real estate and other ventures. He married Kateřina Křížová in 2002, and they have two children. He continues to be a highly respected figure in the Czech Republic, frequently appearing at sporting events and inspiring the next generation of athletes. He was inducted into the Czech Sports Hall of Fame in 2010, recognizing his outstanding contributions to Czech sport. Šebrle’s legacy as one of the greatest decathletes of all time remains secure, marked by his Olympic gold, World Championship title, and consistently high level of performance throughout his career.

title: Charles B. McVay III
text:
Charles Bunker McVay III was born on July 30, 1901, in Ashland, Kentucky, to Charles Bunker McVay Jr., a physician, and his wife, Elizabeth “Lizzie” Kinkead. His early life was marked by frequent relocation due to his father’s profession, spending time in Kentucky, Illinois, and finally settling in Coronado, California, in 1915. It was in Coronado that McVay developed a strong affinity for the sea, spending much of his youth swimming, sailing, and generally being drawn to naval life. He enrolled at the United States Naval Academy in Annapolis, Maryland, in 1918, graduating with the class of 1922, ranked 394th out of 457 midshipmen. 

His initial naval assignments involved service aboard the battleship USS Texas (BB-35) where he served as a junior officer, followed by a tour of duty on the destroyer USS William B. Preston (DD-379). He steadily progressed through the ranks, demonstrating a competence for ship handling and a dedication to duty. In 1932, he completed instruction at the Submarine School in New London, Connecticut. He spent the next decade largely assigned to submarine duty, serving on various vessels including USS S-24, USS S-31, and USS Narwhal (SS-169). He rose to become Executive Officer of the submarine USS Shark (SS-267) in 1939.

World War II saw McVay’s career accelerate. He was promoted to Commander in February 1941 and given command of the destroyer USS Maddox (DD-604) in September of that year. While commanding Maddox, he participated in the Battle of Guadalcanal in November 1942, earning a commendation for his skillful maneuvering and aggressive attacks against Japanese warships.  His performance gained the attention of superiors, and in June 1943, he received command of the heavy cruiser USS Indianapolis (CA-35). 

The Indianapolis’s most significant, and tragically remembered, mission under McVay’s command was a top-secret operation in July 1944. The ship was tasked with delivering crucial components of the atomic bomb, specifically enriched uranium, to Tinian Island.  After successfully completing this mission, the Indianapolis was en route to Leyte Gulf for preparations for the invasion of the Philippines when it was torpedoed by the Japanese submarine I-58 on July 30, 1944—McVay’s 43rd birthday. 

The ship sank in just 12 minutes. Of the 1,196 crew members, approximately 900 made it into the water. What followed was a horrific ordeal of exposure, dehydration, starvation, and shark attacks over the next five days before rescue arrived. Only 316 men were saved. 

Following the disaster, McVay was court-martialed in January 1945 on charges of negligence and endangering his vessel. The trial was controversial, largely because survivors testified that the lack of life rafts and the delayed response to distress signals contributed significantly to the high death toll.  He was convicted of negligence in failing to order all hands to abandon ship immediately and was publicly censured. Despite being cleared of willful misconduct, the conviction and public scrutiny deeply affected him. 

Throughout the rest of his naval career, McVay served in various administrative roles. He was reassigned to sea duty in 1947, commanding the heavy cruiser USS Helena (CA-75). He retired from the Navy in 1949 with the rank of Captain.  

In the decades following his retirement, McVay struggled with depression and alcoholism, haunted by the memory of the Indianapolis tragedy. Numerous investigations were undertaken over the years, largely driven by the dedication of survivors and their families, to determine the full circumstances surrounding the sinking and the rescue delay. In 2000, the U.S. Congress formally exonerated McVay, acknowledging that he had been unfairly blamed for the disaster, and that the circumstances were largely a result of failures in the chain of command and a delayed response due to miscommunication and bureaucratic errors. 

Charles B. McVay III died on November 6, 1968, in Pomona, California, from a heart attack. He was 67 years old. He is buried at Arlington National Cemetery. His story remains a poignant example of the complexities of wartime command and the enduring consequences of tragedy.

title: Shakira
text:
## Shakira: A Biography

Shakira Isabel Mebarak Ripoll, known mononymously as Shakira, was born on February 2, 1977, in Barranquilla, Colombia. Her name, meaning “grateful” in Arabic, reflects her Lebanese ancestry through her father, William Mebarak Chadid. Her mother, Nidia del Socorro Ripoll Torrado, is of Spanish, Catalan, and Italian descent. William, a New York native, moved to Colombia as a young man and established a jewelry business. Shakira spent much of her early childhood in her father’s office, fueling her imagination and introducing her to literature. 

Her musical talent became apparent early. She began writing songs at the age of four, and her father brought home a typewriter as a gift, facilitating this creative outlet. By age eight, she was already performing, inspired by English-language rock music and artists like the Beatles and Blondie, despite limited exposure.  She attended La Enseñanza school in Barranquilla, where she was known for her distinctive voice and performed in school choirs.  

Shakira’s professional career began to take shape in the early 1990s.  In 1990, she signed her first record deal with Sony Music Colombia.
