Despite his significant contribution to parliamentary scrutiny and governance, Feroze remained largely outside the inner circle of power, largely due to his independent spirit and willingness to challenge even those within his wife’s family. He was a vocal advocate for socialist policies and a strong critic of corruption.  His relationship with Indira Gandhi, while initially close, became strained as she rose through the ranks of the Congress party and began to assert her own political authority. 

Tragically, Feroze Gandhi died of a heart attack on September 8, 1960, in Delhi, at the relatively young age of 48. His death was a shock to the nation and prompted an outpouring of grief. He left behind a legacy of integrity, courage, and commitment to public service.  While often remembered as Indira Gandhi’s husband, Feroze Gandhi was a parliamentarian of considerable stature and a significant figure in the early years of independent India, remembered for his unwavering commitment to ethical governance and holding power accountable.

title: Profit (gamer)
text:
Justin “Profit” Krüger was born on December 18, 1999, in Mainz, Germany. He grew up in a relatively standard household with a strong interest in video games from a young age, initially gravitating towards real-time strategy games like *StarCraft II* before ultimately finding his competitive niche in fighting games. His early gaming was largely self-taught, honed through online play and local arcade scenes, developing a particular affinity for the *Tekken* series. He didn’t initially pursue competitive play seriously, viewing it more as a hobby until around age 16.

Profit’s serious competitive career began in earnest in 2015, focusing on *Tekken Tag Tournament 2*. He quickly made a name for himself within the European *Tekken* scene, attending regional tournaments and steadily improving his results. His first notable tournament win was at the Tekken European Tour Brussels in 2016, marking him as a player to watch. This victory, alongside consistent top placements at events like Frosty Faustings 9 in 2017, signaled his potential on a larger stage. He was consistently supported and travelled with his father, Klaus Krüger, who became a crucial element of his early competitive journey, managing logistics and providing encouragement.

The release of *Tekken 7* in 2017 proved to be a turning point. Profit quickly adapted to the new game, mastering the character of Dragunov – a character known for its complex movelist and punishing offense. He rapidly ascended through the rankings, consistently demonstrating a unique, aggressive, and highly technical style. He began to regularly compete in major international tournaments, and his results began to reflect his skill. 

2018 was a breakthrough year. He achieved a second-place finish at CEO 2018 in Orlando, Florida, losing to the reigning world champion, Lee "Infiltration" Seon-woo. This performance established Profit as a legitimate contender for the world title. He followed this with a win at the Summer Jam tournament in Dallas, Texas, cementing his position as a top player globally.  His consistent performances earned him sponsorships from Red Bull Gaming and Razer.

Profit reached the pinnacle of his career in 2019, winning the coveted EVO Championship Series in Las Vegas, Nevada.  He defeated a stacked bracket including notable players like Hyuntae “JDCR” Kim and ultimately defeated Arslan Ashid Siddiqui in the grand finals to claim the title.  This win was significant, not only for the prestige it carried but also for being the first major *Tekken* title won by a European player.  His EVO win earned him $24,000 in prize money.

Following his EVO win, Profit continued to compete at a high level, consistently placing in the top eight of major tournaments. He maintained a strong presence in the *Tekken* Pro League, representing Europe and contributing significantly to his team’s success. Throughout 2020 and 2021, competition was impacted by the COVID-19 pandemic, shifting many events to online formats. Profit adapted, maintaining his competitive edge and remaining a dominant force in the online scene.

In 2022, Profit began a gradual transition away from full-time competitive play. He cited burnout and a desire to explore other avenues as contributing factors. He began streaming more regularly on Twitch, building a dedicated community around his gameplay and personality. While he still participates in select tournaments, his focus has shifted towards content creation and community engagement. 

As of late 2023, Profit continues to stream *Tekken 7* and has begun to focus on the newest installment in the series, *Tekken 8*, released in January 2024. He is considered a highly influential figure in the *Tekken* community, respected for his technical skill, innovative playstyle, and contributions to the game's growth. While no longer chasing tournament dominance with the same intensity, he remains a prominent voice and a beloved figure within the fighting game world. He currently resides in Germany and continues to actively engage with his fans and the broader gaming community.

title: Liam Neeson
text:
Liam Neeson, born William John Neeson on June 7, 1952, in Ballymena, County Antrim, Northern Ireland, is an actor renowned for his commanding presence and versatility. His upbringing was Catholic, and he was the third of four children born to Barbara Neeson, a cook, and Bernard Neeson, a school caretaker. Growing up during The Troubles, Neeson witnessed firsthand the sectarian violence that plagued Northern Ireland, an experience which profoundly impacted him. He was a relatively shy child, finding solace and confidence through participation in school plays. He attended St. Malachy's College, a Catholic grammar school in Belfast, where he excelled in sports, particularly boxing, and continued his theatrical pursuits.

Neeson initially intended to study law at Queen's University Belfast, but dropped out after a year, feeling unfulfilled. He worked in a Guinness brewery and as a teacher at a Catholic primary school to earn money before committing fully to acting. He joined the Belfast Lyric Players in 1976, gaining valuable experience in a repertory theatre environment. This led to a pivotal role with the Abbey Theatre in Dublin in 1978, where he performed in numerous productions, honing his craft and gaining recognition within the Irish theatre scene. 

His early film work began with minor roles in British and Irish productions, including *Excalibur* (1981) and *Krull* (1983). He gained wider attention with roles in *The Mission* (1986), where he played Sergeant Major Toby, and *Alfred Hitchcock Presents* (1987) television series. A significant breakthrough came with Neil Jordan’s *The Last of the High Kings* (1989), showcasing his dramatic range. He moved to the United States in 1988, seeking to expand his career opportunities.

The early 1990s saw Neeson taking on diverse roles, including the title character in *Darkman* (1990), a superhero film directed by Sam Raimi, and as Zeus in *Hercules* (1997). However, it was his portrayal of Oskar Schindler in Steven Spielberg’s *Schindler’s List* (1993) that cemented his status as a leading actor. He received an Academy Award nomination for Best Actor for the role, alongside numerous other accolades. This performance demonstrated his ability to convey profound empathy and moral weight. 

Throughout the late 1990s and early 2000s, Neeson continued to take on a variety of challenging roles, appearing in films such as *Michael Collins* (1996), *Les Misérables* (2000), and *Kinsey* (2004). He explored both dramatic and comedic territory, displaying a breadth of talent.  

A remarkable career resurgence came in 2008 with the release of *Taken*, an action thriller that redefined his public image. The film’s commercial success spawned two sequels (*Taken 2* in 2012 and *Taken 3* in 2014), establishing Neeson as an action star in his 50s and 60s. He subsequently starred in a string of successful action films, including *The Grey* (2011), *Non-Stop* (2014), and *Run All Night* (2015).

Beyond action, Neeson has continued to pursue diverse projects, appearing in dramas like *Silence* (2016) directed by Martin Scorsese, and comedies such as *Love Actually* (2003). He returned to the stage, starring in revivals of Arthur Miller’s *The Crucible* on Broadway in 2016. 

Tragically, Neeson experienced a profound personal loss with the sudden death of his wife, actress Natasha Richardson, in 2009 following a skiing accident. They had married in 1994 and had two sons, Michael and Daniel.  Neeson has since become a vocal advocate for organ donation.  

As of late 2023, Liam Neeson remains an active and highly respected actor, continuing to choose roles that challenge and engage him. He has appeared in over 100 films and numerous theatrical productions, consistently demonstrating his commitment to his craft and his ability to connect with audiences worldwide. He was awarded a CBE (Commander of the Order of the British Empire) in 1999 for his services to drama.

title: D. B. Nihalsinghe
text:
David Bibile Nihalsinghe, commonly known as D. B. Nihalsinghe, was a pivotal figure in the development of Sinhala cinema and a significant intellectual in post-independence Sri Lanka. He was born on June 29, 1910, in Chilaw, a coastal town in the Puttalam District, to Don Bastian Nihalsinghe and Rosalin Perera. His father was a schoolteacher and his mother, a homemaker. Nihalsinghe received his early education at St. Mary’s College, Chilaw, and later attended St. Joseph’s College, Colombo, where he excelled in studies and developed a keen interest in literature and the arts. 

He continued his education at the University of London, earning a Bachelor of Arts degree in English Literature in 1932. Returning to Ceylon (as Sri Lanka was then known), he initially pursued a career in education, teaching English Literature at Prince of Wales' College, Moratuwa, and later at Royal College, Colombo, from 1936 to 1947. It was during his time at Royal College that his passion for cinema began to truly blossom, recognizing its potential as a powerful medium for cultural expression. 

Nihalsinghe’s formal entry into the film industry was in 1947, when he joined South Indian film producer S. M. Nayagam's production, *Ashoka*. He served initially as a dialogue writer and then as an assistant director, gaining practical experience in the technical aspects of filmmaking. This experience led him to co-found his own film production company, Sinhala Cinema Limited, with the intention of creating films distinctly rooted in Sri Lankan culture and narrative. 

His directorial debut came in 1954 with *Prema Thiyaa Pawura* (Love’s Gentle Breeze), a film that is considered a landmark in the history of Sinhala cinema. It wasn't merely a romantic story, but consciously employed techniques of cinematic storytelling previously unseen in the region, moving away from the heavily melodramatic and stage-bound productions prevalent at the time. He followed this with *SuDu Seelaya* (The White Rider) in 1955, a film adapted from a short story by Martin Wickramasinghe. *SuDu Seelaya* is widely regarded as his masterpiece and is considered the first truly artistic Sinhala film. It explored themes of social injustice and the clash between traditional rural life and modern influences, and won the prestigious ‘Diploma of Merit’ at the 1955 Cannes Film Festival – the first Sri Lankan film to receive international recognition. 

Nihalsinghe’s subsequent films included *Hanthane Kathawa* (The Tale of Hanthana) in 1958, another adaptation of a Wickramasinghe novel, exploring the complexities of post-colonial identity and societal expectations. He directed a total of 12 feature films, each marked by his meticulous attention to detail, realistic portrayals of characters, and a sophisticated use of cinematic techniques. He consciously avoided excessive melodrama, opting instead for nuanced performances and a focus on psychological realism.

Beyond filmmaking, Nihalsinghe was a prolific writer and intellectual. He authored several books, including *Sinhala Cinema: A Study* (1967), a critical analysis of the development of Sinhala film, and translated numerous works of English literature into Sinhala. He also served as the Director of the Government Film Unit from 1962 to 1964, contributing to the production of documentaries and educational films. 

In his later life, Nihalsinghe became increasingly disillusioned with the commercialization of Sinhala cinema and the decline in artistic standards. He largely withdrew from active filmmaking in the 1970s, dedicating his time to writing and lecturing. He was awarded the Presidential Award for Lifetime Achievement in 1994 in recognition of his immense contribution to Sri Lankan cinema. D. B. Nihalsinghe passed away on April 20, 1987, in Colombo, leaving behind a legacy as a visionary filmmaker and a cultural icon who fundamentally shaped the landscape of Sinhala cinema. His films continue to be studied and celebrated for their artistic merit and their enduring relevance.

title: Takuma Asano
text:
Takuma Asano was born on November 10, 1994, in Mitake, Kumamoto Prefecture, Japan. His father, Tadashi Asano, was a former professional footballer himself, playing as a defender for several J.League clubs, instilling in young Takuma a passion for the sport.  Asano began playing football seriously during his elementary school years, joining the local youth club, Minami Kumamoto FC. He displayed precocious talent, notable for his blistering pace and determined attacking style. His dedication led him to be scouted by Hiroshima-based high school powerhouse, Kokuryo High School, where he enrolled in 2013.

At Kokuryo, Asano quickly established himself as a key player, primarily as a winger. He led the school to national prominence, reaching the final of the All Japan High School Soccer Tournament in his final year, 2013, though they ultimately lost to Gunma United. This performance significantly raised his profile and drew attention from professional clubs.  He was recognized as one of the nation’s brightest young prospects, and his speed became a defining characteristic, earning him the nickname “The Gazelle of Kumamoto.” 

In July 2013, before even graduating high school, Asano signed a professional contract with Sanfrecce Hiroshima in the J1 League.  He officially joined the club in January 2014, wearing the number 29 shirt. Initially, he spent much of his first season as a substitute, making 7 league appearances and scoring 1 goal. However, he gradually integrated into the first team, showcasing his explosive speed and dribbling skills.  The 2015 season proved to be his breakthrough year. He played 36 league games, netting 8 goals, and became a crucial component of Hiroshima’s attack.  His performances helped Sanfrecce Hiroshima win the J1 League title that year, marking the first league championship of his career. 

Asano’s growing reputation attracted interest from European clubs. In July 2016, he signed a contract with Arsenal in the English Premier League, becoming the first Japanese player to join the club directly from a J.League team. However, work permit issues initially delayed his arrival, and he officially joined Arsenal on August 18, 2016.  His time at Arsenal was largely frustrating. He made a total of 18 appearances across all competitions, but only 11 were in the Premier League, and he scored just once – a memorable goal against Ludogorets in the Champions League group stage on November 1, 2016.

Seeking more regular playing time, Asano was loaned to VfB Stuttgart in Germany's Bundesliga on August 30, 2017, for the 2017-2018 season.  The move proved to be beneficial, and he became a regular starter, scoring 7 goals in 27 Bundesliga appearances.  Stuttgart then exercised their option to sign him permanently in January 2018, securing his services on a contract until June 2021. He continued to be a valuable player for Stuttgart, adding another 9 Bundesliga goals over the next two seasons. 

In August 2020, Asano moved to Partizan Belgrade in the Serbian SuperLiga, signing a two-year contract. He made a significant impact in Serbia, scoring 16 league goals in 30 appearances during the 2020-2021 season, helping Partizan win the Serbian Cup.  He continued to play well in the following season, scoring 8 league goals in 25 games.

In July 2022, Asano returned to the J1 League, signing with Vissel Kobe. He quickly became a key player for Kobe, contributing significantly to their attacking force. In the 2023 season, Asano had a stellar year, scoring 13 goals in 33 league matches and earning a place in the J1 League Best XI. Vissel Kobe also won the 2023 Emperor’s Cup with Asano playing a pivotal role.

Internationally, Asano has represented Japan at various youth levels. He earned his first senior national team cap on November 14, 2014, in a friendly match against Venezuela. He has been a consistent member of the national team squad, participating in the 2018 FIFA World Cup and the 2022 FIFA World Cup in Qatar, where he scored a crucial goal against Spain, helping Japan secure a stunning victory and progress from the group stage. As of November 2023, he has earned over 50 caps for Japan.

title: Joji (musician)
text:
George Kusunoki Miller, known professionally as Joji, was born on September 18, 1992, in Osaka, Japan. His father was an American father of Japanese and Native American descent, and his mother was Japanese. His early childhood was transient; he moved to Macao with his family at the age of two, and subsequently to Melbourne, Australia, when he was eleven in 2003. He attended high school at St Kevin’s College, a Catholic all-boys school in Toorak, Melbourne, graduating in 2012. It was during this period he began experimenting with music production, initially through GarageBand on his computer. He credits his early musical influences as being primarily R&B artists like Frank Ocean and also Japanese city pop.

Before rising to prominence as a solo artist, Miller gained initial recognition online primarily through comedic videos on YouTube under the alias Filthy Frank and his associated channel TVFilthyFrank, beginning around 2011.  These videos were characterized by surreal, often offensive, and deliberately low-budget humor, developing a dedicated, albeit controversial, cult following.  A core component of this online persona was the character Pink Guy, a hyper-masculine, pink-clad alter ego that rapidly became a meme.  Alongside this comedy work, he began uploading music to SoundCloud under the name Pink Season in 2015, offering a stark contrast to his comedic online persona. These early tracks, often lo-fi and melancholic, hinted at the musical direction he would later fully embrace.

In December 2017, Miller abruptly announced the retirement of both the Filthy Frank and Pink Guy characters, citing mental health concerns and the overwhelming nature of the online persona. He explained the performative aspect of the character had become detrimental to his well-being. This decision, though initially shocking to his fanbase, paved the way for him to focus solely on his music.

He officially adopted the stage name Joji and released his debut single, “Winter Strikes,” in March 2018. The song quickly gained traction, amassing over a million plays on Spotify within a month. He followed this with the EP *XXXtentacion* (not affiliated with the rapper of the same name) in September 2018, which further solidified his sound – a blend of lo-fi hip hop, R&B, and ambient electronic music, often characterized by themes of loneliness, heartbreak, and existentialism. The EP peaked at number 31 on the Billboard 200 chart.

Joji's breakthrough came with the single “Slow Dancing in the Dark,” released in October 2018.  The song went viral, driven largely by its emotional resonance and relatable lyrics, and was certified Platinum by the RIAA in December 2020.  He released his debut studio album, *Ballads 1*, in October 2018, which reached number 3 on the Billboard 200 and received generally positive reviews. The album showcased a refined, more polished version of the sound established in his earlier work. 

In 2020, Joji released his second studio album, *Nectar*, in September.  The album featured collaborations with artists like Diplo, Yves V, and Omar Apollo. *Nectar* debuted at number 3 on the Billboard 200, becoming his highest-charting album to date. He supported the album with a planned world tour in 2021, which was significantly affected by the COVID-19 pandemic.

His third studio album, *Smithereens*, was released in October 2022.  It marked a slight shift in sound, incorporating more experimental and darker elements. While not reaching the commercial heights of *Nectar*, it was critically well-received and demonstrated his continued artistic exploration.  

As of late 2023, Joji continues to release music and perform live. He has earned multiple Platinum certifications for his singles and albums.  He maintains a relatively private personal life, rarely granting interviews and largely letting his music speak for itself.  He is currently signed to 88rising, an Asian-American music collective, and remains a significant figure in the contemporary alternative R&B and lo-fi music scenes, with over 14 million monthly listeners on Spotify as of November 2023.

title: Lemuel W. Joiner
text:
Lemuel W. Joiner, born on December 27, 1903, in Richmond, Virginia, was a pivotal figure in the development of modern accounting practices, particularly within the United States federal government. His career spanned over four decades, marked by a commitment to professionalizing government accounting and establishing standardized auditing procedures. Joiner’s early life was relatively modest; he was the son of William and Lucy Joiner, and his father worked as a carpenter. He received his early education in Richmond public schools, graduating from Armstrong High School in 1921. 

He then attended Virginia State College (now Virginia State University), earning a Bachelor of Science degree in Accounting in 1925. This was a significant achievement for an African American man at the time, as educational and professional opportunities were severely limited by racial segregation. Immediately following graduation, Joiner began his government career with the United States Treasury Department in Washington, D.C., as a junior accountant in the Bureau of Internal Revenue, later to become the Internal Revenue Service. 

Joiner quickly distinguished himself through his meticulous work and intellectual curiosity. He passed the Certified Public Accountant (CPA) exam in Virginia in 1932, becoming one of the first African Americans to achieve this credential in the state. His early years at the Treasury focused on auditing and examining the financial records of national banks. Recognizing the inconsistencies and lack of uniformity in government auditing practices, Joiner became a vocal advocate for standardization. 

In 1936, he transferred to the General Accounting Office (GAO), the investigative arm of Congress, where he spent the majority of his career. Within the GAO, he rose steadily through the ranks. He served as a principal assistant examiner, then assistant chief of the budget and accounting branch, and finally, in 1956, he was appointed Chief Accountant of the General Accounting Office, a position he held until his retirement in 1970. This appointment was groundbreaking; Joiner was the first African American to head a major accounting function within the federal government.

As Chief Accountant, Joiner spearheaded numerous initiatives to modernize and improve government financial management. He was instrumental in developing the “Standards for Internal Control in the Federal Government,” often referred to as the “Green Book,” first published in 1974, though its conceptual groundwork was laid during his tenure. This publication provided a framework for federal agencies to establish and maintain effective internal controls, significantly enhancing accountability and reducing fraud. He also played a crucial role in the development of the Government Auditing Standards, providing a comprehensive guide for auditors inspecting federal programs. 

Joiner was a strong proponent of professional development for government accountants. He actively encouraged GAO staff to pursue professional certifications, like the CPA, and he fostered a culture of continuous learning within the agency. He lectured extensively at universities and professional conferences, sharing his expertise and advocating for improved accounting practices. He served on numerous committees and boards related to accounting and auditing, including the Federal Accounting Standards Advisory Board. 

Throughout his career, Joiner faced systemic racism and discrimination, but he consistently overcame these obstacles through his dedication, competence, and integrity. He became a mentor to many young accountants, particularly African Americans, encouraging them to pursue careers in the field. He received numerous awards and accolades for his contributions, including honorary degrees from Virginia State College in 1965 and Howard University in 1969. 

Following his retirement from the GAO in 1970, Joiner remained active in professional circles, continuing to consult and advise on accounting matters. He passed away on January 26, 1984, in Washington, D.C., at the age of 80, leaving behind a legacy of professional excellence and a lasting impact on the field of government accounting. His contributions remain foundational to the financial oversight of the U.S. federal government.

title: Neha Sargam
text:
Neha Sargam was born on December 24, 1988, in Bhubaneswar, Odisha, India, to a musically inclined family. Her father, Dr. Anil Prakash, is a doctor and her mother, Vandana Prakash, is a trained classical singer and a devotee of Rabindranath Tagore’s music, significantly influencing Neha’s early exposure to the arts.  Neha’s grandfather, the late Bansidhar Bhagat, was a renowned tabla player, further solidifying the musical heritage within the family. She spent her formative years in Rourkela, also in Odisha, where she received her primary and secondary education at Carmel School.

Neha began her formal musical training at the age of six, learning Hindustani classical music under the guidance of Pandit Babban Prasad Sharma for eight years.  Alongside classical training, she also received rigorous instruction in Rabindra Sangeet – songs written and set to tune by Rabindranath Tagore – from her mother.  This dual focus would become a defining element of her musical identity.  She actively participated in numerous inter-school and state-level competitions, consistently winning accolades. A significant early achievement was winning the All India Radio competition in 1999 at the age of eleven, a national-level recognition that boosted her confidence and visibility. 

In 2005, at the age of seventeen, Neha moved to Delhi to pursue a Bachelor of Arts degree from Indraprastha College for Women, affiliated with the University of Delhi.  She continued her musical training during her college years, expanding her repertoire and performing at various cultural events within the university circuit. However, her breakthrough moment arrived in 2009 when she auditioned for and was selected as a contestant on the reality television singing competition, *Sa Re Ga Ma Pa Li'l Champs* on Zee TV. 

Although she didn’t win the competition, finishing as a finalist, *Sa Re Ga Ma Pa Li’l Champs* provided her with a national platform.  She impressed the judges – including prominent musicians like Bappi Lahiri, Sadhana Sargam (her namesake, though no relation), and Pritam – with her versatile vocal abilities and particularly her renditions of Rabindra Sangeet, which she introduced to a wider Indian audience.  The show concluded in December 2009. 

Following her appearance on *Li’l Champs*, Neha focused on building a career as a playback singer and independent artist. In 2011, she released her debut album, *Acchha Yakeen*, which featured a blend of Hindi and Bengali songs, heavily influenced by Rabindra Sangeet.  The album garnered positive reviews, especially for its unique musical arrangements and Neha’s emotive vocal delivery.  

Her work as a playback singer began to gain momentum in 2013 with the song "Banjaa Rang" for the film *Chha-e Chha*.  She subsequently lent her voice to several other Bollywood projects, including songs for *Barkhaa* (2015) and *Yeh Jawaani Hai Deewani* (2013), though her work in this area remained relatively modest compared to some of her contemporaries. 

Neha’s passion for Rabindra Sangeet remained central to her work.  She has performed extensively in concerts dedicated to Tagore’s music, both in India and internationally. She has toured the United States, the United Kingdom, and several countries in Southeast Asia, presenting her unique interpretations of Tagore’s songs. In 2018, she released a critically acclaimed album dedicated solely to Rabindra Sangeet titled *Ektu Chowa Lage* (A Gentle Touch). 

In more recent years, Neha has become increasingly involved in music education, conducting workshops and mentoring aspiring singers. She has also begun experimenting with fusion music, blending classical and contemporary elements in her compositions.  As of late 2023, Neha continues to perform regularly and is working on new musical projects, remaining a dedicated exponent of both Hindustani classical music and the timeless legacy of Rabindranath Tagore. She is currently based in Mumbai, India, and actively manages her career through independent platforms and collaborations.

title: Rory Byrne
text:
Rory Byrne, born on February 22, 1959, in Cape Town, South Africa, is a highly respected and influential Formula One car designer, renowned for his pivotal role in the championship-winning success of Benetton and Ferrari during the 1990s and 2000s. His early life offered little indication of the path he would take. He wasn’t initially drawn to motorsport, but possessed a strong aptitude for mathematics and physics, graduating with a degree in Mechanical Engineering from the University of Stellenbosch in 1981. This foundation proved crucial to his future career.

Byrne’s entry into motorsport was somewhat accidental. Following graduation, he initially worked as a structural engineer, but a friend’s involvement in Formula Ford sparked an interest. He began designing and building Formula Ford cars in his spare time, honing his skills and demonstrating a natural talent for aerodynamic understanding. This led to an opportunity in 1986 with Toleman Motorsport, a small Formula One team based in Witney, Oxfordshire, England. He joined as a designer, quickly becoming involved in the development of their TG186 and TG187 chassis. 

In 1989, Byrne made a significant move to Benetton Formula One, joining under the leadership of John Barnard. Barnard, a legendary designer himself, recognised Byrne’s potential, and the pair worked closely together. The following year, 1990, proved to be a breakthrough. Benetton, with Michael Schumacher at the wheel, began a period of dominance. Byrne was instrumental in the design of the B190 and subsequent B191, cars that benefited from a semi-automatic transmission and innovative aerodynamic features. Schumacher secured his first World Championship in 1994 driving the B194, a car largely attributed to Byrne’s design philosophy, focusing on maximizing downforce and mechanical grip.  Benetton also clinched the Constructors' Championship that year. Byrne’s designs continued to be successful, contributing to Schumacher’s championship win in 1995 with the B195.

In 1996, Byrne made the defining move of his career, joining Scuderia Ferrari, the most iconic team in Formula One.  Initially, the task was immense; Ferrari hadn't won a Drivers' Championship since 1979, and the team was struggling.  He was appointed Chief Designer and given a broad remit to rebuild the team's technical foundation. Working alongside Ross Brawn, the then-Technical Director, and with Schumacher joining the team in 1996, Byrne oversaw a complete overhaul of the car’s design. 

The fruits of their labour became apparent in 1999, when Ferrari came close to winning both championships, ultimately losing the Drivers' Championship by a single point. The F399, the car of that season, laid the groundwork for the unprecedented success that followed.  From 2000 to 2004, Ferrari entered a period of complete dominance. Schumacher won five consecutive World Championships (2000, 2001, 2002, 2003, and 2004), and Ferrari secured six consecutive Constructors' Championships (1999-2004). Cars like the F1-2000, F2001, F2002, F2003-GA, and F2004, all bore Byrne’s signature – characterized by exceptional aerodynamic efficiency, powerful engines, and a focus on reliability.  He was promoted to Technical Director in 2006, but the team’s performance began to decline as rivals caught up. 

Byrne officially retired from Ferrari at the end of the 2006 season, though he remained with the team as a consultant until 2009.  During his time at Ferrari, the team won 15 Grand Prix races and 164 podium finishes.  He briefly worked with the A1GP series, assisting the South African team, before largely retreating from the public eye.  

Rory Byrne is known for his understated personality and meticulous attention to detail. He is not a flamboyant figure, preferring to let his designs speak for themselves. He’s often described as a “fundamentals” engineer, focusing on core aerodynamic principles and a strong chassis.  He is widely regarded as one of the most successful Formula One designers of all time, his legacy cemented by the record-breaking achievements of Benetton and Ferrari in the late 1990s and early 2000s. He resides in the UK and maintains a private life, rarely granting interviews or making public appearances.

title: Kion Smith
text:
Kion Smith, born on March 23, 1988, in Miami, Florida, was an American professional basketball player whose career, though relatively short-lived at the highest levels, was marked by impressive athleticism and a compelling personal story of overcoming significant adversity. He was the son of former NBA player and coach Kevin Smith and the brother of professional soccer player Klayton Smith. His early life was deeply intertwined with basketball, growing up around the game through his father’s career. Kevin Smith played for several NBA teams including the Miami Heat, Sacramento Kings, and Orlando Magic during the 1980s and 90s, and later coached in the NBA Development League. 

Kion Smith’s high school career took place at American Heritage High School in Plantation, Florida, where he quickly established himself as a standout player. He led the Patriots to a Florida Class 2A State Championship in 2006, averaging 23.4 points, 8.2 rebounds, and 3.1 assists per game during his senior year. He was named the 2006 Florida Class 2A Player of the Year and a McDonald's All-American, solidifying his status as a highly sought-after recruit. He finished his high school career with 1,803 points, a school record at the time.

He committed to the University of Florida, joining the Gators basketball program under coach Billy Donovan. Smith played for the Gators from 2006 to 2010. While he showed flashes of brilliance, his college career was hampered by a series of knee injuries. He suffered a torn anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) in his left knee during a practice in November 2007, causing him to miss the entire 2007-2008 season. He would later injure the same knee again, requiring further rehabilitation. Despite these setbacks, Smith managed to contribute significantly when healthy, showcasing his scoring ability and defensive prowess.  He finished his college career with 721 points over 88 games, averaging 8.2 points per game. 

Despite the injury concerns, Kion Smith was drafted by the Fort Wayne Mad Ants of the NBA Development League (now the NBA G League) in 2010. He had a brief stint with the Mad Ants before being called up to the NBA by the Cleveland Cavaliers on February 24, 2011, signing a 10-day contract. He played in three games for the Cavaliers, scoring a total of 9 points and grabbing 2 rebounds. Following the expiration of his contract, he was released by the Cavaliers.

He continued to bounce between the NBA G League and short stints with international teams. He played for the Iowa Energy (now the Iowa Wolves) in the 2011-2012 season, averaging 12.7 points per game in 34 appearances. He then spent time playing professionally in Turkey with Mersin Büyükşehir Belediyesi Spor Kulübü in 2012-2013, and later in South Korea with the Jeonju KCC Egis in the 2013-2014 season. Throughout these international experiences, he demonstrated his scoring abilities, often being a key offensive contributor for his teams.

However, the persistent knee injuries continued to plague his career, limiting his opportunities and impacting his performance. He attempted several comebacks, joining training camps with NBA teams, but was ultimately unable to secure another sustained position in the league.  

Kion Smith’s later life saw him transition away from professional basketball. Details regarding his post-basketball career have been kept relatively private. As of late 2023, he is involved in mentoring young basketball players, drawing on his experiences to guide them through the challenges of the sport. He resides in Florida and occasionally participates in basketball-related events. While his NBA career was brief, Kion Smith remains a respected figure in Florida basketball circles, remembered for his high school success, his resilience in the face of adversity, and his dedication to the game.

title: Shigeru Fukudome
text:
Shigeru Fukudome was born on December 22, 1933, in Nagoya, Aichi Prefecture, Japan, into a family with a strong artistic inclination. His father was a calligrapher, and this early exposure profoundly influenced his aesthetic sensibilities. Fukudome’s childhood coincided with the tumultuous years leading up to and during World War II, experiences that subtly shaped his later artistic concerns with fragility and impermanence. He attended Aichi Prefectural Arts and Crafts School, graduating in 1952, where he initially focused on traditional Japanese painting. However, a pivotal encounter with the work of Lucio Fontana, an Argentinian-Italian artist known for his slashed and punctured canvases, during a 1956 exhibition in Tokyo, radically altered his artistic trajectory. Fontana’s exploration of spatial concepts resonated deeply with Fukudome, prompting him to move away from traditional painting and towards three-dimensional work.

Fukudome formally began his career as a sculptor in 1958. He quickly distinguished himself by pioneering a unique approach to sculpture that challenged conventional notions of form and materiality. Rather than adding material to create a sculpture, Fukudome focused on *removing* it, creating works defined by negative space and delicate structures. He primarily worked with plaster, a material he favored for its inherent fragility and its ability to capture subtle textures. His early works, appearing in the late 1950s and early 1960s, were characterized by thin, plaster walls, often intricately patterned with holes and fissures. These pieces weren't simply solid forms with voids; they were, essentially, the voids themselves given form by the remaining plaster.

A key moment in his recognition came in 1964 when he participated in the Tokyo International Color School exhibition. This exposure broadened his audience and established him as a leading figure in the emerging Japanese avant-garde.  He began exhibiting internationally throughout the 1960s, including shows in Paris, Germany, and the United States.  In 1967, he represented Japan at the São Paulo Bienal, a significant platform for international contemporary art.  This period saw the development of his signature “Work” series, which continued and refined his exploration of negative space and the inherent qualities of plaster. These weren’t sculptures intended to be ‘looked at’ in the traditional sense; they were designed to be experienced spatially, with the viewer’s movement around the work altering their perception of its form. 

Throughout the 1970s and 80s, Fukudome’s work became increasingly architectural in scale. He began creating large-scale installations, often site-specific, that transformed entire spaces.  A notable example is his work for the 1978 Paris Biennale, where he created a labyrinthine structure of delicate plaster walls that invited viewers to physically navigate the artwork.  He also held a solo exhibition at the Guggenheim Museum in New York in 1985, further solidifying his international reputation.  He received numerous awards throughout his career, including the Minister of Education's Art Encouragement Prize in 1978 and the Japan Art Academy Prize in 1995.

Fukudome's artistic philosophy was deeply rooted in Zen Buddhism, emphasizing concepts of emptiness, impermanence ( *mujō*), and the beauty of imperfection (*wabi-sabi*).  He saw his work as a meditation on these themes, creating structures that were both physically fragile and conceptually profound. He deliberately avoided applying paint or other surface treatments to his plaster, allowing the raw material to speak for itself, revealing its inherent texture and vulnerability.

Shigeru Fukudome continued to work and exhibit until his death on March 2, 2009, in Tokyo, at the age of 75.  His influence on contemporary sculpture is considerable, particularly in the realm of installation art and minimalist abstraction. He left behind a legacy of work that challenges conventional artistic boundaries and invites viewers to contemplate the nature of space, form, and perception.  His works are held in major museum collections worldwide, including the Museum of Modern Art in New York, the Centre Pompidou in Paris, and the National Museum of Modern Art, Tokyo.

title: Vladimir Lenin
text:
Vladimir Ilyich Ulyanov, later known as Vladimir Lenin, was born on April 22, 1870, in Simbirsk, Russia (now Ulyanovsk). His father, Ilya Nikolayevich Ulyanov, was a school inspector, and his mother, Maria Alexandrovna Blank, was a teacher. The family, though not wealthy, belonged to the educated middle class and enjoyed a comfortable upbringing. Vladimir was the third of six children. A pivotal moment in his childhood occurred on January 21, 1886, when his father died unexpectedly, profoundly impacting young Vladimir and contributing to a growing sense of resentment towards the autocratic Tsarist regime.

He attended the Simbirsk Classical Gymnasium, showing academic aptitude but also attracting the attention of authorities due to his father’s past political activities. Following his father’s death, the family faced financial hardship. In 1887, his older brother, Aleksandr, was arrested and executed for involvement in a plot to assassinate Tsar Alexander III – a tragedy that further radicalized Vladimir. He was subsequently denied access to higher education and completed his schooling privately, passing his exams in 1888. 

In 1891, Lenin moved to Kazan and briefly attended Kazan University but was expelled in December of that year for participating in a student protest. He continued his self-education, focusing on Marxist theory. In 1893, he moved to St. Petersburg and became involved in Marxist study circles. In 1895, he travelled to Western Europe, particularly Germany and Switzerland, spending time in Berlin, Paris, and London. During this period he met prominent Marxists like Wilhelm Liebknecht and Georg Plekhanov. 

He formally adopted the pseudonym “Lenin” in 1895. In 1898, he participated in the First Congress of the Russian Social Democratic Labour Party (RSDLP) in Minsk, which formally established the party. However, the RSDLP soon fractured into two factions: the Bolsheviks (“majority”), advocating for a disciplined revolutionary party, and the Mensheviks (“minority”), favouring a broader, more inclusive approach. Lenin became a leading figure of the Bolsheviks. 

From 1900 to 1917, Lenin lived primarily in exile, moving between Germany, Switzerland, and France to evade Tsarist authorities. He wrote extensively during this time, including “What Is to Be Done?” (1902), outlining his vision for a vanguard party of professional revolutionaries. He actively participated in the 1905 Russian Revolution, returning briefly to Russia, but the uprising was ultimately suppressed. Following the failed revolution, he again went into exile. 

The February Revolution of 1917, which overthrew Tsar Nicholas II, provided Lenin with an opportunity to return to Russia, facilitated by the German government who hoped he would destabilize the country. He arrived in Petrograd (St. Petersburg) in April 1917 and issued his “April Theses,” calling for an immediate socialist revolution, “All power to the Soviets,” and withdrawal from World War I. 

In October 1917 (November according to the Gregorian calendar), Lenin led the Bolsheviks in a successful armed insurrection, overthrowing the Provisional Government and establishing a socialist state. He became the Chairman of the Council of People's Commissars, effectively the head of government of the Russian Soviet Federative Socialist Republic.  The subsequent Russian Civil War (1917-1922) saw the Bolsheviks, or “Reds,” fight against a variety of opponents, known as the “Whites”. Lenin implemented “War Communism”, a policy of nationalization and forced grain requisitioning, to support the Red Army. 

In 1922, the USSR (Union of Soviet Socialist Republics) was formally established. Lenin, however, suffered a series of strokes beginning in May 1922. His health deteriorated rapidly.  He retired from active politics and appointed Joseph Stalin to the position of General Secretary of the Communist Party, a decision that would later have profound consequences.  Vladimir Lenin died on January 21, 1924, in Gorki, near Moscow, at the age of 53. His body was embalmed and placed in a mausoleum in Red Square, Moscow, where it remains to this day.

title: Jonathan Roy
text:
Jonathan Roy was born on January 29, 1967, in Montreal, Quebec, Canada, to parents Jean-Guy Roy, a musician and composer, and Lorraine Dénommé, a visual artist. He was immersed in a creative environment from a young age, growing up in a household where music was central. His father, a jazz pianist and arranger, exposed him to a wide range of musical genres including jazz, classical, and pop. Roy began learning piano at the age of five, quickly demonstrating a natural aptitude for the instrument. He continued his musical education at the Conservatoire de musique du Québec à Montréal, studying classical piano and composition. However, his interests soon broadened to include contemporary music and particularly, the burgeoning world of electronic music. 

Roy’s professional career began in the early 1990s, initially as a session musician and arranger. He worked with numerous Quebecois artists, honing his skills in production and arrangement. A pivotal moment arrived in 1996 when he began a long and fruitful collaboration with the iconic Quebec singer-songwriter, Céline Dion. He served as her musical director for over two decades, a role that would define much of his career. This began with the *Falling into You* tour in 1996-1997, a massive undertaking that played to over 1.6 million people across 85 shows. 

As musical director, Roy was responsible for overseeing all aspects of Dion’s live performances, including vocal arrangements, instrumentation, and the overall sonic landscape of her concerts. He was instrumental in translating her studio recordings into dynamic and engaging live experiences. He spearheaded the arrangements for numerous albums, including *Let's Talk About Love* (1997), *A New Day Has Come* (2002), and *Taking Chances* (2007).  His arrangements often incorporated orchestral elements alongside contemporary pop production, becoming a hallmark of Dion's sound.

Beyond his work with Dion, Roy has also collaborated with a diverse roster of artists. He produced and arranged for artists such as Garou, Patrick Fiori, and Isabelle Boulay, all prominent figures in the French-speaking music scene. He also contributed to the soundtrack of the 2003 film *Le Baron*.  In 2008, Roy released his first solo album, *Éphémère*, a collection of instrumental piano compositions showcasing his classical training and compositional abilities. The album received positive reviews and demonstrated his versatility beyond his work as an arranger and producer.

Roy’s contributions to music have been recognized with numerous awards and nominations. He has won multiple Félix Awards, the Quebec equivalent of the Juno Awards, including awards for Arranger of the Year. He has also received several nominations for Juno Awards, Canada’s national music awards, in categories relating to production and arrangement. In 2016, he received a lifetime achievement award from the Quebec Association des professionnels de l'industrie musicale (APIM). 

Throughout his career, Roy maintained a relatively private personal life. He is married and has two children.  He continued to work closely with Céline Dion until her health challenges began in 2022, when she announced she was suffering from Stiff-Person Syndrome. He was deeply involved in the planning for her planned 2023-2024 Courage World Tour, which was ultimately postponed due to her condition. 

As of late 2023, Jonathan Roy remains an active figure in the music industry, continuing to work on various production and arrangement projects while also focusing on his own solo work. He consistently emphasizes the importance of musical education and mentorship, frequently participating in workshops and masterclasses for aspiring musicians, carrying on the legacy of his father. He resides in Montreal with his family.

title: Stephen J. Mackwell
text:
Stephen Joseph Mackwell was born on October 27, 1928, in Hartford, Connecticut, the son of Joseph and Helen Mackwell. His father was a physician, and his mother a homemaker. He grew up in a relatively privileged environment, attending the prestigious Loomis School in Windsor, Connecticut, graduating in 1946. This preparatory education laid the groundwork for his subsequent academic pursuits. He then enrolled at Yale University, earning a Bachelor of Arts degree in English in 1950. It was at Yale he began to demonstrate an aptitude for finance, though his initial degree was in the humanities. Following graduation, Mackwell served in the United States Navy during the Korean War, reaching the rank of Lieutenant and fulfilling his service obligation between 1951 and 1953. 

Upon completing his military service, Mackwell pivoted fully towards a career in finance. He joined the investment banking firm of Dominick & Dickerman in 1954, beginning as a trainee and quickly ascending through the ranks. He spent twelve years with the firm, gaining significant experience in corporate finance, mergers and acquisitions, and international transactions. In 1966, he left Dominick & Dickerman and co-founded the investment banking boutique, Lazard Frères & Co. (US) with André Lazard and Felix Rohatyn. This proved to be a pivotal moment in his career.

At Lazard Frères, Mackwell quickly became a key player, specializing in restructuring troubled companies. He possessed a reputation for being a pragmatic and unflinching negotiator, a quality that proved invaluable in navigating complex financial situations. The firm, under his and his partners’ guidance, became a leading advisor in corporate restructurings throughout the 1970s and 1980s. Mackwell’s expertise was particularly sought after during the period of significant corporate raiding and leveraged buyouts. He was instrumental in the restructuring of companies like International Harvester (later Navistar International) in 1980, a particularly challenging case that involved negotiating with both labor unions and creditors to avoid bankruptcy. He also played a critical role in the 1984 restructuring of Revlon, a landmark case in the history of junk bond financing. 

Beyond these specific cases, Mackwell advised on numerous other high-profile restructurings, including those of Pan American World Airways, Montgomery Ward, and Chrysler Corporation, the latter in 1979-1980, securing a federal loan guarantee that helped save the automaker from collapse.  He was known for his ability to quickly assess a company’s financial realities and devise a plan for survival, often involving difficult decisions regarding layoffs and asset sales.  He was described by colleagues as possessing a sharp intellect coupled with a cool demeanor, enabling him to remain calm under pressure.

Mackwell’s success at Lazard Frères translated into significant personal wealth. By the late 1980s, he was one of the most highly compensated individuals in the investment banking industry, earning an estimated $24 million in 1988 alone.  He was a member of the Council on Foreign Relations and served on the boards of several corporations and non-profit organizations. 

In the early 1990s, Mackwell began to reduce his involvement in the day-to-day operations of Lazard Frères, though he remained a partner. He transitioned towards philanthropic pursuits, focusing on education and the arts. He was a substantial donor to Yale University, establishing the Stephen J. Mackwell Fund for undergraduate scholarships. He also supported the Metropolitan Museum of Art and other cultural institutions. 

Stephen J. Mackwell passed away on August 22, 2019, in New York City, at the age of 90. He was survived by his wife, Katharine, and two daughters. His career left a lasting mark on the field of corporate finance, particularly in the realm of restructuring, and his philanthropic endeavors continued to benefit future generations. He is remembered as a shrewd financial strategist, a meticulous negotiator, and a dedicated philanthropist.

title: F. Gwynplaine MacIntyre
text:
F. Gwynplaine MacIntyre, a highly influential figure in the field of human factors and aviation safety, was born on October 23, 1904, in New Westminster, British Columbia, Canada. His full name was Francis Gwynplaine MacIntyre, but he was almost universally known as Gwyn. His early life was marked by a strong connection to the burgeoning aviation industry. His father, Frank MacIntyre, was a pioneering aviator and barnstormer who established the first flying school in Western Canada in 1913 at Steveston, near Vancouver. Gwyn spent his childhood immersed in the world of flight, assisting his father with aircraft maintenance and observing flying techniques. This formative experience instilled in him a lifelong fascination with the complexities of human-machine interaction.

He received his formal education at the University of British Columbia, graduating with a Bachelor of Science degree in Physics and Mathematics in 1926. Following graduation, he initially pursued a career as a pilot himself, flying with the Vancouver Aviation Company. However, a near-fatal crash in 1928, while attempting a forced landing in adverse weather near Hope, British Columbia, dramatically altered his trajectory. The incident, which left him with a fractured skull and other serious injuries, forced him to abandon flying, but simultaneously ignited his focus on understanding *why* pilots crashed.

MacIntyre believed that many accidents weren't due to mechanical failure, but to errors in pilot judgment and the inadequacies of cockpit design. He began a systematic study of accident reports and pilot performance, developing a keen interest in the psychological factors contributing to flight errors. This led him to pursue further education, obtaining a Master of Arts degree in Psychology from the University of Washington in Seattle in 1931. He then completed his Ph.D. in Psychology at Harvard University in 1934, specializing in experimental psychology with a focus on perception and psychomotor skills. His doctoral dissertation, “The Flashlight-Vestibular Interaction in Spatial Orientation,” explored the impact of visual stimuli on a pilot’s sense of balance and spatial awareness, a topic directly relevant to flight safety. 

During World War II, MacIntyre’s expertise was highly sought after. He joined the US Navy in 1942 and was assigned to the Naval Aviation Psychological Research Unit at the University of Maryland. He rose to the rank of Lieutenant Commander and spearheaded research aimed at improving pilot training and reducing accidents. He developed the “Link Trainer” concept further, building upon Charles Lindbergh’s original design, to create more realistic and effective flight simulators. He also pioneered the use of statistical control methods in flight training, identifying critical skills that predicted successful pilot performance. He led a team that analyzed over 10,000 pilot records, identifying factors like visual acuity, reaction time, and spatial orientation that correlated with accident rates.

After the war, in 1945, MacIntyre joined the Civil Aeronautics Authority (later the Federal Aviation Administration, or FAA) as a research psychologist. He established the Human Factors Laboratory at the FAA’s National Aviation Facilities Experimental Center in Atlantic City, New Jersey, and served as its director until his retirement in 1972.  During his tenure, he oversaw research into a wide range of topics, including cockpit design, instrument displays, air traffic control procedures, and pilot workload. He was instrumental in the development of standardized cockpit layouts and the implementation of improved pilot training programs.  He published over 80 scientific papers and reports, becoming a leading voice in the emerging field of human factors.

MacIntyre was awarded the Robert J. Allen Award from the Aerospace Medical Association in 1968, recognizing his significant contributions to aviation safety. He was a fellow of the American Psychological Association and a member of numerous professional organizations. Following his retirement, he continued to consult on aviation safety issues until the late 1980s.  F. Gwynplaine MacIntyre died on December 20, 1993, in Atlantic City, New Jersey, leaving behind a legacy of groundbreaking research that continues to influence aviation safety practices today. He is considered a foundational figure in the field of human factors, and his work remains relevant in the ongoing effort to improve the safety and efficiency of air travel.

title: Hiren Gohain
text:
Hiren Gohain, a prominent intellectual, author, and academic of Assam, was born on September 28, 1942, in Nagaon, Assam, India. His parents were Prabhat Chandra Gohain, a teacher, and Monorama Gohain. He grew up in a household deeply immersed in literature and a strong sense of social consciousness, values that profoundly shaped his later life and work. Gohain received his early education at Nagaon Government Boys’ Higher Secondary School, completing his matriculation in 1958. He continued his studies at Cotton College, Guwahati, graduating with a Bachelor of Arts degree in English in 1962 and securing the first position in the state merit list. 

He then pursued his postgraduate studies at the University of Delhi, earning a Master of Arts degree in English in 1964, again topping the university. Gohain’s academic trajectory led him to King’s College, Cambridge, where he completed his PhD in 1968, focusing on the socio-political context of early Assamese literature. His doctoral thesis explored the themes of identity and resistance in the writings of Lakshminath Bezbaroa, a pivotal figure in Assamese nationalism. 

Returning to India in 1969, Gohain joined the Department of Assamese at Gauhati University as a lecturer. He quickly rose through the ranks, becoming a reader in 1976 and a professor in 1982. He served as the Head of the Department of Assamese on several occasions – from 1988 to 1990, and again from 1998 to 2000. He officially retired from Gauhati University in 2002, but continued his association with the institution as an emeritus professor.

Gohain's contribution to Assamese literature and intellectual discourse is substantial. He authored over twenty books, encompassing literary criticism, essays, political analysis, and translations. Notable works include "Asomiya Sahityar Buranji” (History of Assamese Literature), published in 1986, which remains a seminal text in the field, and "The Politics of Identity in Assam," released in 1991, a critical examination of the complex ethnic and political dynamics of the state. He translated prominent works of Western literature, including Albert Camus’ “The Rebel,” into Assamese, making them accessible to a wider readership. 

Beyond academic publications, Gohain was a prolific columnist, regularly contributing articles to leading Assamese newspapers like *Asomiya Pratidin* and *Janasanyukta Barta*. His writings often tackled contemporary socio-political issues, advocating for secularism, human rights, and the rights of marginalized communities. He was a vocal critic of communalism, ethnic nationalism, and authoritarian tendencies. 

Gohain was actively involved in various social and political movements throughout his life. He was a key figure in the Assam Movement (1979-1985), a student-led agitation demanding the detection and deportation of illegal immigrants. However, he later became critical of the movement’s exclusionary aspects and the rise of aggressive ethnic nationalism it fostered. He consistently championed a broader, more inclusive understanding of Assamese identity. In 2015, Gohain was arrested along with activist Akhil Gogoi under the National Security Act for allegedly inciting violence during protests against the proposed amendments to the Citizenship Act. He was later released.

Throughout his career, Gohain received numerous accolades for his literary and intellectual contributions. He was awarded the Sahitya Akademi Award in 1996 for his collection of essays, *Mur Bibhajan Abhinaya* (My Partition Play). He also received the Assam Sahitya Sabha Award in 2007 and the Lifetime Achievement Award from the Asom Jatiya Bidyalay in 2018. Hiren Gohain continued to write and engage in public discourse until his passing on November 27, 2023, in Guwahati, at the age of 81, leaving behind a legacy as one of Assam’s most important public intellectuals.

title: Vujadin Savić
text:
Vujadin Savić was born on January 27, 1930, in the village of Grabovac, near Gornji Milanovac, in the Kingdom of Yugoslavia. His parents, Milosav and Milica, were farmers. He grew up in a modest household alongside his brother, Predrag, and sister, Radmila. Savić’s early life was marked by the hardships of rural existence and the looming shadow of World War II. He received his primary education in Grabovac and later attended the gymnasium (high school) in Gornji Milanovac, completing his studies in 1949.

Following his gymnasium graduation, Savić enrolled in the Faculty of Electrical Engineering at the University of Belgrade in 1949. He successfully completed his undergraduate studies in 1953 and continued his education, earning a Master of Science degree in 1956. He remained at the University, becoming a teaching assistant and beginning a research career focused on high-voltage engineering and electrical insulation.  He defended his doctoral dissertation in 1961, earning a PhD in Electrical Engineering, and was subsequently appointed as a docent (assistant professor) at the same faculty.

Savić’s career trajectory was rapid. He was promoted to associate professor in 1965 and full professor in 1970.  His research quickly gained international recognition, specializing in the breakdown voltage of insulating materials, particularly under pulsed high-voltage stress. He became a leading authority in the field, publishing over 200 scientific papers in prestigious international journals and presenting his work at numerous conferences across Europe, North America, and Asia.  A significant portion of his research revolved around the development of new insulating materials and techniques for high-voltage equipment, contributing directly to advancements in power transmission and distribution.

In 1973, Savić was elected as a full member of the Serbian Academy of Sciences and Arts (SANU), a prestigious recognition of his scientific accomplishments. He served actively within SANU, holding various positions and contributing to numerous studies and initiatives. He became a corresponding member in 1969 before gaining full membership.  He championed the importance of scientific research for national development and advocated for increased investment in technological innovation within Yugoslavia. 

Beyond his academic and research work, Savić played a critical role in the development of Yugoslavia’s electrical energy sector. He consulted with major power companies and industrial enterprises, providing expertise on high-voltage systems and equipment. He was involved in the design and testing of transformers, circuit breakers, and other critical components of the national power grid. He was also a key figure in establishing national standards for high-voltage testing and safety.  He received the "October Award" – a significant Yugoslavian national award for science and technology – in 1977 for his contributions to the field.

Throughout his career, Savić mentored numerous students, many of whom went on to become prominent engineers and researchers themselves. He was known for his rigorous academic standards and his dedication to fostering a new generation of scientists. He held visiting professor positions at several international universities, including the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign in the United States, further disseminating his knowledge and expertise globally.

Following his retirement from the University of Belgrade in 1993, Savić continued his research and remained an active member of SANU. He remained a highly sought-after consultant for industry and government agencies.  He was a recipient of numerous other accolades, including the Nikola Tesla Award in 1989, recognizing his lifetime achievements in electrical engineering.  Vujadin Savić passed away on December 12, 2015, in Belgrade, at the age of 85. His legacy continues through his extensive body of work and the impact he had on the advancement of electrical engineering in Yugoslavia and beyond.
